card.dispute: An estate broker sued the property owner for commission after finding buyers willing to pay Rs. 1,10,000, but the owner sold to the same buyers for Rs. 1,05,000 and refused to pay the claimed commission.
issues_decided: Whether the agent's authority to 'secure a purchaser' entitled him to commission upon finding ready and willing buyers at the stipulated price, even if the principal later sold at a lower price.
Whether the term 'purchaser' in the commission note required a binding contract of sale or merely a ready and willing buyer at the agreed price.
holdings: An agent employed to secure a purchaser is entitled to commission if he finds a ready and willing buyer at the price fixed by the principal, even if the principal refuses to complete the sale.

The word 'purchaser' in such contracts should be understood in its ordinary, loose sense as a person ready and willing to buy, not necessarily one with a binding contract, unless the contract clearly indicates otherwise.
provisions: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 227 (Agent's right to remuneration)
doctrines: Doctrine of vested right in agency upon performance of contractual condition
Doctrine of liberal interpretation of commercial contracts based on common usage

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed the proper construction of a will, specifically whether certain bequests to the testator's daughters and wife remained valid despite the failure of a primary adoption contingency.
issues_decided: Whether paragraphs 5, 6, and 7 of the will, benefiting the testator's wife, daughters, and mother, were contingent solely on the adoption of the testator's daughter's son.
Whether the bequest of the Kothangudi village to Nagammal for life under paragraph 5 remained operative even when the primary adoption condition failed.
Whether the omission to repeat the Rs. 5,000 payment to Alamelu in later paragraphs invalidated the bequest.
holdings: The provisions in paragraphs 5, 6, and 7 were not contingent on the adoption of the daughter's son and were intended to take effect immediately upon the testator's death under all contingencies.
The bequest of Kothangudi village to Nagammal for life under paragraph 5 remained valid even when the adoption condition failed, as the provision was not altered in later paragraphs.
The failure to repeat the Rs. 5,000 bequest to Alamelu in later paragraphs did not invalidate it, as the testator had meticulously provided for all dispositions and omissions were likely inadvertent.
doctrines: Construction of wills to ascertain testator's intention
Presumption against intestacy
Integration of testamentary clauses across contingencies
Use of surrounding circumstances in interpreting wills

card.dispute: The adopted son of the testator's nephew sued to recover possession of certain properties after the death of a life tenant, while the testator's daughter claimed absolute ownership under the will.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions in the will regarding the Kothangudi property in favor of the testator's daughter Nagammal and her daughter Alamelu remained operative despite the adoption of a nephew's son instead of the daughter's son.
Whether the adoption of a nephew's son nullified earlier bequests made in the first part of the will.
holdings: The provisions in the will favoring the testator's daughters, widow, and adoptive mother remained valid and were not revoked by the adoption of a nephew's son.

The reversionary interest in the Kothangudi property was validly left to the appellant daughter subject to payment of Rs. 5,000 to Alamelu, even though the adoption under the alternative clause took place.
provisions: Hindu Law of Wills and Inheritance
doctrines: Rule against intestacy
Doctrine of testamentary intention
Principle of harmonious construction of wills

card.dispute: The dispute was between Gorakhram Sadhuram (a firm) and Laxmibai, wife of Inderlal Nandlal, over whether Laxmibai could enforce specific performance of an agreement to transfer a bungalow to her in lieu of debt settlement.
issues_decided: Whether Laxmibai was a party to the agreement and thus entitled to seek specific performance
Whether the suit was barred by Section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC)
Whether the suit was belated and whether the defendants' position had changed to defeat the claim
holdings: A person who is intended to be the promisee and benefits directly from an agreement, and who undertakes obligations under it, is a party to the contract and can enforce specific performance.

Section 66 CPC does not bar a suit for specific performance where the defendant purchased property in their own name to fulfill a prior agreement to transfer it to the plaintiff for a greater debit amount.
A suit for specific performance is not barred by delay where the plaintiff has been in possession, incurred expenses, made improvements, and the defendant has substantially performed the agreement.
doctrines: Doctrine of privity of contract with exception for intended beneficiaries
Substantial performance of contract
Equitable doctrine of part performance (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act, implied)

card.dispute: The defendants first party challenged the plaintiffs' title to certain lands acquired via a sale deed from the defendants second party, disputing the inheritance and possession claims over the property.
issues_decided: Whether the pedigree-table in the plaint correctly established the line of inheritance from Gobind Rai and Kari Rai to Bator Rai and Singhasan Rai as nearest reversioners.
Whether the defendants first party had acquired Shikmi rights or occupancy rights over the disputed lands.
Whether the trial court could base its decision on a Shikmi settlement not pleaded by the defendants first party.
Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for possession despite not proving prior personal possession within 12 years before the suit.
holdings: The High Court correctly upheld that Bator Rai and Singhasan Rai inherited the shares of Gobind Rai and Kari Rai as nearest reversioners, and the plaintiffs acquired valid title through a registered sale deed.
The defendants first party failed to prove any Shikmi settlement or payment of rent as Shikmidars; their possession was permissive, not adverse.
A court cannot base a decision on a case not pleaded by the parties, especially when it contradicts their pleaded title.

The plaintiffs were entitled to possession because permissive occupation by the defendants first party did not extinguish the defendants second party’s possession, which continued constructively until the assertion of adverse title shortly before the sale.
doctrines: Constructive possession
Principle of pleaded case
Permissive possession does not ripen into adverse possession
Reversioner's right under Hindu law

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, as ijaradars, sued to eject the defendant, claiming he was a trespasser due to the absence of a registered lease deed, while the defendant relied on an unregistered agreement of lease and part performance under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered lease agreement, supported by written correspondence and part performance, can protect a lessee from eviction
Whether secondary evidence of the lease agreement (Ex. 181) is admissible in the absence of primary documents
Whether the defendant’s possession and payment of rent constituted part performance under Section 53-A
holdings: An agreement to lease, evidenced by written correspondence and government sanction, coupled with possession and rent payment, satisfies Section 53-A, protecting the lessee from eviction despite no registered lease deed.
Secondary evidence of the lease agreement is admissible when primary documents are in the opponent’s possession and not produced despite notice.
Taking possession and paying rent under an unregistered lease agreement constitutes part performance, invoking the equitable protection of Section 53-A.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Equitable protection against forfeiture for non-registration
Admissibility of secondary evidence under the Indian Evidence Act

card.dispute: The mortgagor and his adopted son challenged the validity of a court auction of their village property in execution of a mortgage decree, seeking relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938, while the mortgagee claimed the sale was valid and final.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagor remained an 'agriculturist' under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938, after the execution sale of his village property.
Whether the decree was deemed satisfied upon the execution sale, thereby barring relief under the Act.
Whether the High Court could simultaneously uphold the sale and grant relief under the Act, despite the logical inconsistency.
holdings: A judgment-debtor cannot claim relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act if the decree has been satisfied by a valid execution sale, as the debt ceases to exist.
If a sale is treated as effective and title passes, the decree is satisfied, and the debtor loses standing to claim relief under the Act.
The High Court’s position was inconsistent in upholding the sale while allowing relief under the Act, as both cannot coexist logically; the sale and satisfaction must stand or fall together.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 90
doctrines: Doctrine of consistency in judicial decisions
Doctrine of indefeasibility of title upon confirmation of execution sale
Doctrine of logical coherence in applying relief statutes

card.dispute: Ram Gopal (representing Nand Lal) challenged the High Court's decision that Mst. Meria received only a life interest in properties gifted to her, arguing instead that she received an absolute estate.
issues_decided: Whether the use of the word 'Malik' in the Tamliknama conveyed an absolute estate or a limited interest to Mst. Meria
Whether the purpose of the gift—maintenance—restricted the interest to a life estate
Whether the inclusion of the gifted properties in a subsequent relinquishment deed indicated a limited interest
holdings: The term 'Malik' in a document, unless contextually restricted, conveys full proprietary rights including the right to alienate, and is sufficient to create an absolute estate in favor of a Hindu female.
A gift made for the maintenance of a female does not, by itself, limit her interest to a life estate if the language of the document clearly conveys absolute ownership.

The inclusion of gifted properties in a relinquishment deed does not negate an absolute interest, especially when the two documents form part of a single transaction to settle disputes and perfect title.
provisions: Principles of Document Construction under Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (implied)
doctrines: Presumption of absolute ownership from use of 'Malik'
Distinction between motive and legal effect in gift deeds
Rule of harmonious construction of related documents in a transaction

card.dispute: The principal (Mohanlal) sued to set off the loss from uninsured goods destroyed in an explosion against the agent's (Pannalal Jankidas) claim for indemnity, alleging the agent's failure to insure caused the loss.
issues_decided: Whether the principal's counterclaim for loss due to the agent's failure to insure arose out of the explosion and was barred by the Bombay Explosion (Compensation) Ordinance, 1944
Whether the loss from non-insurance was a direct or remote consequence of the agent's breach
Whether the Ordinance displaced ordinary rules on remoteness of damage in contract
holdings: The principal's counterclaim arose out of the explosion and was barred by section 18(2) of the Ordinance, which extinguished all rights to compensation for explosion-related losses outside the Ordinance.

The loss of compensation was not a direct result of the agent's failure to insure, but stemmed from the statutory scheme distinguishing insured and uninsured property, not natural consequences of the breach.

The Ordinance did not abrogate standard rules on remoteness of damage or invalidate exclusion clauses in insurance policies; it created a separate compensation regime without altering contractual or common law principles.
doctrines: Remoteness of damage in contract
Statutory bar on legal remedies
Inconsistent legal positions estoppel

card.dispute: The widow of Mrityunjoy Mullick claimed joint shebaitship of a Hindu religious endowment (deity Nitto Gopal Jew) against her minor stepson, the deceased's only biological child.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 includes shebaitship as 'property' that a widow can inherit
Whether the widow is entitled to joint shebaitship under the terms of the 1934 indenture creating the endowment
holdings: The term 'property' in the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 includes shebaitship, and a widow can succeed to it unless expressly excluded.

The 1934 indenture does not limit 'heirs' to issue only; since the deceased left a son, the proviso allowing appointment of a shebait does not apply, and the widow is entitled to joint shebaitship with the son.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (Act XVIII of 1937 as amended by Act XI of 1938), Section 3
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Contextual interpretation of deeds
Presumption against implied exclusion in inheritance

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sued for ejectment of the lessees (respondents) after lease expiry; the dispute centered on whether the Bombay Rents Control Act, 1947 applied to pending appeals.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 applies to appeals pending when the Act came into force.
Whether Section 12 of the Act has retrospective operation to protect tenants in pending appeals.
Whether Section 50 of the Act extends the application of the Act to execution proceedings and appeals.
holdings: The Bombay Rents Control Act, 1947 does not apply to appeals pending at the time of its commencement; its retrospective effect is limited to suits and proceedings transferred under Section 50.
Section 12 of the Act is prospective, not retrospective, and applies only to suits instituted after the Act came into force.
Section 50 excludes execution proceedings and appeals from the transfer and application of the Act’s provisions, which apply only to transferred suits and proceedings.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 50
doctrines: Prospective vs. retrospective operation of statutes
Statutory interpretation of repeal and saving clauses
Doctrine of implied exclusion in legislative provisions

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, after attaining majority, challenged a compromise decree in a partition suit, claiming it was obtained by coercion and undue influence and that the division was unfair.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise decree in a partition suit involving a minor is binding when the court sanctioned it, even if prior court sanction for the guardian's compromise was not obtained
Whether the mere unfairness of a partition entitles a minor to set aside a decree after attaining majority
Whether allegations of coercion and undue influence were sufficiently pleaded and proved
Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to seek partition of undivided properties in the present suit
holdings: A decree based on a compromise in a suit involving a minor is valid and binding if the court sanctioned it, even without prior court approval of the guardian's authority to compromise.
A minor cannot set aside a partition decree on the ground of unfair division alone if he was properly represented; he must prove fraud or negligence by his guardian.
Allegations of coercion and undue influence must be specifically pleaded with particulars and cannot be based on general assertions; failure to provide details renders the claim unsustainable.
The plaintiffs' right to seek partition of undivided properties need not be decided here due to a pending suit between the same parties for the same relief.
doctrines: Binding effect of court-sanctioned compromise involving minors
Rule against setting aside partition decrees for mere inequality when minor is represented
Requirement of specific pleading in cases of fraud, coercion, and undue influence

card.dispute: Members of a joint Hindu family fought over succession to an impartible zamindari estate after the extinction of one branch, disputing whether prior agreements had extinguished rights of succession by survivorship.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise and release deed of 1890 effected a partition or renunciation of future rights of succession in the impartible estate.
Whether Sundara Pandiya validly renounced the right of his branch to succeed by survivorship in favour of another branch.
Whether general words of release in a deed operate to extinguish contingent rights of succession not specifically mentioned.
holdings: An impartible estate remains joint family property unless there is clear express or implied intention by junior members to renounce their future right of succession by survivorship.
A valid renunciation of succession rights in an impartible estate must be in favour of the head of the family or all family branches, not a stranger like a widow.
General words of release in a deed are limited to rights then in contemplation and do not extinguish unmentioned contingent rights like future succession by survivorship.
provisions: Principles of Construction of Deeds under Indian Contract Act, 1872
doctrines: Doctrine of survivorship in Hindu joint family property
Doctrine of renunciation of succession rights
Rule of construction of release deeds based on parties' contemplation

card.dispute: The appellant (Karnani Industrial Bank) and the respondent (Province of Bengal) disputed whether the lease ended by efflux of time or continued by holding over, and who owned the materials left on the land after the lease ended.
issues_decided: Whether the lease terminated by efflux of time or was renewed by holding over under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the lessor became entitled to the lessee's materials left on the property after lease expiry
Whether the lessor could obtain an injunction to prevent removal of materials claimed as its property
holdings: Section 116 does not apply where rent is paid before lease expiry; no holding over occurred as there was no assent to continue possession after termination.
Under the lease, materials like bricks and tiles left after the permitted period became the property of the lessor, but machinery and plant were not covered by 'other materials'.
A lessor can obtain an injunction to protect property rights in materials, even without current possession, once ownership is established under the lease terms.
doctrines: Holding over under Section 116 requires possession after lease termination and assent by lessor
Interpretation of lease clauses based on context and commercial purpose
Injunction available to protect property rights upon clear ownership

card.dispute: The Collector of Bombay assessed land owned by the Municipal Corporation of Bombay to land revenue, and the Corporation challenged the legality of the assessment, claiming exemption based on a 1865 government resolution promising no rent (assessment) would be charged.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's resolution of 1865 exempting the Municipal Corporation from payment of rent amounted to a binding exemption from land revenue assessment under the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876
Whether the right to levy land revenue could be lost by adverse possession or equitable estoppel
Whether the principles of part performance or equitable estoppel applied to prevent the Government from assessing the land after decades of non-assessment
holdings: A government resolution promising no rent (assessment) on land granted to a municipality creates an equitable obligation that binds the Government, especially when the Corporation acted on it by giving up other land and incurring heavy expenditure.
The prerogative right of the Government to levy land revenue cannot be lost by adverse possession, as such a right is not susceptible to being possessed adversely.

Even if the original grant was invalid, the Government is estopped from assessing land revenue where it made a clear representation that no assessment would be charged and the Corporation substantially acted on it to its detriment.
provisions: Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, Section 8
doctrines: Equitable estoppel
Part performance
Prerogative right to tax
Adverse possession

card.dispute: The dispute was between coparceners of a Hindu joint family over whether the family remained joint after one member separated, affecting rights of survivorship in property.
issues_decided: Whether the separation of one coparcener leads to the presumption of separation among the rest of the family
Whether cohabitation and joint business dealings after separation indicate continued joint family status under Mitakshara law
Whether statements made by a deceased coparcener about family separation are admissible under the Evidence Act
What properties and mesne profits the plaintiff was entitled to upon proving separation
holdings: The separation of one coparcener does not presume the separation or continuation of the joint status of the others; it is a question of fact based on intention.
Mere cohabitation or joint business activity after separation does not re-establish joint family status under Mitakshara law without a clear re-union.

Statements by a deceased person that he was separated from the joint family and had no interest in joint property are admissible under Section 32(3) of the Evidence Act as declarations against interest.
The plaintiff is entitled to succeed on the finding of separation, but the decree must be remanded to determine the specific properties and mesne profits due.
doctrines: Presumption of joint family under Mitakshara law
Doctrine of separation and re-union in Hindu joint families
Admissibility of dying declarations and declarations against interest
Burden of proof in establishing family status

card.dispute: The Karnani Industrial Bank and the Province of Bengal disputed whether a new tenancy arose after the original lease expired and whether the lessor could claim ownership of materials left on the premises and obtain an injunction against their removal.
issues_decided: Whether acceptance of rent before the expiry of a lease creates a new tenancy under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the lessor could claim ownership of bricks and other materials left on the premises after lease expiry
Whether the lessor could obtain an injunction to prevent removal of such materials despite not being in physical possession
holdings: Acceptance of rent before the lease expires, without any assent to continued possession, does not create a new tenancy under Section 116.
Materials like bricks and tiles left beyond the permitted period become the absolute property of the lessor under the lease terms upon expiry.
A lessor can obtain an injunction to prevent removal of materials that have become their property, even without physical possession, to protect proprietary rights.
doctrines: Doctrine of holding over
Doctrine of implied assent to tenancy renewal
Proprietary right over leasehold improvements

card.dispute: Co-mortgagors disputed whether contribution should be based on the value of their respective properties or on the benefit each derived, and whether an oral agreement modifying contribution rights was valid.
issues_decided: Whether the right to contribution between co-mortgagors is governed by Section 43 of the Indian Contract Act or Sections 82 and 92 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether an unregistered oral agreement among co-mortgagors altering contribution rights was valid and enforceable
Whether the plaintiff's claim for contribution and charge was properly framed in the absence of a personal covenant
holdings: The right to contribution between co-mortgagors is governed by Sections 82 and 92 of the Transfer of Property Act, not Section 43 of the Indian Contract Act, as the former is a special law on the subject.
In the absence of a valid contract to the contrary, co-mortgagors must contribute proportionately to the value of their respective shares in the mortgaged property, not by benefit derived.
An unregistered oral agreement allegedly modifying contribution rights was not proved, especially where a party withheld crucial evidence and the circumstances suggested hesitancy.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIV, Rule 2(1)
doctrines: Special law prevails over general law
Contribution among co-mortgagors based on property value
Requirement of registration for certain agreements affecting immovable property
Substantial justice over technical pleading

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sought to evict tenants (respondents) for alleged non-payment of rent, and the tenants challenged the Controller's eviction order in civil court.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to question an eviction order passed by the Controller under the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, on the ground of non-payment of rent.
Whether the Controller's determination of 'non-payment of rent' is final and not subject to judicial review in a civil court.
holdings: The Controller has exclusive jurisdiction under the Act to determine whether there is non-payment of rent, and his decision on this issue is final and cannot be questioned in a civil court.

Even if the Controller wrongly decided the question of non-payment of rent, his order remains valid and immune from challenge in civil proceedings, as the Act provides a complete adjudicatory mechanism.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 16
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 18(3)
doctrines: Finality of administrative tribunal decisions
Jurisdictional immunity of quasi-judicial authorities
Statutory ouster of civil court jurisdiction

card.dispute: Reversioners challenged a Hindu widow's deed of release in favor of her daughter and son-in-law jointly, claiming it was invalid and seeking mesne profits.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow can validly surrender her husband's estate to her daughter and son-in-law jointly under Hindu law
Whether mesne profits can be awarded to reversioners from the date of the widow's death when an alienation is voidable but not void
Whether a conditional decree for possession bars a claim for mesne profits
holdings: A Hindu widow cannot validly surrender her husband's estate to the next reversioner and a stranger jointly; such a transaction is not a valid surrender and does not bind ultimate reversioners.

Mesne profits can be awarded to reversioners from the date of the widow's death even if the alienation is voidable, as the reversioner's suit for possession treats the alienee's possession as unlawful from that date.
A conditional decree for possession does not bar mesne profits if the reversioner is required to pay only interest on the amount to be deposited for the benefit of the estate.
doctrines: Doctrine of surrender under Hindu law
Voidable alienation by a Hindu widow
Election theory in reversionary rights
Award of mesne profits in suits by reversioners

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant, who had paid annual rent for two years under an inoperative kabuliyat for ten years, claiming he was a monthly tenant thereafter.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy created in 1925 was a monthly tenancy under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the payment and acceptance of annual rent in 1926 created a tenancy for another year
Whether a subsequent tenancy arose after 1926 in the absence of rent payment or demand
holdings: In the absence of a valid lease agreement, a tenancy for non-agricultural purposes is deemed to be from month to month under Section 106, unless a valid contract to the contrary exists.
Payment of annual rent cannot imply a yearly tenancy if the lease is invalid and not registered as required by Section 107, and no valid contract for a yearly tenancy exists.
No tenancy arose after 1926 as there was no rent payment or acceptance, and the defendant remained a monthly tenant by implication under Section 106.
doctrines: Implied tenancy
Presumption of monthly tenancy under Section 106
Requirement of registration for leases exceeding one year under Section 107
Rule of construction in absence of valid contract

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the respondent's right to claim protection under the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940, regarding a pre-existing mortgage and sub-mortgage, particularly whether a proceeding in execution was pending on January 1, 1939, and whether a sub-mortgagee qualifies as an 'assignee' entitled to protection under Section 36(5).
issues_decided: Whether a proceeding in execution was pending on or after January 1, 1939, within the meaning of Section 2(22) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940, when the execution case was struck off but attachment continued.
Whether a sub-mortgagee, who received an assignment of the mortgage debt and all rights of the mortgagee, qualifies as an 'assignee' under Section 36(5) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940.
holdings: A proceeding in execution was pending on January 1, 1939, because the attachment remained in force until June 2, 1939, and the dismissal of the execution case did not terminate the proceeding so long as the attachment continued under Order 21, Rule 57, CPC.

A sub-mortgagee who receives an assignment of the mortgage debt and all rights of the mortgagee is an 'assignee' under Section 36(5) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act and is entitled to protection, as such assignment creates a direct debtor-creditor relationship with the original mortgagor.
doctrines: Pendency of execution proceedings despite dismissal of execution application when attachment continues
Assignment of mortgage debt creating an assignee-creditor relationship under fiscal relief statutes
Doctrine of privity of estate distinguished from debtor-creditor relationship in mortgage assignments

card.dispute: The dispute was between the shebait (religious manager) of a deity and permanent lessees over whether the leases granted by past shebaits were valid beyond their lifetimes due to legal necessity.
issues_decided: Whether a permanent lease granted by a shebait in 1848 was valid in the absence of evidence on the necessity for the transaction.
Whether a later mokrari lease created in 1869 was valid when the property was dedicated only after the lease was created.
Whether the appellants could recover outstanding dues from a 1886 usufructuary mortgage.
holdings: Where a permanent lease by a shebait is challenged long after it was granted and original parties are unavailable, courts should presume it was made for legal necessity and is valid beyond the grantor's life.
A lease created before dedication of property to a religious endowment is valid if the income was dedicated and used for the deity’s worship and repairs, especially when not questioned for decades.
Concurrent findings by lower courts on factual issues, such as satisfaction of a mortgage, will not be overturned by the Supreme Court without strong contrary evidence.
provisions: Religious Endowments Act (if applicable, though not explicitly named, context implies general law on religious endowments and shebait powers)
doctrines: Presumption of legal necessity in old religious endowment transactions
Doctrine of acquiescence and non-challenge over long periods validating leases
Principle of non-interference with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell a house, claiming he paid Rs. 30,000 as price and was given possession; the defendants claimed the amount was a loan and possession was for facilitating interest payment.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff's claim for specific performance was valid based on the evidence.
Whether the plaintiff could be granted a decree for recovery of Rs. 30,000 as a loan despite not pleading it, when the defendant claimed the payment was a loan.
holdings: The court upheld the finding that no concluded contract for sale was proved and specific performance could not be granted.

The plaintiff is entitled to a decree for recovery of Rs. 30,000 and interest as a loan, since the defendant admitted receiving the amount as a loan and pleaded it as a defense, making it unjust to deny relief on technical grounds.
doctrines: Relief on an alternative plea not pleaded but admitted by the defendant
Restitution under Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with by appellate court

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the respondent widow's right to succeed to Birbhum ghatwali tenures, claiming that as a widow she was not a 'descendant' under Regulation XXIX of 1814 and that the property should pass to the nearest male agnate.
issues_decided: Whether a widow can succeed to a Birbhum ghatwali tenure in preference to the nearest male agnate when the holder dies without lineal descendants, even if the family is joint.
Whether Regulation XXIX of 1814 restricts succession to lineal descendants only, excluding widows.
Whether custom modifies Hindu law in determining succession to Birbhum ghatwali tenures.
holdings: Among Birbhum ghatwals, a widow succeeds in preference to the nearest male agnate when the holder dies without direct lineal descendants, even if the family is joint.
The term 'descendants' in Regulation XXIX of 1814 is used loosely to mean 'heirs' and does not exclude widows from succession.
Custom and usage are significant in governing succession to ghatwali property and may modify the application of Hindu law, particularly where consistent practice supports female succession.
doctrines: Custom overriding general Hindu law
Loose interpretation of statutory terms in light of context and practice
Distinction between ancestral and separate property under Mitakshara
Rejection of strict application of survivorship in ghatwali tenures

card.dispute: The dispute was between a co-operative housing society (lessee) and a sub-lessee over whether a suit for eviction was maintainable in the City Civil Court, given the applicability of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 applies to a suit by a lessee of a local authority against a sub-lessee?
Whether the building constructed by the lessee on land leased from a local authority belongs to the lessee or the local authority?
Whether the City Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain the eviction suit?
holdings: The Bombay Rents Act does not apply to premises belonging to a local authority, even when the suit is brought by the lessee against a sub-lessee, as the immunity under Section 4(1) extends to such cases.

The building erected by the lessee on land leased from a local authority belongs to the local authority, as per the lease terms and the Transfer of Property Act, since ownership does not pass to the lessee.
A civil court has inherent jurisdiction to decide its own jurisdiction, and thus the City Civil Court could validly entertain the suit even if the Act did not apply.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 4(1)
doctrines: Inherent jurisdiction of civil courts to determine their own jurisdiction
Ownership of fixtures under lease agreements
Statutory immunity for premises belonging to government or local authorities

card.dispute: Two branches of a family disputed ownership of property said to have belonged to Shanker Lal, with plaintiffs claiming reversionary rights after the death of his daughter’s widow, while defendants relied on an arbitration award granting her absolute ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award granted Mst. Mohan Dei an absolute estate in the suit properties
Whether Brijlal and his successors were estopped from challenging Mst. Mohan Dei's absolute title
Whether Kishan Lal, as a reversioner, was estopped from denying Mst. Mohan Dei's absolute estate after her death
Whether the plaintiffs, claiming through Kishan Lal, were bound by the same estoppel
holdings: The arbitration award effectively granted Mst. Mohan Dei absolute ownership of the suit properties, which was accepted by all parties at the time.
Brijlal, having accepted benefits under the award and taken possession of other properties pursuant to it, was estopped from later challenging Mst. Mohan Dei's title.

Kishan Lal, having knowingly retained and benefited from the property for forty years under the award, was estopped from denying Mst. Mohan Dei's absolute estate even when he became the presumptive reversioner.
The plaintiffs, deriving their title through Kishan Lal, inherited his estoppel and could not challenge the validity of the award or the alienation.
provisions: Hindu Law of Inheritance and Succession (unspecified statutory source)
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel (constructive and promissory)
Doctrine of Reversionary Rights under Hindu Law
Principle of Acceptance of Benefit under a Transaction
Rule against re-opening settled family arrangements

card.dispute: One co-mortgagor redeemed a mortgage by paying less than the full amount due and sought contribution from other co-mortgagors based on the full mortgage debt, leading to a dispute over the basis of contribution.
issues_decided: Whether a co-mortgagor who redeems a mortgage by paying less than the full amount due can claim contribution from other co-mortgagors based on the full amount of the mortgage debt or only on the amount actually paid?
What is the extent of subrogation rights of a co-mortgagor who redeems a mortgage in a jurisdiction governed by equity, justice, and good conscience rather than the Transfer of Property Act?
holdings: A co-mortgagor who redeems a mortgage by paying less than the full amount due is entitled to contribution from other co-mortgagors only on the basis of the amount actually paid, not the full amount of the mortgage debt.

The right of subrogation allows the redeeming co-mortgagor to stand in the shoes of the mortgagee only to the extent necessary for equitable protection, not to enforce the full original mortgage liability against co-debtors.
provisions: Mercantile Law Amendment Act, 1856 (England), Section V
doctrines: Equity, justice and good conscience
Subrogation
Contribution among co-debtors
Fiduciary relationship between co-mortgagors

card.dispute: The decree-holder and judgment-debtor disputed whether the Asansol Court had jurisdiction to proceed with execution after an earlier dismissal for default and transmission of a certificate under Section 41, CPC.
issues_decided: Whether the Asansol Court had jurisdiction to proceed with execution after the earlier application was dismissed for default and a certificate under Section 41, CPC was sent to the Calcutta High Court.
Whether the judgment-debtor was precluded by the principle of constructive res judicata from raising the jurisdictional objection in subsequent execution proceedings.
Whether an erroneous decision on jurisdiction by a court operates as res judicata between the parties in execution proceedings.
holdings: A court's jurisdiction to execute a decree is not automatically lost upon dismissal of an earlier application for default and transmission of a certificate under Section 41, CPC, especially when the decree-holding court later grants liberty to proceed with execution.

The principle of constructive res judicata applies to execution proceedings: a party who fails to challenge a court's jurisdiction at the appropriate stage is barred from raising it later, even if the court's decision was legally incorrect.

An erroneous judicial decision on a point of law, including jurisdiction, operates as res judicata between the parties if not appealed, provided the court had the capacity to act and the matter was directly in issue.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 90
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Waiver of jurisdictional objection
Finality of unappealed orders

card.dispute: The dispute was between the sons of a deceased Muslim man over the succession to his estate, particularly concerning the validity of a settlement deed executed by the eldest son on behalf of a minor brother and the legitimacy of certain claimants born to a woman alleged to be the deceased's wife.
issues_decided: Whether a de facto guardian can validly convey immovable property of a minor under Muslim law
Whether a settlement deed, void due to lack of legal guardianship, can be upheld as a family arrangement
Whether prolonged cohabitation raises a presumption of valid marriage under Muslim law
Whether mesne profits can be awarded when not specifically claimed in the plaint
holdings: A de facto guardian has no power to alienate a minor's immovable property, and any such transaction is void, irrespective of whether it benefits the minor.
A deed void due to lack of legal authority cannot be validated merely by characterizing it as a family arrangement.
Under Muslim law, prolonged and continuous cohabitation as husband and wife, in the absence of an insurmountable legal obstacle to marriage, raises a presumption of a valid marriage.
Mesne profits cannot be awarded if not specifically claimed in the plaint, even if the relief sought includes possession with all appurtenant rights.
provisions: Mahomedan Law (unspecified statutory source, as personal law)
No specific statutory provisions cited; decision based on case law and principles of Muslim personal law
doctrines: De facto guardian's lack of power to alienate minor's property
Invalidity of transactions by unauthorized guardians under Muslim law
Presumption of marriage from cohabitation in Muslim law
Family arrangement cannot override legal incapacity to contract

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's decree allowing an illegitimate son to claim a share in the separate property of his father after his death, including the right to seek partition.
issues_decided: Whether the two brothers, Budparkash Das and Nandkishore Das, were living as a joint Hindu family or had separated in status during their lifetimes.
Whether an illegitimate son of a Sudra is entitled to a share in the separate property of his father after the father's death in the presence of legitimate sons.
Whether the illegitimate son can maintain a suit for partition despite not being in possession of the property.
Whether defendant No. 5 (Kuldip Das) has a claim over properties beyond those listed in schedules C and D.
holdings: The court held that although there was no formal partition, Budparkash Das and Nandkishore Das were divided in status, with separate enjoyment of property shares, supported by oral evidence and documentary letters indicating account adjustments between them.

An illegitimate son of a Sudra, while not entitled to partition during the father's lifetime, can enforce partition after the father's death if the father left separate property and had legitimate sons, and is entitled to a coparcenary share (half of what a legitimate son would receive).
A co-sharer in joint family property is entitled to sue for partition even without possession, provided there is no pleaded and proved exclusion or ouster.
Defendant No. 5 (Kuldip Das) is entitled only to a share in the properties listed in schedules C and D and has no claim over other properties, as conceded by his counsel.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statute, based on Mitakshara doctrine)
doctrines: Mitakshara coparcenary rights of illegitimate sons
Separation in status without formal partition in Hindu joint families
Right to partition despite lack of possession
Doctrine of constructive partition through division of usufruct

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued to remove the defendant as head of a religious institution and declare the temple properties as part of a public religious and charitable trust, alleging breach of trust, while the defendant claimed the properties were his private assets and no public trust existed.
issues_decided: Whether a suit under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code can sustain a declaration that properties belong to a public religious and charitable trust when allegations of breach of trust are not proved and no directions for administration are sought?
Whether the High Court was justified in making a declaration about the existence of a public trust when the suit was dismissed for lack of cause of action under Section 92?
holdings: A suit under Section 92, CPC, requires either an allegation of breach of trust or a need for court directions in trust administration; without these, the suit lacks cause of action and cannot support any relief under the section.

A declaration that properties belong to a public trust is not a relief contemplated under Section 92, CPC, when the plaintiff's case fails on merits; such a finding is obiter dictum and cannot be part of the decree.
doctrines: Obiter dictum
Cause of action under special statutory suit
Ancillary relief doctrine

card.dispute: The dispute was between reversioners and a widow (and her transferees) over whether a compromise agreement, by which the widow settled succession rights in favor of non-heirs, was binding on the reversioners.
issues_decided: Whether a surrender of a Hindu widow's estate in favor of the next reversioner and a stranger is valid under Hindu law.
Whether a compromise entered into by a Hindu widow during litigation binds the reversioners.
Whether a transferee can claim protection under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act against reversioners after the widow's death.
holdings: A surrender by a Hindu widow of her estate in favor of the next reversioner and a stranger in equal shares is not a valid surrender under Hindu law, as surrender can only be made to the next heir of the husband.

A compromise by a Hindu widow binds reversioners only if it is bona fide, prudent, and made in the interest of the estate, not for her personal benefit; the compromise here was not binding as it ignored the reversioners' interests.

Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act does not protect a transferee against reversioners after the death of a widow with a limited estate, as the protection under that section is limited to the duration of the limited owner’s interest.
doctrines: Bona fide compromise doctrine
Limited estate of Hindu widow
Doctrine of surrender to lawful heir only
Protection of transferee under ostensible owner doctrine (Section 41, Transfer of Property Act)

card.dispute: The plaintiff and defendant contested ownership of a ginning and pressing factory at Khamgaon, each claiming a valid sale agreement from Sir Hukumchand and his son.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff's prior agreement of sale dated 3-11-1939 was valid and binding over the defendant's later agreement of 6-11-1939.
Whether the plaintiff had taken possession of the property before the defendant, and whether such possession was lawful.
Whether the defendant could claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
holdings: A prior valid contract of sale, followed by possession and later perfected by a registered deed, takes precedence over a subsequent unregistered contract, even if the latter is acted upon earlier on the ground.
Possession taken by the plaintiff's agent before the defendant's claim arose, and not relinquished with consent, supports the plaintiff's title under part performance of contract.
Section 53A does not protect a subsequent purchaser who has notice of an earlier contract and whose transaction is not fully completed for valuable consideration.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance under Section 53A
Priority of contracts based on date and performance
Estoppel by conduct or consent

card.dispute: The appellant, a purchaser at a revenue sale, claimed rights as a purchaser of an entire estate under the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, to annul under-tenures, while the respondents contested this, arguing the sale was only of separate shares, not the entire estate.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of all shares in an estate with separate revenue accounts constitutes a sale of the entire estate under the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859
Whether the purchaser at such a sale is entitled to the privileges under Section 37 of the Act, including the right to annul under-tenures
Whether a fresh notification under Section 6 is required to sell the entire estate when separate accounts exist
holdings: A sale of all shares in an estate with separate revenue accounts does not amount to a sale of the entire estate unless the Collector merges the accounts and issues a notification for the sale of the entire estate under Section 6.

The purchaser is not entitled to the privileges under Section 37 of the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, including the right to annul under-tenures, unless the sale is of the entire estate in compliance with statutory procedure.
A fresh notification under Section 6 is mandatory to sell the entire estate when separate accounts exist; without it, the sale remains limited to the defaulting shares.
provisions: Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, Section 6
Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, Section 13
Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, Section 14
Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, Section 37
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of revenue sale procedures
Notice and procedural compliance as condition precedent to valid sale
Protection of co-sharers under separate revenue accounts

card.dispute: Raja Suriya Pal Singh and other zamindars challenged the validity of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, which abolished zamindari holdings without providing immediate or adequate compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 is valid despite not providing for prompt and adequate compensation?
Whether the Act violates the requirement of 'public purpose' under the Constitution?
Whether the Act constitutes a fraud on the Constitution or improper delegation of legislative power?
Whether the private property of rulers under covenants of merger is protected from acquisition under Article 362?
holdings: The Act is valid in its entirety as the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, through Articles 31-A, 31-B and 31(4), bars judicial review of compensation provisions in land reform laws.
The abolition of zamindari serves a public purpose, as the concept is elastic and determined by societal needs, not rigid definitions.
The Act does not involve a fraud on the Constitution or improper delegation of legislative power, as the legislature has laid down sufficient policy and guidance.
Article 362 does not confer an absolute right to private property for rulers under merger covenants, and such property can be acquired under valid land reform laws.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950: Article 31, Article 31-A, Article 31-B, Article 362, Article 363
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (Act I of 1951): Sections 18, 65, 68
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule: List II, Entry 18; List III, Entry 42
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine
Eminent domain
Fraud on the Constitution
Delegation of legislative power
Implied limitations from constitutional spirit

card.dispute: The plaintiff, claiming to be the sole Saranjamdar of the Gajendragad estate, sued family members and the State of Bombay for declarations regarding his rights, challenging government actions affecting the estate.
issues_decided: Whether the suit is barred by section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, as a claim against the Crown relating to lands held as Saranjam.
Whether the claim against private defendants can be adjudicated separately from the claim against the government.
Whether seeking a declaration against the government amounts to a 'claim' within the meaning of section 4(a).
holdings: The suit is a claim against the Crown under section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, because it challenges government actions regarding Saranjam lands, even if no direct relief is sought.
The claim against the private defendants cannot be separated from the claim against the government, as the rights asserted depend on the validity of government orders.
Seeking a declaration that binds the government constitutes a 'claim against the Crown' under section 4(a), thus ousting civil court jurisdiction.
provisions: Bombay Rent Free Estates Act, 1852, Rule 10
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Indivisibility of claims when relief depends on government action
Interpretation of 'claim against the Crown' to include declaratory reliefs binding on government

card.dispute: The sons of a deceased Hindu joint family manager contested the execution of a money decree against their partition-allotted properties for a pre-partition debt claimed by a creditor of their father.
issues_decided: Whether a decree against the estate of a deceased father can be executed against ancestral property in the hands of sons after partition
Whether the liability of sons under Hindu law to pay their father's debts extends to properties allotted to them in partition
Whether questions of illegality or immorality of the debt and adequacy of arrangements at partition for debt payment can be raised in execution proceedings under Section 47, CPC
holdings: A decree against the estate of a deceased father can be executed against ancestral property in the hands of sons if the debt is a legitimate pre-partition liability under Hindu law.

Section 53 of the Civil Procedure Code deems sons in possession of ancestral property liable to satisfy their father's debts as legal representatives, even if the property was obtained by survivorship or partition.

Sons can challenge the execution of a decree on grounds of the debt being illegal or immoral, or absence of proper provision for payment at partition, through objections under Section 47 CPC, which must be decided by the executing court.
doctrines: Pious obligation of Hindu sons to pay ancestral debts
Legal fiction of sons as legal representatives under Section 53 CPC
Execution of decree against ancestral property under Hindu law liability

card.dispute: Landlords and religious institutions challenged the constitutional validity of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, which abolished intermediaries in land ownership and provided for compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the Act violates the requirement of public purpose and just compensation under the Constitution
Whether the Act amounts to a fraud on the Constitution or improper delegation of legislative power
Whether the private property rights of the Maharaja of Kapurthala are protected under Article 362 of the Constitution
Whether property already dedicated to a public purpose (by religious institutions) can be acquired for another public purpose
holdings: The Act serves a clear public purpose and provides for compensation as required by the Constitution, even if the method is deferred and rule-based.
The Act does not involve fraud on the Constitution or excessive delegation, as the legislative framework is sufficient and protected under Article 31B.
Article 362 does not confer enforceable rights over private property, and disputes under covenants of merger are barred by Article 363.
Religious endowments can be acquired for public purpose; conversion of immovable property into monetary compensation does not violate dedication to public use.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 18
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 65
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 68
doctrines: Public purpose in land reform
Just compensation under eminent domain
Bar on judicial review under Article 363
Protection of laws under Article 31B (Ninth Schedule)
Non-justiciability of covenants of merger

card.dispute: A family dispute over the succession and rights to the Gajendragad saranjam estate, where one branch claimed sole rights under a 1932 government resolution, while others relied on a 1936 resolution recognising shared hereditary shares, leading to a suit challenging the validity of the 1936 resolution and seeking declarations against both rival family members and the Government of Bombay.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was a claim against the Crown within the meaning of Section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, by virtue of impleading the Government and seeking relief against it.
Whether the suit related to lands held as saranjam, thereby attracting the jurisdictional bar under Section 4(a).
Whether the plaintiff could maintain a claim against the private defendants (family branches) independently of the claim against the Government.
holdings: A suit is a claim against the Crown under Section 4(a) if the plaintiff seeks any relief against the Government, even if the primary dispute is with private parties, and refuses to drop the government as a party.

The suit relates to lands held as saranjam when the reliefs challenge government resolutions affecting rights over saranjam lands, including rights to revenues and succession, which are inseparable from the land.

The claim against private defendants cannot be severed from the claim against the Government where the plaintiff's rights against them depend on invalidating government orders, and the decree sought would bind the Government indirectly.
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction in matters involving government and hereditary land grants
Indivisibility of claims when relief against private parties depends on invalidating state action
Doctrine of necessary party in relation to Crown immunity

card.dispute: Thakur Gokalchand claimed to be the lawful husband of a deceased Gurkha woman, Ram Piari, and sought succession to her self-acquired property under a Rajput customary law, while Parvin Kumari, his daughter by Ram Piari, opposed the claim.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff proved that he was lawfully married to the deceased Ram Piari.
Whether the plaintiff was governed by a valid customary law entitling him to succeed to the self-acquired property of his wife.
Whether succession to a wife's self-acquired property is governed by the husband's family custom when the spouses belong to different communities.
holdings: The plaintiff failed to clearly establish that his marriage with Ram Piari was lawful and valid under applicable personal or customary law.

A custom must be proven to have long, invariable usage with general acceptance; the alleged rule of succession in this case lacked such foundation due to the rarity of inter-tribal marriages like the one claimed.

Where spouses belong to different tribes and customs, it cannot be assumed that the husband’s custom governs succession to the wife’s self-acquired property, especially without evidence of long-standing practice.
doctrines: Proof of custom requires long and invariable usage
No presumption of applicability of customary law
Riwaj-i-am as strong but rebuttable evidence of custom
Drift from agricultural life affects applicability of agrarian custom

card.dispute: Rival claimants and a mortgagee contested the right to compensation for acquired land, leading to a suit over title after earlier acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the decision on title in land acquisition proceedings operates as res judicata in a subsequent suit between the same parties.
Whether a Land Acquisition Judge's decision binds a mortgagee who participated in the proceedings.
Whether the court deciding the prior issue must be competent to try the subsequent suit for res judicata to apply.
Whether the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation or by section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code.
holdings: A decision on title between rival claimants in land acquisition proceedings operates as res judicata in a subsequent suit on the same title, even if the properties differ.
A mortgagee who intervenes and defends title in acquisition proceedings is bound by the decision if it goes against the mortgagor.
For res judicata under general principles, it is sufficient that the prior court had competent jurisdiction; it need not have been competent to try the subsequent suit.
The suit was not barred by section 47 or limitation, as the earlier decree became unexecutable and a fresh cause of action arose.
doctrines: Res judicata
Identity of title test for res judicata
Binding effect of judgments from courts of special jurisdiction

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and other parties challenged the constitutional validity of land reform acts that abolished zamindari rights, while zamindars contested the adequacy and fairness of compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the State Legislatures were competent to enact laws abolishing zamindari rights under the Constitution.
Whether the acquisition of arrears of rent and deduction for 'cost of works of benefit' under the Bihar Land Reforms Act constituted a violation of Article 14.
Whether money and choses in action can be compulsorily acquired under the power of eminent domain.
Whether the impugned provisions amounted to confiscation rather than lawful acquisition with compensation.
holdings: State Legislatures have the competence to enact laws abolishing zamindari rights, provided such laws do not violate constitutional limitations.
The Bihar Act's provisions for acquiring arrears of rent and deducting arbitrary amounts for 'works of benefit' are arbitrary and violate Article 14.
Money and choses in action cannot be compulsorily acquired under eminent domain as they are not subject to such power without violating constitutional principles.
Provisions that result in virtual confiscation without reasonable relation to public purpose are unconstitutional, even if part of a larger reform measure.
doctrines: Eminent domain
Arbitrariness under Article 14
Confiscation vs. acquisition with compensation
Colourable legislation

card.dispute: The tenant, W.H. King, was prosecuted for receiving 'pugree' money from another person taking possession of his flat, and the dispute was whether this constituted an illegal relinquishment of tenancy under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether handing over possession of a flat to a third party in exchange for 'pugree' amounts to 'relinquishment of tenancy' under Section 19(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947.
Whether the conviction under Section 19(2) of the Act can be sustained if the transaction is an assignment rather than a relinquishment.
holdings: The act of handing over possession to a third party in return for payment, without surrendering tenancy rights to the landlord, does not constitute 'relinquishment of tenancy' under Section 19(1).

A relinquishment under Section 19 requires mutual agreement with the landlord and termination of the tenant's rights; a unilateral transfer to a third party is an assignment, not a relinquishment, and thus does not attract penal liability under the section.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 19
Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Sections 15, 18, and Section 108(i)
doctrines: Strict construction of penal statutes in favour of the accused
Distinction between assignment and surrender/relinquishment of tenancy

card.dispute: The State of Bihar fought with Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh and other zamindars over the constitutional validity of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, which abolished zamindari without providing compensation and sought to acquire arrears of rent and deduct costs for public works.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, falls under 'lands and land tenures' or 'acquisition of property' in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
Whether the State is constitutionally obligated to pay compensation when acquiring property under entry 36 of List II.
Whether the provisions allowing acquisition of arrears of rent and deduction for 'cost of works' constitute a colourable exercise of legislative power or confiscation.
Whether sections 4(b) and 23(f) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, are unconstitutional.
holdings: The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, is a law on 'acquisition of property' under entry 36 of List II, not 'lands and land tenures' under entry 18.

There is no constitutional obligation under entry 36 of List II or the spirit of the Constitution to pay compensation; challenges based on non-compensation are barred by Articles 31-B and 31(4) for laws in the Ninth Schedule.
The acquisition of arrears of rent and arbitrary deduction for 'cost of works of benefit' under section 23(f) are colourable legislation and amount to confiscation, violating constitutional limits.
Sections 4(b) and 23(f) of the Act are unconstitutional; however, the rest of the Act remains valid as these provisions are severable.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 18
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 36
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 42
Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 (Act XXX of 1950), Section 4(b)
Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 (Act XXX of 1950), Section 23(f)
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Severability
Eminent domain
Public purpose
Constitutional immunity of laws in the Ninth Schedule

card.dispute: The proprietors of Hamgir, Serapgarh, and Nagra zamindaries challenged the Orissa State government's notification under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1952, claiming their properties were not 'estates' held by 'intermediaries' and thus could not be taken over by the state.
issues_decided: Whether the proprietors of Hamgir, Serapgarh, and Nagra were 'intermediaries' within the meaning of Section 2(h) of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1952
Whether the properties held by the petitioners constituted 'estates' under Section 2(g) of the Act
Whether the State Government had jurisdiction under Section 3 to issue notifications taking over these properties
holdings: The proprietors of Hamgir and Serapgarh were not intermediaries under Section 2(h) because no deed or instrument established them as zamindars in a municipal, as opposed to political, relationship with the Raja of Gangpur.

The Nagra zamindar was not an intermediary under Section 2(h) because the Ekrarnama, relied on as evidence, was not produced and secondary evidence did not prove surrender of municipal independence or creation of a landlord-tenant relationship.
Since the petitioners were not intermediaries, their lands did not qualify as 'estates' under Section 2(g), and the State had no authority under Section 3 to take over the properties.
The State could not rely on historical or political documents to establish intermediary status; only legally recognized deeds or instruments defining such status were relevant.
doctrines: Ejusdem generis
Strict construction of statutory definitions
Requirement of primary evidence for establishing legal status
Distinction between political subordination and municipal (revenue) subordination

card.dispute: The archakas (temple priests) of a temple were sued for ejectment by the temple's management, who claimed ownership of land granted as inam, while the archakas claimed rights over the land based on tradition and alleged lost grant.
issues_decided: Whether a presumption of a lost inam grant in favour of the archakas can be raised despite clear documentary evidence of the grant being in favour of the temple
Whether the inam grant comprised only melvaram (revenue) rights or included both melvaram and kudivaram (land and cultivation) rights
Whether equitable considerations in favour of long-serving archakas can prevent their ejectment in a suit based on legal title
holdings: Where there is clear documentary evidence of the nature and recipient of an inam grant, no presumption of a lost grant in favour of archakas can be raised.
An inam grant includes both melvaram and kudivaram rights if the records show a grant to the temple and no indication that only revenue rights were granted.
Equitable claims of archakas based on long service cannot override legal title in a suit for ejectment, especially when they assert adverse title.
provisions: Hindu Religious Endowments Act (if implied, though not explicitly named)
doctrines: Presumption of lost grant
Distinction between melvaram and kudivaram rights in inam grants
Equity cannot prevail over legal title in ejectment suits

card.dispute: The dispute was between brothers over whether properties bequeathed by their father to each of them under his will became ancestral property in their hands or remained self-acquired, affecting rights of subsequent generations.
issues_decided: Whether property gifted or bequeathed by a father to a son becomes ancestral property in the hands of the son
Whether the will in question conferred absolute ownership or created ancestral property
How to determine the intention of a testator when bequeathing property to sons
holdings: A property given by a father to a son does not automatically become ancestral property; it remains self-acquired unless the father intended it for the benefit of the son's branch.
Where a will grants a son absolute rights with powers of alienation, the property is held as self-acquired, not ancestral.
The intention of the testator must be gathered from the will's language and surrounding circumstances; there is no presumption in favour of gift or partition.
doctrines: Doctrine of ancestral property under Mitakshara law
Doctrine of intention in construction of wills
No presumption of partition or gift in absence of clear words

card.dispute: A Hindu father's insolvency and the sale of joint family property by a Receiver led to a dispute over whether his sons could redeem the property and whether the purchaser could claim relief under agrarian debt relief laws.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu father's power to alienate his sons' interest in joint family property for antecedent debts passes to the Receiver upon insolvency under the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920 (as amended in 1948)
Whether the sons can redeem the joint family property after a sale by the Receiver
Whether a purchaser of the equity of redemption can claim relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938, if the original debt was payable by an agriculturist on the date the Act commenced
holdings: Under s. 28A of the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920 (as amended in 1948), a Hindu father’s power to alienate his sons’ interest in joint family property for antecedent debts passes to the Receiver as 'property', even if the sale occurred before the 1948 amendment.
Upon sale by the Receiver, the sons’ interest in the joint family property vests in the purchaser, and only the purchaser can exercise the right of redemption.

A purchaser of the equity of redemption can claim relief under s. 7 of the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938, if the original debt existed and was payable by an agriculturist on 22 March 1938, and the purchaser is an agriculturist at the time of application.
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutory amendments
Alienation of sons' interest by Hindu father under Mitakshara law
Vesting of property in Receiver upon insolvency
Successor's right to claim agrarian debt relief

card.dispute: The adopted son of a Hindu manager of a Muslim shrine (Darga) claimed exclusive rights to manage the shrine and receive its offerings, against a Muslim claimant who asserted managerial rights as Mutawalli.
issues_decided: Whether the second plaintiff has the right to be declared guardian and manager of the Darga of Haji Malang and entitled to its offerings.
Whether the defendant or his legal representatives have any right to the offerings deposited in the Kalyan Treasury.
Whether the management of the Darga falls under Hindu or Muslim law, or is governed by a special custom or public trust law.
Whether a de facto manager can be granted a declaration of continuing rights without a formal trust suit.
holdings: The Darga, being a composite shrine with both Muslim and Hindu associations and receiving offerings from all communities, is not governed by either Hindu or Muslim personal law but by the general law of public religious and charitable trusts.

No valid custom was pleaded or proved to establish hereditary managerial rights in the plaintiff's family, and the vague claims of lineage and succession do not support a legal declaration of exclusive management.
The defendant had no hereditary claim and only asserted managerial rights, which died with him; thus, his legal representatives have no right to the offerings.

The second plaintiff, as de facto manager from 1938 to 1946, may retain collected offerings for the trust’s benefit if no formal suit under Section 92, Civil P.C., is filed within six months; otherwise, disposal will follow a court-approved scheme.
doctrines: De facto manager doctrine
Public religious and charitable trust
Doctrine of hereditary succession in religious management
Doctrine of laches and acquiescence in religious rights

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's declaration that he was not the legitimate son of the respondent, disputing the finding of non-access between his parents at the time of his conception.
issues_decided: Whether the presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act can be rebutted by evidence of non-access.
Whether the husband's subsequent statements and conduct could be used to prove non-access.
Whether the evidence on record was sufficient to displace the presumption of legitimacy.
holdings: The presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 is conclusive unless rebutted by clear and satisfactory evidence of non-access between the spouses at the time of conception.
Subsequent statements or conduct of the husband, made after estrangement, cannot be treated as part of res gestae or used to prove non-access if they contradict earlier evidence and documents.
The evidence in this case did not conclusively establish non-access, and the High Court erred in relying on speculative inferences rather than proven facts to rebut legitimacy.
doctrines: Conclusive presumption of law
Rebuttal of presumption by non-access
Res gestae
Familial legitimacy protection

card.dispute: The head of a math (religious institution) sued a Jain Sabha to recover possession of land that had been permanently leased by a prior head and later gifted by the lessee to the Sabha for a school, claiming the lease was invalid and the Sabha had no title.
issues_decided: Whether the decree for possession obtained by the math head against the heirs of the lessee in a prior suit bound the Jain Sabha as a sub-lessee.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 134-B of the Limitation Act, and whether Section 10 of the Limitation Act saved the suit.
holdings: The decree in the prior suit did not bind the Jain Sabha because the suit was not for eviction of a tenant but to recover property based on title, and the Sabha was not a sub-lessee but a donee under a gift deed.

The suit was barred by limitation as it was filed beyond 12 years from the death of the previous math head, and Section 10 of the Limitation Act did not apply because the lease was for valuable consideration, even if inadequate.
doctrines: Decree binding on privies
Valuable consideration vs. adequate consideration
Limitation in suits involving trust property

card.dispute: The executor-nominee sought probate of a will that provided for the testator's daughter and dedicated property to a deity; the daughter objected, challenging the will's execution and validity.
issues_decided: Whether the probate court can reject a will on the ground that a bequest is void for uncertainty
Whether the will was duly executed with valid attestation
Whether the evidence of the sole surviving attesting witness could be relied upon
holdings: A probate court cannot reject a will on grounds of uncertainty in a bequest; its role is limited to verifying due execution and testamentary capacity.
The will was duly executed and attested; non-registration of a will does not affect its validity or probative value.
The evidence of the sole surviving attesting witness, a reputable advocate, was credible and sufficient to prove due execution, especially when supported by surrounding circumstances.
doctrines: Probate jurisdiction limited to execution and testamentary capacity
Rule of two attesting witnesses under probate law
No requirement of will registration
Credibility of attesting witness in contested wills

card.dispute: Kalyanpur Lime Works Ltd. sued the State of Bihar for specific performance of a lease agreement for quarrying limestone, after the State granted the lease to another party following a prior invalid forfeiture.
issues_decided: Whether the Government had an imperfect title when entering into the lease agreement in 1934, making Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act applicable
Whether the plaintiff could claim partial specific performance under Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act for the unexpired lease period after March 31, 1948
Whether the plaintiff had fulfilled the condition of relinquishing all claims to further performance and compensation for the earlier period under Section 15
Whether specific performance should be granted when only a short unexpired period remained
holdings: The Government had an imperfect title when contracting to grant the lease in 1934 due to the subsisting lease in favor of Kuchwar Company, making Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act applicable.
The plaintiff could seek partial specific performance under Section 15 for the unexpired term up to March 31, 1954, as the impediment to performance had been removed after the prior lease expired.
The plaintiff validly relinquished claims to further performance and compensation for the period before April 1, 1948, satisfying the requirements of Section 15.
Specific performance was denied due to the minimal unexpired lease period, but the plaintiff was entitled to compensation for the entire period from April 1, 1948, to March 31, 1954.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, 1908, Order VI, Rule 8
Civil Procedure Code, 1908, Order VIII, Rule 2
doctrines: Doctrine of imperfect title under Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act
Doctrine of partial specific performance under Section 15
Doctrine of equitable relief in specific performance

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant for non-payment of rent without serving a written notice, under a lease deed executed before the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, where the lease provided that default in rent would terminate the lessee's rights.
issues_decided: Whether a written notice of termination is necessary under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act for leases executed before 1st April, 1930
