The words 'eviction' and 'vacation' mean more than physical removal of the occupant; they entail restoration of the land to its original agricultural condition.
doctrines: Incidental powers doctrine
Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Termination of occupancy rights upon lawful eviction

card.dispute: The parties disputed over possessory title to a property, with neither having legal title, and the issue centered on whether attornment by tenants to claimants without payment of rent was sufficient to establish possessory title.
issues_decided: Whether attornment by tenants to persons claiming title but having no legal title requires actual payment of rent to be effective.
Whether the High Court could remand the case for a fresh finding on attornment and possession in second appeal.
Whether a document creating a new lease with different terms constitutes valid attornment.
holdings: Attornment is complete upon the tenant's agreement to recognize a new landlord; subsequent payment of rent is not necessary for attornment to be effective.
The High Court erred in remanding for a fresh finding on possession without first holding that attornment was legally ineffective.

A document that grants a new lease with altered terms, such as duration, area, and rent, is not attornment but a fresh lease and cannot establish possessory title in favor of claimants without legal title.
doctrines: Attornment as estoppel
Possessory title through recognized tenancy
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the marriage of Bangaru Ammal was an Asura marriage (involving payment for the bride) or a Brahma marriage (a gift of the bride without consideration).
issues_decided: Whether the marriage of Bangaru Ammal was in the Asura form or Brahma form under Hindu law.
Whether the expenditure by the bridegroom's party constituted consideration for the marriage, making it an Asura marriage.
Whether the absence of proof of 'Kanyadan' ceremony invalidated the presumption of a Brahma marriage.
holdings: A Hindu marriage is presumed to be in the Brahma form unless proven otherwise; the burden lies on the party alleging it to be Asura.
Expenditure by the bridegroom's party, without more, does not constitute 'sale' of the bride and cannot convert a marriage into Asura form if no consideration passed for the bride.
The presumption of 'Kanyadan' (gift of the bride) arises when no consideration is paid; absence of explicit proof of the ritual does not negate the Brahma form if the circumstances imply a gift.
provisions: Hindu Law (customary and textual principles regarding marriage forms)
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in Hindu marriages (Brahma form)
Essential distinction between Asura and Brahma marriage based on presence or absence of consideration
Kanyadan as a constitutive element of valid Hindu marriage
Burden of proof in challenging the form of a Hindu marriage

card.dispute: The appellant, a hereditary trustee of a temple in Hyderabad, challenged the state's orders taking over temple management and removing him from trusteeship under the Hyderabad Endowments Regulations, 1940, without a proper inquiry.
issues_decided: Whether the orders of June 13 and 14, 1960, taking over management of the temple and vesting it in the Director of Endowments were valid under the Hyderabad Endowments Regulations, 1940
Whether a trustee can be removed without an inquiry and without being given a show-cause notice under the Regulations
Whether the authority passing the removal orders had the power to do so under the Rules
holdings: The orders taking over management and effectively removing the trustee were ultra vires because they were passed without a mandatory inquiry and show-cause notice as required by Rule 67.
Removal of a trustee under the Regulations requires a finding of incompetence after an inquiry by a competent officer, which did not occur here.
Only the Minister for Endowments (Government) has the power to remove a trustee under Rule 68, not a Member of the Board of Revenue.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (reading provisions in context)

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued his brothers for a declaration that their partnership in a sugar mill was dissolved on May 13, 1944, when one brother filed a prior suit for dissolution, along with claims for accounts and appointment of a receiver, while one defendant challenged the suit as time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 106 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the date of filing or service of summons in a prior dismissed suit for dissolution determines the date of dissolution of the partnership
Whether the High Court could entertain a limitation plea raised for the first time in appeal without framing an issue or allowing amendment of pleadings
holdings: A suit for dissolution of partnership does not automatically determine the date of dissolution; the date must be fixed by court or by notice under Section 43(1) of the Partnership Act, and service of summons does not amount to such notice.

The High Court erred in treating the plea of limitation as purely a question of law; it was a mixed question of fact and law, and could not be raised for the first time in appeal without affording parties an opportunity to amend pleadings.

Where a plea of limitation is raised for the first time before the High Court and affects the merits, the court must frame an issue and remit for a finding if necessary, rather than dismiss the suit outright.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 15
doctrines: Mixed question of fact and law
Doctrine of proper opportunity to amend pleadings
Date of dissolution of partnership under statutory and procedural law

card.dispute: Coal mining companies challenged the Janapada Sabha's notices demanding coal tax at 9 pies per ton and seeking to reopen past assessments for coal exported out of Madhya Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether the increase in coal tax from 3 pies to 9 pies per ton was valid without prior sanction of the State Government under Section 51(2) of the Central Provinces Local-Self Government Act, 1920
Whether the Janapada Sabha could legally reopen final assessments to demand additional tax for coal exported out of the state
Whether the coal tax was a sales tax or excise duty, thereby subject to constitutional limitations under Articles 277 and 286
holdings: A tax rate increase under Section 51(2) of the Act is invalid unless it has the prior sanction of the State Government; the increase to 9 pies per ton lacked such sanction and is therefore void.
Assessments made under the Rules become final under Rule 10, and the Janapada Sabha cannot reopen them to demand additional tax for past periods.
It is unnecessary to decide whether the tax is a sales tax or excise duty, as the notices are invalid on procedural grounds under the Act and Rules.
provisions: Central Provinces Local-Self Government Act, 1920, Section 51
Central Provinces Local-Self Government Act, 1920, Section 79(1)
Central Provinces Local-Self Government Act, 1920, Rule 2, Rule 3, Rule 10
doctrines: Principle of finality of assessment
Prior government sanction for tax increases
Doctrine of legislative competence regarding taxation

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment of the tenant for non-payment of rent arrears, and the tenant challenged the validity of the notice to quit and claimed relief upon depositing arrears after suit was filed.
issues_decided: Whether a valid notice to quit was required before filing a suit for ejectment under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947,
Whether the tenancy was converted from the Indian Calendar to the British Calendar under Section 27 of the Act and Rule 4 of the Rules,
Whether the tenant was entitled to relief against forfeiture by depositing arrears of rent after the institution of the ejectment suit
holdings: A valid notice to quit determining the tenancy is a prerequisite for filing an ejectment suit under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947, as the Act does not create an independent right to evict without termination of tenancy.

Section 27 of the Bombay Rents Act and Rule 4 do not convert a tenancy from the Indian Calendar to the British Calendar; they only standardize the period for rent recovery, not the tenancy period itself.

Deposit of arrears after filing of the ejectment suit does not entitle the tenant to relief from eviction under Section 12(3)(a), as the statutory conditions for decree are mandatory and the court has no discretion to withhold eviction.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 27
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
doctrines: Notice to quit as a condition precedent to ejectment
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions
No relief against forfeiture where statute provides mandatory conditions for eviction

card.dispute: The dispute was between property owners and claimants of pre-emption rights under various state laws, challenging the constitutional validity of pre-emption provisions restricting the right to sell property freely.
issues_decided: Whether Section 10 of the Rewa State Pre-emption Act, 1946 violates Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution
Whether Section 16 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 offends Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution
Whether Chapter XIV of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928 is inconsistent with Article 19(1)(f)
holdings: Section 10 of the Rewa State Pre-emption Act, 1946 is valid as the restriction on sale to neighbors serves a reasonable public purpose and does not violate the right to property under Article 19(1)(f).
Section 16 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 does not violate Article 14 as business premises like shops and katras can be excluded from pre-emption, forming a valid classification.

Chapter XIV of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928 is constitutionally valid as the pre-emption right promotes consolidation of agricultural holdings, which outweighs the restriction on property rights under Article 19(1)(f).
provisions: Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, Chapter XIV (Sections 173–187)
doctrines: Reasonable restriction on fundamental rights
Classification test under Article 14
Balancing of property rights with public interest
Consolidation of agricultural holdings as a valid state objective

card.dispute: The appellant, a transferee of property, challenged the rejection of his claim to set aside an attachment by a decree-holder who alleged the sale was fraudulent to defeat creditors.
issues_decided: Whether a plea under Section 53(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, that a transfer was fraudulent and voidable, can be raised by an attaching decree-holder as a defence in a suit to set aside a summary order under Order 21, Rule 63 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
Whether such a plea must be raised only in a representative suit by creditors after the amendment to Section 53(1).
holdings: A decree-holder can raise the plea that a transfer is voidable under Section 53(1) as a defence in a suit to set aside a summary order under Order 21, Rule 63, CPC, without filing a representative suit.
The amendment to Section 53(1) does not require a defence based on fraud against creditors to be brought in a representative capacity; it only governs how a plaintiff must frame a suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 8
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 58 to 63
doctrines: Fraudulent transfer doctrine
Defence of avoidance of transfer at creditor's instance
Representative suit doctrine

card.dispute: Budhu Ram, a displaced person, was prosecuted for using a forged document to claim compensation, and challenged the validity of the prosecution and the legal interpretation of using a forged document under the Indian Penal Code.
issues_decided: Whether a complaint under Section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is required when only a copy of a forged document is produced before a court or tribunal.
Whether the use of an attested copy of a forged document amounts to 'using as genuine' under Section 471 of the Indian Penal Code.
holdings: No complaint under Section 195(1)(c) CrPC is required if only a copy of a forged document is produced, as the section applies only when the forged document itself is produced or given in evidence in court.

Producing an attested copy of a forged document with knowledge that it is forged amounts to using the original forged document as genuine under Section 471 IPC, especially when the copy serves the legal purpose of the original.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Rules
doctrines: Use of forged document as genuine
Secondary evidence and production in court
Requirement of complaint under Section 195 CrPC

card.dispute: The appellant, a manganese ore mine-owner, challenged the constitutional validity of government notifications that restricted his right to export ore by channeling exports through state-controlled agencies, allegedly infringing his fundamental right to carry on business.
issues_decided: Whether the government's canalisation of manganese ore exports through state agencies constituted a reasonable restriction on the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Whether a virtual monopoly created by administrative action, without a specific law, violates the right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g).
Whether the impugned restrictions were protected under Article 19(6) of the Constitution as amended.
holdings: The government's export canalisation policy, which effectively granted a monopoly to the State Trading Corporation without clear rules or quotas, imposed an unreasonable restriction on the appellant's right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g).
A virtual monopoly created solely through administrative action, without a law authorizing exclusion of citizens from trade, cannot be sustained as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6).
The amended Article 19(6) does not empower the state to create monopolies via executive action; such action must be supported by a valid law to be protected under the provision.
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6)
State monopoly and fundamental rights
Canalisation of trade through state agencies

card.dispute: Gurbaksh Singh (appellant) claimed exclusive title to agricultural land against Nikka Singh (respondent), contesting the validity of a corrected revenue mutation entry that recognized shared ownership between Teja Singh and Jhandha Singh.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to interfere in a second appeal when the first appellate court did not decide the question of title
Whether the appellant was a bona fide purchaser for value under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether a presumption of correctness arose in favor of the corrected mutation entry under the Punjab Land Revenue Act
holdings: The High Court could interfere in second appeal because the first appellate court failed to decide the question of title, leaving it open for determination.
The appellant was not a bona fide purchaser in good faith as he had knowledge of the defective title and did not take reasonable care to verify the transferor's authority.

A presumption of correctness attached to the corrected mutation entry under Section 44 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, as it was made in accordance with facts proved before the revenue authorities and the appellant failed to rebut it.
doctrines: Presumption of correctness of revenue records
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Concurrent findings exception in second appeal
Ostensible ownership under Section 41

card.dispute: Two government officials were accused of contempt of court for dispossessing a person despite a High Court stay order, which they claimed they did not officially receive.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were guilty of contempt for disobeying a prohibitory order of the High Court without official communication of the order?
Whether knowledge of a court order aliunde (from a source other than official service) is sufficient to bind public officials for contempt?
holdings: In cases of contempt for disobedience of a prohibitory order, actual knowledge of the order aliunde can be sufficient, even without formal service.
However, in this case, the evidence did not conclusively prove that the appellants had reliable or authentic knowledge of the extended stay order before acting.
provisions: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (principles applicable by precedent, though case predates Act)
doctrines: Contempt by disobedience of court orders
Knowledge aliunde as a basis for contempt
Requirement of authentic communication to public officials

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of an agreement of sale, which the respondent challenged as forged and unsupported by consideration; the High Court reversed the trial court’s decree in favour of the appellant.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's finding on the genuineness and validity of the agreement and its consideration.
Whether the High Court erred in using strong language to criticize the trial judge and witnesses.
holdings: The trial court's finding that the agreement was genuine, valid, and supported by consideration was correct; the High Court erred in overturning it based on a different view of the evidence.
Appellate courts must avoid extravagant or intemperate language in criticizing trial judges or witnesses; imputing corrupt motives without clear proof undermines judicial decorum and fairness.
doctrines: Judicial restraint in appellate criticism
Presumption of judicial impartiality
Proper appreciation of witness testimony

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, successors of Santokhi Jha, sued to declare that a 1935 sale of land did not transfer raiyati interest because such interest was inalienable under Regulation III of 1872, while the defendants claimed the sale was valid and the land had lost its raiyati character.
issues_decided: Whether the raiyati interest of a tenant merges into the superior landlord's interest upon acquisition of the latter, thereby extinguishing the raiyati status.
Whether a sale of land with inalienable raiyati interest under Regulation III of 1872 can validly transfer such interest to the purchaser.
Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to decide title disputes involving inalienable raiyati interests or if remedy lies solely under the Regulation.
holdings: Acquisition of the superior landlord's interest by a raiyat does not automatically merge or extinguish the raiyati interest; the two interests can coexist unless there is a clear intention to merge.
A sale of land with inalienable raiyati interest under Regulation III of 1872 does not transfer the raiyati interest to the purchaser if such transfer is not permitted by law.
Civil courts have jurisdiction to decide title disputes involving inalienable raiyati interests, and the remedy under Section 27(3) of the Regulation is not exclusive.
doctrines: Doctrine of merger
Mixed question of law and fact
Res judicata
Inalienability of raiyati interest

card.dispute: The Trustees of the Port of Bombay sued Kanji Manji, an assignee of a leased property, for ejectment to regain vacant possession of land and buildings after termination of a monthly tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for ejectment was governed by the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, 1947, thereby requiring it to be filed in the Small Causes Court
Whether notice served on one of the joint assignees was sufficient
Whether the suit was bad for non-joinder of the legal representatives of a deceased co-assignee
Whether the impossibility of evicting sub-tenants under the Rent Control Act rendered the obligation to deliver vacant possession unenforceable
holdings: The suit for ejectment of a lessee from land held under a local authority is not governed by the Rent Control Act when the land is involved, and thus the City Civil Court has jurisdiction.
Notice served on one of the joint assignees under a monthly tenancy is sufficient to terminate the tenancy.
The suit is not bad for non-joinder of the legal representatives of a deceased co-assignee where the surviving assignee continues in possession and the tenancy is determinable at will.
The inability of an assignee to evict sub-tenants due to rent control protections does not render the obligation to deliver vacant possession impossible or unenforceable against the local authority.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 4(4)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 5(8)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 15
doctrines: Doctrine of severability of land and building for jurisdictional purposes under rent control laws
Doctrine of privity of contract in lease assignments
Doctrine of supervening impossibility not applying to contractual obligations where third-party rights are involved

card.dispute: The appellants, a mining company, challenged the validity of an agreement to pay enhanced royalty to the State Government, claiming it was void and that they were entitled to a refund of amounts paid under protest.
issues_decided: Whether the Mining Rules of 1913 had statutory force and bound the Government, making the agreement void if violated
Whether the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, applied to the agreement dated January 11, 1949
Whether the agreement was vitiated by misrepresentation or undue influence
Whether the enhanced royalty terms amounted to deprivation of property without authority of law under Article 31(1) of the Constitution
holdings: The 1913 Rules were departmental instructions, not statutory, and did not bind the Government; the Governor, as lessor, could validly approve exceptions, making the agreement enforceable.
The 1949 Rules had no retrospective effect and did not apply to an agreement finalized in January 1949, before their enforcement on October 25, 1949.
There was no misrepresentation or vitiating factor; the appellants entered the agreement voluntarily and with full knowledge.
Payment under a valid contract does not amount to deprivation of property under Article 31(1), as it is authorized by law.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 4
doctrines: Non-statutory administrative rules as departmental instructions
Presumption of validity in governmental contracts when authorized by competent authority
No retrospective application of statutory rules
Contractual liability does not equate to constitutional deprivation of property

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant to carry out repairs, but the tenant had already repaired the building, leading to a dispute over whether eviction was justified under the Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's revision powers under s. 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 are limited to questions of jurisdiction like under s. 115 CPC
Whether the landlord required vacant possession for carrying out extensive repairs that could not be done with the tenant in occupation
Whether the appellate court could consider subsequent events, such as repairs completed after the eviction application was filed
holdings: The High Court's powers under s. 15(5) of the Act are wider than those under s. 115 CPC and are not confined to jurisdictional errors.
Eviction under s. 13(3)(a)(iii) is only justified if repairs are so extensive that they require the tenant to vacate; minor repairs do not justify eviction.
Courts may consider events occurring after the filing of the eviction application, including completion of repairs, when deciding if eviction is necessary.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(5)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Purpose and scheme of rent control legislation
Revisional jurisdiction beyond jurisdictional errors

card.dispute: The company challenged the validity of the Madras Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1954, which validated the acquisition of its electricity undertaking and determined compensation under three prescribed bases.
issues_decided: Whether the Madras Act 29 of 1954, which validated the earlier acquisition under an ultra vires law, is constitutionally valid.
Whether the compensation mechanisms under Section 5 of the 1954 Act violate Article 31(2) of the Constitution by not providing a 'just equivalent' of the acquired undertaking.
holdings: The impugned Act, though validating prior illegal acquisition, is valid as it is within the legislative competence of the State and does not violate constitutional provisions.

The compensation scheme under Section 5, offering three alternative bases, does not per se violate Article 31(2); in absence of concrete evidence, the Court cannot hold that the prescribed methods fail to provide a just equivalent.
provisions: Madras Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1949, Section 4
Madras Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1954, Sections 5, 24
doctrines: Validation of acts done under an ultra vires law
Principle of just equivalent under Article 31(2)
Burden of proof in challenging compensation adequacy

card.dispute: The appellants (trustees) challenged the Director of Endowments' order to register their trust under the Hyderabad Endowment Regulation and the Wakf Act, arguing it was a public charitable trust, not a wakf.
issues_decided: Whether the trust created by the Nizam of Hyderabad is a wakf within the meaning of the Wakf Act, 1954
Whether the trust is governed by the Hyderabad Endowment Regulation, 1348-F (1939)
Whether the provisions of the Wakf Act apply to a trust with charitable purposes not restricted by religion
holdings: A trust is not a wakf if its charitable purposes extend beyond those recognized under Muslim law, even if some features resemble a wakf.
The dominant intention of the settlor to create a secular, comprehensive public charitable trust defeats classification as a wakf.
Where two constructions are possible, the one giving effect to all clauses of the document must be preferred; here, treating it as a public charitable trust does so.
The vesting of legal title in trustees and their wide discretionary powers indicate a trust under English law principles, not a wakf.
doctrines: Rule of harmonious construction
Doctrine of dominant purpose
Presumption against invalidating clauses in a document
Distinction between wakf and public charitable trust under secular law

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed their respective landholding statuses in a draft record of rights, with the respondent claiming to be a lessee under the appellant, who claimed to be a raiyat, while the Settlement Officer recorded the appellant as a tenure holder and the respondent as a temporary lessee.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere under Article 227 with concurrent findings of revenue authorities on the status of the respondent as a temporary lessee.
Whether the Settlement Officer had jurisdiction to determine the appellant's status as a tenure holder when the Government did not object.
Whether the lack of a recorded oral evidence in the settlement proceedings violated principles of natural justice or undermined the appeal mechanism.
holdings: The High Court cannot act as a court of appeal under Article 227; it may only interfere if revenue tribunals exceeded jurisdiction, acted without material, or rendered perverse findings—none of which were present here.
The Settlement Officer had jurisdiction to decide the appellant’s status because the respondent raised a valid objection affecting that status, even though the Government did not challenge it.

Though rules do not require recording of oral evidence, a record must be maintained to preserve the effectiveness of the statutory right of appeal, as a reasoned order and access to evidence are essential for meaningful appellate review.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 44
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 59
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Rules 30(2) and 17(2)
doctrines: Limited scope of judicial review under Article 227
Concurrent findings of fact by tribunals not to be disturbed without jurisdictional error or perversity
Implication of statutory duty to maintain records to give effect to statutory appeal rights
Natural justice in quasi-judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The Lambardars (appellants) challenged the validity of a revenue sale of their property, arguing that the arrears for which the sale was conducted were not actually due at the time of the sale proclamation.
issues_decided: Whether a revenue sale can be set aside in a civil court if the arrear for which the property was sold was not due at the time of the sale proclamation.
Whether subsequent accrual of arrears after the sale proclamation validates a sale initially based on non-existent arrears.
Whether inaccuracies or irregularities in the amount of arrears shown in the sale proclamation can invalidate a revenue sale under the C.P. Land Revenue Act, 1947.
holdings: Section 149(2) of the C.P. Land Revenue Act, 1947 grants the property owner a right to have a revenue sale set aside in civil court if the arrear for which the sale was held was not due.
Arrears that accrue after the sale proclamation is issued cannot be considered in validating the sale; each arrear must be separately proceeded against under the Act.
A sale conducted for an arrear that was not due falls outside the category of mere procedural irregularities and is invalid, as it violates the statutory basis of the sale under the Act.
provisions: C.P. Land Revenue Act, 1947 (Central Provinces and Berar Act II of 1917), Section 149(2)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of revenue sale provisions
Validity of administrative action based on due arrears
Distinction between procedural irregularities and fundamental illegality in revenue sales

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of Om Prakash Gupta on grounds of rent default and personal need, while Gupta denied being a tenant, claiming the premises were let to a union, not him.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to proceed when the appellant denied the landlord-tenant relationship.
Whether the Rent Controller could strike out the appellant's defence under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act for non-deposit of rent.
Whether the appellant could benefit from the Act while denying its applicability by contesting tenancy.
holdings: A mere denial of the landlord-tenant relationship does not oust the Rent Controller's jurisdiction; the tribunal must first determine if such a relationship exists.
When a tenant invokes the protection of the Rent Control Act, such as seeking deposit orders under Section 15, they accept the jurisdiction and cannot later challenge it.
Orders under Section 15(7) for striking out defence are valid if the tenant fails to comply with deposit directions, especially when the tenant has sought benefits under the Act.
doctrines: Jurisdictional assumption based on conduct
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct
Limited jurisdiction of rent tribunals
Res judicata in administrative orders

card.dispute: The appellant, Pearey Lal, refused to vacate a portion of a house bequeathed under a will; the respondent, Rameshwar Das, claimed ownership through a chain of bequests starting from Girdhari Lal's will and sought eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'Malik' in Girdhari Lal's will conveyed an absolute interest or a limited estate to his wife, Mst. Kishen Dei.
Whether the bequest to the wife and the subsequent gift over to the adopted son were repugnant, and if so, how they should be reconciled.
Whether the failure of the gift over to the adopted son resulted in the wife acquiring an absolute interest.
holdings: The term 'Malik' in the will, when read in context and with judicial precedents, conveyed absolute ownership unless restricted by surrounding terms; here, no such restriction existed.

The two bequests—to the wife and then to the son—can be reconciled by construing the son's bequest as a defeasance clause, not creating a remainder but cutting down the wife’s interest only if the son survived her.
Since the adopted son predeceased the testator, the defeasance clause failed, and the wife’s estate became absolute, enabling her to dispose of the property by will.
doctrines: Rule of construction of wills: the entire will must be read as a whole to ascertain the testator’s intention.
Principle of harmonious construction: where possible, all terms of a will should be given effect rather than rendering any inoperative.
Presumption against intestacy: a construction that avoids partial intestacy is preferred when reasonably possible.

card.dispute: The sons of Ramalingam fought with the executors of his will over whether the properties he disposed of were joint family property or his self-acquired property, and whether the Mysore High Court's decision could bind the Madras suit regarding properties in Madras.
issues_decided: Whether the Mysore High Court's judgment deciding the nature of the property as self-acquired had binding effect in a subsequent suit in Madras over immovable and movable properties located there.
Whether a foreign or out-of-jurisdiction court's decision on status and ownership can conclusively determine rights in properties situated outside its territorial jurisdiction.
Whether the shares of a company registered in Madras could be effectively adjudicated by the Mysore High Court.
holdings: A judgment by a competent court on the status and ownership of property between parties is binding in subsequent suits even if some properties are located outside the original court’s territory, provided the court had jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter.

Courts in India cannot adjudicate on immovable property situated outside their territorial jurisdiction, but a decision on ownership based on personal status is conclusive between the same parties if it arose in a competent proceeding.

The Mysore High Court could validly decide ownership of company shares as ancillary to its main decree, especially when the share certificates were within its jurisdiction and the company complied with the order.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified provisions regarding joint family property)
doctrines: Res judicata
Conclusive effect of foreign judgments under Section 13 CPC
Jurisdiction based on effectiveness and presence of movable property
Distinction between in rem and in personam jurisdiction in private international law

card.dispute: The parties disputed the validity of a widow's adoption of a son without her husband's express authority and whether the widow's declared share in a partition suit became her absolute property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether a Jain widow can adopt a son without express authority from her deceased husband
Whether a preliminary decree in a partition suit confers 'possession' of property on a Hindu widow within the meaning of Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the widow's share in joint family property became her absolute property and devolved on her heirs upon her death
holdings: A sonless Jain widow can validly adopt a son without express authority from her husband, based on a long-standing custom recognized among Jains outside Madras and Punjab.

A preliminary decree in a partition suit declaring a Hindu widow's share in joint family property confers 'possession' within the meaning of Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, making her interest an absolute estate.
The widow's declared share became her absolute property and, upon her intestate death, devolved on her sons under Section 15 and 16 of the Act, not to the adopted son of another branch.
doctrines: Customary adoption rights among Jains
Conversion of limited estate into absolute estate under Section 14
Overriding effect of statutory law over personal law under Section 4
Rule of succession for female Hindus dying intestate

card.dispute: Raghav Prapanna Tripathi and others were convicted for the murder of Kamla and her son and for destruction of evidence; they challenged the convictions based on circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the circumstantial evidence was sufficient to convict Raghav of murder under Section 302 IPC?
Whether Ramanuj Das and Jai Devi were rightly convicted under Section 201 IPC for causing evidence of the offence to disappear?
Whether Ramanuj Das was rightly convicted under Section 176 IPC for failing to report a cognizable offence?
Whether Mohan Singh and Udham Singh were rightly convicted under Section 201 IPC for abetment in destruction of evidence?
holdings: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain pointing exclusively to the guilt of the accused and must be inconsistent with innocence; in this case, the circumstances were sufficient to uphold Raghav’s conviction for murder.

Mere presence in the house and absconding are not sufficient to prove active participation in destruction of evidence; hence, conviction of Ramanuj Das and Jai Devi under Section 201 IPC was not sustained.
A person who has knowledge of a cognizable offence and fails to inform the police can be convicted under Section 176 IPC; Ramanuj Das’s conviction under this section was upheld.
Accused persons who accompanied the principal offender and participated in removing the bodies can be convicted under Section 201 IPC based on circumstantial inference, even without direct evidence.
doctrines: Chain of circumstantial evidence
Exclusive hypothesis of guilt
Inference from conduct (absconding, false explanation)
Duty to report cognizable offence

card.dispute: Radhakrishnadas, a minor, challenged the validity of a sale deed executed by him and his father, claiming it was not binding due to lack of legal necessity for the full amount and that cultivatory rights in sir lands were not transferred.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of joint family property by a father and his minor son is binding on the minor
Whether legal necessity for part of the sale consideration justifies the entire alienation
Whether the sale deed transferred cultivatory rights in sir land under the C.P. Tenancy Act, 1920
holdings: A sale of joint family property by a father as manager, even if joined by a minor son, is binding on the minor if the transaction was for legal necessity.
The alienee need only prove legal necessity for the transaction; it is not necessary to show that the entire consideration was used for family purposes.

The phrase 'all rights and privileges' in the sale deed sufficiently transfers cultivatory rights in sir land, satisfying the express transfer requirement under Section 49(1)(a) of the C.P. Tenancy Act, 1920.
doctrines: Legal necessity in alienation of joint family property
Manager's authority under Hindu law to bind minor coparceners
Doctrine of express transfer of cultivating rights in sir land

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of a notice of assessment under the U.P. Large Land Holdings Tax Act, 1957, claiming it was beyond the state's legislative power and violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the State Legislature had the competence to enact the U.P. Large Land Holdings Tax Act, 1957 under Entry 49, List II of the Seventh Schedule?
Whether the Act violated Articles 14, 19(1)(b), and 31 of the Constitution?
Whether the tax rates prescribed under the Act were invalid for being unreasonably high or confiscatory?
Whether a taxing statute can be struck down as a colourable legislation on the ground that its effect is to confiscate property?
holdings: The term 'land' in Entry 49, List II, Seventh Schedule includes all lands, agricultural or non-agricultural, and thus the State Legislature had competence to pass the impugned tax law.
The Act does not violate Articles 14, 19(1)(b), or 31, as it is a valid exercise of taxing power and does not infringe fundamental rights.
A taxing statute cannot be invalidated merely because the tax burden is high; unreasonableness in rate is not a ground to strike down a tax law if it is otherwise constitutionally valid.

A tax law may be struck down as colourable legislation only if there is evidence of a design to confiscate property under the guise of taxation, not merely from high rates; no such design was proven here.
provisions: U.P. Large Land Holdings Tax Act, 1957, Section 7(2)
U.P. Large Land Holdings Tax Act, 1957, Section 5(1)
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Liberal construction of legislative competence
Presumption of constitutionality of taxing statutes
Distinction between excessive taxation and confiscatory design

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of revenue sales of his land conducted by the government for a nominal price of Re. 1, arguing they were not genuine public auctions, while the respondents claimed the suit was time-barred and barred by estoppel and statutory provisions.
issues_decided: Whether a sale for a predetermined nominal price of Re. 1 without competitive bidding constitutes a valid public auction under the Bombay Land Revenue Code?
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 11 of the Indian Limitation Act?
Whether the suit was barred by Sections 4(c) and 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876?
Whether the appellant was estopped from challenging the sale under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act?
holdings: A sale at a predetermined nominal price without competitive bidding is not a valid public auction under Section 167 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code and does not constitute a legal sale.
The suit is not barred by limitation because no valid sale occurred, and Article 11 of the Indian Limitation Act applies only where a sale exists to be set aside.
Sections 4(c) and 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act do not bar the suit, as there was no valid sale to set aside and no appealable order under Section 203 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code.
Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply because the government had no title to convey, and there was no representation by the appellant that could create estoppel.
doctrines: Doctrine of valid public auction requiring competitive bidding
Doctrine of no estoppel where no representation or prejudice exists
Doctrine of exhaustion of alternative remedies under revenue statutes
Doctrine that no title passes in a non-statutory sale

card.dispute: Roop Chand challenged the State Government's revision of an appellate officer's order in a land consolidation matter, claiming it lacked power under the Act to overturn its own delegate's decision.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government could revise an order passed by an officer to whom it had delegated appellate powers under s. 41(1) of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948?
Whether the revisional power under s. 42 of the Act applied to orders made by a delegated appellate authority?
Whether the State Government's action in setting aside the Assistant Director's order violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 32?
holdings: Section 42 of the Act empowers the State Government to revise any order passed by an officer under the Act, including one exercising delegated appellate powers under s. 21(4).
The revisional power under s. 42 is distinct from appellate powers and allows the State Government to ensure legality and propriety of all consolidation orders, even those made by its delegates.
The State Government’s exercise of revisional power does not infringe fundamental rights when it corrects orders that may vitiate the entire consolidation scheme.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 21(4)
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 41(1)
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 42
doctrines: Delegation of powers
Revisional jurisdiction vs. appellate jurisdiction
Finality of administrative orders
Legality and propriety in administrative action

card.dispute: Co-sharers disputed whether a partition award had absolutely dedicated a village (Mouza Telibandha) to a temple or merely granted it to one co-sharer with a charge to spend income on the temple.
issues_decided: Whether the partition award created an absolute dedication of Mouza Telibandha in favour of the temple.
Whether a partition award can validly create a dedication to a deity under Hindu law.
Whether the subsequent Bagchi award modified or superseded the original partition award.
Whether the conduct of the parties in managing the property affects the nature of the dedication.
holdings: The partition award absolutely dedicated Mouza Telibandha to the Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple, with Ramsaranlal as trustee and manager.
A partition award, made with the consent of all co-sharers, can validly create a dedication to a deity as it amounts to an act of the collective owners.
The Bagchi award did not legally supersede the partition award; it had no effect on the prior valid dedication.
Subsequent conduct of the trustee in treating the property as family asset does not alter the absolute nature of a clear dedication.
provisions: Registration Act, 1908 (implied by registration of award)
doctrines: Doctrine of dedication under Hindu law
Constructive trust
Principle of unambiguous document interpretation
Non-derogation from valid religious dedication

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh and the respondent, Duvvuru Balarami Reddy, fought over whether shrotriem inamdars had the right to grant mining leases for mica, and whether the State was bound to renew them after resuming the estate.
issues_decided: Whether shrotriem inamdars had rights in sub-soil minerals to grant mining leases.
Whether the inclusion of poramboke (unculturable land) in the inam grant implied transfer of sub-soil rights.
Whether the State was obligated to renew mining leases granted by inamdars.
holdings: Shrotriem inamdars did not have sub-soil rights unless explicitly granted; mere ownership of inam land does not include mineral rights.
Inclusion of poramboke in the grant indicates full surface rights but does not automatically confer sub-soil rights.
Leases for mining granted by inamdars without sub-soil rights are legally ineffective, and the State is not bound to renew them.
provisions: Board of Revenue Standing Orders (1890 and 1907)
Madras Irrigation Cess Act, No. 7 of 1865
doctrines: Sub-soil rights do not pass with surface rights unless expressly granted or clearly inferred.
Presumption of full proprietary rights from inclusion of poramboke does not extend to mineral rights.
Government holds mineral rights unless grant explicitly provides otherwise, per Srinivasa Chariar's case.

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the government's notification under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming the acquisition was not for a public purpose and that the government's contribution to compensation was not substantial.
issues_decided: Whether the government's declaration of public purpose under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act is justiciable
Whether a nominal contribution by the government towards compensation satisfies the requirement of 'partly out of public funds' under the proviso to Section 6
holdings: The court can examine whether the government's declaration of public purpose is genuine and not a colourable exercise of power.
The government must contribute a substantial part of the compensation from public funds; a token amount does not satisfy the statutory requirement.
doctrines: Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of substantial compliance
Principle of justiciability of public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal challenged the Union of India's power to acquire coal-bearing lands owned by the State under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957 applies to lands owned by a State.
Whether Parliament has the legislative competence to enact a law for the acquisition of State-owned property.
Whether the acquisition of State property by the Union violates the federal structure of the Indian Constitution.
holdings: The Coal Bearing Areas Act, 1957 applies to coal-bearing lands owned by the State, as its language does not exclude State property.
Parliament lacks legislative competence to acquire property belonging to a State unless the Constitution expressly authorizes it.
The federal structure of the Constitution prohibits one coordinate entity (Union) from encroaching upon the property of another (State) without constitutional authorization.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 52
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 54
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 97
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 23
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 24
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 42
doctrines: Federalism in the Indian Constitution
Ultra vires doctrine
Principle of constitutional supremacy
Separation of legislative fields between Union and States

card.dispute: The eldest son of a predeceased eldest son claimed succession to a talukdari estate, challenging the validity of a wakf-alal-aulad deed created by the original owner in favour of his descendants and charities.
issues_decided: Whether the wakf-alal-aulad deed violated Section 12 of the Oudh Estates Act, 1869, by postponing vesting beyond permissible periods
Whether a wakf-alal-aulad is valid under the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, even if benefits to charity are deferred until the extinction of the family
Whether the Oudh Estates Act, 1869, allows transfers by way of wakf as valid inter vivos gifts
holdings: A wakf-alal-aulad does not violate Section 12 of the Oudh Estates Act because the property vests immediately in God upon creation, so there is no postponement of vesting.
Under the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, a wakf for family maintenance with ultimate benefit to charity is valid, even if the charity's benefit is deferred until the family's extinction.

The Oudh Estates Act, 1869, permits wakf as a valid transfer inter vivos, as it falls under voluntary gifts within Section 11, and the Act recognizes religious and charitable uses under Indian personal law.
doctrines: Rule against perpetuity as applied in Section 12 of the Oudh Estates Act
Wakf-alal-aulad as a valid religious dedication under Muslim law
Immediate vesting of property in God in a wakf, distinguishing it from English trust law

card.dispute: Tenants of non-residential buildings in Tanjore challenged the constitutional validity of an amendment that withdrew their statutory right to purchase leased land, while retaining such rights in other towns, alleging violation of rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the withdrawal of tenants' right to purchase leased land under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, as amended, violated Article 14 (equality before law)?
Whether the amendment restricting the right to purchase constituted an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f)?
Whether the statutory right to apply for purchase of leased land is a 'right in property' protected under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31?
holdings: The classification between Tanjore and other towns was based on intelligible differentia and bore a rational relation to the object of the law, hence did not violate Article 14.
A statutory right to apply for purchase of land does not constitute a 'right in property' under Article 19(1)(f); therefore, its withdrawal does not infringe the fundamental right to property.

Article 19(1)(f) protects both abstract and concrete rights in property, but the law must still satisfy the test of reasonableness and public interest under clause (5) when property is deprived by law.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921 (III of 1922), Section 9
doctrines: Classification test under Article 14
Right to property under Article 19(1)(f)
Distinction between proprietary and non-proprietary statutory rights
Harmonious construction of Articles 19 and 31

card.dispute: Tata Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. challenged the levy of cess on annual net profits from its iron ore mines in Bihar, arguing that no profit was made since the ore was not sold but used internally for manufacturing steel.
issues_decided: Whether a mining company that uses extracted ore for internal manufacturing, rather than selling it, can be said to derive 'profit' from the mine under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880 as amended in Bihar.
Whether the absence of a specific assessment mechanism for internally consumed ore renders the cess unenforceable.
holdings: Where a mine owner processes extracted ore into finished products for sale, the profit from mining is embedded in the final sale and can be legally disintegrated and taxed under the Act.

The lack of a detailed machinery for profit apportionment does not invalidate the cess, as the assessing authorities can determine profits using permissible methods, including a statutory fallback under Section 76.
provisions: Bengal Cess Act, 1880 (Ben. 9 of 1880), as amended in Bihar, Section 5
Bengal Cess Act, 1880 (Ben. 9 of 1880), as amended in Bihar, Section 6
Bengal Cess Act, 1880 (Ben. 9 of 1880), as amended in Bihar, Section 72
Bengal Cess Act, 1880 (Ben. 9 of 1880), as amended in Bihar, Section 76
doctrines: Literal interpretation of taxing statutes
Embedded profit doctrine in integrated mining and manufacturing operations
Presumption against tax liability in case of ambiguity (rejected due to clear statutory language)

card.dispute: The Jumma Masjid, Mercara and another claimed a half share in property based on a gift and a release deed, while the respondents claimed title through a prior sale by reversioners who represented they had a present interest in the property.
issues_decided: Whether a transfer by a reversioner who only had spes successionis but represented having a present interest is void under Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the transferee can acquire a valid title under Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act if the transferor later acquires title
Whether the doctrine of estoppel under Section 43 applies when the transferor makes a fraudulent or erroneous representation about having a present interest
holdings: A transfer made by someone with only spes successionis is not void if they represent having a present interest and the transferee acts on that representation for consideration.
If a transferor later acquires title to property they previously transferred while only having spes successionis, the transferee can claim the benefit of Section 43 and obtain valid title.
Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act applies regardless of whether the representation was made fraudulently or innocently, as long as the transferee acted on it in good faith.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel
Spes successionis
Representation and good faith under Section 43
Interpretation of statutory provisions in light of equitable principles

card.dispute: The Lodna Colliery Co. Ltd. challenged whether Bhola Nath Roy, as successor to proprietors of resumed invalid Lakhraj land, had rights over sub-soil minerals.
issues_decided: Whether a person with whom resumed invalid Lakhraj land was permanently settled holds rights in sub-soil minerals.
Whether the principle denying mineral rights to tenure-holders applies to proprietors of resumed Lakhraj land.
holdings: The right of property in resumed invalid Lakhraj land, once permanently settled, is equivalent to that of zamindars and includes rights to sub-soil minerals.
The rule that mineral rights do not pass to tenure-holders unless expressly granted does not apply where the holder is a proprietary owner under permanent settlement, not a subordinate tenant.
doctrines: Proprietary right in soil includes sub-soil minerals
Permanent settlement confers full proprietary rights
Distinction between proprietary ownership and subordinate tenures

card.dispute: The heirs of an inamdar challenged the applicability of two Madras land reform Acts to their Shrotriem village, arguing it was not an 'inam estate' and that the tribunal's dismissal of their appeal was invalid due to improper constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Shrotriem village of East Thakkellapadu fell within the scope of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, as an 'inam estate'.
Whether the Settlement Officer had jurisdiction to determine that the property was an 'inam village'.
Whether the Tribunal's order dismissing the appeal was void for lack of proper constitution under Section 8 of the Abolition Act.
holdings: The Settlement Officer could only determine whether an 'inam village' was an 'inam estate'; he lacked jurisdiction to finally decide whether a property was an 'inam village', a question open to challenge in civil courts.

The finding that East Thakkellapadu was an 'inam village' having been established, the Settlement Officer was competent to decide it was an 'inam estate' under the Act, and that decision was within his exclusive jurisdiction.
An order by a two-member bench of the Tribunal was void under Section 8, but this did not nullify the Settlement Officer’s order; it only left the appeal pending, not disposed of.
provisions: Madras Estates (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947 (Act XXX of 1947)
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 (Act XXVI of 1948), Section 2(7), Section 8, Section 9(1)
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of statutory tribunals
Doctrine of implied exclusion of civil court jurisdiction
Conditional jurisdiction based on pre-existing facts
Void vs. voidable orders in administrative proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed over the inheritance of joint family property, specifically whether an adoption was valid and whether a partition or severance in status occurred prior to the death of a family member.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of Venkayya by Pitchayya was validly proved.
Whether a severance in status in the joint Hindu family occurred during the lifetime of Chimpirayya.
Whether the declaration of intention to separate, as expressed in a will, could take effect without knowledge by the other family members.
What is the correct date for determining severance in status: the date of expression of intention or the date it was communicated to affected members?
holdings: The burden of proving adoption lies on the party asserting it, and mere assertion without clear evidence does not establish a valid adoption.
A declaration of intention to sever joint status must be communicated to the affected family members to be effective; an uncommunicated declaration is no more than a personal intention.
Severance in status relates back to the date of expression of intention, but only if it does not affect vested rights created between the date of expression and communication.
Rights acquired by coparceners during the period between the formation of intention to separate and its communication are protected and cannot be disturbed by retroactive application of severance.
doctrines: Doctrine of relation back
Burden and onus of proof
Severance in status in joint Hindu family
Communication of intention to separate

card.dispute: The appellant company, which occupied part of a building under a sub-lease from Maneklal, fought the respondents (owners) over whether it could retain possession after Maneklal's tenancy was terminated and a decree for eviction was passed.
issues_decided: Whether a statutory tenant can lawfully sublet the premises after the determination of the contractual tenancy?
Whether a sub-lessee of a statutory tenant acquires independent tenancy rights under the Bombay Rents Act upon termination of the head tenancy?
Whether the doctrine of 'lis pendens' under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act protected the sub-lessee when the sub-letting occurred during the pendency of the eviction suit?
holdings: A statutory tenant has only a personal right to occupation and no transferable interest in the property; thus, cannot lawfully sublet the premises.
A sub-lessee of a statutory tenant acquires no independent tenancy rights under Section 14 of the Bombay Rents Act because the statutory tenant has no estate to transfer.

The doctrine of 'lis pendens' does not protect a sub-lessee when the sub-letting is void ab initio due to lack of transferable interest in the statutory tenant, and the Bombay Amendment Act did not apply to the suit in Ahmedabad.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Sections 12, 14, 15
Indian Registration (Bombay Amendment) Act, XIV of 1939
Transfer of Property (Bombay Provision for Uniformity and Amendment) Act, 57 of 1959
doctrines: Statutory tenant vs. contractual tenant distinction
No transfer of interest by statutory tenant
Lis pendens (Section 52, Transfer of Property Act)
Conditional application of lis pendens under Bombay Amendment Act

card.dispute: The nearer sapindas of a deceased man's wife challenged the validity of her adoption of a boy, claiming their refusal of consent was proper and that the remote sapinda who consented was disqualified due to lack of faith in Hinduism.
issues_decided: Whether the refusal of consent to adoption by the nearer sapindas was improper
Whether a remote sapinda who does not believe in certain Hindu rituals and doctrines is legally competent to give valid consent to an adoption
holdings: The refusal of consent by the nearer sapindas was improper as it was motivated by self-interest and not an impartial assessment of the adoption's religious necessity.

A sapinda's consent to adoption remains valid even if he disbelieves in certain Hindu rituals or doctrines, as long as he is intellectually capable and applies his mind to the matter; non-belief does not negate his status as a Hindu or his legal capacity to consent.
The act of giving consent to adoption is a protective and advisory function, not a religious act per se, and thus does not require religious belief for validity.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules, Order XVI Rule 4
Supreme Court Rules, Order XVIII Rule 3(2)
doctrines: Hindu law of adoption
Sapinda consent in adoption
Judicial review of religious acts based on spiritual rather than proprietary considerations
Continuity of Hindu identity despite doctrinal disbelief

card.dispute: The appellants (Cutchi Memons) challenged the revision of a 1927 scheme for the administration of the Jumma Masjid in Bangalore, arguing it should remain under their exclusive management, while the respondents (Sunni Muslims, including non-Cutchi Memons) sought a revised scheme reflecting broader community ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the 1927 scheme for the Jumma Masjid, based on Cutchi Memon representation, could be revised on the ground that the mosque belonged to all Sunni Muslims of Bangalore.
Whether the plea of res judicata barred the respondents' suit given the earlier 1924 suit under Section 92 of the CPC.
Whether the existing scheme should be entirely replaced or only modified to ensure fair representation.
holdings: The mosque and its properties were established for the benefit of the entire Sunni Muslim community of Bangalore, not exclusively for the Cutchi Memons, warranting revision of the scheme to reflect this.
The plea of res judicata did not apply because the earlier suit was filed on behalf of only the Cutchi Memon community, and thus did not represent the interests of all Sunni Muslims.
An entirely new scheme was unnecessary; instead, specific clauses of the 1927 scheme should be modified to ensure equitable administration by including all Sunni Muslim worshippers of Bangalore.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 6
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 8
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11, Explanation VI
doctrines: Representative suit
Res judicata
Equitable administration of public religious trusts
Doctrine of proper representation in suits affecting public rights

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the validation of a sale deed in favor of the respondent, which had been previously declared invalid under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, after amendments introduced Section 84A allowing validation of such transfers.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings initiated by villagers under Section 84 of the Bombay Tenancy Act constitute proceedings under that section.
Whether the Collector has the power to formally declare a sale deed invalid under Section 84.
Whether the Collector's order declaring the sale invalid became final before the introduction of Section 84A in 1956.
Whether Section 84A applies to validate a transfer that was under adjudication but not finally decided before its commencement.
holdings: Proceedings initiated by villagers under Section 84, treated as such by lower authorities, can be considered proceedings under Section 84.
The Collector lacks power to formally declare a sale deed invalid; he can only decide on invalidity for the purpose of determining unauthorized possession.
The Collector’s order did not become final before August 1, 1956, as the matter was remanded by the High Court before Section 84A came into force.
Section 84A applies prospectively and allows validation of a transfer even if proceedings challenging it were pending, provided no final declaration of invalidity had been made.
provisions: The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 84
The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 84A
The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Sections 63 and 64
Code of Civil Procedure, Order IX Rule 8, Order XVII Rule 2
doctrines: Prospective operation of statutory amendments
Finality of administrative orders
Jurisdictional limits of revenue authorities
Distinction between declaratory and adjudicatory powers

card.dispute: The heirs of Chandrappa and a third-party purchaser claimed a 5/6th share in property against Nagayya's sons, who claimed Nagayya acquired the property through an oral contract to marry a relative and manage the estate.
issues_decided: Whether an oral contract for inheritance, without a registered instrument, can transfer an interest in property under Indian law.
Whether the English doctrine of part performance applies in India in the absence of compliance with Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.
holdings: An oral contract purporting to transfer an interest in immovable property does not confer any title if it is not evidenced by a registered instrument as required by law.

After the enactment of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, the doctrine of part performance can only apply where its statutory conditions are satisfied; equity cannot override the requirement of a registered document.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Equity cannot override statutory requirements for transfer of property

card.dispute: Brahm Parkash, a mortgagee of properties A and B, challenged the right of Mukhamal Gokul Chand, a purchaser and mortgagee of another property of the same mortgagor, to claim marshalling of mortgage debt against unsold property.
issues_decided: Whether a purchaser who is also a mortgagee of other property of the mortgagor can claim the benefit of marshalling under Section 56 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether marshalling under Section 56 prejudices the rights of a subsequent mortgagee as a matter of law
holdings: A purchaser remains entitled to marshalling under Section 56 even if he is also a mortgagee of other properties of the same mortgagor, provided those properties are not involved in the current proceedings.

Marshalling does not automatically prejudice a subsequent mortgagee; the question of prejudice depends on factual circumstances, particularly the value of the property to be first proceeded against, and must be specifically pleaded and proved.
doctrines: Doctrine of marshalling
Principle of prejudice in equitable remedies

card.dispute: The plaintiff Fateh Chand sued to forfeit Rs. 25,000 received from Balkishan Das under a sale agreement and claimed compensation for use of property after the sale failed; the defendant contested forfeiture and compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff could forfeit Rs. 25,000 as penalty for the defendant's breach of contract
What amount of mesne profits the plaintiff was entitled to for being kept out of possession
holdings: Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, a party cannot forfeit a stipulated amount as penalty without proving actual loss; reasonable compensation must be based on actual damage, not arbitrary percentages.
Mesne profits must be based on the actual or potential income from the property, not on a percentage of its market value; the trial court's award of Rs. 140 per mensem was upheld with interest at 6%.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 12(1)(c)
doctrines: Reasonable compensation for breach of contract
Forfeiture not allowed without proof of loss
Mesne profits based on user value, not capital value

card.dispute: The wife and child sought maintenance from the husband who had lived with them in India before moving to Africa; the dispute was over whether the Magistrate in Ludhiana had jurisdiction to entertain the maintenance petition.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate in Ludhiana had jurisdiction under Section 488(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, to entertain the maintenance petition when the husband was last in India temporarily and had since returned to Africa.
Whether the word 'is' in Section 488(8) includes a person's physical presence in a district at the time of filing the petition, even without permanent residence.
Whether the jurisdictional issue could be raised for the first time in the High Court.
holdings: The Magistrate has jurisdiction under Section 488(8) if the husband last resided with his wife in a district in India, even if that residence was temporary.
The word 'is' in Section 488(8) refers to the physical presence of the person in the district when the petition is filed, regardless of animus manendi or duration of stay.
The jurisdiction of the Magistrate to entertain a maintenance petition is a mixed question of fact and law, but in this case, the presence and last residence in Ludhiana established jurisdiction.
doctrines: Presumption against extraterritorial application of statutes
Jurisdiction based on physical presence ('is') in addition to residence or last residence
Liberal interpretation of maintenance provisions to serve social purpose

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of properties sold by his father, challenging a decree in favor of the respondents who had purchased the properties in execution of a prior decree, arguing the sale to him was genuine and that the appellate forum was improperly constituted.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deed executed by the appellant's father in his favor was genuine or a sham transaction
Whether the appellant could challenge the decree in a suit to which he was not a party
Whether the appeal before the High Court was invalidly heard by a Division Bench of two judges instead of a Full Bench of three as previously required
holdings: A sale deed from father to son, with no independent proof of consideration and suspicious recitals, can be held to be a sham transaction, especially when possession remained effectively with the father.

A person not a party to a decree cannot challenge it on merits unless the decree is shown to be a nullity, which is not the case when the decree is validly passed and the transaction underlying it is found to be genuine.
The right to appeal before a Full Bench was procedural and not a vested right; the legislature could validly abolish such a requirement, and the appeal heard by a two-judge bench was valid.
provisions: Travancore High Court Act, 1099 (IV of 1099), Section 11(1)
doctrines: Vested rights in appellate forum
Procedural vs substantive rights
Sham transaction doctrine
Principle of constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The senior widow and other family members fought over the validity of adoptions, gifts, and partition of joint family property after the death of the patriarch, including claims by a posthumous son and an adopted son.
issues_decided: Whether the existence of a son in embryo at the time of adoption invalidates the adoption.
Whether the gifts made by the father to his daughters and others were valid under Hindu law.
Whether an adopted son among Sudras is entitled to an equal share as a natural-born son in joint family property upon partition.
holdings: The existence of a son in embryo does not invalidate an adoption, as the unborn child has no legal status until birth.
Gifts made by a Hindu father to his daughters and relatives from joint family property are valid if reasonable and made during his lifetime, especially when he was the sole coparcener.

Among Sudras in the Bombay Presidency, an adopted son is entitled only to one-fifth of the share of a natural-born son, not an equal share, based on prevailing regional customs and judicial precedent.
provisions: Hindu Law (customary), Mitakshara, Vyavahara Mayukha, Dattaka Chandrika
doctrines: Doctrine of reasonable alienation by a Hindu father
Regional variation in Hindu law based on customary practices
Principle of stare decisis in application of regional Hindu law
Validity of adoption despite potential posthumous heir

card.dispute: The appellant (Hari Narain) fought the respondent (Badri Das) over his eviction from rented premises, claiming he had not defaulted on rent and that the courts below misinterpreted the rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant made inaccurate, untrue, and misleading statements in his petition for special leave to appeal?
Whether special leave to appeal should be revoked on the ground of misrepresentation in the petition?
holdings: The appellant made wholly untrue statements in his special leave petition, including that the landlord did not rely on defaults prior to December 2, 1958, and that he did not default after that date, both of which were factually incorrect.
Special leave to appeal must be revoked when obtained by making inaccurate or misleading statements, as such conduct betrays the confidence of the Court and undermines the integrity of the process.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(a)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(4)
doctrines: Judicial integrity in special leave petitions
Revocation of special leave on grounds of misrepresentation

card.dispute: The retiring partners (appellants) and continuing partners (respondents) disputed the valuation of the firm's assets, particularly goodwill, upon dissolution, challenging the arbitrator's award as exceeding his jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator exceeded his jurisdiction in valuing the goodwill and other assets contrary to the partnership deed
Whether the Civil Court could set aside the award on the ground of an error apparent on the face of the record
holdings: The arbitrator exceeded his jurisdiction by including depreciation and appreciation of assets in the goodwill valuation, which contradicted the clear terms of the partnership deed that fixed goodwill at five years' net profits without such adjustments.

An error in interpreting the contract is within the arbitrator's jurisdiction unless it results in a legal error apparent on the face of the award; however, acting beyond the scope of the reference constitutes jurisdictional excess, which courts can invalidate.
doctrines: Excess of jurisdiction by arbitrator
Severability of arbitration clause
Error apparent on the face of the record
Finality of arbitral awards unless jurisdictional limits are breached

card.dispute: The appellant claimed exclusive possession of properties as the sole heir of her mother, while respondents challenged her title and argued that her brothers were necessary parties to the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the property purchased in the mother's name with money from the father is governed by Section 10(2)(b) (gift) or Section 10(2)(d) (self-acquired) of the Mysore Hindu Women's Rights Act, 1933
Whether the suit was invalid due to non-joinder of the appellant's brothers as necessary parties
holdings: The property purchased in the wife's name using money gifted by the husband does not automatically fall under Section 10(2)(b) as a gifted property; the transaction must show a clear intention to gift the property, not just the funds.

Where a mother dies intestate leaving multiple heirs, a suit for recovery of her property must include all co-heirs as necessary parties; failure to do so renders the suit incompetent, even if the plaintiff claims exclusive title.
provisions: Mysore Hindu Women's Rights Act, 1933, Section 10(2)(b)
Mysore Hindu Women's Rights Act, 1933, Section 12
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 10(2)
doctrines: Necessary parties doctrine
Benami transaction doctrine
Rule against splitting causes of action
Doctrine of constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The landlord recovered possession of a vacant plot from tenants on grounds of personal occupation, but tenants sought re-possession claiming he failed to occupy it within one month as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the one-month period in Section 17(1) of the Bombay Rents Act applies to decrees passed under Section 13(1)(g) for personal occupation as well as under Section 13(1)(i) for construction.
Whether the tenant is entitled to regain possession if the landlord fails to occupy the premises within one month of recovery of possession.
holdings: The one-month requirement in Section 17(1) applies equally to decrees under Section 13(1)(g) for occupation and Section 13(1)(i) for construction, as the provision treats both cases similarly.

If a landlord fails to occupy the premises within one month of recovering possession under Section 13(1)(g), the original tenant is entitled to regain possession under Section 17(1), provided the application is made within thirteen months.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(i)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17(2)
