The land acquisition for staff-quarters cannot be sustained under Clause (aa) due to lack of material showing that the work for which quarters were needed was a public-purpose industry or work.
Although staff-quarters could fall under Clause (a), the government did not consider this clause, as evidenced by the agreement and notification, so the acquisition cannot be validated under it.
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine
Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of necessity of material on record to justify acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant, Uttamchand, leased a Dal Mill building with machinery from the respondent, S.M. Lalwani, and sought rent fixation under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, which the respondent contested on the ground that the lease was not for 'accommodation' under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the lease of a Dal Mill building with machinery constitutes a lease of 'accommodation' within the meaning of Section 3(a)(y) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955.
Whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to fix rent under Section 9(1) of the Act in this case.
holdings: A lease is for 'accommodation' under the Act only if the dominant intention is to lease the building for its own use; where the building is leased merely to facilitate the use of machinery or a mill, it does not qualify as 'accommodation'.

The Rent Controller lacks jurisdiction to fix rent under Section 9(1) of the Act when the lease is not for 'accommodation' as defined by Section 3(a)(y), regardless of the absence of an express exemption for mills in the Act.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, Section 3(a)(y)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, Section 9(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, Section 2(1)
doctrines: Dominant intention test
Statutory interpretation of 'accommodation'
Jurisdiction based on statutory definition

card.dispute: The landlord sought recovery of possession on grounds of rent default, while the tenant challenged the interim order to deposit rent, claiming an agreement to set off professional fees against rent and a tax department notice blocking payment.
issues_decided: Whether an order under Section 15(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for deposit of rent can be made at an interlocutory stage before final trial
Whether a notice under Section 46(5A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 operates as a garnishee order, prohibiting the tenant from depositing rent with the Rent Controller
holdings: An order under Section 15(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act is preliminary and can be made at an interlocutory stage after affording parties a hearing, even before final determination of disputes.

A notice under Section 46(5A) of the Indian Income-tax Act does not amount to a garnishee order; the tenant may deposit rent with the Rent Controller without incurring personal liability if the amount is held pending tax clearance.
doctrines: Interim relief in rent control proceedings
Garnishee order distinction under tax law

card.dispute: The Union of India and others fought against Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd. over whether a pre-Constitution tax exemption agreement with the former Gwalior State bound the Indian government after the state became part of Madhya Bharat, a Part B State.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement dated April 7, 1947, granting tax exemption to the respondent company, remained valid and binding on the Union of India after the integration of the Gwalior State into Madhya Bharat.
Whether Article 278(1)(a) of the Constitution applies to private agreements between former princely states and individuals regarding tax exemptions.
Whether the Finance Act, 1950 and the Part B States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950 preserved the tax exemption granted under the 1947 agreement.
holdings: The 1947 tax exemption agreement with the Gwalior State did not bind the Union of India after the state’s merger, as such private agreements are not covered by Article 278(1)(a) of the Constitution.
Article 278(1)(a) only permits agreements between the Union and Part B States regarding the levy, collection, and distribution of taxes, not the enforcement of pre-existing private tax concessions.

The obligations under the 1947 agreement were not preserved under Article 295(1)(b) or the Finance Act, 1950, and the company could not claim continued tax exemption beyond the constitutional framework.
provisions: Part B States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950, Clause 16
doctrines: Doctrine of Succession of Governments
Doctrine of Constitutional Limitation on Executive Agreements
Doctrine of Legislative Competence
Doctrine of Harmonious Construction

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of arrears of rent and personal need; the tenant paid all arrears during the suit and challenged the eviction, arguing the law protected her right to pay during proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could be evicted under the amended Section 12(3)(a) despite paying arrears during the pendency of the suit
Whether the notice served before the amendment of the Act was valid under the amended provision
Whether the tenant had a vested right to pay arrears at the hearing of the suit, which the amendment could not retrospectively affect
holdings: A decree for eviction can be passed under Section 12(3)(a) if the tenant failed to pay arrears within one month of notice, even if payment is made later during the suit.
A notice served before the amendment of Section 12(3)(a) is valid if it complies with Section 12(2), and no fresh notice is required after the amendment.
The tenant does not have a vested right to pay arrears at the hearing of the suit; the amended provision applies to all suits filed after its enactment, regardless of when the notice was served.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of statutory provisions
Prospective application of amendments
No vested right in procedural benefits unless explicitly conferred

card.dispute: Shrotriemdars and tenants disputed whether a grant of a named village constituted an 'estate' under the Madras Estates Land Act, determining the tenants' occupancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether a grant expressed to be of a named village is presumed to be an estate under Explanation 1 to Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, as amended in 1945.
Whether the presumption under Explanation 1 is rebuttable and subject to conditions.
Whether the presumption under Section 23 of the Act applies to cases arising after the 1936 amendment.
holdings: A grant expressed to be of a named village is presumed to be an estate under Explanation 1 to Section 3(2)(d), regardless of whether some lands were previously granted or reserved.
The presumption is rebuttable by evidence, but not by facts covered under the non-obstante clause of the Explanation.
Section 23's presumption applies only to cases arising before the 1936 amendment; post-amendment cases are governed by Explanation 1.
provisions: Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, Section 3(2)(d), Explanation 1
doctrines: Presumption of law (rebuttable)
Non obstante clause interpretation
Onus of proof in civil cases

card.dispute: Trustees of a Hindu deity sued lessees and their successors for possession of temple lands, claiming the lessees' possession was not adverse and the suit was not barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the 1851 sanad created a permanent lease or a year-to-year lease of the suit lands
Whether the defendants acquired title by adverse possession
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under the Indian Limitation Act
holdings: The 1851 sanad granted a lease from year to year only, not a permanent lease, and the non-production of the sanad by the defendants raises a presumption against them.

The possession of the defendants and their predecessors was not adverse to the deity, as they were tenants who could not deny the landlord's title during the tenancy under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act.
The suit was not barred by limitation as it was filed within 12 years of the tenancy's termination in 1949, and Article 134-B does not apply to lawful leases continuing beyond a manager's tenure.
doctrines: Section 116 presumption against tenants denying landlord's title
Adverse possession cannot be claimed by a tenant during the continuance of tenancy
Presumption against non-production of a document under the Evidence Act
Lawful lease by temple manager binding beyond his tenure

card.dispute: The Mutawalli of a public trust sued to restrain the Municipal Committee from encroaching on property claimed as trust property, based on its registration under the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act; the Committee denied the trust's claim and asserted its own title.
issues_decided: Whether the Registrar's entry under the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act that a property belongs to a public trust is conclusive against a third party not involved in the registration proceedings.
Whether the Municipal Committee, not being a party to the registration process, was bound to file a suit under Section 8(1) to challenge the trust's registration.
holdings: The Registrar's finding that property belongs to a public trust does not affect the title of a third party who was not a participant in the registration proceedings and had no opportunity to object.
The finality of the Registrar’s order under the Act applies only to persons interested in the trust and does not bind outsiders who dispute the existence of the trust or ownership of the property.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 4(5)
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 5(2)
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 7(2)
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 8(1)
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 9
doctrines: Principle of constructive res judicata
Doctrine of notice and opportunity to be heard
Finality of administrative findings limited to parties in interest

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued the defendant for ejectment and arrears of rent, claiming tenancy, while the defendant argued he constructed the house and was entitled to remain until reimbursed, leading to a dispute over the nature of possession—tenancy or licence.
issues_decided: Whether the defendant was a tenant or a licensee in possession of the suit property
Whether a decree for ejectment can be granted on the ground of licence when tenancy is not proved, despite the plaint not specifically pleading licence
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to future mesne profits after ejectment
holdings: Where the defendant's possession is permissive and based on the plaintiff's permission, and tenancy is not proved, the relationship may be that of owner and licensee, entitling the plaintiff to ejectment.
A decree for ejectment on the ground of licence can be granted even if not specifically pleaded, provided both parties led evidence on the permissive nature of possession and were not prejudiced.
A decree for ejectment must include a direction for payment of future mesne profits at a reasonable rate from the date of the decree until possession is delivered.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XVIII, Rule 17
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Doctrine of substantial justice over technical pleading
Doctrine of mesne profits in ejectment suits

card.dispute: The appellants (Bharat Singh and another) sued to declare that the respondent (Bhagirathi) was wrongly recorded as owner of property in village records after her husband's death, claiming the family remained joint, while she claimed severance and ownership since 1925.
issues_decided: Whether the mutation of the widow's name in revenue records is sufficient proof of severance of a joint Hindu family?
Whether admissions made by a party in earlier pleadings and documents can be used against her even if not confronted during her deposition as a witness?
Whether the suit was barred by limitation?
holdings: Mutation of a widow's name in revenue records does not by itself prove severance of a joint Hindu family; the burden lies on the party alleging severance to prove it.

Admissions in earlier pleadings and documents, if duly proved, are substantive evidence under Sections 17 and 21 of the Indian Evidence Act and can be used against a party even if not confronted during cross-examination under Section 145.
The suit was not barred by limitation as there was no clear adverse possession or ouster by the respondent before 1950, when the dispute arose.
doctrines: Presumption of jointness in Hindu families
Admissions as substantive evidence
Test for adverse possession in family property disputes

card.dispute: The tenant (Bishan Paul) challenged his eviction by the landlord (Mothu Ram), who purchased the property at auction, over the date from which rent was due and whether the tenant had validly deposited rent.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord acquired title and could demand rent from the date of confirmation of sale (October 3, 1956) or only from the date of issuance of the sale certificate (December 4, 1956)?

Whether the tenant's deposit of rent, though short of the full amount and made after the eviction petition was filed, was sufficient to avoid eviction under Section 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949?
Whether the Rent Controller had discretion to refuse eviction despite non-payment of rent as required under Section 13?
holdings: Title passed to the auction-purchaser on the date of confirmation of sale (October 3, 1956), not on the date of issuance of the sale certificate, especially where full payment was made and possession was effectively delivered.

The tenant’s deposit of rent was insufficient and untimely under Section 13(2)(i) as it was made after the eviction petition was filed and did not cover the full arrears, costs, and interest, thus failing to cure the default.
The word 'may' in Section 13 does not confer unfettered discretion; once the statutory conditions for eviction are met, the Controller is obligated to order eviction, as clarified by precedent.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 29
doctrines: Relation back of title upon confirmation of sale
Mandatory interpretation of eviction provisions in rent control laws
Relief against forfeiture not available when statutory conditions are not met

card.dispute: The Commissioner and temple authorities fought the trustees of the Samaradhanai Fund over whether the fund for feeding Brahmins during a temple festival constituted a 'religious charity' subject to state regulation under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether the Samaradhanai Fund for feeding Brahmins during the Rathotsavam festival is a 'religious charity' under s. 6(13) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
Whether a charity must be under the control of temple authorities to be 'associated with' a Hindu religious festival
holdings: A public charity is a 'religious charity' if it is connected with or related to a Hindu festival of religious character, even if not managed by temple authorities.
The term 'associated with' in s. 6(13) means 'connected with' or 'in relation to' and does not require control or integration with the festival's administration by temple authorities.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 6(13)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on context, scheme, and object of legislation
Meaning of 'association' in statutory definition does not imply control or integration

card.dispute: The appellant landlord fought the income tax authorities over whether amounts received from a mining lessee as 'local fund cess' were taxable as income.
issues_decided: Whether amounts received by the lessor from the lessee described as 'local fund cess' are taxable as income under the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the appellant was acting as a government agent in collecting the amounts, thereby making them non-taxable.
Whether the nature of the receipt was casual or non-recurring, thus exempt from taxation.
holdings: Amounts received under a lease covenant related to rent and royalty, even if mistaken, are taxable as income if appropriated by the recipient.
The appellant did not act as a government agent in collecting the amounts, so the receipts are not shielded from taxation.
Receipts under a contractual obligation, even if based on a mistake, are not casual or non-recurring if they arise from regular business dealings.
doctrines: Inclusive definition of income
Receipts in the nature of rent or royalty are taxable
Taxability determined at time of receipt, regardless of subsequent claims for restitution

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax challenged whether the assessee was a validly existing firm for the assessment year 1950-51 after one karta died and was not immediately replaced by a legal representative.
issues_decided: Whether a partnership continued between the representatives of two joint Hindu families after the death of one karta in 1945.
Whether the assessee qualified as a 'firm' under Section 16(1)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1950-51.
Whether a widow or guardian of minor coparceners could act as a partner or representative of a joint Hindu family in a partnership.
holdings: A partnership cannot continue with a deceased partner; a new partnership must be formed by legal representatives or coparceners who are competent to contract.
The assessee became a valid firm only from December 13, 1949, when a minor coparcener attained majority and could legally represent his family in the partnership.
A widow, though a guardian, cannot be a manager or partner of a joint Hindu family as she is not a coparcener; only a coparcener can represent the family in a partnership.
doctrines: Karta can represent a joint Hindu family in a partnership
No partnership by succession without agreement or competence
Coparcenership as prerequisite for managerial authority in a joint Hindu family

card.dispute: The mutawallis of two wakfs challenged the acquisition of their estates by the State of West Bengal, claiming exemption under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act on the ground that the properties were held for charitable or religious purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the wakf properties were held exclusively for charitable or religious purposes within the meaning of Section 6(1)(i) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953?
Whether family endowments under Muslim law can be considered 'charitable purposes' under the Act?
holdings: The purposes outlined in the wakf deeds were not exclusively charitable or religious, as they included substantial family and secular benefits, and thus did not qualify for exemption under Section 6(1)(i).

A trust that primarily benefits the wakif's family, even if partly used for religious or charitable purposes, does not constitute a 'charitable purpose' unless there is a clear element of public benefit.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 6(1)(i)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of public benefit in charitable trusts
Doctrine of exclusivity in statutory exemptions
Judicial interpretation of 'charitable purpose' in light of statutory definition and public utility

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over possession of land previously held by Raj Kaur, with the respondents claiming as her heirs and the appellants asserting possession through a prior decree and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was governed by Article 142 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 144 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the possession of successive trespassers could be tacked together to complete adverse possession
holdings: Article 142 does not apply because the plaintiffs were never in initial possession of the property and did not discontinue possession; their claim arose by succession, not possession.
Article 144 applies to the suit, but the suit is not time-barred because the defendant failed to prove continuous adverse possession for 12 years through a jural chain.
The possession of independent trespassers cannot be tacked together; there must be a jural relationship or continuity through succession for tacking to be valid.
doctrines: Doctrine of independent trespassers
Tacking of possession
Adverse possession under the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The appellant family claimed depreciation on a sugar mill based on the auction price at partition, while the tax authorities insisted on using the original cost to the joint family.
issues_decided: Whether the value for claiming depreciation under s. 10(2)(vi) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 should be the auction price at partition or the original cost to the joint family.
Whether a co-sharer acquiring another co-sharer's interest in a joint family asset through auction can treat the entire auction value as the cost of acquisition for depreciation purposes.
holdings: For depreciation under s. 10(2)(vi), the cost of an asset to a co-sharer is the original cost to the joint family for their own share, not the auction price.
The auction price paid to acquire another co-sharer's interest determines only the cost of that acquired share, not the entire asset or the acquirer's pre-existing share.
doctrines: Substance over form in partition transactions
Original cost rule for depreciation allowance
Distinction between acquisition of own share and purchase of another's share in partition

card.dispute: The surviving widow and the daughter of a deceased co-widow fought over possession of the deceased widow's share of inherited property after a partition.
issues_decided: Whether co-widows can validly partition property and relinquish their mutual right of survivorship under Hindu Law
Whether such a partition and relinquishment is repugnant to Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the right of survivorship is automatically extinguished by partition between co-widows
Which party bears the burden of proving an agreement to relinquish the right of survivorship
holdings: Co-widows under Hindu Law can partition inherited property and each may lawfully relinquish her right of survivorship in the other's share as part of the partition agreement.
Such a relinquishment is not prohibited by Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which only bars transfer of a bare chance of survivorship, not a transfer coupled with present interest.
Mere partition between co-widows does not extinguish the right of survivorship; it continues unless clearly and expressly relinquished.
The party asserting that there was an agreement to relinquish the right of survivorship must prove it by clear and cogent evidence.
doctrines: Right of survivorship under Hindu Law
Doctrine of clear and cogent evidence for relinquishment of survivorship rights
Validity of oral partition under Hindu Law
Interpretation of partition deeds in absence of express terms

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, arguing that the tenant's failure to deposit rent in court after the suit began—instead depositing with the Rent Controller—justified striking out the tenant's defence under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can continue to deposit rent with the Rent Controller under Section 21 after a suit for eviction is filed, instead of depositing in court under Section 17(1).
Whether the defence of a tenant can be struck out under Section 17(3) if rent was deposited with the Rent Controller but not in court during the pendency of the suit.
Whether deposit of rent under Section 21 with the Rent Controller constitutes valid payment to the landlord under Section 22(3), thereby negating default under Section 17(3).
holdings: Section 17(1) creates a mandatory statutory obligation to deposit rent in court within one month of service of summons in an eviction suit, overriding any prior practice of depositing with the Rent Controller under Section 21.

Deposits made under Section 21 with the Rent Controller are governed by contractual payment terms, whereas Section 17(1) imposes a distinct statutory mode and timeline for payment during litigation, which must be followed.

Section 22(3), which treats deposit with the Controller as payment to the landlord, does not apply once a suit is pending, as Section 17(1) carves out a separate and exclusive scheme for rent payment during litigation.

A tenant who fails to deposit rent in court as required by Section 17(1) is in default, and the landlord may invoke Section 17(3) to strike out the tenant’s defence, even if rent was deposited with the Controller.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 21
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 22
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 4
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 24
doctrines: Statutory interpretation: harmonious construction of related provisions
Complete code doctrine: Section 17(1) as a self-contained scheme during pendency of eviction proceedings
Legislative intent: distinction between contractual and statutory modes of rent payment

card.dispute: The landlord's assignee sued the tenant for eviction after an earlier ejectment decree could not be executed due to the Slum Areas Act; the tenant claimed protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act as a continuing 'tenant'.
issues_decided: Whether a person against whom an ejectment decree has been passed remains a 'tenant' under s. 2(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, despite non-execution of the decree under s. 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956.
Whether a civil court is barred by s. 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act from entertaining a suit for eviction of such a person on the ground that they are a trespasser.
holdings: A tenant against whom an ejectment decree has been passed does not remain a 'tenant' under s. 2(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, merely because the decree remains unexecuted under s. 19 of the Slum Areas Act.

Section 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act bars civil court suits only for eviction of a 'tenant' as defined by the Act; it does not bar a suit against a person who has ceased to be a tenant and is now a trespasser.
provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'tenant' based on plain meaning
Jurisdictional bar of civil courts under rent control legislation
Non-derogation from statutory definitions by implication

card.dispute: Madhya Pradesh Industries Ltd. challenged the Central Government's rejection of its revision application against the State of Maharashtra's refusal to grant it a mining lease for manganese ore.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government was obligated to provide detailed reasons for rejecting a revision application under Rule 55 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960
Whether the appellant was entitled to a personal hearing before the Central Government decided the revision
Whether the Government of Bombay's 1959 order amounted to a valid grant of mining lease
Whether Section 17 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 applied to the reservation of mines for the public sector
holdings: The Central Government is not required to give elaborate reasons when rejecting a revision application if the order shows that it agreed with the reasoning of the lower authority.
A personal hearing is not a mandatory requirement in revision proceedings before the Central Government under the Mineral Concession Rules.
An order by a State Government granting a mining lease is only recommendatory if it lacks prior approval from the Central Government as required by law.

Section 17 of the Mines and Minerals Act does not govern the reservation of mines for public sector exploitation but applies only when the Central Government itself intends to undertake mining operations.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 17
doctrines: Principle of reasoned orders in administrative decisions
Doctrine of limited scope of Article 136 discretionary jurisdiction
Doctrine of statutory compliance for mining leases
Distinction between recommendatory and final administrative orders

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Commissioner's declaration that part of the income from family properties set aside for charities constituted a 'specific endowment' under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether a charge on property for payment of specified charitable amounts constitutes a 'specific endowment' under Section 6(16) of the Act
Whether there must be a divestment of ownership or transfer of title to constitute a 'specific endowment'
Whether the endowment was for a fixed sum or a percentage of income
holdings: A 'specific endowment' can exist even if it consists merely of a charge on property without transfer of title, as contemplated by Section 32(1) of the Act.
Divestment of ownership is not necessary to create a 'specific endowment'; partial dedication through a charge suffices under Hindu law and the Act.
The endowment was for a fixed annual sum of Rs. 1,590, not 15.9% of income, subject to slight discretionary variation by the proprietors.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 6(14)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 6(16)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 32(1)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 62(ii)
doctrines: Partial dedication in Hindu law
Charge as an endowment
Statutory interpretation of 'specific endowment'

card.dispute: The landlord (A. C. Estates) challenged the Controller's order declaring the sub-tenant (Serajuddin & Co.) a direct tenant under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, after the tenant had been ejected.
issues_decided: Whether the Controller had the power to rescind the August 9, 1956 order declaring the sub-tenant a direct tenant after the tenant was ejected on August 22, 1956.
Whether the sub-tenant was entitled to invoke Section 16(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, despite the tenant's ejectment after the declaration.
holdings: An order under Section 16(3) declaring a sub-tenant a direct tenant is final and cannot be rescinded by the Controller based on subsequent events, even before rent fixation.
A sub-tenant is entitled to the benefit of Section 16(3) if the tenant was still in possession on the date of the declaration, regardless of later ejectment.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 2(h)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 16(3)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 29
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLVII
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Prospective application of tenancy protection laws
Inclusive definition of 'tenant' under tenancy statutes

card.dispute: The appellant firm disputed with the tax authorities over whether royalty payments for a mining lease were deductible as revenue expenditure or were non-deductible capital expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the annual royalty payments made by the assessee for a mining lease constitute revenue or capital expenditure under the Income-tax Act.
Whether the test of 'enduring advantage' applies to classify royalty payments as capital expenditure in the absence of a lumpsum payment.
holdings: Annual royalty payments under a mining lease, when related to the extraction of raw material and not to acquisition of an enduring capital asset, are revenue expenditure deductible from taxable income.
The 'enduring advantage' test does not automatically render expenditure capital in nature; where payments are periodic and tied to material extracted, they remain revenue in character.
doctrines: Enduring advantage test
Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Revenue deduction for periodic royalty and dead-rent payments

card.dispute: The appellant Ruler of a former Indian State challenged the attachment of his privy purse payments in execution of a decree obtained by the respondent based on an arbitration award.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award required registration under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the arbitration proceedings were invalid for lack of Central Government consent under Sections 86(1) and 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the privy purse payments are liable to attachment in execution of a decree under Section 60(1)(g) of the Code of Civil Procedure
holdings: The arbitration award did not create or declare any interest in immovable property and therefore did not require registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908.

Arbitration proceedings under Sections 14 and 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 do not amount to a suit and thus do not require prior consent of the Central Government under Sections 86(1) and 87B of the CPC.

Privy purse payments are political pensions under Section 60(1)(g) of the CPC, made under treaty obligations and political considerations, and are not liable to attachment or sale in execution of a decree.
doctrines: Political pension doctrine
Doctrine of non-justiciability of treaty obligations involving sovereign acts
Doctrine of immunity of privy purse from execution

card.dispute: The trustees of a trust (appellants) fought against the State of Maharashtra and another over the validity of an order requisitioning and allotting a room to a person evicted from it, after the appellants had obtained possession on grounds of bona fide requirement.
issues_decided: Whether a room from which a tenant was evicted on the ground of the landlord's bona fide requirement qualifies as 'premises' under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, and can be requisitioned by the State.
Whether the order of requisition and allotment made by the Accommodation Controller was mala fide.
holdings: A room that became vacant due to eviction of a tenant, even on grounds of the landlord’s bona fide requirement, is 'premises' under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, and can be requisitioned for public purpose.
The requisition and allotment order was not mala fide, as the State Government acted within its powers under the Act, and there is no conflict between the Rent Act and the Requisition Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of public purpose in requisitioning property

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the deed of settlement created a partial or absolute religious endowment in favor of the deity, and whether a joint shebait could challenge a decree affecting the nature of the endowment.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of settlement created an absolute or partial dedication to the deity
Whether a provision for maintenance and residence of shebaits invalidates the endowment
Whether invalidity of certain charges in favor of non-deity beneficiaries affects the validity of the endowment
Whether a joint shebait has the right to appeal against a decree declaring the endowment as partial when the deity is represented by a guardian
holdings: A deed creates an absolute endowment if the property is wholly dedicated to the deity with no beneficial interest reserved; a partial endowment arises if a charge is created in favor of the deity and residue vests with the settlor.
A reasonable provision for remuneration, maintenance, and residence of shebaits does not invalidate an otherwise absolute endowment, as management must necessarily be entrusted to human agents.
If a charge in favor of persons other than the deity is invalid, the benefit reverts to the deity in case of an absolute endowment, and does not affect the validity of the dedication.

A joint shebait has a proprietary interest in the shebaiti right and is entitled to challenge a decree that affects the nature of the endowment, even if the deity is represented by a guardian ad litem.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 33
doctrines: Absolute vs. partial dedication
Shebaiti as a proprietary right
Doctrine of reverter in invalid charges
Appellate power to grant relief to non-appealing parties under Order 41 Rule 33

card.dispute: The appellant mining company fought the State over whether export duty and sales tax could be deducted from the selling price when computing royalty payable on manganese ore under mining leases.
issues_decided: Whether export duty under the Sea Customs Act can be deducted as a charge incurred in delivering ore to purchasers under F.O.B. sales.
Whether sales tax under the Central Provinces and Berar Sales Tax Act can be deducted as a charge incurred in delivering ore to purchasers under F.O.R. sales.
holdings: Export duty is not a charge incurred in conveying or delivering ore to buyers and thus cannot be deducted from the selling price for royalty calculation.
Sales tax is a fiscal obligation of the dealer and not a cost incidental to conveyance or delivery; hence, it is not deductible in computing the pit's mouth value of ore.
provisions: Mining Manual of the Central Provinces and Berar
Sea Customs Act, 1878, Section 28 and Section 137
Indian Tariff Act, 1934, Section 2 and Second Schedule, item No. 7
Central Provinces and Berar Sales Tax Act, 1947, Section 4
doctrines: Literal interpretation of lease terms
Principle of ejusdem generis in interpreting 'such other charges'
Distinction between fiscal taxes and transportation costs

card.dispute: The appellant, a bona fide purchaser of mortgaged property, challenged the respondents' recovery of possession under the Bengal Agriculturists' Debtors Act, claiming protection as a third-party purchaser.
issues_decided: Whether the Debt Settlement Board had jurisdiction to entertain the application under Section 37-A despite the decree value exceeding Rs. 5,000
Whether Section 37-A of the Bengal Agriculturists' Debtors Act applies to a bona fide purchaser for value from an auction-purchaser (decree-holder)
holdings: The Board had jurisdiction because, even if the decree exceeded Rs. 5,000, the proviso to Rule 144 allowed the Collector’s subsequent sanction, curing any jurisdictional defect.

Section 37-A(8) applies to all persons in possession, including bona fide purchasers for value from the decree-holder, as the sale is set aside and possession must revert to the debtor, unless the transfer falls within the four exceptions in Section 37-A(1)(c).
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Legislative intent behind debtor relief statutes
Effect of setting aside a sale in execution

card.dispute: The appellant, claiming to be the son of a deceased Muslim mortgagor, challenged a prior mortgage enforcement decree and sale, arguing he was not impleaded as an heir and thus the decree should not bind him.
issues_decided: Whether a decree in a mortgage enforcement suit binds all heirs of a deceased Muslim debtor when only some heirs were impleaded after a bona fide inquiry by the creditor.
Whether the personal law of the deceased (Muslim law) affects the binding nature of a decree passed against some heirs in a suit for debt recovery.
holdings: A decree in a suit to enforce a mortgage binds the entire estate of a deceased debtor if the creditor, after a bona fide and diligent inquiry, impleads those heirs known to be in possession and representing the estate, even if other heirs are not joined.
The rule that a decree binds all heirs upon sufficient representation is procedural and applies regardless of the personal law of the deceased, including Muslim law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22 Rule 4
doctrines: Sufficient representation doctrine
Bona fide inquiry exception to party representation
Binding effect of decree on absent heirs in representative suits

card.dispute: The tenant-occupants built structures on leased land in breach of a covenant not to build and sought protection under the Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1922, including a right to purchase the land, while the landlord sought their ejectment.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant who constructed buildings in breach of a covenant not to build is entitled to compensation under Section 3 of the Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1922
Whether such a tenant can claim the benefit of Section 9 of the Act to compel the landlord to sell the land
Whether an unregistered covenant not to build can exclude a tenant’s rights under the Act
holdings: A tenant remains entitled to compensation under Section 3 of the Act regardless of a contractual covenant not to build, as the Act defines 'tenant' independently of private agreements.
A tenant entitled to compensation under Section 3 can invoke Section 9 to require the landlord to sell the land, provided the application is timely and the suit is pending.
Section 12 of the Act nullifies contractual restrictions unless stipulations about building erection are in writing and registered; an unregistered lease covenant cannot bar statutory rights.
provisions: Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1922, Section 2(4)
Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1922, Section 3
Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1922, Section 9
Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1922, Section 12
doctrines: Statutory rights prevail over private contracts when legislation so provides
Preamble cannot override unambiguous statutory language
Doctrine of tenancy by holding over
Interpretation of statutes: enacted text prevails over legislative motive

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the High Court's refusal to revise a lower court's order granting the landlord possession of the premises over a dispute on whether rent was inclusive of taxes and electricity charges.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere under Section 115, CPC, with a decision based on an erroneous interpretation of Section 12 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947?
Whether an error in law by a subordinate court amounts to lack of jurisdiction or material irregularity justifying revision under Section 115, CPC?
holdings: An erroneous construction of a statutory provision by a subordinate court does not constitute a lack of jurisdiction or material irregularity, and thus does not justify interference under Section 115, CPC.

The High Court cannot exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, CPC merely because a subordinate court decided a point of law incorrectly; such error must go to jurisdiction to warrant revision.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
doctrines: Jurisdictional error vs. error of law
Limits of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, CPC

card.dispute: The appellant-landlord evicted the respondent-Mahant from land, and the successor Mahant sued for possession, claiming the Akhara was the occupancy tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for possession was barred by limitation due to adverse possession
Whether the occupancy tenancy was extinguished upon eviction by the landlord
Whether the successor Mahant could sue after a period of more than 12 years of the appellant's possession
Whether adverse possession could run against the Akhara during the period when no Mahant was in office
holdings: The occupancy right merged with the landlord's ownership upon eviction, and continuous possession for over 12 years extinguished any tenancy rights.
The appellant's possession under eviction decrees was adverse to the Akhara, whether the Mahant represented it or not.
The successor Mahant could not maintain the suit after 12 years of adverse possession, as the cause of action was extinguished.
There was always a competent person (the previous Mahant or court-appointed Receiver) who could sue on behalf of the Akhara, so limitation ran uninterrupted.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Merger of tenancy rights into ownership
Successor bound by prior litigation involving predecessor
Cause of action accrues when a person can legally sue

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's decree granting the first defendant (co-heir) possession of her half share in inherited properties and awarding her past and future mesne profits, arguing estoppel, liability for improvements, lack of transposition as plaintiff, and improper award of mesne profits.
issues_decided: Whether the first defendant was estopped by her conduct from claiming possession of her share under Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act or the principle of equitable estoppel
Whether the first defendant could be required to pay for half the cost of improvements made by the second defendant
Whether a decree could be granted to a defendant who was not formally transposed as a plaintiff
Whether future mesne profits could be awarded to a defendant who did not claim them in the plaint
holdings: The first defendant's conduct did not amount to estoppel under Section 115 or equitable estoppel, as there was no representation or concealment inducing a mistaken belief in the adverse party.
The first defendant could not be made liable to pay for improvements made by the second defendant without her consent, as he spent money on the property knowing he had no title.

A court may decree relief in favor of a defendant who did not seek transposition as plaintiff if both parties claim under the same title and complete justice requires it, especially when the appellate court has jurisdiction to adjust claims.
Future mesne profits can be awarded under Order XX Rule 2 CPC even if not specifically claimed, to prevent multiplicity of litigation and ensure complete justice, particularly in partition suits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order I Rule 10(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XX Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLI Rule 33
doctrines: Equitable Estoppel
Doctrine of Acquiescence
Principle of Complete Justice
Suo Motu Powers of Court
Relief not barred by technicalities

card.dispute: Two appellants, Saravanabhavan and Govindaswamy, challenged their conviction and death sentence for murder, arguing that the prosecution's case based on an approver's uncorroborated testimony lacked reliable evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of the approver was sufficiently corroborated to connect Saravanabhavan with the commission of the crime.

Whether the evidence of the approver was sufficiently corroborated to connect Govindaswamy with the crime, particularly through the thumb impression on the lamp chimney and recovery of blood-stained clothes.
Whether the conviction of the appellants could be sustained solely on the basis of the approver's uncorroborated and incredible testimony.
holdings: The evidence of Muthuswamy Goundar regarding Saravanabhavan’s visit and request to burn blood-stained clothes was unreliable and did not constitute valid corroboration due to its inherent improbabilities and the witness’s role in destroying evidence.

The presence of Govindaswamy’s thumb impression on the lamp chimney did not corroborate the approver’s story, as it was more plausible that it resulted from prior visits and cleaning rather than from carrying the lamp during the crime.
The approver’s evidence was inherently incredible and lacked independent corroboration in material particulars; thus, the convictions of both appellants were unsafe and unsustainable.
doctrines: Corroboration of approver's evidence
Inherent improbability of evidence
Principle of benefit of doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The appellant (landowner) fought the tax authorities over whether excess payments received from a mining lessee for local fund cess constituted taxable income.
issues_decided: Whether the excess amounts received by the lessor from the lessee for local fund cess constituted taxable income under the Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the appellant was acting as a government agent in collecting the cess, thereby making the receipt non-taxable
Whether the receipt was of a 'casual and non-recurring' nature and thus exempt from taxation
holdings: Receipts from a lessee under a mining lease agreement, even if exceeding statutory cess liability, are taxable as income if received under a contractual obligation related to rent and royalty.
The lessor does not become an agent of the government merely by collecting cess from the lessee under the lease; such receipts remain personal income.
Receipts arising from contractual obligations, even if based on a mistake, are not 'casual or non-recurring' if they are connected to regular income-generating activity.
doctrines: Definition of income as inclusive and broad under tax law
Receipts under contractual obligation linked to rent/royalty treated as income
Distinction between agent of government and private contractual收款

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant's assignee after the tenant company was dissolved, claiming the assignment was without consent under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller could make an order for recovery of possession against the assignee after the tenant ceased to exist due to dissolution
Whether clause 7 of the lease, defining 'lessee' to include assigns, amounted to written consent to assignment under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act
holdings: The Rent Controller cannot proceed with an eviction application under Section 14(1)(b) after the tenant is dissolved and no legal representative exists, as the jurisdiction to make an order for possession ceases due to a legal lacuna.

A lease clause defining 'lessee' to include assigns does not constitute written consent to assignment under Section 14(1)(b); such consent must be express or implied in fact, not merely by contractual definition.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1) proviso (b)
doctrines: Jurisdictional limitation due to statutory lacuna
Strict interpretation of statutory consent
Doctrine of legal personality and corporate dissolution

card.dispute: The appellant, a trustee of a temple, challenged the State of Madras's extension of a notification placing the temple under government supervision without being given a chance to object.
issues_decided: Whether a reasonable opportunity to show cause must be given before extending a notification under Section 64(4) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
Whether the High Court was correct in rejecting the writ petition on procedural and factual grounds
holdings: The process under Section 64(4) for extending a notification is quasi-judicial and requires compliance with principles of natural justice, including giving the trustee a reasonable opportunity to show cause.

The High Court erred in holding that the plea was not raised and that the notification would soon expire, as the plea was properly raised in rejoinder and the notification was statutorily extended beyond the date assumed.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 64(3)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 64(4)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 63
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial character of administrative action
Prospective and retrospective operation of statutory amendments

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications issued by the State of U.P. for a water-works scheme, arguing that procedural safeguards were bypassed.
issues_decided: Whether Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be invoked to dispense with Section 5-A inquiry for non-waste or non-arable land with buildings.
Whether the notifications under Section 4(1) and Section 6 were valid in law given the procedural defect under Section 17(4).
Whether fresh acquisition proceedings for the same land after abandonment of prior proceedings are permissible without fresh grounds.
holdings: Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act applies only to waste or arable land and cannot be used to exclude Section 5-A inquiry for land with buildings.
A notification under Section 6 issued without complying with the mandatory procedure under Section 5-A is invalid.
The court did not decide on the validity of fresh acquisition proceedings due to lack of evidence on whether prior proceedings were abandoned on finality of objections.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Finality of quasi-judicial orders
Ultra vires doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants (alienees) sued for declaration of title and injunction against respondents (temple trustees) who sought possession of temple lands allegedly alienated by a former manager; the dispute centered on whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 134-B of the Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether Article 134-B of the Limitation Act applies to alienations by a manager of a Hindu religious endowment who transferred properties as his own separate property
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 134-B, particularly whether more than 12 years had elapsed since the alienator was removed from management
holdings: Article 134-B applies to all transfers by a previous manager of a Hindu religious endowment for valuable consideration, regardless of whether the manager claimed the property as his own; representations by the manager are irrelevant to the applicability of the article.

The suit was not barred by limitation under Article 134-B because the evidence showed the alienator had been removed from management and de facto managers had managed the temple for over 25 years, thus more than 12 years had elapsed since removal, extinguishing the temple’s right to sue.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
doctrines: Adverse possession against religious endowments
De facto management as evidence of removal of trustee
Applicability of limitation to suits involving religious properties

card.dispute: The appellant math and the respondent's legal representatives fought over ownership of math properties, with the respondent claiming title by adverse possession after long-term occupation without payment of rent.
issues_decided: Whether adverse possession against a math can commence in the absence of a legally appointed mathadhipathi
When the limitation period under Article 144 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 begins to run in cases involving endowed math properties
Whether the appointment of a new mathadhipathi after the expiration of limitation revives the right to sue for recovery of property
holdings: Adverse possession against a math begins when possession becomes hostile, irrespective of whether a legally appointed mathadhipathi exists.
Limitation under Article 144 starts from 1915, when the lease ended with the death of the previous mathadhipathi, and continued to run despite the absence of a legal manager.
The appointment of a mathadhipathi in 1939 did not restart limitation or restore the right to sue, as the math’s title had already been extinguished by adverse possession by then.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Juristic personality of religious institutions
Extinction of title by prescription

card.dispute: The trustee of a temple challenged the High Court's modification of a 1919 administrative scheme by appointing an Executive Officer and adding provisions for additional trustees, despite no proven mismanagement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could appoint an Executive Officer to manage a temple's administration without proof of mismanagement under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
Whether the Commissioner's recommendation alone is sufficient to justify structural changes in temple administration
Whether a scheme can be modified to dilute the trustee's powers when no mismanagement has been established
holdings: The appointment of an Executive Officer who effectively displaces the trustee is not justified unless there is proven mismanagement or exceptional circumstances warranting such intervention.
The Commissioner's advice or recommendation does not override the court’s duty to independently assess whether changes to a temple’s administration are necessary based on evidence.
A scheme modifying temple administration cannot be altered to subordinate the trustee’s authority in the absence of proven mismanagement or a legal basis under the applicable Act.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 62(3)(a)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 39
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 45
doctrines: Principle of proven mismanagement as prerequisite for state intervention in religious administration
Judicial review of administrative schemes under religious endowments law
Separation of supervisory and managerial functions in temple administration

card.dispute: The brothers disputed whether certain properties were joint family assets subject to partition or the self-acquired property of one brother, and whether a written family arrangement required registration.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in question were joint family properties or the self-acquired property of the appellant
Whether the written family arrangement (Exhibit 3) required compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act
holdings: The properties were treated as joint family properties based on the family arrangement, and the court assumed antecedent title among the brothers despite acquisition with mother's funds.
A written memorandum of a family arrangement does not require registration if it merely records an oral agreement and is not intended to serve as a document of title.
doctrines: Family arrangement doctrine
Doctrine of antecedent title in family arrangements
Doctrine of non-registration for memoranda of family arrangements

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan refused to extend a mining lease for the full period mandated by rule 30, leading the lessee to challenge the decision, seeking mandatory extension and renewal of the lease as per the rules.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Chapter IV of the Rajasthan Mines and Mineral Concession Rules, 1958 apply to mining leases granted under Chapter V by auction
Whether rule 30 applies to leases granted under Chapter V
Whether the word 'may' in rule 30 is directory or mandatory in nature regarding the period and extension of the lease
Whether the High Court exceeded the relief claimed by directing inclusion of an option for second renewal
holdings: Provisions of Chapter IV apply to leases under Chapter V to the extent they cover essential incidents of mining leases not provided for in Chapter V.
Rule 30 applies to leases granted under Chapter V as there is no corresponding rule in Chapter V and Chapter IV rules fill the gaps.
The word 'may' in the main part and proviso of rule 30 must be read as 'shall', making the grant of a 5-year lease and its extension mandatory if conditions are met.
The prayer for renewal under rule 30 necessarily includes the option for a second renewal; thus, the High Court did not exceed the relief claimed.
provisions: Rajasthan Mines and Mineral Concession Rules, 1958, Chapter IV, Rule 30
Rajasthan Mines and Mineral Concession Rules, 1958, Chapter V, Rules 38 and 39
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of 'may' where context demands
Gap-filling by applying general rules to specific procedures
Doctrine of necessary implication in interpreting statutory conditions

card.dispute: The tenant (V. N. Sarin) resisted eviction by the new landlord (Major Ajit Kumar Poplai), who acquired the property through partition of a Hindu undivided family, arguing that such acquisition was a 'transfer' under the Delhi Rent Control Act, disqualifying the landlord from seeking eviction on personal need.
issues_decided: Whether a share in property allotted to a coparcener on partition of a Hindu undivided family amounts to 'acquisition by transfer' under Section 14(6) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the word 'transfer' in Section 14(6) should be interpreted the same way as in Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act or Section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Registration Act.
holdings: Partition of a Hindu undivided family does not amount to 'acquisition by transfer' under Section 14(6) because each coparcener already has an antecedent title, and partition merely crystallizes that pre-existing interest.
The term 'transfer' in Section 14(6) implies acquisition by a person who had no prior title, unlike in partition where the coparcener's title is transformed, not newly acquired.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on context and object
Partition under Hindu law as crystallization of pre-existing title
Principle of consistency in statutory definitions across different legal contexts

card.dispute: The Zamindar's sons and other family members claimed a share in the compensation for the abolished Seithur Zamindari, arguing it was an ancestral impartible estate, while the Zamindar claimed it as his separate property entitled solely to him.
issues_decided: Whether the Seithur Estate was an ancestral impartible estate or the Zamindar's separate property
Whether the appellants were entitled to share in the compensation under Section 45 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
Whether the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904 converted a self-acquired impartible estate into a joint family property
holdings: An impartible estate may be either ancestral or self-acquired; the mere fact of impartibility does not make it joint family property.
Section 4 of the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904 did not convert a self-acquired impartible estate into a joint family property; it only restricted the holder’s power of alienation.

Section 45 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 applies only to ancestral impartible estates; since the Seithur Estate was self-acquired, the compensation was solely payable to the Zamindar.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 44
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 45
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 54-A
doctrines: Doctrine of impartible estates in Hindu law
Doctrine of blending (merger) of separate property into joint family property
Rule of succession and compensation distribution under abolition statutes

card.dispute: The step-mothers of a man contested the legitimacy of his son and the validity of a gift of joint family immovable property made by the man to his second wife.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was the legitimate son of the deceased R.
Whether the gift of ancestral immovable property by R to his second wife was valid under Hindu law.
holdings: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act creates a conclusive presumption of legitimacy if a child is born during a valid marriage and access between spouses is not disproven; the appellants failed to prove non-access, so the son's legitimacy stands.
A gift of ancestral immovable property by a husband to his wife, even out of love or to fulfill a father's wish, does not constitute a 'pious purpose' and is not valid under Hindu law.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory source, as personal law)
doctrines: Conclusive presumption of legitimacy
Doctrine of pious obligation
Limited power of gift of ancestral immovable property under Hindu law

card.dispute: The appellant, a small landholder within the ceiling limit, challenged the validity of a land consolidation scheme that took a portion of his land for a common pool managed by the Gram Panchayat, arguing it amounted to acquisition by the State requiring compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the Consolidation Officer could be validly appointed retrospectively after the repartition was completed.

Whether the transfer of a portion of proprietors' land to a common pool managed by the Gram Panchayat amounted to 'acquisition by the State' under the second proviso to Article 31A(1) of the Constitution, requiring payment of market-value compensation.
holdings: The court did not rule on the retrospective appointment issue as the appeal was decided on the broader constitutional question of acquisition and compensation.

The transfer of land to a common pool managed by the Gram Panchayat, with ownership vested in a proprietary body but all management and income rights vested in the Panchayat for public benefit, constitutes 'acquisition by the State' under the second proviso to Article 31A(1), requiring compensation at market value even if the land taken is small in proportion.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948
Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Rules, 1949, Rule 16(ii)
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Substance over form
Deprivation of property under Article 31
Acquisition by the State under Article 31A

card.dispute: Basant Singh and Janki Singh disputed over property rights following the death of Ramyad Singh, specifically whether Ramyad Singh died in 1939, affecting inheritance under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a party can rely on an admission in a pleading in a prior suit even if they do not accept the truth of other statements in that pleading.
Whether an admission made in a pleading in one suit is admissible as evidence against the party in a subsequent suit.
holdings: A party may rely on a specific admission in a prior pleading even if they reject other statements in the same pleading; the court may accept some statements and reject others.
An admission in a pleading signed and verified by a party is admissible under Section 17 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, in subsequent suits, though it is not conclusive and may be rebutted.
doctrines: Admission under Section 17 of the Indian Evidence Act
Selective reliance on admissions in pleadings
Use of prior judicial admissions in subsequent litigation

card.dispute: The landlord sought to eject the tenant from rented land, claiming personal use for building a residence, while the tenant argued the law only permits ejectment for business or trade purposes.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can obtain an ejectment order under Section 13(3)(a)(ii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 for any purpose claimed as 'for his own use', including residential construction.
Whether the phrase 'for his own use' in Section 13(3)(a)(ii) must be read restrictively in light of sub-clauses (b) and (c) to apply only to business or trade purposes.
holdings: The phrase 'for his own use' in Section 13(3)(a)(ii) is restricted to use for business or trade and does not include personal residential use.
Sub-clauses (b) and (c) imply that the legislature intended to limit ejectment rights to cases where the landlord needs the land for business, otherwise those restrictions would be meaningless.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)(ii)
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Restrictive interpretation of landlord rights in tenant protection statutes

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, members of two Joint Hindu families in a partnership, disputed whether an unregistered document recording the dissolution of their partnership and settlement of accounts was admissible in evidence, given that the partnership owned immovable property.
issues_decided: Whether a document evidencing dissolution of a partnership and relinquishment of a partner's share in partnership assets, including immovable property, is compulsorily registrable under Section 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether an unregistered deed of release by a partner of his share in a partnership owning immovable property is admissible in evidence
holdings: A document that merely records the dissolution of a partnership and relinquishment of a partner's share, without conveying immovable property expressly or by necessary implication, does not require compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act, 1908.

The interest of a partner in partnership assets, including immovable property, is treated as movable property; thus, a deed releasing such interest does not require registration and is admissible in evidence even if the firm owns immovable property.
doctrines: Doctrine of partnership property as movable interest
Doctrine of compulsory registration for conveyance of immovable property

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated by the Commissioner, arguing that the delegation of legislative power to the State Government under the Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1958, was excessive and unconstitutional, and that the amended definition of 'public purpose' in the Land Acquisition Act was ultra vires.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3(3) and 3(4) of the Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1958, involve excessive delegation of legislative power to the State Government
Whether the State Government's power to amend other enactments via notification under Section 3(4) amounts to an unconstitutional abdication of legislative function
Whether the notifications issued under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, based on powers conferred via Section 3(4), are valid
holdings: Sections 3(3), 3(4), and 3(5) of the Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1958, constitute an impermissible transfer of legislative power to the executive and are ultra vires for amounting to excessive delegation.

The power conferred on the State Government under Section 3(4) to amend other enactments to confer powers on the Commissioner involves the power to amend or repeal laws, which is an essential legislative function and cannot be delegated.
Notifications issued under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, which relied on amendments made under Section 3(4) of the 1958 Act, are invalid and are quashed.
provisions: The Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1958 (Bom. Act 8 of 1958), Sections 3(3), 3(4), 3(5)
Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (Act 1 of 1894), Section 3(f)(2) as amended by Bombay Amendment Act 35 of 1953
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Doctrine of essential legislative function
Conditional legislation
Delegated legislation

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sued for eviction of the tenant (respondent) claiming he made unauthorized material alterations to the rented shops, while the tenant argued the alterations did not substantially diminish the property's value and thus eviction was not permissible without the District Magistrate's permission.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(1)(c) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 requires both material alteration and substantial diminution in value, or either condition separately
Whether the tenant's unauthorized structural changes constituted 'material alterations' within the meaning of Section 3(1)(c)
holdings: Section 3(1)(c) provides two independent grounds for eviction without the District Magistrate’s permission: material alteration of the accommodation or likelihood of substantial diminution in its value; the word 'or' is disjunctive and not conjunctive.

Lowering the floor, door, staircase, and chabutra without consent amounted to material and structural alterations, which alone justified eviction under Section 3(1)(c), irrespective of whether the property's value was diminished.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(1)(c)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Disjunctive interpretation of statutory language
Material alteration in property law

card.dispute: Bihar Mines Ltd fought the Union of India over the validity of the termination of its mining lease and sub-leases after the vesting of estate rights in the State, and whether the Controller had authority to terminate (not just modify) the lease under mining laws.
issues_decided: Whether subsisting mining leases deemed vested in the State under Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 are 'existing mining leases' under Rule 2(c) of the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956
Whether the Controller of Mines had the power to terminate, rather than merely shorten, a mining lease exceeding 20 years under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Whether the termination orders passed without notice to sub-lessees in some cases were invalid
holdings: Leases deemed to be granted by the State under Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 are 'existing mining leases' and remain subject to modification under central mining laws.

The Controller may terminate an existing mining lease exceeding 20 years for minerals like soapstone, as the law requires conformity with the 20-year limit from the original commencement date, not a new lease.
Though termination orders on sub-leases without notice were irregular, they were valid as the head lease was lawfully terminated, automatically ending sub-leases.
provisions: Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 10(1) and (2)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 8, Section 16
Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956, Rule 2(c), Rule 4, Rule 6
doctrines: Deeming fiction in statute
Continuity of subsisting leases post-vesting
Automatic termination of sub-leases upon termination of head lease

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax challenged the registration of a partnership firm (Juggilal Kamalapat) formed between a trust and an individual, arguing it lacked legal validity due to an unregistered deed of relinquishment concerning firm assets, including immovable property.
issues_decided: Whether the new partnership firm legally came into existence despite the unregistered deed of relinquishment by former partners in favor of a trust.
Whether a deed of relinquishment of a partner's interest in firm assets, including immovable property, requires registration under the Registration Act, 1908.
Whether the Tribunal's rejection of the firm's registration application was justified on the ground of legal invalidity.
holdings: A partnership firm can legally exist even if a deed of relinquishment by former partners is unregistered, provided the partnership deed is valid and partners contribute capital or interest.

A partner's interest in partnership assets, including when comprising immovable property, is movable in nature and thus a deed transferring such interest does not require registration under Section 17(1) of the Registration Act, 1908.

Even if the deed of relinquishment were invalid concerning immovable property, it remained valid for movable assets, and the firm's existence and registration could not be denied solely on that ground.
doctrines: Doctrine of severability of contractual terms in unregistered deeds
Partnership interest as movable property
Distinction between questions of law and questions of fact under tax referral provisions

card.dispute: The appellants (Gomathinayagam Pillai and others) refused to execute a sale deed for land they had agreed to sell to the respondent (Pallaniswami Nadar), who sued for specific performance of the contract.
issues_decided: Whether time was of the essence of the contract for the sale of land
Whether the respondent was disentitled to specific performance due to delay
Whether the respondent was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract
holdings: Time was not of the essence of the contract merely because a date was stipulated for completion; the appellants were required to give reasonable notice to complete before cancelling the agreement.
Delay in performance, without more, does not bar specific performance if the party is otherwise ready and willing and there is no waiver or abandonment.

The respondent was ready and willing to perform his obligations throughout, as shown by partial payments and prompt deposit of the balance upon notice; lack of immediate readiness on a fixed date does not prove unwillingness.
doctrines: Specific performance
Readiness and willingness in contracts
Time as essence of contract
Laches and delay in equitable relief

card.dispute: The petitioners, as landowners in Daman, challenged the constitutional validity of the Daman (Abolition of Proprietorship of Villages) Regulation, 1962, which abolished village proprietorship, arguing it violated Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution, while the Union of India claimed protection under Article 31-A.
issues_decided: Whether the Daman Regulation falls within the protection of Article 31-A of the Constitution by virtue of the definition of 'estate' under Article 31-A(2)(a)(iii)
Whether the Regulation is severable insofar as it applies to lands not covered by the definition of 'estate' in Article 31-A
Whether the expropriation of non-agricultural lands such as salt pans, hilly areas, quarries, and lands within municipal areas is constitutionally valid
holdings: The Regulation is protected by Article 31-A only in respect of lands used for agriculture or horticulture, including waste and forest land used for cultivation or related purposes, which fall within the constitutional definition of 'estate'.
The Regulation is severable; it remains valid for lands qualifying as 'estate', but does not enjoy constitutional protection under Article 31-A for lands outside that definition.

Lands such as salt pans, hilly tracts, quarries, and areas within municipal limits do not vest in the Government under Article 31-A and require compensation assessed independently of the Regulation if acquired.
provisions: Daman (Abolition of Proprietorship of Villages) Regulation, 1962
doctrines: Doctrine of Severability
Agrarian Reform under Article 31-A
Presumption of Constitutional Validity within Legislative Competence

card.dispute: Collateral members of a Hindu undivided family disputed whether a preliminary decree specifying shares in 1924 amounted to partition and whether a later suit for partition and accounts, including benami properties, was barred by law.
issues_decided: Whether specification of individual shares in a preliminary decree of partition amounts to actual severance of status under Hindu law
Whether a suit claiming a share in properties purchased at court auction in another's name is barred by Section 66(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether a claim for rendition of accounts survives the death of the parties
holdings: Specification of shares in a preliminary decree does not by itself amount to partition or severance of joint family status unless there is a clear intention to separate.

A suit seeking a share in joint family property held in another's name is not barred by Section 66(1) CPC if the claim is that the property was acquired with joint family funds, not that it was purchased benami on behalf of the plaintiff.
A claim for rendition of accounts is not a personal action and does not abate upon the death of a party; the liability to account survives against the estate.
provisions: Hindu Law (general principles of joint family and partition)
