doctrines: Doctrine of adverse possession
Doctrine of extinguishment of right by limitation
Principle that a right cannot be barred before it accrues

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an arbitrator's award for compensation on the ground that the arbitrator lacked jurisdiction due to an invalid appointment.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator was validly appointed under the Arbitration Act, 1940, or the Defence of India Act, 1939.
Whether the agreement dated January 27, 1944, formed a valid basis for the arbitration proceedings despite not being executed by the government.
Whether the arbitrator had jurisdiction to pass the award when the Union of India was not a party to the original arbitration reference.
holdings: The arbitrator was appointed under Section 20(4) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, not under the Defence of India Act, 1939, as the appointment orders consistently referred to the 1944 agreement and court order in Suit No. 169 of 1948.

The appointment under the Arbitration Act was invalid because the Union of India was not a party to the suit and the agreement was never executed by the government, rendering the reference ineffective against it.
The arbitrator lacked jurisdiction to pass the award, as the appointment was based on a non-binding agreement and a court order not applicable to the Union of India.
doctrines: Jurisdictional validity of arbitration appointments
Requirement of valid agreement and proper reference for arbitration
Distinction between statutory arbitration under Defence of India Act and consensual arbitration under Arbitration Act

card.dispute: The appellants, who raised a bund on government land, were accused of murder when one of them shot and killed three people from a rival group that had come to forcibly remove the bund.
issues_decided: Whether the accused had the right of private defence of person and property when the deceased and their group attempted to remove the bund by force
Whether the right of private defence extends to causing death in the circumstances of this case
Whether the court can consider the right of private defence even if the accused raised a plea of alibi and did not specifically plead self-defence
holdings: The right of private defence of the body extends to causing death when there is reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt or death due to an assault, especially when the accused is confronted with a violent mob.
The right of private defence can be exercised even against a group acting as aggressors, particularly when public authorities have failed to act and the attack is sudden and severe.

A court may grant the benefit of private defence to an accused even if not pleaded, provided the evidence on record supports such a conclusion, and the failure to plead it does not amount to estoppel.
doctrines: Right of private defence
Reasonable apprehension of danger
No estoppel against raising right of private defence
Preventive, not punitive, nature of self-defence

card.dispute: Hanuman Pershad (landlord) fought with Roop Narain (occupant) over whether Roop Narain's possession of a house was adverse and had ripened into ownership, barring eviction under a 1953 decree.
issues_decided: Whether Roop Narain acquired title by adverse possession against the landlord during the subsistence of a lease to Bishan Chand?
Whether the finding of adverse possession by the appellate court could be overturned in second appeal?
Whether the landlord's inaction after denial of title amounted to acquiescence in adverse possession?
holdings: Possession of a third party (Roop Narain) during the subsistence of a lease cannot be adverse to the landlord, even if title is denied, unless there is a fresh assertion of adverse possession after the lease ends.
A finding of fact by an appellate court based on sufficient evidence cannot be disturbed in second appeal merely because another view is possible.
A landlord is not obligated to file an ejectment suit immediately upon denial of title by a tenant or occupant, especially when rent continues to be paid and possession remains permissive.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Constructive possession through tenant
Res judicata
Principle of permissive possession not ripening into adverse possession during lease

card.dispute: Hereditary trustees challenged the validity of provisions in the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, which imposed restrictions on their management rights, claiming violation of Article 19 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the office of a hereditary trustee constitutes 'property' within the meaning of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
Whether Sections 15, 17, 27, 36, and 97 of the Andhra Pradesh Act violate Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
Whether the restrictions imposed by the impugned provisions are reasonable and in the public interest.
holdings: The office of a hereditary trustee, who holds only a bare right to manage and administer without proprietary or beneficial interest, is not 'property' under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
Even if such office were considered property, the restrictions imposed by the Act are saved by Article 19(5) as they are reasonable and in the interest of the general public.
The impugned provisions do not violate Article 19(1)(f) as they ensure efficient management of religious institutions while preserving religious practices and safeguarding the trustee's role.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Sections 15, 17, 27, 36, 97
Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(f), Article 19(5), Article 14, Article 26(d), Article 31
doctrines: Bare right to manage without beneficial interest is not property under Article 19(1)(f)
Reasonable restrictions in public interest under Article 19(5)
Distinction between office and property in religious management roles
Doctrine of precedent: obiter dicta in Sambudamurthi Mudaliar distinguished

card.dispute: The state and the complainant appealed the acquittal of the appellants in a case where they were accused of dishonestly cutting and removing paddy crops, but the complainant died during the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal under Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C. abates upon the death of the complainant.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal by the first appellate court based on re-evaluation of evidence.
holdings: An appeal under Section 417 of the Cr.P.C. does not abate upon the death of the complainant; it only abates upon the death of the accused, as per Section 431 Cr.P.C.

The High Court should not interfere with an acquittal unless the lower court's conclusion was palpably wrong, based on an error of law, or leads to grave injustice; reappreciation of evidence alone is insufficient.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Principle of double jeopardy and finality of acquittal
Doctrine of limited appellate review in acquittal cases

card.dispute: The daughter and wife of Narasimha Bhatta challenged the validity of a settlement deed and will executed in favor of respondent No. 1, alleging undue influence and lack of mental capacity due to senility and illness.
issues_decided: Whether Narasimha Bhatta was of sound disposing mind when executing the settlement deed Ext. B-3 in December 1955?
Whether the settlement deed Ext. B-3 was executed under undue influence or pressure by respondent No. 1?
Whether the burden of proof lay on respondent No. 1 to prove the voluntary execution of the deed given suspicious circumstances?
Whether the non-production of medical records and the will itself raises an adverse inference against respondent No. 1?
holdings: An aged and diabetic person suffering from senility and mental weakness cannot be presumed to have had sound disposing mind without clear evidence.
A settlement deed making unnatural dispositions in favor of a person who took charge of the executant raises a presumption of undue influence.
Where circumstances suggest incapacity or coercion, the burden shifts to the beneficiary to prove voluntary and informed execution.
Failure to produce medical records, case sheets, or the will itself, despite their existence, justifies an adverse inference against the beneficiary.
provisions: Registration Act, 1908, Section 30 (Registration at place other than office)
doctrines: Presumption of undue influence in transactions between dominant and dependent parties
Burden of proof shifting in cases of suspicious circumstances
Rejection of attesting witness testimony lacking proper medical examination
Adverse inference from non-production of relevant documents

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Luka Mathai challenged the validity of a revenue sale of agricultural land hypothecated to the government, arguing misdescription of survey numbers and inclusion of non-hypothecated properties.
issues_decided: Whether misdescription of survey numbers in the proclamation of sale vitiated the sale when the identity of the property was not in doubt.
Whether the sale was vitiated by the inclusion of properties not hypothecated to the government.
Whether the government had legal authority to recover the dues under the bond as arrears of public revenue.
Whether the entire sale became void due to the inclusion of non-hypothecated properties in a composite sale.
holdings: A misdescription of survey numbers in a proclamation of sale does not vitiate the sale if the identity of the property is clear and there is no resulting prejudice.
The inclusion of non-hypothecated properties in a revenue sale invalidates the entire sale when all properties are sold as one lot.
The government's power to recover dues as arrears of public revenue requires a written agreement or enabling regulation, which was absent here.
A sale conducted under revenue recovery proceedings is void if it includes properties beyond those legally subject to attachment and sale.
provisions: Travancore Revenue Recovery Regulation 1 of 1068 M.E., Section 32(2)
Travancore Revenue Recovery Regulation 1 of 1068 M.E., Section 59
doctrines: Misdescription vs. mistaken identity
Vitiation of entire sale for inclusion of non-hypothecated property
Procedural compliance in revenue sale notices
Doctrine of severability in attachment proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant (Maharajadhiraj of Burdwan) and respondent (Subodh Gopal) fought over ownership and share in joint lands in Mouja Alipore, including rights to compensation and mesne profits from acquired land.
issues_decided: Whether the suit lands were joint properties of the Toujis and the respondent had a share in them
Whether the appellant acquired exclusive rights by long possession
Whether the respondent was entitled to a share in the compensation amount for acquired lands
Whether a decree for mesne profits could be granted against the appellant
holdings: The suit lands, to the extent of 25 Bighas 2 Cottahs 1 Chittak and 45 Sq. Feet, are joint properties of Toujis 1 to 6, 8 to 16, 33, 51, 53 and 91, and the respondent is entitled to an undivided 1 anna 3 gondas share.
Mere long possession by a co-owner, without adverse possession, does not confer exclusive rights over joint property.
The respondent is entitled to a proportionate share of the compensation amount, as acquisition proceedings do not confer title on the possessor.
A decree for mesne profits is maintainable against a co-owner in possession, as such possession can be unlawful in relation to other co-owners' shares.
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are not disturbed unless based on ignored evidence or irrelevant considerations
Adverse possession doctrine: possession by a co-owner is not adverse unless there is a denial of co-ownership
Acquisition proceedings do not confer title; compensation follows property rights

card.dispute: The landlord (Mylapore Hindu Permanent Ltd.) and tenant (K. S. Subramania Iyer) disputed whether the tenant was entitled to compensation under Section 3 and the right to purchase the land under Section 9 of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, despite contractual limitations in a registered lease deed.
issues_decided: Whether the stipulations in the registered lease deed limiting compensation for buildings erected by the tenant fall within the proviso to Section 12 of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, as amended in 1955.
Whether the tenant could claim compensation under Section 3 of the Act despite agreeing to a cap on such compensation in the lease deed.
Whether the tenant could exercise the option to purchase the land under Section 9 of the Act if not entitled to full compensation under Section 3.
holdings: A stipulation in a registered lease deed that limits or regulates the compensation payable for buildings erected by the tenant constitutes a 'stipulation as to the erection of buildings' within the proviso to Section 12 of the Act and overrides the tenant's rights under Section 3.
Where a tenant agrees in a registered lease deed to a limited compensation amount for constructions, he is not entitled to claim full market value compensation under Section 3 of the Act.

The right to purchase the land under Section 9 is contingent upon the tenant being entitled to compensation under Section 3; if barred from such compensation by contractual stipulations in a registered deed, the tenant cannot invoke Section 9.
provisions: The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922 (Madras Act 3 of 1922), as amended by Madras Act 19 of 1955, Section 3
The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, as amended by Madras Act 19 of 1955, Section 9
The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, as amended by Madras Act 19 of 1955, Section 12
doctrines: Statutory override of contractual terms in tenancy law
Conditional statutory rights dependent on fulfillment of prerequisites
Interpretation of 'stipulation as to the erection of buildings' under proviso to Section 12

card.dispute: The mortgagee's legal representatives sued to eject the mortgagor after a time-barred application for a final mortgage decree; the dispute was whether the ejectment suit was maintainable despite the expired right to enforce the mortgage by sale.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee's right to sue for ejectment survived the expiry of the limitation period for obtaining a final decree for sale of the mortgaged property
Whether the rights under the rent note merged with the preliminary mortgage decree
Whether Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 extinguished the mortgagee's right to possession under the rent note after the limitation period for final decree expired
holdings: A mortgagee who fails to apply for a final decree within the limitation period loses the right to sell the property but retains other rights, including those under a separate rent note.
Rights under a rent note executed alongside a mortgage do not merge into the preliminary mortgage decree and remain enforceable independently.
Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 does not extinguish a mortgagee's right to sue for possession under a valid rent note once the limitation for a final mortgage decree has expired.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 34, Rule 14
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 34, Rule 4
doctrines: Merger of rights doctrine
Independent enforceability of collateral agreements
Doctrine of extinction of right under limitation law

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad fought with New Shorock Spg. & Wvg. Co. over the legality of property tax collection and refusal to refund amounts already collected, especially after a court had declared the assessments invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Corporation could lawfully retain property tax amounts collected without a valid assessment under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, as amended.
Whether sub-section (3) of Section 152A, introduced by an Ordinance, which allowed the Corporation to withhold refunds despite court orders, was constitutionally valid.
holdings: The Corporation could not retain tax amounts in the absence of a lawful assessment under the Act and its rules, as no valid assessment orders were passed in accordance with the law.
Sub-section (3) of Section 152A was unconstitutional because it attempted to override judicial orders, thereby violating the separation of powers and the rule of law under the Constitution.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 152A
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation (Gujarat Amendment and Validity Provisions) Ordinance, 1969, Section 152A(3)
doctrines: Separation of powers
Rule of law
Limitations on retrospective legislation
Invalidity of forced loans under the Constitution

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's eviction petition under the Mysore Rent Control Act, claiming the landlord could not evict unless the building was in a condition requiring immediate demolition.
issues_decided: Whether the condition of the building must be such that immediate demolition is necessary for eviction under Section 21(1)(j) of the Mysore Rent Control Act
Whether the landlord's intention to redevelop the property for more profitable use satisfies the requirement of 'reasonably and bona fide required' under the Act
holdings: The requirement under Section 21(1)(j) is based on the landlord's reasonable and bona fide need to demolish and redevelop, not on the physical condition of the building.

A landlord may evict a tenant under Section 21(1)(j) if the intention to demolish and rebuild is bona fide and reasonable, even if the building is not structurally unsafe or in immediate need of demolition.
doctrines: Bona fide requirement of landlord
Reasonableness in eviction for redevelopment
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions

card.dispute: The appellants (Parbhat General Agencies) and the Union of India disputed whether a new arbitrator could be appointed when the designated arbitrator (Judicial Commissioner, Himachal Pradesh) refused to act, despite the arbitration clause naming only that official.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitrator can be appointed in place of the Judicial Commissioner when he refuses to act, under an arbitration clause specifying only that officeholder as arbitrator.
Whether the parties' agreement indicates an intention not to fill the vacancy if the named arbitrator is unable or unwilling to act.
Whether Section 8(1)(b) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 applies to allow appointment of a substitute arbitrator in such circumstances.
holdings: Section 8(1)(b) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 allows appointment of a substitute arbitrator unless the agreement shows the parties intended not to fill the vacancy.
The mere designation of an arbitrator by reference to an office does not imply that the parties intended to leave the vacancy unfilled if the officeholder refuses to act.
The arbitration agreement in question did not indicate an intention not to supply the vacancy; hence, a new arbitrator may be appointed by the court.
doctrines: Doctrine of effective arbitration: arbitration agreements should not be rendered infructuous by failure to appoint a named arbitrator.
Doctrine of party autonomy in arbitration: the intention of the parties governs whether a vacancy in arbitration may be filled.
Principle of statutory interpretation: Section 8(1)(b) is to be applied unless the agreement clearly shows an intention not to supply the vacancy.

card.dispute: The appellants (vendees) sued for specific performance of an agreement to purchase a plot from the respondents (vendors), whose title was initially imperfect and required government sanction, which was later granted but not communicated to the vendees.
issues_decided: Whether the vendors could avoid specific performance by claiming the vendees failed to perform their part when the vendors themselves had not perfected title or obtained required sanction
Whether time was made the essence of the contract by the vendors' letters, rendering the agreement void due to uncertainty
Whether the vendees were ready and willing to perform their part of the contract, including having sufficient funds
Whether the vendees were precluded from appealing for specific performance after accepting a decree for refund of earnest money
holdings: A vendor cannot insist on the vendee's performance without first fulfilling their own obligation to obtain necessary sanction and perfect title.
Mere expressions of uncertainty about government sanction do not make time the essence of the contract or render it void.
The vendees demonstrated continuous readiness and willingness to perform, including financial capacity, and thus were entitled to specific performance.
Accepting a decree for refund while appealing for specific performance does not constitute approbation and reprobation where conduct consistently shows rejection of the trial court's decision.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform
Approbation and reprobation
Discretion in granting specific performance
Vendors must first perform their obligations before claiming vendee's default

card.dispute: The son of Perumal Nadar and Annapazham, born after Perumal's alleged prior marriage, claimed a share in the joint family property, leading to a dispute over the validity of the marriage and the child's legitimacy.
issues_decided: Whether Annapazham, originally an Indian Christian, was validly converted to Hinduism before her marriage to Perumal Nadar.
Whether the marriage between Perumal and Annapazham was void due to bigamy under the Madras Hindu (Bigamy Prevention and Divorce) Act, 1949.
Whether the child born from the marriage was legitimate under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act.
holdings: A person born in another faith can become a Hindu through bona fide intention and unequivocal conduct; no formal purification ceremony is required for conversion.
The Madras Hindu (Bigamy Prevention and Divorce) Act, 1949 applies only to those domiciled in Madras, and since domicile was not pleaded or proved, the Act did not invalidate the marriage.
Under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, a child born during a valid marriage is presumed legitimate unless non-access is conclusively proven, which was not done here.
provisions: Madras Hindu (Bigamy Prevention and Divorce) Act, 1949, Sections 3 and 4(1)
doctrines: Conversion to Hinduism by intention and conduct
Domicile as a requirement for application of personal law statutes
Conclusive presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Radha Nath Seal sued Haripada Jana and others to declare title and recover possession of a tank property, claiming purchase of tenancy rights from original tenants, against defendants asserting valid termination of tenancy and subsequent settlement.
issues_decided: Whether the original tenants had a permanent raiyati tenancy under the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, or merely a jalkar (fishery) right.
Whether the tenancy was validly terminated by notice under Section 100, CPC, and whether the High Court could interfere with findings of fact.
Whether the plaintiff acquired valid rights through purchase from the original tenants despite alleged termination of tenancy.
holdings: The tenancy between the Duleys and the landlord was governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, and became permanent after 12 years, granting occupancy rights.
The High Court could interfere with factual findings due to material evidence being ignored and assumptions made by lower courts.
The notice Ext. P.3 did not legally terminate the permanent tenancy under the Act, and thus the plaintiff validly acquired rights through purchase from the tenants.
doctrines: Permanent tenancy under Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885
Interference with findings of fact in second appeal under Section 100, CPC
Survival of tenancy rights despite notice if not in compliance with statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant claimed entitlement to land settled by his father upon respondents 1 and 2, contesting their right to possession after he dispossessed them in 1946.
issues_decided: Whether the settlement of land by the Raja in 1936 in favor of respondents 1 and 2 was valid and binding on the joint family estate.
Whether the respondents were entitled to a decree for possession and mesne profits despite the absence of a plea regarding legal necessity in the written statement.
Whether the High Court was justified in confirming the trial court's findings of fact regarding possession and dispossession.
holdings: The settlement in favor of respondents 1 and 2 was upheld as an act of prudent management beneficial to the joint family estate, supported by familial loyalty and past services.
Even without a plea of legal necessity, an alienation by a joint family manager is voidable, not void, and possession can be restored to the alienee if dispossessed wrongfully.
Concurrent findings of fact by the trial and appellate courts are not interfered with by the Supreme Court unless perverse, and no such perversity was found here.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact
Manager's power of alienation in Hindu joint family law
Legal necessity and benefit to estate doctrine
Voidability of alienation without legal necessity

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings for a housing scheme undertaken by a cooperative society, arguing it was not for a public purpose and that procedural requirements were not met.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition for a housing scheme by a cooperative society qualifies as a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether non-compliance with Sections 40 to 42 of the Land Acquisition Act invalidates the acquisition when the purpose is public.
Whether the government applied its mind in issuing the Section 6 notification.
Whether the notifications under Sections 4 and 6 were vague or invalid.
holdings: An acquisition for a housing scheme undertaken by a cooperative society with state sanction qualifies as a public purpose under the amended Section 3(f)(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Sections 40 to 42 of the Land Acquisition Act need not be complied with if the acquisition is for a public purpose, even if it benefits a company or cooperative society.
The government is presumed to have applied its mind when issuing a Section 6 declaration, especially after a Section 5A enquiry and review of the report.
Notifications under Sections 4 and 6 are valid if they specify the public purpose and are in the usual form; mere vagueness is not a ground for invalidation.
provisions: Gujarat Unification and Amendment Act 30 of 1965
doctrines: Conclusive presumption of public purpose under Section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act
Doctrine of legislative competence to define public purpose
Presumption that government applies its mind in administrative action
Fraud exception to conclusiveness of public purpose declaration

card.dispute: The sons of a Hindu female challenged the validity of a sale deed executed by her, claiming it was not supported by legal necessity and was induced by undue influence.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deed executed by the Hindu female was supported by legal necessity under the Dayabhaga school of Hindu law
Whether the recitals in the sale deed regarding financial need and debt repayment are sufficient to prove legal necessity
Whether the alienee must prove actual payment of consideration and how burden of proof operates on that issue
Whether the appeal abates due to the death of one of the defendants before the appeal was heard
holdings: A sale by a Hindu widow governed by the Dayabhaga system is valid if supported by legal necessity, which includes serious pressure on the estate, not actual compulsion.
Recitals of legal necessity in a deed are not conclusive but gain significant evidentiary value when the party challenging the sale withholds relevant evidence within their knowledge.

The burden to disprove receipt of consideration lies on the party attacking the deed; absence of direct evidence from the alienee does not invalidate the sale if recitals and witness testimony support payment.
An appeal does not abate due to the death of a non-substantial defendant when no relief was sought against them and the main issue concerns the validity of the alienation.
provisions: Evidence Act, Section 90 (presumption as to documents 30 years old)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22, Rule 4 (abatement of suits on death)
doctrines: Legal necessity in Hindu law
Burden of proof in challenging alienations by limited owners
Evidentiary value of recitals in deeds
Doctrine of constructive res judicata

card.dispute: Rustom Cavasjee Cooper challenged the constitutional validity of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969, which nationalised 14 major Indian banks, arguing that the President's satisfaction for issuing the enabling ordinance was not genuine and that the law violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the President's satisfaction for promulgating an ordinance under Article 123 is subject to judicial review.
Whether the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969, violates the fundamental rights of shareholders under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31.
Whether the lack of disclosure of materials behind the President's satisfaction renders the ordinance or the Act invalid.
Whether the petitioners had locus standi to challenge the acquisition.
holdings: The President's satisfaction under Article 123 is subjective and cannot be questioned in court unless mala fide or bad faith is proven, which was not alleged or established in this case.

The Act violates the fundamental rights of shareholders under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) as it does not provide for compensation and is not supported by a valid law making provision at the time of acquisition.
Non-disclosure of materials forming the basis of the President’s satisfaction does not invalidate the ordinance or the Act, as the Court cannot demand disclosure of executive or state secrets.

The petitioners, as shareholders and depositors, had sufficient locus standi to challenge the law affecting their rights, though the Court ultimately decided the matter on merits without relying on this objection.
provisions: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969, Sections 4, 5, 6, 15(2), and Schedule II
doctrines: Subjective satisfaction of the President under Article 123
Judicial review of executive action limited to mala fide
Violation of fundamental rights under Right to Property
Doctrine of severability and unconstitutionality of acquisition without compensation

card.dispute: The appellants, as Mahant of a religious institution displaced after Partition, claimed land in India in lieu of lands lost in Pakistan, but the allotment was challenged on the ground that the institution could not be re-established in India.
issues_decided: Whether the institution 'Gaddi Kacha Pacca' could be re-established in India for the purpose of land allotment under rehabilitation schemes.
Whether the doctrine of cy-pres applies to the rehabilitation of displaced persons and institutions under the Land Resettlement Manual.
Whether lands recorded in the name of the Mahant as Muafidar were eligible for rehabilitation allotment independently of the institution's status.
holdings: A religious institution of historical nature, like 'Gaddi Kacha Pacca', which is tied to a specific location, cannot be re-established elsewhere and thus does not qualify for land allotment in India.
The doctrine of cy-pres is inapplicable to the statutory scheme of rehabilitation of displaced persons and cannot justify land allotment in lieu of institutional property lost across the border.
The claim for allotment based on personal ownership of land (as Muafidar) was not raised before the High Court and cannot be considered for the first time in appeal.
doctrines: Doctrine of cy-pres
Principle of res judicata and estoppel by record
Finality of findings due to failure to raise arguments at the earliest opportunity

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961, arguing that the state lacked legislative competence to create the Maharashtra Development Corporation and that the Act violated principles of fair compensation and non-discrimination in land acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961 falls within the legislative competence of the State under Entry 24 of the State List or encroaches upon Entry 43 of the Union List as it pertains to a trading corporation.
Whether there is procedural discrimination between land acquisition under the impugned Act and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, particularly in acquiring land for companies.
Whether the proviso to Section 33 of the Act restricts the judicial power of the Collector in determining compensation.
holdings: The pith and substance of the Act relates to industrial development, which falls under Entry 24 of the State List; the Maharashtra Development Corporation is an agency of the State for industrial growth, not a trading corporation, hence the Act is valid.

The Act is a special law with a distinct public purpose—planned industrial development—and does not provide for acquisition of land for private companies; thus, no procedural discrimination exists with the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

The proviso to Section 33 does not fetter the Collector’s judicial function; it merely requires government approval for compensation exceeding a specified amount, with final determination preserved through judicial appeal.
provisions: The Constitution of India, Entry 24 of List II (State List), Entry 43 of List I (Union List)
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine against fettering of judicial power

card.dispute: The appellant, Sheshanna Bhumanna Yadav, challenged his conviction for murder, house-breaking, and theft, arguing lack of corroboration of the approver's evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of the approver was sufficiently corroborated in material particulars against both accused (father and son).
Whether the conviction for murder could be sustained in the absence of direct evidence of actual participation in the killing.
Whether the theft and murder were part of the same transaction, supporting joint liability.
holdings: The evidence of the approver was reliable and sufficiently corroborated by independent evidence connecting both accused with the crime.
Corroboration need not prove the exact act of killing, but must connect the accused with the crime in material particulars, which was satisfied here.
The close temporal and factual connection between the murder and theft established them as parts of a single transaction committed by the same persons.
doctrines: Corroboration of accomplice evidence in material particulars
Doctrine of joint criminal liability in a composite transaction
Reliability test for approver's testimony

card.dispute: The State of Mysore levied an education cess on 'shop-rent', 'tree-tax', and 'tree-rent' collected from excise contractors, who challenged the validity of the levy.
issues_decided: Whether 'shop-rent' constitutes excise revenue under Entry 51 of List II of the Constitution, making it liable to education cess
Whether the State could lawfully levy education cess on 'tree-tax' and 'tree-rent' after they were merged into 'shop-rent'
Whether the expression 'now being levied' in the amended Schedule means 'lawfully being levied'
Whether the State could rely on Entry 62 of List II to levy education cess as a tax on luxuries
holdings: Shop-rent, being a payment for the exclusive privilege of selling toddy and not linked to production or manufacture, is not excise revenue under Entry 51 of List II and cannot be taxed with education cess.

Even if 'tree-tax' and 'tree-rent' were excise revenue, they merged into 'shop-rent' in 1907, and since no lawful education cess was being levied on them before 1955, the State cannot enforce liability for such cess.
The phrase 'now being levied' in the amended Schedule must be read as 'lawfully being levied', and in absence of lawful authority under Article 265, the levy is invalid.
Education cess cannot be sustained under Entry 62 of List II as it is not an independent tax on luxuries but a dependent levy on specific revenues like excise, which 'shop-rent' is not.
provisions: Constitution of India, List II, Entry 8
Constitution of India, List II, Entry 51
Constitution of India, List II, Entry 62
doctrines: No tax without legislative authority (Article 265)
Incidental and subsidiary powers do not include power to tax
Merger of separate levies into a single composite levy
Statutory interpretation of 'now being levied' as 'lawfully being levied'

card.dispute: The State of Orissa and the Union of India fought with Kalinga Construction Co. over whether the company was entitled to additional payment for machine leads, lifts, ramp construction, and interest arising from earthwork at the Hirakud Dam site.
issues_decided: Whether the contract contemplated manual labour only or included use of machinery for earthwork.
Whether the company was entitled to payment for extra leads beyond the contracted average of 10, in the absence of a written order from the Chief Engineer.
Whether the Superintending Engineer's letter (Ext. P-6) could bind the Chief Engineer and allow payment for lifts converted into leads.
Whether the Government was estopped from denying liability for extra payments despite conduct suggesting approval of the work.
holdings: Where a contract requires a written order from a specified authority for extra payment, failure to obtain such order bars the contractor's claim, even if work was performed.

An arbitrator's factual findings based on credible evidence, especially credibility determinations, cannot be overturned in setting aside an award merely because a court might have reached a different conclusion.

A letter issued by a subordinate officer (Superintending Engineer) in the name of a superior (Chief Engineer) does not bind the superior unless authority or ratification is proved; the burden lies on the party asserting such authority.
Courts cannot sit in appeal over an arbitral award under Sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940; they may only interfere if there is an error apparent on the face of the award.
doctrines: Finality of arbitral awards
No appeal on factual findings in arbitration
Error apparent on the face of the award
Estoppel by conduct (discussed but not applied)

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal and the Dalhousie Institute Society disputed over the title to the compensation amount awarded for the land at premises No. 34 Dalhousie Square, which was acquired by the state.
issues_decided: Whether the Dalhousie Institute Society acquired a valid grant of the land from the Government in 1865.
Whether the Society perfected title to the land by adverse possession despite the grant being invalid in law.
holdings: The Government intended to and did make an unconditional grant of the land to the Institute in 1865, as evidenced by official correspondence, and the grant was treated as effective despite lack of formal legal compliance.
The Institute’s open, continuous, and uninterrupted possession for over 60 years under colour of an invalid grant matured into a limited title by adverse possession, entitling it to the compensation.
provisions: West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section II
doctrines: Adverse possession
Title by prescription under colour of title
Government estoppel by conduct

card.dispute: Tea plantation owners challenged the constitutional validity of a uniform tax imposed under the Kerala Plantation (Additional Tax) Act, arguing it violated equality under Article 14 due to unequal incidence across differently productive lands.
issues_decided: Whether the uniform tax on plantations under the impugned Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the method of assessment based on land use without regard to productivity or potential yield constitutes arbitrary classification
Whether the Kerala legislature had the competence to levy such a tax on plantations
holdings: A uniform tax on plantations without rational classification based on productivity or potential yield violates Article 14 by creating unequal burden among similarly situated taxpayers.
The tax is arbitrary and invalid under Article 14 because it is based solely on land use, ignoring factors like soil quality, situation, and yield capacity.
The charging provision of the Kerala Plantation (Additional Tax) Act, as amended, is void to the extent it imposes tax on tea plantations without rational or equitable classification.
provisions: Kerala Plantation (Additional Tax) Act, 1960 (Act 17 of 1960), Section 3
Kerala Plantation (Additional Tax) Amendment Act, 1967 (Act 19 of 1967)
doctrines: Equal protection under Article 14
Test of rational classification in taxation
Prohibition of arbitrary state action under Article 14

card.dispute: The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation sought to recover arrears of municipal taxes from a property purchased at a court auction by Haji Abdulgafur, who claimed he was a transferee without notice and thus not liable.
issues_decided: Whether Section 141(1) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, read with Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, allows enforcement of municipal tax arrears against a transferee for consideration without notice.
Whether the auction purchaser had constructive notice of the arrears of municipal taxes due on the property.
holdings: Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act bars enforcement of a charge against a transferee for consideration without notice, unless a specific law provides otherwise; Section 141(1) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act does not override this protection.

Constructive notice cannot be imputed merely because municipal taxes are a statutory charge; it depends on facts showing wilful abstention or gross negligence, which were absent here given the purchaser’s reasonable reliance on the receivers’ conduct.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 141(1)
doctrines: Constructive notice
Transferee for value without notice
Statutory charge on property

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought with The Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd over whether cess could be levied on coal supplied from the company's colliery to its own factories and the method of profit computation for such cess.
issues_decided: Whether the supply of coal from a colliery to the owner's own factory constitutes a 'sale' for the purpose of computing profits under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880.
Whether the mode of valuation of coal at the controlled rate for cess assessment can be challenged in a civil suit.
holdings: The supply of coal from a colliery to the owner's factory forms part of an integrated process of production, and the profit from mining is embedded in the final product; thus, it is valid to include such supply in profit computation for cess.

The mode of computation of profits under the Act cannot be challenged in a civil suit if the Act provides a finality clause and a specific appellate procedure; the remedy lies within the statutory mechanism, not in court.
doctrines: Finality of statutory assessment orders
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction when adequate statutory remedies exist
Integration of mining and manufacturing as a single economic activity

card.dispute: The Bihar State Board of Religious Trusts sought to enforce accountability under the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act against Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das, who claimed the Kamlabari asthal and its properties as his personal, non-trust estate.
issues_decided: Whether the properties of the Kamlabari asthal constituted a public religious trust under Section 2(1) of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1951
Whether the succession of Mahants from Guru to Chela creates a presumption of a public religious trust
Whether the mode of usage and declarations by Mahants can establish a public religious trust in the absence of a formal deed of dedication
holdings: The onus of proving that properties constitute a public religious trust lies on the Board; failure by the Mahant to produce sanads does not justify an adverse inference that the properties were granted for public religious purposes.

Succession from Guru to Chela in a Mahant lineage does not, by itself, indicate that the properties are religious or charitable trusts; secular character of originally acquired property is not lost due to such succession.

Mere description of properties as 'appertaining to the asthal' or the presence of a temple does not establish a public trust; there must be clear evidence of dedication to public religious or charitable use, which was lacking here.
provisions: Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1951, Section 2(1)
doctrines: Burden of proof in establishing a public religious trust
No presumption of trust from mode of succession
Requirement of clear dedication for public religious trust
Distinction between private and public mutts

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the election of the Chief Minister to the State Legislative Assembly, alleging that his public welfare actions before the election amounted to corrupt practice under the Representation of the People Act.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Order 42, Rule 22 of the Civil Procedure Code apply to appeals under Section 116C of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
Whether the Chief Minister's actions in ordering public works and grants before the election constituted a corrupt practice under Section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
holdings: The Supreme Court can uphold a judgment in favor of a respondent on grounds not upheld by the High Court, even if the respondent has not filed an appeal, as procedural rules under Section 116C allow application of Order 41, Rule 22, CPC.
Mere performance of public welfare acts by a minister-candidate close to elections does not amount to corrupt practice unless there is clear evidence of a quid pro quo to induce votes.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 116C
Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 123(1)
doctrines: Application of civil appellate procedure to election appeals
Distinction between bona fide public acts and corrupt practice in elections
Principle of judicial review of findings of fact when crucial evidence is overlooked

card.dispute: The appellants, former lessees of a plot in Bombay, continued in possession after their lease expired and challenged the lessors' eviction suit, claiming a new tenancy by holding over under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants became tenants by holding over under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act after the lease ended.
Whether acceptance of rent by the landlord after expiry of the lease created a new contractual tenancy.
Whether the statutory protection under the Bombay Rents Act prevented the creation of a tenancy by holding over.
holdings: Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply where a tenant remains in possession due to statutory protection, not the landlord's assent.
Acceptance of rent by a landlord under a Rent Control Act does not imply agreement to a new tenancy if the tenant stays due to statutory rights.
A tenancy by holding over requires mutual intention; mere payment and acceptance of rent under a Rent Act does not establish such intention.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 13(1)
doctrines: Tenancy by holding over
Statutory tenancy vs. contractual tenancy
Consensus ad idem in contract formation
Interplay between rent control statutes and common law tenancies

card.dispute: The Bombay Panjrapole, a charitable institution for animal care, contested whether its activities constituted an 'industry' under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, after its workers raised a dispute over wages and service benefits.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Panjrapole's activities fall within the definition of 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
Whether commercial activities like milk production and sale transform a charitable animal welfare institution into an 'industry'
holdings: An institution originally established for charitable purposes can become an 'industry' if its activities evolve into systematic economic production, such as large-scale milk sales.

The commercial scale of milk production and use of stud bulls for breeding to maintain milk supply indicates an undertaking analogous to trade or business, bringing it within Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act.
doctrines: Test of 'industry' under Section 2(j) based on functional activity rather than institutional purpose
Doctrine of evolution of character: an institution's legal classification may change with its economic activities

card.dispute: The appellant Balakrushna Swain challenged his conviction for murder and life sentence, arguing that the eyewitness testimony was unreliable and contradictory.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of the appellant for murder could be sustained based on the eyewitness testimony.
Whether contradictions and improvements in the statements of key prosecution witnesses affected the reliability of their evidence.
Whether the use of deposition under Section 288 of the CrPC after the close of prosecution evidence was properly considered by the High Court.
Whether the circumstantial details indicated fabrication or collusion among witnesses.
holdings: The conviction cannot be sustained if the eyewitness testimony contains material contradictions and shows signs of being tailored or fabricated.
Where a witness changes material aspects of their statement between committal and trial court, and fails to explain the discrepancy, their testimony becomes unreliable.
It is unsafe to base a conviction on evidence that appears to be the result of confabulation or consultation among witnesses after the incident.
The presence of suspicious circumstances, such as delayed examination of witnesses and unnatural conduct at the scene, raises doubt about the prosecution's version.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Improvement in testimony
Corroboration of material evidence

card.dispute: The appellant claimed permanent lease rights and easements of light, air, and passage over a strip of land adjacent to his leased property, which the respondent disputed.
issues_decided: Whether the lease deed created a permanent lease and included the disputed strip of land
Whether the appellant acquired easementary rights by prescription over the strip of land for light, air, and passage
Whether the obstruction to light and air amounted to substantial damage justifying a suit under the Easements Act
holdings: The lease did not extend to the disputed strip of land, and the appellant’s own conduct, including property descriptions in transfer deeds, negated inclusion of the strip in the lease.
Easement by prescription cannot be claimed where the use was permissive or under a claim of ownership, as there is no hostile, continuous, and uninterrupted use for 20 years.
An obstruction to light or air is actionable only if it causes substantial damage, such as materially diminishing the value of the property or affecting physical comfort, which was not proven here.
doctrines: Easement by prescription requires hostile, continuous, and uninterrupted use for 20 years
Permissive use cannot form the basis of a prescriptive easement
Substantial damage is required to maintain a suit for disturbance of easement under Section 33
A party who claims ownership of land cannot later claim an easement over the same land by prescription

card.dispute: The dispute was between rival claimants to the Dhanora Zamindari and associated malguzari lands, involving questions of succession, proprietary rights, and entitlement to compensation under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether the zamindari devolves on the eldest male in the senior line or the nearest male relative by age under the rule of primogeniture
Whether the Governor's order conferring the zamindari on one claimant bars civil court jurisdiction over succession
Whether the Compensation Officer's order under Section 14 of the Act determining entitlement to compensation is final and binding in the absence of a timely suit
holdings: The expression 'nearest male relative' in the Wajib-ul-arz refers to propinquity of blood, not seniority by age; succession follows lineal primogeniture, not mere age.
Orders by the Governor or revenue authorities do not bar the civil court's jurisdiction to decide questions of kinship and succession to zamindari rights.

Section 14 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act allows the Compensation Officer to decide only proprietary rights qua the State, not competing private claims; such orders are not conclusive if no suit is filed within two months, and civil courts can adjudicate title.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, Section 14
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, Section 35(7)
doctrines: Primogeniture in zamindari succession
Civil court jurisdiction not ousted by executive or revenue orders
Summary adjudication under compensation statutes does not bar due process of law for title disputes

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of the Andhra Pradesh (Krishna and Godavari Delta Area) Drainage Cess Act, 1968, which imposed a cess on delta lands for flood and drainage control.
issues_decided: Whether the Act violates Article 14 by treating unequals equally within the delta area.
Whether the right of appeal under Section 5 of the Act is illusory.
Whether the Act involves excessive delegation of legislative power by not prescribing a minimum cess rate.
holdings: The classification of lands in the delta area for cess imposition is reasonable and based on intelligible differentia, and does not violate Article 14, as the flood and drainage issues vary across regions and equal burden per acre within a division is justified.
The right of appeal under Section 5 is not illusory, as it allows aggrieved persons to challenge the area or ownership basis of the cess, even if the rate is fixed by notification.
There is no excessive delegation of legislative power, as the Act prescribes a maximum cess rate and links the rate to the cost of drainage schemes, providing sufficient legislative guidance.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Krishna and Godavari Delta Area) Drainage Cess Act, 1968, Section 3
Andhra Pradesh (Krishna and Godavari Delta Area) Drainage Cess Act, 1968, Section 4
Andhra Pradesh (Krishna and Godavari Delta Area) Drainage Cess Act, 1968, Section 5
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Presumption of constitutionality
Doctrine of non-excessive delegation with guidelines

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued for possession of properties based on a sale deed from the first defendant, while the second defendant contested ownership, claiming the properties were his after a family partition.
issues_decided: Whether the suit properties fell to the share of the first defendant or the second defendant in a family partition.
Whether the sale deed executed by the first defendant in favor of the plaintiffs was genuine and validly proved despite the loss of original records.
Whether the second defendant was estopped or his admission in a written agreement could be used to establish the plaintiffs' title.
holdings: The suit properties fell to the first defendant’s share in the partition, as conclusively admitted by the second defendant in a written agreement.
The sale deed was proved through secondary evidence, including an official extract and witness testimony, satisfying the requirements of the Evidence Act despite destruction of original records.

The admission by the second defendant in a written agreement that the first defendant owned and sold the properties is binding evidence, though not creating estoppel, and supports the plaintiffs' title.
doctrines: Admission as evidence
Secondary evidence in case of lost documents
Partition in joint family property

card.dispute: The landlords (plaintiffs) sought to enforce a lease clause giving them the option to buy buildings erected by the tenant on leased land, which the tenant refused, citing protection under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921.
issues_decided: Whether clause 4(d) of the lease deed, granting the lessor an option to purchase the buildings, could be enforced despite the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, as amended in 1955
Whether the stipulations in the lease deed fell within the proviso to Section 12 of the Act, allowing written and registered agreements regarding building erection to override statutory protections
holdings: The stipulations in the lease deed, particularly clause 4(d), constitute a valid written and registered agreement as to the erection of buildings, and thus fall within the proviso to Section 12 of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921.

The tenant cannot claim statutory protection under the Act to defeat the landlord's contractual right to purchase the buildings, as the Act does not protect rights created contrary to express written stipulations regarding building erection.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 12 (proviso)
doctrines: Contractual stipulations as to building erection override statutory tenant protections if in writing and registered
Statutory protection does not extend to tenants who have contracted out of rights through express lease terms

card.dispute: The tenant-firm sought special leave to appeal a eviction order for non-payment of rent, claiming a conflict between High Courts on the interpretation of the Bombay Rents Act, while the landlord moved to revoke the leave alleging the Court was misled.
issues_decided: Whether the special leave to appeal should be revoked on grounds of misrepresentation or suppression of facts
Whether the petitioners made false or misleading averments about the High Court being apprised of a conflicting decision
holdings: Special leave to appeal will not be revoked unless there is a deliberate misstatement of material facts or suppression intended to mislead the Court.

Mere legal contentions highlighting a conflict between High Courts, even if they create an impression that a decision was brought to the lower court's attention, do not constitute false or misleading statements if factually accurate in substance.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Judicial discretion in granting special leave under Article 136
Principle against misstatement or suppression of material facts in special leave petitions

card.dispute: The descendants of Bhakats and the heirs of the original grantee fought over whether land granted by an Ahom King was a Dharmottar (religious endowment) or a personal Brahmottar grant, and whether the suit was maintainable without complying with Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was maintainable without compliance with Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the land grant was a Dharmottar (charitable/religious trust) or a personal Brahmottar grant
holdings: A suit seeking declarations about religious rights and possession tied to a religious institution does not require compliance with Section 92 CPC unless it specifically seeks reliefs like appointment of trustees or directions for trust administration.

The use of the term 'Brahmottar' in the grant does not conclusively make it a personal grant; the grant was for religious purposes and intended to benefit the institution, thus having the character of a Dharmottar.
provisions: Assam Land and Revenue Regulations, Regulation 1 of 1886
doctrines: Section 92 CPC applies only to suits involving public religious or charitable trusts seeking specific reliefs for trust administration
Substance over form in determining the nature of a grant: the purpose and conditions of the grant determine whether it is a personal or religious endowment

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, sons of a deceased Hindu father, disputed over partition of the father's estate, including whether the appellant had separated from the family and whether certain deposits were gifted to one son.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had separated from the joint family before the father's death
Whether fixed deposits in the father's name were gifted to the first respondent
Whether a cheque and deposit in favour of the daughter-in-law constituted a valid gift
holdings: Mere emotional disagreements or expressions of disinterest do not prove separation from a Hindu joint family; a clear and communicated intention is required.
Transferring fixed deposits to joint names does not amount to a gift in favour of the son unless there is clear evidence of the father's intention to make an irrevocable gift during his lifetime.
A gift to a daughter-in-law was validly proved by the father's conduct, including depositing money in her name and handing over the receipt, showing clear intention to benefit her.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, Section 123 (for gifts of immovable property)
doctrines: Presumption of jointness in Hindu families
Requirement of clear intention for separation from joint family
No presumption of advancement in Indian law
Resulting trust in absence of proven gift intention

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of the Madras Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, after it was revived via inclusion in the Ninth Schedule, arguing it was void ab initio and beyond state legislative competence.
issues_decided: Whether Article 31-B of the Constitution can validate a law previously struck down as unconstitutional with retrospective effect
Whether the Madras Land Reforms Act, 1961, falls within the legislative competence of the State Legislature under Entry 18, List II, and Entry 42, List III of the Seventh Schedule
holdings: Article 31-B, as amended by the Seventeenth Amendment, validates laws included in the Ninth Schedule from their original enactment date, curing any prior unconstitutionality on grounds of fundamental rights.

Entry 18 of List II, read with Entry 42 of List III, empowers state legislatures to enact land ceiling and agrarian reform laws to implement Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c), including acquisition of surplus land with compensation.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 18
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 42
Madras Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961
doctrines: Doctrine of curative validation by constitutional amendment
Pith and substance doctrine
Liberal interpretation of legislative entries
Principle of retrospective validation under Article 31-B

card.dispute: The company claimed deductions for road, public works, and education cesses paid under Bengal Acts, but the tax authorities disallowed them under s. 10(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, leading to a dispute over whether these cesses were based on business profits.
issues_decided: Whether the Road and Public Works Cess under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880, and the Education Cess under the Bengal (Rural) Primary Education Act, 1930, fall within the scope of s. 10(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1922.

Whether cesses assessed on 'annual net profits' determined under separate statutes can be considered as assessed 'on the basis of profits and gains' as defined under s. 10 of the Income Tax Act, 1922.
holdings: The phrase 'profits and gains of any business, profession, or vocation' in s. 10(4) refers only to profits determined under s. 10 of the Income Tax Act, not to profits computed under other laws.

Cesses assessed under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880, and the Bengal (Rural) Primary Education Act, 1930, based on net profits calculated independently, do not fall within s. 10(4) and are allowable deductions under s. 10(2)(ix) or (xv).
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Distinction between tax based on profits and tax merely correlated with profits
Precedent of Privy Council in Commissioner of Income Tax, Bengal v. Gurupada Dutta

card.dispute: The tenant and landlord disputed whether the tenant was entitled to protection under the U.P. Rent Control Act after reconstructing the building post-1951, despite an agreement to apply the Act.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can waive the benefit of Section 1A of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, which exempts buildings constructed after January 1, 1951, from the Act's applicability.
Whether an agreement between landlord and tenant to apply the Rent Control Act despite Section 1A is void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
holdings: A landlord may waive the benefit of Section 1A of the U.P. Rent Control Act, as it is a personal benefit and not against public policy to do so.

An agreement to apply the Rent Control Act despite Section 1A is not void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, as its performance does not require violation of law or contravention of public policy.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 1A
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
doctrines: Waiver of statutory benefit for personal advantage
Public policy exception to contractual validity
Cuilibet licet renuntiare juri pro se introducto

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the state's acquisition of their land for setting up a factory, arguing lack of public purpose, urgency, and improper use of land acquisition provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition was for a public purpose and not merely for the benefit of a company
Whether the urgency clause under Section 17(2)(c) of the Land Acquisition Act was validly invoked
Whether Section 17(2)(c) should be interpreted narrowly using the ejusdem generis rule in light of clauses (a) and (b)
holdings: Acquisition for establishing an industry serves a public purpose if it benefits the public at large, even if a company operates it.
The appropriate government's opinion on urgent public importance is sufficient to invoke Section 17(2)(c), and courts will not second-guess it absent mala fides.
Section 17(2)(c) is not subject to the ejusdem generis rule because clauses (a), (b), and (c) involve different authorities, conditions, and purposes, and do not form a distinct class.
doctrines: Ejusdem Generis
Presumption of Public Purpose in Industrial Development
Deference to Government Opinion in Urgency Determinations

card.dispute: The heirs of Nagappa Setty sued for partition of family properties, claiming entitlement under a will or family arrangement, while the other family members contested the validity of the will and the nature of the business carried on after 1940.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated 1st January 1933 was valid and effective to confer a 4-anna share on Nagappa Setty
Whether the arbitration agreement of 11th July 1940 amounted to a partition of the joint family business
Whether the defendants were liable to account for profits and acquisitions from the business run after 1940
What properties and assets should be included in the partition and how accounts should be settled
holdings: The will was not validly executed and did not operate to create a 4-anna share in favor of Nagappa Setty, nor did it constitute a binding family arrangement.
The arbitration agreement of 11th July 1940 did not amount to a formal partition but marked the severance of joint status, leading to separate businesses being carried on by the parties.
After severance of joint status, each party's business became their separate venture; thus, no party is entitled to claim a share in the profits or acquisitions of the other's business.

Joint family properties for partition include all movable and immovable assets as of 11th July 1940; parties must account for rents, profits, and dividends from family assets in their possession, but not from their separate businesses.
provisions: Hindu Law (as applicable to joint family and partition)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 (for execution and decree clarification)
doctrines: Severance of joint family status
Tenancy in common after partition
No trust presumption on funds after severance
Family arrangement and validity of will under Hindu Law

card.dispute: The appellants, Madhusudan Gordhandas & Co., sought to wind up Madhu Woollen Industries Pvt. Ltd. on grounds of insolvency and disputed debts, while the company resisted, asserting bona fide disputes and a viable future business plan.
issues_decided: Whether the company was unable to pay its debts within the meaning of Section 433(c) of the Companies Act, 1956.
Whether there was a bona fide dispute regarding the debts claimed by the appellants.
Whether the substratum of the company had disappeared, justifying winding up.
Whether the petition for winding up was an abuse of the court's process due to improper motive.
holdings: A winding-up order is not justified if there is a bona fide and substantial dispute over the debt, especially where the company provides prima facie proof supporting its defence.
The court will not order winding up if creditors, representing a significant portion of debt, oppose the petition and the company shows a reasonable prospect of continuing business.
The mere existence of losses or sale of assets does not mean the substratum of the company is gone; the company must have abandoned its objects, which was not proved here.
A winding-up petition may be dismissed as an abuse of process if it is filed with an improper motive, such as to coerce settlement of disputed claims.
doctrines: Bona fide dispute doctrine in winding-up petitions
Doctrine of substratum disappearance
Abuse of process in creditor petitions
Creditors' wishes in winding-up discretion

card.dispute: The landlord (Sain Das Berry) sought eviction of the tenant (Madan Lal Puri) on grounds of bonafide personal requirement, which the tenant challenged based on concurrent findings against such requirement by lower authorities.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 39(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, to interfere with concurrent findings of the Rent Controller and Rent Control Tribunal on the landlord's bonafide requirement?
Whether a finding on the bonafide requirement of a landlord under Section 14(1)(e) is a question of fact or a mixed question of law and fact?
holdings: The High Court has jurisdiction under Section 39(2) to consider the correctness of findings on bonafide requirement if it involves a substantial question of law.
A finding on whether a landlord's requirement is bonafide under Section 14(1)(e) is a mixed question of law and fact, not purely factual, and thus subject to review by the High Court.
doctrines: Mixed question of law and fact
Substantial question of law in second appeal

card.dispute: Mohan Lal (appellant) fought with Anandibai and others (respondents), the daughters of Bhiwa, over ownership and possession of property allegedly sold by Bhiwa to Mohan Lal, which the respondents claimed they already owned via gift deeds.
issues_decided: Whether the gift deed (Ext. P-3) executed by Bhiwa in favor of the respondents was fraudulent and invalid?
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the lower courts' findings on fraud and antedating of the gift deed despite lack of pleadings?
Whether the appellant should be allowed to amend his written statement to include pleas of fraud and antedating at a late stage?
holdings: The gift deed (Ext. P-3) executed by Bhiwa was not proved to be fraudulent, and the respondents acquired title through it, making prior title claims unnecessary to decide.

The High Court was justified in setting aside the lower courts' findings on fraud and antedating because those issues were not properly pleaded or tried, and parties were unaware they would be decided.
The appellant cannot be permitted to amend his written statement at a late stage to raise new pleas of fraud and antedating, as they constitute a new cause of action and would be time-barred.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI, Rule 17 (Amendment of Pleadings)
Limitation Act, 1963, Article 58 (For suits relating to immovable property)
doctrines: Res judicata
Amendment of pleadings to allow new case
Principle of fair trial and proper pleading

card.dispute: The appellant, as attorney for Mahant Santosh Dass, filed a criminal complaint alleging trespass and theft by the respondents who managed a Gurdwara, claiming they destroyed an orchard on land owned by his principal; the respondents sought discharge from prosecution, asserting the dispute was essentially civil over title.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in discharging the accused under Section 253(2) of the CrPC on the ground that the dispute was civil in nature and related to title?
Whether a criminal court can proceed with prosecution for offences of criminal trespass and mischief despite a pending civil dispute over title to the land?
Whether the Magistrate must discharge accused persons if a civil court has previously ruled against the complainant on title?
holdings: A criminal court is concerned with possession and alleged criminal acts, not title, which is to be decided by civil courts; the existence of a civil dispute does not bar criminal prosecution for trespass or mischief.
If the allegations in the complaint are true, they disclose cognizable offences under IPC; the question of whether they are proved is for trial, not grounds for discharge at the preliminary stage.

The High Court erred in discharging the accused under Section 253(2) CrPC merely because a civil court had dismissed a suit related to title; criminal liability depends on possession and conduct, not title.
doctrines: Separation of civil and criminal jurisdiction
Prima facie case in criminal prosecution
Possession vs. title in criminal trespass cases

card.dispute: The appellant, Karmi, claimed ownership of properties under a will by Nihali, while respondents Amru and Bhagtu claimed under a prior will of Jaimal, Nihali's husband, leading to a dispute over rightful succession.
issues_decided: Whether Nihali inherited the properties under Jaimal's 1937 will or as his heir by operation of law
Whether Nihali could pass absolute title to the appellant via her own will
holdings: Nihali acquired the properties under Jaimal's valid 1937 will, which granted her only a life estate, not absolute ownership.
A life estate under a will cannot transform into absolute ownership under the Hindu Succession Act, so Nihali could not bequeath the property by will.
doctrines: Doctrine of testamentary succession
Life estate cannot ripen into absolute estate under Hindu Succession Act

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay fought with private plot owners (Advance Builders) over whether the Corporation was legally obligated to remove unauthorized huts from private plots under a town planning scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Corporation had a statutory duty to remove unauthorized structures from private plots under the Bombay Town Planning Scheme, 1954
Whether the respondents were disqualified from seeking a writ of mandamus due to collecting rent from hut occupants
holdings: The Corporation, as the local authority, had an exclusive and non-discretionary duty under the Town Planning Act, 1954 to implement the scheme, including removing unauthorized structures from private plots.
Mere collection of rent or compensation by plot owners from hut occupants does not disqualify them from seeking mandamus, as they have no statutory duty to remove such structures themselves.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Sections 88, 89, 90, 165
doctrines: Mandamus to enforce statutory duty
Statutory duty as non-discretionary function
Clean hands doctrine in writ petitions

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents contested entitlement to compensation for acquired land, with appellants claiming res judicata from a prior acquisition proceeding where the respondent's predecessor's claim was dismissed for default.
issues_decided: Whether the earlier decision in land acquisition proceedings, where a claim was dismissed for default, operates as res judicata in a subsequent proceeding involving the same title?
Whether a decision not contested or heard on merits can constitute a final adjudication for the purpose of res judicata?
holdings: A decision in land acquisition proceedings dismissed for default without contest or hearing on merits does not operate as res judicata, even if the same title is involved in a later proceeding.

For res judicata to apply, the prior decision must have been on merits after a full contest; a dismissal in appeal on preliminary grounds confirms a merits-based trial decision, but a default dismissal at first instance does not.
doctrines: Res judicata
Identity of title test in res judicata
Finality of decisions on merits

card.dispute: The appellant Ram Gopal was convicted of murdering Zingrooji Sita Ram by poisoning and challenged the conviction, arguing that the evidence was insufficient.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant administered poison to the deceased in a cup of tea?
Whether the conduct of the appellant after the collapse of the deceased amounted to an incriminating circumstance?
Whether the forensic and circumstantial evidence supported the conviction for murder?
holdings: The testimony of eyewitnesses regarding the administration of poisoned tea was inconsistent and unreliable, and therefore could not form the basis of a conviction.
The appellant's conduct after the incident, including his phone call to the police, did not constitute an admission of guilt, especially in light of the unproven allegations.
The absence of physical evidence, such as the alleged cup or traces of poison in the tumbler, and contradictions in oral testimony rendered the prosecution's case unproven.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The appellants, recorded as Sir Khudkasht holders, contested the adhivasi status of respondents recorded as subtenants in 1356 Fasli, claiming the entries were fictitious, while consolidation authorities upheld the respondents' adhivasi rights under the Zamindari Act.
issues_decided: Whether a fictitious entry in revenue records in 1356 Fasli can confer adhivasi rights under Section 20(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951
Whether the Allahabad High Court's interpretation of Section 20(b) as ignoring the fictitious nature of entries is still good law
Whether the appeal abated due to non-joinder of a legal representative of a deceased party
