holdings: The Supreme Court may depart from concurrent findings of fact if there are exceptional circumstances showing a serious miscarriage of justice.
The prosecution failed to prove the murder charge beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts, lack of forensic corroboration, and unexplained gaps in evidence.
Absconding or failure to surrender, without more, does not establish guilt, nor does family inaction amount to an admission of culpability.
When material contradictions and omissions undermine the prosecution’s case, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt, warranting acquittal.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Rejection of unsafe eyewitness testimony
Prohibition of using Section 162 statements to circumvent procedural bars
Insufficiency of mere suspicious circumstances to prove guilt

card.dispute: Landlords fought with tenants over eviction for unauthorized commercial use of residential property leased under restrictions from the Delhi Improvement Trust.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord is estopped from seeking eviction when they themselves permitted commercial use of the property in violation of lease terms?
Whether the lease becomes void ab initio if the property is used for unauthorized commercial purposes?

Whether the Controller under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1952 must choose between eviction or compensation under Section 14(11), and can award compensation without the Development Authority's presence?
Whether Section 14 of the Delhi Development Act applies to enforce restrictions on land use in this case?
holdings: A landlord is not estopped from seeking eviction even if they permitted commercial use, as there can be no estoppel against a statute.
A lease is not void in inception merely because the property is used for unauthorized commercial purposes contrary to the land lease conditions.
The Controller must choose one of the two alternatives under Section 14(11): eviction or compensation, but compensation cannot be awarded in the absence of the Delhi Development Authority.
Section 14 of the Delhi Development Act does not apply to enforce lease conditions; the relevant restrictions arise from the Improvement Trust’s lease, not that Act.
provisions: The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 14
doctrines: No estoppel against statute
Statutory interpretation to give effect to legislative intent
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Lease not void for unauthorized use unless expressly provided

card.dispute: The dispute was between the successors of Aswini Kumar Mandal and Fani Bhushan Kundu over title and possession of 10 Cottahs of land in Howrah, following conflicting claims based on court auctions and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the land in question was agricultural land governed by the Bengal Tenancy Act or 'Niskar' homestead land exempt from it.
Whether the landlords could validly file a rent suit against Purshottam Sonar and sell the property in execution despite Shewpujan's earlier purchase in a mortgage auction in 1932.
Whether Fani Bhushan Kundu acquired valid title through the court auction in the rent suit, and whether Aswini Kumar Mandal’s subsequent purchase from Shewpujan could override that title.
Whether the suit by Aswini Kumar was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act.
holdings: The land was agricultural ('Danga Paratan Patit') and subject to the Bengal Tenancy Act, as evidenced by its classification and rent entry in the record of rights.

Despite Shewpujan's 1932 auction purchase, his failure to mutate his name in the landlord's Sherista meant Purshottam Sonar remained the recognized representative of the holding, enabling the rent suit and sale.
Fani Bhushan acquired valid title through the 1946 court auction in the rent suit; Aswini Kumar’s 1949 purchase from Shewpujan conveyed no title as neither Shewpujan nor Aswini Kumar had possession.
The suit was barred by limitation because neither Aswini Kumar nor his predecessor was in possession within 12 years before the suit, and no title was established.
doctrines: Presumptive validity of record of rights under tenancy law
Requirement of mutation for recognition as tenant under the Bengal Tenancy Act
Title by adverse possession
Limitation based on possession under the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The dispute was between family members over whether a male member of an Aliyasantana joint family, who had claimed partition, could dispose of his interest in the family property by will or whether that interest could devolve by intestate succession.
issues_decided: Whether a male member of an aliyasantana kavaru who has claimed partition retains an undivided interest in the joint family property under Section 7(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether such a member's interest in the property can be disposed of by will under Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 enlarged the life interest of a male member under Aliyasantana law into an absolute interest
holdings: A demand for partition by a member of an aliyasantana kavaru disrupts the jointness, and such a member ceases to have an undivided interest in the property, thus falling outside the scope of Section 7(2) of the Hindu Succession Act.

Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act allows testamentary disposition only of an undivided interest in a kutumba or kavaru; once partition is claimed and jointness ends, the interest is no longer capable of being bequeathed by will.

The Hindu Succession Act does not convert a male member's life interest under Aliyasantana law into an absolute interest; such an interest remains non-heritable and cannot devolve by intestacy or be disposed of by will.
doctrines: Survivorship in matriarchal joint families under Aliyasantana law
Doctrine of severance of status by partition in joint family property
Principle that statutory succession overrides customary law where inconsistent
Doctrine of limited interest not being heritable or testamentary unless expressly enlarged by statute

card.dispute: The cooperative dairy farm appealed against an arbitral award that dismissed its claims and ordered it to return government land, challenging the arbitrator's conduct and interpretation of the agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator misconducted the proceedings by refusing to admit certain documents on grounds of privilege
Whether the arbitrator had jurisdiction to decide on the return of government land used by the appellant
Whether the arbitrator's interpretation of the agreement dated 6-5-1953 was correct, particularly the term 'provisional' regarding cattle cost
Whether the appellant waived its right to object to the arbitrator's ruling on privilege
holdings: The arbitrator did not misconduct the proceedings in ruling on document privilege, as the award was not affected by the exclusion of those documents.
The arbitrator had jurisdiction to decide on the return of land, as the appellant itself raised the issue of land transfer in its claim.
The term 'provisional' in the agreement did not entitle the appellant to claim depreciation benefits, as the final cost could be higher and the appellant had acknowledged the uncertainty.
The appellant waived its right to challenge the privilege ruling by not raising a timely objection during the arbitration proceedings.
doctrines: Waiver of procedural objections in arbitration
Arbitrator's authority to interpret contracts as a question of law
Presumption against a party benefiting from its own delay or afterthought arguments

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Jaydayal Poddar contested the ownership of a property, claiming it was benami in the name of Hakimunnissa, while Bibi Hazra (Hakimunnissa's daughter) asserted her mother was the real owner.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction in which Hakimunnissa purchased the property was a benami transaction in favor of her husband Abdul Karim
Whether the burden of proving the benami nature of the transaction was discharged by the plaintiffs
Whether previous judicial findings in execution proceedings could be treated as conclusive proof of a benami transaction
holdings: The burden of proving a transaction is benami lies on the person asserting it and must be discharged by definite and legal evidence, not conjecture.
The source of purchase money is the most important factor in determining a benami transaction, and here, the preponderance of probability indicated Hakimunnissa provided the funds.
A finding in earlier execution proceedings that a transaction is benami is not conclusive if not res judicata and can be outweighed by stronger evidence on the overall circumstances.
Joint possession, role in negotiations, and custody of title deeds by the husband do not negate the wife’s ownership where she is a pardanashin woman and acting through her husband as agent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 57
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 103
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Burden of proof in benami cases
Res judicata
Presumption of agency in favor of pardanashin women

card.dispute: The appellant co-sharer claimed bhumidhari rights in joint property under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, 1950, against respondents who were in exclusive possession but had not pleaded ouster.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could claim rights under s. 18(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, despite not being in physical possession of the land.
Whether possession by one co-sharer can be deemed possession on behalf of all co-sharers in the absence of a plea of ouster.
Whether the terms 'held' and 'deemed to be held' in s. 18(1)(a) include constructive possession or require actual cultivation.
holdings: Under s. 18(1)(a), lands in constructive possession of a co-sharer are covered if no ouster is pleaded, as possession by one co-sharer benefits all.
The term 'possession' in s. 18(1)(a) includes constructive possession, not merely physical or cultivatory possession.
The expressions 'held' and 'deemed to be held' refer to legal title or right, not actual cultivation, and thus co-sharers with declared rights are entitled to bhumidhari status.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 18(1)(a)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 9
doctrines: Constructive possession of co-sharers
Fiction of deemed holding
Lawful possession includes legal title, not mere physical control

card.dispute: The daughter claimed a half share in her father's property based on a special custom of patnibhagam allowing daughters to inherit, against her half-brother and others who opposed it.
issues_decided: Whether a special custom of patnibhagam allowing daughters to inherit was proved in the Krishnanwaka community.
Whether prior judicial decisions can establish a custom without evidence being adduced in those cases.
Whether a custom becomes part of general law so as to shift the burden of proof under Section 57(1) of the Evidence Act.
holdings: A custom becomes part of general law only if established by a series of decisions each based on evidence; otherwise, it must be specifically proved in each case.
A single judicial observation, not based on evidence or necessary for the decision, cannot establish a binding custom.
The special form of patnibhagam allowing daughters to inherit was not proved, as the relied-upon decisions did not rest on evidentiary findings.
doctrines: Proof of custom in Hindu law
Judicial recognition of custom as part of general law
Burden of proof under Section 57(1) of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The landlord filed for eviction on grounds of bonafide requirement, and after a compromise decree, the tenant challenged the court's jurisdiction to pass an eviction order without independently verifying the landlord's bonafide need.
issues_decided: Whether a court can pass an eviction order based solely on a compromise decree without making independent findings on the jurisdictional fact of the landlord's bonafide requirement under Section 10(3)(a)(i) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
Whether the court must independently satisfy itself about the existence of statutory grounds for eviction even when the tenant consents or compromises.
holdings: An eviction order based on a compromise is valid if the statutory grounds for eviction existed at the time of the order and sufficient material was before the court to justify its satisfaction.

The court need not make explicit judicial findings if it had applied its mind to the facts and the tenant’s consent implied admission of the landlord’s statutory ground, provided there is no dispute and the compromise is not contrary to the Act.
provisions: Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(i)
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Judicial satisfaction in rent control proceedings
Validity of consent decrees in statutory eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The petitioner, a religious leader, challenged land reform laws and constitutional amendments that affected his property rights, arguing they violated fundamental rights, while the state defended the amendments as valid exercises of parliamentary power.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament has unlimited power to amend the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights under Article 368
Whether the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments are valid
Whether judicial review of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule is permissible
Whether the 'basic structure' of the Constitution can be amended
holdings: Parliament has wide but not unlimited power to amend the Constitution; it cannot alter its basic structure or essential features.
The 24th Amendment is valid as it merely clarifies Parliament's pre-existing power to amend the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
Section 3 of the 25th Amendment, which introduced Article 31C, is valid but subject to judicial review to ensure a law has a direct nexus with Directive Principles in Article 39(b) or (c).
Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule via the 29th Amendment are protected from judicial review under Articles 14, 19, and 31, but not if they violate the Constitution's basic structure.
doctrines: Basic Structure Doctrine
Parliamentary Sovereignty vs Constitutional Supremacy
Judicial Review
Doctrine of Prospective Overruling

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant, alleging she had sublet the shop premises to her partner Sohan Singh, while the tenant claimed they were living as husband and wife and no subletting occurred.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's status as the legally married wife of Sohan Singh was a necessary finding in the eviction proceeding.
Whether the finding of subletting involved a substantial question of law warranting interference in second appeal.
holdings: In an eviction proceeding under the Delhi Rent Control Act, it is sufficient to determine whether the tenant and another person are living as husband and wife; a formal finding on legal marriage is not required.

The question of whether subletting occurred, based on cohabitation and joint business operation, is a factual inference and not a mixed question of law and fact, so it does not justify High Court interference in second appeal.
doctrines: Onus of proof in subletting cases lies on the landlord
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts not to be disturbed in second appeal without substantial question of law
Distinction between questions of fact, mixed questions of law and fact

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) challenged the renewal of a cinema licence in favour of the tenant (respondent) who continued in possession after the lease expired.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant, whose lease has expired and who is not protected under rent control laws, can be said to be in 'lawful possession' under Rule 13 of the Madras Cinemas (Regulations) Rules, 1957?
Whether the licensing authority could renew the cinema licence in favour of such a tenant?
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to interfere under Article 226 of the Constitution with the Board of Revenue's reversal of the licensing authority's order?
holdings: A non-statutory tenant cannot be in 'lawful possession' of the property after the lease expires and the landlord has not consented to continued possession.
Rule 13 of the Madras Cinemas (Regulations) Rules, 1957 requires documentary evidence of lawful possession, which an ex-lessee without statutory protection cannot provide.
The Board of Revenue was correct in overturning the licence renewal; the High Court should not have declined to interfere under Article 226 as there was no manifest error of law.
provisions: Madras Cinemas (Regulations) Act, 1955, Section 5(1), Section 5(7), Section 5(5)(a)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
doctrines: Lawful possession requires a legal right or juridical relationship, not merely physical control or protection against forcible dispossession
Distinction between juridical possession and lawful possession
No interference under Article 226 in absence of manifest error of law

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether, upon default in payment, the respondents were entitled to regain both possession and title to the property, and whether the arbitral award was executable.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' default in payment entitled the respondents to regain both possession and title to the property
Whether the arbitral award was merely declaratory and thus inexecutable
Whether the clause allowing respondents to retake possession was penal and unenforceable
holdings: Default by the appellants in discharging their obligations under the award resulted in both possession and title to the property passing to the respondents, as the award created a conditional transfer enforceable upon breach.
The award was executable because it clearly intended to confer enforceable rights, not merely declare them, and the decree based on it was binding like a consent decree.
The clause allowing repossession upon default was not penal but a legitimate condition tied to the transfer of rights, and could be enforced in execution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXIII, Rule 3
doctrines: Privity of contract
Executability of arbitral awards
Conditional transfer of title
Penal clause doctrine

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell a house, after the defendant sold it to third parties, with the defendant claiming the agreement was obtained by misrepresentation or unfair advantage.
issues_decided: Whether the presumption under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, that specific performance is the proper remedy for breach of a contract to sell immovable property, is rebutted by a clause stipulating liquidated damages.
Whether the bar under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, against specific performance when damages are adequate, applies automatically if the presumption under Section 12 is rebutted.
Whether the trial court properly exercised its discretion in refusing specific performance on grounds of 'unfair advantage'.
holdings: A stipulation for payment of liquidated damages does not, by itself, rebut the presumption under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877; it is merely one factor to consider in determining whether specific performance is appropriate.

The bar under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, does not automatically apply even if the presumption under Section 12 is rebutted; the court must still determine on facts whether monetary compensation is adequate.
The trial court erred in refusing specific performance on the ground of 'unfair advantage' where no evidence supported it, and the High Court rightly corrected this misuse of judicial discretion.
doctrines: Presumption in favor of specific performance for contracts relating to immovable property
Discretionary nature of specific performance guided by judicial principles
Ineffectiveness of liquidated damages clause to oust equitable jurisdiction
Correction of erroneous exercise of judicial discretion on appeal

card.dispute: The appellant and the Municipal Board disputed whether their contract was a lease or a licence, and whether the appellant had statutory protection against eviction under a now-repealed rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the contract between the parties was a lease, a licence, or a composite of both
Whether the appellant had the status of a tenant entitled to protection under the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947
Whether rights under a temporary rent control statute survive its repeal or expiration
holdings: A contract granting exclusive possession of property for a period with the right to sub-let creates a lease, not merely a licence, especially when the arrangement resembles proprietary interest.
The appellant was a statutory tenant under the 1947 Act with respect to the sheds and shops, but only a licensee regarding pavements, which do not qualify as 'accommodation' under the Act.
Rights created under a temporary statute, such as protection from eviction, do not survive its repeal or expiration in the absence of a saving clause, and cannot be treated as vested rights.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 2 and Section 3
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence
Doctrine of survival of rights post-repeal
Principle of statutory interpretation regarding temporary laws
Appellate court's power to consider supervening changes in law

card.dispute: The appellants sued the respondents for possession of land after a prior suit ended in their favor, but the respondents claimed adverse possession during the pendency of that earlier suit.
issues_decided: Whether banjar land can be subject to adverse possession
Whether Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908 applies to the case
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act arrests the running of limitation
holdings: Banjar land, though uncultivable, can be physically possessed for purposes like building or storage and is capable of adverse possession.
Article 142 of the Limitation Act applies to suits for possession, but no provision excludes the time during which a prior suit was pending.
Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act does not halt the running of limitation; it does not substitute for provisions in the Limitation Act regarding exclusion of time.
doctrines: Lis pendens
Adverse possession
Statutory limitation and exclusion of time
Possession follows title

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of abetting forgery of a sale deed in the name of Smt. Sukh Devi; they challenged the conviction on grounds of procedural legality and sufficiency of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether prosecution for an offence under Section 465 IPC requires prior complaint by a court under Section 195(1)(c) CrPC when the forgery occurred before the document was used in court proceedings
Whether the High Court could rely on the testimony of the accused's own counsel regarding the authenticity of the complainant's thumb impression
Whether the conviction under Section 109/465 IPC was legally sustainable based on the evidence
holdings: Section 195(1)(c) CrPC does not bar private prosecution for forgery under Section 465 IPC if the forgery was committed before the accused became a party to judicial proceedings, as the offence must have a close nexus with the court proceeding to attract the bar.

The testimony of an accused's counsel about facts observed in court, such as the taking of a thumb impression, can be relied upon by the court even if it goes against the accused, as it is not an admission binding the accused but factual evidence.
The conviction under Section 109/465 IPC was valid where the evidence showed the sale deed was forged and the appellants abetted the forgery by falsely identifying the impersonator as the real owner.
doctrines: Strict construction of Section 195(1)(c) CrPC
Close nexus test for applicability of court's exclusive power to complain
Admissibility of counsel's factual testimony against the accused

card.dispute: Ram Narain challenged his conviction for forgery and criminal conspiracy in connection with the alleged fraudulent issuance of land pattas by a defunct Gram Panchayat.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant committed forgery under Section 467, I.P.C. by creating fake land pattas that qualify as valuable securities?
Whether the appellant was guilty of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B, I.P.C. to commit forgery and cheating?
Whether the approver's testimony, unsupported by reliable corroboration, is sufficient to sustain convictions for forgery and conspiracy?
holdings: The conviction under Section 467, I.P.C. for forgery of pattas as valuable securities cannot be sustained due to lack of reliable evidence corroborating the forgery of signatures or documents.

The charge under Section 120B, I.P.C. for criminal conspiracy cannot stand independently when the substantive offence of forgery is not proven and the approver's testimony lacks credibility and corroboration.
The approver’s uncorroborated testimony, especially when inconsistent and unimpressive, is insufficient to base a conviction for either forgery or conspiracy.
doctrines: Requirement of corroboration for approver's testimony
Forgery of valuable security under IPC
Inference of criminal conspiracy from circumstantial evidence
Presumption of innocence and benefit of doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The landlord, Raval & Co., sought fixation of a higher fair rent during a subsisting contractual tenancy, which the tenant challenged as not permissible under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 applies to contractual tenancies for fixation of fair rent during the subsistence of the contract.
Whether a landlord can apply for fixation of fair rent under Section 4(1) of the Act while a contractual tenancy is still in force.
Whether the term 'landlord' in Section 4(1) includes a landlord under a continuing contractual tenancy.
holdings: The Act does not permit a landlord to apply for fixation of fair rent under Section 4(1) during the subsistence of a contractual tenancy.
The term 'landlord' in Section 4(1) must be interpreted restrictively to exclude a landlord of a continuing contractual tenant, in line with the protective purpose of rent control legislation.
Rent control laws are intended to protect tenants from unreasonable rent, not to grant landlords new rights during an ongoing contractual tenancy.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 4(1)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 7
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes in light of legislative object and purpose
Binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution
Restricted meaning of 'landlord' in rent control laws
No oral variation of registered lease deed under Section 92 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the first respondent's right to execute a compromise decree for transfer of properties, claiming partnership debts and procedural non-compliance barred execution.
issues_decided: Whether the first respondent could execute the decree under Clause (3) without final ascertainment of the amount due to him.
Whether only Shree Radhakissen Cotton Mills, and not the first respondent, could execute the decree.
holdings: The decree is executable without final ascertainment of the sum due, as the value of properties to be transferred (Rs. 4,50,000) was fixed and not conditional on further accounting.

The first respondent retained the right to execute the decree even if he failed to nominate Shree Radhakissen Cotton Mills, as the failure resulted from other partners' non-performance of prior obligations under the agreement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of executability of compromise decrees
Doctrine of conditional obligations in decrees
Principle of concurrent findings in appellate review

card.dispute: The dispute was between landowners/lessees and the State of U.P. over whether a leased plot in Meerut, allegedly used for non-agricultural purposes, could be declared an 'agricultural area' and vested in the State under the U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'agricultural area' in Section 2(1)(d) of the U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956 includes land leased for erecting buildings even if not used for agriculture?
Whether land not proven to be used for agricultural or horticultural purposes can be acquired by the State under Section 8 of the Act?
Whether the High Court was correct in abating the suits and appeals under Rule 39 of the U.P. Land Reforms Rules?
holdings: Section 2(1)(d) of the Act must be interpreted to apply only to land actually used for agriculture, horticulture, or pasture, not merely leased for agricultural purposes.
The State cannot issue a notification under Section 8 of the Act unless it is first established that the land was an 'agricultural area' being used for agricultural purposes on the relevant date.

The abatement of suits and appeals by the High Court under Rule 39 was premature and invalid; the matters must be restored and decided on merits after the appropriate authority determines the land's agricultural status.
provisions: U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956, Section 2(1)(d)
U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956, Section 17(1)(b)
U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956, Section 8
U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1956, Section 3, 4, 5
U.P. Urban Areas Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1957, Rule 39
doctrines: Doctrine of ejusdem generis
Principle of harmonious construction
Presumption against retrospective application of statutes
Protection under Article 31A for agrarian reform laws

card.dispute: The temple sued to declare certain lands as its Devadayam property and sought possession; the archakas and their alienees claimed ownership based on long possession.
issues_decided: Whether item 2 of Schedule A (R.S. No. 1057) was Devadayam land belonging to the temple
Whether stray revenue entries in the temple's name could override a long course of consistent entries in favor of the archakas
holdings: Mere stray entries showing the temple as ryot in a single year do not establish title against a continuous chain of revenue records in favor of the archakas.
A finding in a prior suit that land belonged to a temple is not binding if the appellate court did not affirm it on merit and the right to sue was the only issue decided.
provisions: Revenue Record Entries (Settlement Register, Diglet Register, Resettlement Register, Patta)
Indian Evidence Act, Section 90 (presumption as to documents 30 years old)
doctrines: Presumption of ownership from long and continuous possession reflected in revenue records
Limited precedential value of findings not challenged in appeal

card.dispute: The State of Kerala and the Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd. disputed whether the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, which acquired private forest lands held under Janman rights without compensation for agrarian reform, was protected under Article 31A of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Kerala Private Forests Act, 1971 qualifies for protection under Article 31A(1) of the Constitution
Whether forest lands held under Janman rights can be considered 'agricultural lands' under Article 31A(2)(iii)
Whether the Act constitutes colorable legislation or lacks a genuine nexus with agrarian reform
Whether non-payment of compensation violates constitutional rights despite Article 31A protection
holdings: Article 31A protects laws acquiring estates for agrarian reform even if they do not provide compensation, provided the law falls within the defined categories of 'estate'.
Forest lands held under Janman rights can be part of an 'estate' under Article 31A(2)(i) and need not be classified as agricultural land under sub-clause (iii).
The Act has a real and direct nexus with agrarian reform as it reserves forests for use in promoting agriculture or rural welfare, satisfying the requirements of Article 31A.
Non-payment of compensation is not grounds to invalidate a law protected by Article 31A, though legislatures are expected to provide just compensation except in exceptional socio-historical contexts.
provisions: The Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 10
The Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 17
doctrines: Doctrine of Colorable Legislation
Doctrine of Nexus
Agrarian Reform as a Constitutional Objective
Judicial Post-Audit of Executive Action

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan and others fought against Sajjanlal Panjawat and others over whether certain provisions of the Rajasthan Public Trusts Act, 1959, violated fundamental rights under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution regarding management of Jain temples.
issues_decided: Whether Section 17(3) of the Rajasthan Public Trusts Act, 1959, which imposes a registration fee, is a tax or a fee and thus constitutionally valid.
Whether Sections 52(1)(d) and (e) read with Section 53 of the Act violate Article 26 by interfering with the management rights of religious denominations.
Whether the State's application of the Act to specific Jain temples infringes upon the religious rights of the Jain denomination.
holdings: A levy under Section 17(3) is a fee, not a tax, because it is intended to contribute toward administrative expenses, even if deposited into the Consolidated Fund, provided collections are less than expenditures.
Section 52(1)(d) and (e) read with Section 53 do not violate Article 26 if safeguards exist for denomination control and appointments can be challenged by affected members.

The State may apply the Act to temples previously under its management before the Constitution, but ownership must be determined by the appropriate authority before applying the Act to disputed private properties.
provisions: Constitution of India, List II, Entry 3, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Distinction between tax and fee
Essential religious practices test
Denominational rights under Article 26
Doctrine of severability

card.dispute: The Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs appealed against the acquittal of Birendra Chandra Chakravarty, who was accused of criminal breach of trust for selling land and misappropriating its profits, allegedly held as a benamidar for the real owner, Saila Bala Devi.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the parties is essentially civil or criminal in nature.
Whether criminal liability under Section 409 IPC can be determined without first establishing title to the disputed immovable property.
holdings: A dispute involving questions of ownership and benami relationships in immovable property must be resolved through civil proceedings before criminal liability for breach of trust can be established.
Criminal liability under Section 409 IPC cannot be fastened beyond reasonable doubt without first adjudicating the civil rights and title to the property in question.
doctrines: Primacy of civil adjudication in title disputes
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases involving civil disputes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's finding that the respondent had a prior charge over a property based on an alleged agreement to sell, claiming the transaction was actually a loan and not a genuine sale.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff proved the execution and payment of consideration under the agreement to sell (Ext. 49).
Whether the High Court was justified in relying on unproduced account books to determine the receipt of earnest money.
Whether the transaction in question amounted to a genuine agreement to sell immovable property attracting a statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act.
holdings: The plaintiff failed to prove payment of consideration as his oral testimony was unreliable and the account books were not properly admitted in evidence.
The High Court erred in examining original account books not produced during trial, as this amounted to admitting fresh evidence without opportunity for cross-examination.
The transaction did not constitute a genuine agreement to sell immovable property, and thus no statutory charge arose under Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act.
doctrines: Principle of judicial review of evidence
Rule against admission of unverified documents
Doctrine of statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings for the Boring Road Development Scheme, alleging procedural irregularities and malafide intent.
issues_decided: Whether the government validly invoked emergency provisions under Section 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act to bypass Section 5A objections.
Whether the Collector's notification under Section 4 was valid despite being based on the satisfaction of the government, not the Collector.
Whether the acquisition for a private company (Samiti) required compliance with Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the delay in filing the petition under Article 226 rendered the challenge inadmissible due to laches.
holdings: The government's approval for invoking emergency provisions under Section 17(4) was presumed valid despite absence of documentary proof, based on circumstantial evidence and official records.
A notification under Section 4 is valid if it reflects the government's satisfaction, even if issued by the Collector; concurrent power under Bihar Amendment Act XI of 1961 permitted this.
Acquisition for a private entity does not automatically require Part VII procedures if the land is acquired for a public purpose and later transferred after development.
The petitioners' delay in challenging the acquisition, despite knowledge of possession and development, amounted to laches, justifying dismissal of the writ petition.
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in official acts
Doctrine of laches in writ petitions
Public purpose in land acquisition
Concurrent jurisdiction under state-amended statutes

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition for Delhi's planned development, alleging procedural irregularities and improper purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act was valid in absence of a declared 'development area' under the Delhi Development Act
Whether the acquisition was for a cooperative housing society, thus attracting Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act
Whether delay in challenging the acquisition rendered the petitions barred by laches and acquiescence
holdings: A valid notification under Section 4 is a sine qua non for land acquisition, and its validity cannot be challenged after long delay due to laches and acquiescence.
The acquisition for planned development under the Delhi Development Act does not require prior declaration of a development area or a master plan; actual development may follow acquisition.
Acquisition is not for a 'company' under Part VII merely because land is later allotted to cooperative housing societies; such allotment does not alter the public purpose.
doctrines: Laches and acquiescence
Procedural unreasonableness
Public purpose in land acquisition
Separation between acquisition and development

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired by the Government of Hyderabad, claiming a higher rate than determined by the Land Acquisition Officer and upheld by the High Court.
issues_decided: What was the appropriate market value of the acquired land for compensation purposes?
Whether the High Court was justified in relying solely on the Land Acquisition Officer's award?
Whether the Trial Court's method of averaging sale prices was legally sound?
holdings: The market value of the acquired land should be based on the resale rate of a nearby comparable plot, which was sold at Rs. 3/- per sq. yard, leading to a reasonable compensation of Rs. 2.50 per sq. yard after adjustments.
The High Court erred in wholly relying on the Land Acquisition Officer's award when it lacked evidentiary support, especially in light of more relevant sale evidence available.
Compensation must reflect fair market value, and where evidence is sparse, a reasonable inference from proximate and comparable sales should guide the award.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales for determining market value in land acquisition
Requirement of just and reasonable compensation based on relevant and proximate evidence
Use of reasonable inference in absence of direct market evidence

card.dispute: Religious denominations challenged the Gujarat Devasthan Inams Abolition Act, 1969, claiming it violated their right to own and manage religious property under Article 26(c) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Gujarat Devasthan Inams Abolition Act, 1969 violates Article 26(c) by acquiring property of religious denominations
Whether the Act is protected under Article 31A despite not explicitly mentioning Article 26
Whether the adequacy of compensation under the Act can be challenged under Article 26(c)
holdings: Article 26(c) guarantees the right to own and acquire property for religious purposes, but does not bar the state from acquiring such property under Article 31(2); the right ceases upon lawful acquisition.
The Act is protected under Article 31A as part of agrarian reform, and the omission of Article 26 in Article 31A's protection does not invalidate this, as fundamental rights are not absolute.
Challenges to compensation adequacy under Article 26(c) are not maintainable when the law falls under Article 31A's protection for agrarian reform.
provisions: Gujarat Devasthan Inams Abolition Act, 1969 - Sections 5, 8, 9, 31
doctrines: Balancing of fundamental rights with state power for social welfare
Non-absolute nature of fundamental rights
Doctrine of harmonious construction
State's power of compulsory acquisition under constitutional provisions

card.dispute: The daughter of a seller challenged the dismissal of her pre-emption suit after the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973 came into force, barring courts from decreeing such suits.
issues_decided: Whether an appellate court, in confirming a decree for pre-emption, passes a decree in a suit for pre-emption within the meaning of Section 3 of the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973.
Whether the appellate court can take into account a law that came into force after the original decree was passed.
holdings: An appellate court, when confirming a decree for pre-emption, passes a decree of its own and thus would be acting contrary to Section 3 of the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973 if it upheld such a decree after the Act's commencement.
An appeal is a re-hearing, and the appellate court is entitled to consider facts and events, including new legislation, that arise after the original decree.
doctrines: Re-hearing doctrine in appeals
Appellate court's power to consider subsequent events

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) sued for eviction of the respondent (tenant) who contested on the ground that co-sharers also had ownership rights and thus the appellants alone could not claim eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could contest the eviction suit on the ground of title after his defence was struck out for non-compliance with a rent deposit order under Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947.
Whether the denial of sole ownership by the tenant amounts to a denial of the landlord-tenant relationship.
holdings: The tenant had admitted the landlord-tenant relationship by paying rent to the appellants and recognizing them as landlords; thus, his plea that co-sharers also had ownership rights was a defence qua tenant, not a denial of the relationship.

Since the defence was struck out for non-compliance with a Section 11A order, all defences raised by the tenant in his capacity as tenant, including the co-ownership plea, were barred, making the ex-parte eviction decree valid.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11A
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 2(d)
doctrines: Striking out of defence under rent control law bars all tenant-defences if compliance is not met
Admission of landlord-tenant relationship through conduct prevents denial of such relationship in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The landlord (Anita Pan) sued to recover possession of premises from the tenant (B. Banerjee); the tenant challenged the constitutional validity of retrospective application of an amendment to the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, which delayed the landlord's right to sue.
issues_decided: Whether the retrospective application of sub-section (3A) of Section 13 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, violates Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution?
Whether the retrospective application of amended Sections 13(1)(f) and (ff) of the Act is constitutionally valid?
Whether the right to evict a tenant is a 'right to property' protected under Article 19(1)(f)?
holdings: The retrospective application of sub-section (3A) to pending suits and appeals imposes an unreasonable restriction on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) and is not in the general public interest; hence, it is ultra vires.
The retrospective application of Sections 13(1)(f) and (ff), which grant additional protections to tenants, is reasonable and valid as it serves the general public interest in secure tenancy.

The right to evict a tenant is an essential incident of the right to hold property under Article 19(1)(f), and thus, the restriction on this right must satisfy the test of reasonableness and public interest.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(f)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(ff)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(3A)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 25
doctrines: Reasonable restriction under Article 19(5)
Prospective and retrospective operation of statutes
Incidents of the right to property under Article 19(1)(f)
Ultra vires doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants, charge-holders under a compromise decree, fought with subsequent simple mortgagees over whether their prior charge could be enforced against the mortgaged property despite lack of registration and the mortgagees' lack of notice.
issues_decided: Whether a simple mortgagee is protected under the proviso to Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, against a prior unregistered charge of which they had no notice?
Whether the prior charge could prevail over subsequent simple mortgages in the absence of notice and registration?
Whether Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act could confer priority on the charge-holder over subsequent transferees?
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens applied to bar the subsequent mortgages?
holdings: The proviso to Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act protects a simple mortgagee who takes property for consideration without notice of a prior charge, even if the charge arose from a decree.
A prior charge cannot be enforced against a subsequent simple mortgagee who acted without notice and for value, as the proviso to Section 100 bars such enforcement.
Section 48 does not apply where one of the interests is a charge and not a transfer, and the priority is governed by Section 100, not the general rule in Section 48.
The doctrine of lis pendens does not apply when the property was not the subject of the original suit and no execution proceedings were pending at the time of the mortgage.
doctrines: Equity follows the law
Qui prior est tempore potior est jure
Lis pendens
Notice and priority in property transfers

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict tenants, claiming he needed the premises for 'his business' under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, but the business was a partnership including his brothers.
issues_decided: What is the meaning of 'his business' in Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961?
Whether the landlord's need for the premises for a family partnership business qualifies as 'his business' under the Act?
holdings: The phrase 'his business' in Section 12(1)(f) must be interpreted in light of the Act's object to ensure accommodation is used by those in genuine need.

A landlord cannot claim 'his business' under Section 12(1)(f) if the business is a partnership where he lacks exclusive or substantial managerial control and does not personally occupy the premises for business.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on object and context
Requirement of direct and substantial personal occupation for eviction under rent control laws

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of agricultural land from the tenant for failure to pay rent for three years, while the tenant argued he was entitled to relief against forfeiture despite partial payments.
issues_decided: Whether partial payment of rent for three consecutive years constitutes 'failure to pay rent for three years' under Section 25(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
Whether the aggregate amount of arrears must exceed two years' rent for Section 25(2) to apply
Whether the decisions in Raja Ram's case and Vithal's case support a different interpretation of 'default for three years'
holdings: A tenant who fails to pay full rent within the statutory period for any three years is a persistent defaulter under Section 25(2), even if only part payments are made each year.
The total arrears need not exceed two years' rent for Section 25(2) to apply; the focus is on the number of years with default, not the quantum of arrears.
The provisions of Section 25(2) are mandatory and leave no discretion to grant relief against forfeiture when there is default in three years, regardless of equitable considerations.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 25(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 14
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Mandatory nature of statutory forfeiture provisions
No relief against forfeiture for persistent defaulters under special tenancy laws

card.dispute: The Bihar State Board of Hindu Religious Trusts and the shebait of a temple disputed whether the temple was a public religious trust under the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act or a private family endowment.
issues_decided: Whether the temple constituted a religious trust in which the public were interested under Section 2(g) of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act.
Whether the management structure, including the role of non-family panches, indicated public interest in the trust.
Whether user by the public and provisions for sadhus and festivals were relevant to determining the public character of the trust.
holdings: A trust is public if the founders divest themselves of all interest and the deity becomes the owner, even if family members serve as managers.
The appointment of outsider panches with power to remove the shebait shows public association with management, indicating a public religious trust.
Provision for public worship, festivals, and service to sadhus supports the inference of a public dedication when the endowment is made directly to the deity.
The mere location of a temple within compound walls separate from residence, combined with public access, supports its public character.
provisions: Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, Section 2(g)
Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, Section 2(1)
doctrines: Public religious trust doctrine
Complete divestiture test for dedication to deity
Management participation as indicator of public interest
Presumption of public character from user and structure

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the adequacy of compensation awarded for land acquired by the Union of India, claiming it should reflect increased market value since a prior acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for the acquired land should reflect a rise in market value since a previous acquisition in the same area.
Whether factors like loss of frontage and lower land level justified reducing the compensation below the doubled rate of the prior award.
holdings: The appellant is entitled to Rs. 16 per square yard as compensation, being double the rate awarded in the earlier acquisition due to a proven 100% rise in land prices.
The reduction in compensation based on loss of frontage and lower land level is not valid, as these factors were already considered in the prior award of Rs. 8 per square yard.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales in land valuation
Consideration of severance and consequential loss in compensation
Rejection of double deduction for same disadvantage

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be co-sharers, sued to pre-empt a sale of land by respondents, but the High Court dismissed their suit, holding they failed to prove continued co-ownership at the time of decree.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had established co-ownership in the suit land on the date of the decree for pre-emption under the Punjab Pre-emption Act?
Whether the omission to produce the sale deed of the appellants' own transfer of co-ownership rights justifies an adverse inference?
holdings: To claim pre-emption under Section 15(b)(iv) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, the plaintiff must prove co-ownership not only at the time of sale but also up to the date of decree.
The failure to produce a registered sale deed within the appellants' possession, which could prove retention of co-ownership, permits an adverse inference that no such right existed.
doctrines: Adverse inference from non-production of document
Continuity of co-ownership requirement for pre-emption

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, claiming to be reversioners of a Bhumihar Brahmin estate, sued for succession based on a special family custom, while the defendants contested the existence of such a custom and the maintainability of the appeals due to non-joinder of legal representatives.
issues_decided: Whether the special family custom claimed by the plaintiffs was proved sufficiently to displace ordinary Hindu succession law.
Whether the appeals before the High Court were maintainable despite failure to implead a legal representative of a deceased plaintiff.
Whether the High Court could grant relief to respondents under Order 41, Rule 33 of the CPC even though they had not filed cross-appeals.
holdings: The evidence of custom was insufficient as only 3 out of 52 instances pertained to the relevant family; evidence relating to distant ancestors was inadmissible and of little evidentiary value.

The appeal before the High Court was not abated by failure to implead a legal representative of a deceased plaintiff where the decree was a combination of separate decrees in favor of distinct plaintiffs.

Under Order 41, Rule 33 CPC, the High Court could grant relief to respondents not appealing where reversal of part of a composite decree would not create inconsistency, and the interests were not joint or indivisible.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
doctrines: Proof of special custom in Hindu law requires clear, consistent, and family-specific evidence.
Order 41, Rule 33 CPC allows appellate courts to grant relief to non-appealing parties in exceptional circumstances.
Decrees in favor of multiple plaintiffs with separate interests are severable and do not abate collectively.

card.dispute: The appellant (H.V. Rajan) claimed possession of a cinema theatre leased to him under a 1946 lease deed, against the respondents who continued possession after the lease period ended and entered into a fresh lease despite the appellant's prior rights.
issues_decided: Whether the lease deed (Exhibit D) created a present demise (lease in presenti) or was merely an agreement to lease in future.
Whether the appellant was entitled to possession of the theatre despite the subsequent lease between the first respondent and the second respondent.
Whether the doctrine of frustration applied to render the lease agreement void due to Rent Control legislation.
Whether the appellant's right to possession had lapsed due to the expiration of the lease period under Section 110 of the Transfer of Property Act.
holdings: A lease deed creates a demise in presenti even if possession is to be delivered at a future date; delivery of possession is not a condition precedent under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act.

The appellant had a vested interest in the property under the lease and was entitled to sue for possession, irrespective of any compromise or fresh lease between the original landlord and the previous tenant.
The doctrine of frustration does not apply to a lease that has already created a present interest; the lease was not merely executory and thus not void due to Rent Control laws.
The lease period begins from the date of delivery of possession, not the date of execution of the lease, as per the terms of the lease agreement; thus, the lease had not expired.
doctrines: Demise in presenti
Doctrine of frustration
Privity of contract
Lessee's right to sue for possession

card.dispute: Kayjay Industries (P) Ltd. (the highest bidder) challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a court-ordered auction sale of mortgaged properties, which the District Court had approved, over a dispute on whether the sale was validly conducted despite inadequate bidding.
issues_decided: Whether there was a material irregularity in the conduct of the court-ordered sale under Order 21, Rule 90 of the CPC.
Whether the inadequacy of the sale price alone is sufficient to set aside a court auction.
Whether the District Court properly exercised its judicial discretion in confirming the sale.
holdings: A material irregularity under Order 21, Rule 90 of the CPC exists when the court fails to apply its mind to whether the bid price is substantially inadequate, especially when it mechanically approves the sale without considering fair market value.
Substantial inadequacy of price, without material irregularity in the conduct of sale, is not sufficient to set aside a court auction; both irregularity and injury must coexist.

The District Court properly exercised its discretion in confirming the sale at Rs. 11.5 lakhs, considering all relevant factors, and thus no material irregularity occurred, warranting the sale to stand.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
doctrines: Material irregularity and substantial injury test
Judicial discretion in confirmation of court sales
Principle of fair valuation in public auctions

card.dispute: The appellant, a legatee of a person who purchased a half share in the shebaiti right of a temple, claimed entitlement to that right, which was denied by the heirs of the original shebait.
issues_decided: Whether the shebaiti right can be transferred by sale for pecuniary consideration.
Whether a transfer of shebaiti right is valid if made in the interest of the deity and to meet a pressing necessity.
Whether the doctrine of benefit to the deity allows alienation of shebaiti rights by sale.
holdings: Shebaiti right, though heritable, cannot be freely transferred as it is inseparable from the duties of managing the deity’s affairs and such transfer would violate public policy.
A transfer of shebaiti right for pecuniary benefit is void, even if intended to serve the deity’s interests, because it amounts to delegation of a religious office.
The doctrine of necessity or benefit to the deity does not justify sale of shebaiti rights; it only permits limited actions for preservation of temple property, not alienation of spiritual rights.
doctrines: Rule against alienation of religious offices
Doctrine of benefit to the deity
Public policy in Hindu religious endowments
Heritability without transferability of shebaiti rights

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the municipal resolution permitting conversion of a lecture hall into a cinema in a residential area, alleging violation of the Town Planning Scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the municipal resolution approving conversion of a building into a cinema theatre in a residential area violated the Town Planning Scheme.
Whether expenditure incurred by the third respondent validates an otherwise illegal construction sanctioned in breach of statutory planning regulations.
Whether a resident has standing to enforce statutory duties imposed on municipal authorities for the benefit of the community.
holdings: A municipal authority cannot approve construction or conversion of a cinema in a residential area contrary to a statutory Town Planning Scheme, as it lacks power to override or modify the scheme.
Excess of statutory power cannot be validated by acquiescence or estoppel, and courts will not uphold illegal actions even if money has been spent in reliance on them.

Residents have a legal right to enforce statutory duties owed by municipalities to uphold town planning regulations, as they have a special and substantial interest in preserving the character of residential areas.
provisions: Madras Place of Public Resorts Act
doctrines: Illegality cannot be cured by estoppel or acquiescence
Enforcement of statutory duty by public authorities for public benefit
Standing of residents to challenge ultra vires municipal actions

card.dispute: Kuju Collieries Ltd. sued Jharkhand Mines Ltd. to recover money paid under a mining lease, claiming it was void and seeking restitution under the Contract Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could claim restitution under Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act for money paid under a void agreement?
Whether Sections 70 or 72 of the Contract Act applied to the facts of the case?
Whether the mining lease was void ab initio due to non-compliance with statutory rules?
holdings: Section 65 applies only when a party discovers an agreement to be void after entering into it; it does not apply when both parties knew or should have known of the illegality at the time of agreement.
Sections 70 and 72 do not apply where payment was made unlawfully, without mistake, coercion, or lawful benefit.
A mining lease violating statutory rules, such as lacking government approval or involving illegal premiums, is void ab initio and unenforceable.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 4
doctrines: In pari delicto potior est conditio defendentis
Unclean hands doctrine
Void ab initio agreements
Restitution under Section 65 of the Contract Act

card.dispute: The appellant, an inamdar with abkari rights, challenged the state's abolition of his rights and denial of separate compensation after the repeal of the 1967 abolition Act was struck down.
issues_decided: Whether the striking down of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1967, revived the Hyderabad Inams Abolition Act, 1955
Whether abkari rights attached to inam lands were abolished under the 1955 Act
Whether compensation under Section 12 of the 1955 Act includes compensation for the abolition of abkari rights
holdings: The invalidation of Act 9 of 1967 revived the 1955 Inams Abolition Act, and the vesting of inam lands in the state remained effective.
Abkari rights, being appurtenant to inam lands and part of the estate, were abolished along with the inam under the 1955 Act.
Compensation under Section 12 of the 1955 Act includes abkari rights as they are inseparable from the land, and no separate compensation is required.
provisions: Hyderabad Inams Abolition Act, 1955, Section 2(2), Section 3(1), Section 3(2), Section 4, Section 5, Section 12
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1967, Act 9 of 1967
Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1317 Fasli, Section 2(1-b)
doctrines: Revival of repealed legislation upon invalidation of repealing Act
Appurtenance of rights to land
Compensation under agrarian reform laws being part of a valid legislative scheme

card.dispute: The Mahants of certain shrines challenged the constitutional validity of provisions of the Sikh Gurudwaras Act, 1925, as amended, which placed their institutions under the management of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), arguing violations of Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 26 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3, 7, and 8 of the Sikh Gurudwaras Act, 1925, as amended, violate Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 26 of the Constitution?
Whether Section 3(4) of the Act, which makes the notification declaring a place as a Sikh Gurudwara conclusive and non-justiciable, infringes the fundamental rights of hereditary office holders?
Whether the appellants have locus standi to challenge the notifications issued under Sections 3 and 7 of the Act?
holdings: Section 3(4) does not violate Article 19(1)(f) or Article 26, as it does not bar claims over the physical property; individuals may still claim rights over the land or buildings by asserting ownership or religious affiliation without using the term 'Gurdwara'.

The long-standing judicial interpretation by the Lahore High Court and the continuity of transactions based on it require that Section 3(4) be upheld to avoid legal uncertainty, supporting its constitutional validity.

The appellants have locus standi to challenge the notifications as they were in possession of the disputed properties and had pending claims before the Tribunal, giving them a sufficient legal interest to invoke Article 226.
provisions: Sikh Gurudwaras Act, 1925 (Punjab Act 8 of 1925), Section 3
Sikh Gurudwaras Act, 1925 (Punjab Act 8 of 1925), Section 3(4)
Sikh Gurudwaras Act, 1925 (Punjab Act 8 of 1925), Section 7
Sikh Gurudwaras Act, 1925 (Punjab Act 8 of 1925), Section 8
doctrines: Presumption of constitutional validity
Stare decisis and settled interpretation of statutes
Locus standi in writ petitions
Distinction between religious institution and physical property

card.dispute: The landlord, Radhe Lal, sought eviction of tenant Mattulal on grounds of bona fide requirement for starting an iron and steel business, which the tenant contested.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement of the landlord for the premises was bona fide under Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the first appellate court's finding of fact in second appeal.
Whether the finding of bona fide requirement is a question of fact or a mixed question of law and fact.
holdings: A finding of bona fide requirement under Section 12(1)(f) is a finding of fact, not a mixed question of law and fact, and thus not easily reversible in second appeal.
The High Court erred in reversing the first appellate court’s finding, as it was based on sufficient evidence and was not arbitrary, perverse, or unreasonable.
Mere assertion of need by a landlord is insufficient; the court must apply an objective test to determine if there is genuine need, with burden of proof on the landlord.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Objective test for bona fide requirement
Principle of finality of findings of fact in second appeal
Error of law as a ground for interference in second appeal under Section 100 of CPC

card.dispute: The appellants, including a former Sarpanch and an advocate, were convicted for criminal misappropriation and forgery; they challenged the conviction based on oral evidence contradicting written documents and the illiteracy of the complainant.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under IPC Sections 409, 467, and 109 can be sustained solely on oral evidence that contradicts written admissions signed by the complainant.
Whether the illiteracy of a complainant justifies disbelieving documentary evidence and accepting oral testimony.
Whether a prior civil court finding that accounts were settled bars criminal conviction for misappropriation of the same amount.
holdings: Oral evidence that contradicts a written admission signed by a party is inherently weak and insufficient to sustain a criminal conviction without strong corroboration.
Illiteracy does not absolve a party from the consequences of their signed documents or justify ignoring material inconsistencies in oral testimony.
A criminal conviction cannot stand if it is incongruous with a prior civil court finding that the accounts in question had already been settled.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Primacy of documentary evidence over oral testimony
Incongruity between civil and criminal findings
Limits of illiteracy as a defense

card.dispute: The appellant, Mulkh Raj Sikka, challenged his conviction and death sentence for the murder of his brother Satish Chander, disputing the admissibility of evidence and the sufficiency of proof.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of Dhan Bahadur recorded before the committing magistrate was admissible under Section 33 of the Evidence Act.
Whether the appellant had the right and opportunity to cross-examine Dhan Bahadur in the committing court.
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant committed the murder of his brother.
holdings: The evidence of Dhan Bahadur recorded before the committing magistrate was admissible because the witness could not be found despite reasonable efforts to trace him.

The appellant had both the right and opportunity to cross-examine Dhan Bahadur, as provided under Sections 207 and 207A of the CrPC, and his counsel’s decision to reserve cross-examination did not invalidate the procedure.
The prosecution established the appellant’s presence at the scene and his suspicious conduct post-murder, which, combined with circumstantial evidence, proved his guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Sections 207 and 207A
doctrines: Admissibility of evidence under former judicial proceedings
Right to cross-examination as a condition for admissibility under Section 33
Use of circumstantial evidence to establish guilt in murder cases

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant after mistakenly filing an eviction application before the Rent Controller for a building constructed in 1958, which was outside the Rent Control Act's scope; the tenant argued the landlord was barred by waiver, res judicata, or estoppel.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord waived his right to evict by filing an application before the Rent Controller for a building outside the Rent Control Act's jurisdiction.
Whether the suit was barred by res judicata due to the prior dismissal by the Rent Controller.
Whether the landlord was estopped from denying the applicability of the Rent Control Act.
holdings: There can be no waiver of a right that does not exist; since the Rent Controller lacked jurisdiction, the landlord did not waive any right by mistakenly approaching it.
A decision by a forum lacking jurisdiction cannot create res judicata, as want of jurisdiction renders proceedings coram non judice and without conclusive effect.
Estoppel cannot confer jurisdiction or create a status under rent control laws; a party cannot be estopped from asserting that a building is outside the Act’s ambit based on a mistake of fact.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction Control) Act, 1960
doctrines: Waiver
Res judicata
Estoppel
Jurisdiction coram non judice
In rem operation of rent control statutes

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants from the ground floor of Hill Bungalow for personal use, claiming reasonable and bonafide need, while tenants resisted on grounds of greater hardship.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's requirement of the premises was reasonable and bonafide under Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rent Act
Whether the High Court could interfere with the lower court's finding on greater hardship under Section 13(2)
Whether juridical possession of another premises by the landlord negates his need for the tenanted premises
holdings: A landlord's need for premises is not negated by juridical possession of another property if that property is not practically available for occupation due to existing leave and licence arrangements.
The burden of proving greater hardship does not shift entirely to the tenant; both parties must adduce evidence, and the court must weigh the hardship to both sides.
The High Court erred in re-appreciating evidence and substituting its finding on hardship without any supporting evidence, especially when the tenant led no evidence of hardship.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1957, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1957, Section 13(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1957, Section 29(3)
doctrines: Reasonable and bonafide requirement for personal occupation
Balancing of hardship under rent control legislation
Revisional jurisdiction limited to cases of miscarriage of justice due to error of law

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the fixation of standard rent by apportionment after structural changes to the leased premises, arguing that the original tenancy had changed and apportionment was no longer applicable.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of apportionment under the Bombay Rent Act applies when parts of a leased property are re-let after structural alterations?
Whether the courts below erred in fixing standard rent by apportioning the original rent despite changes to the premises?
Whether the value of land should be assessed as of 1940 (basic date) or 1948 (date of new lease) for rent fixation?
holdings: The principle of apportionment may be applied to determine standard rent even after partial reconstruction, provided the original identity of the premises largely remains.
Courts may consider apportionment as a relevant factor alongside fairness and justice, especially to prevent evasion of rent control laws by splitting properties.

The value of land for new structures may be assessed as of the date of reconstruction, but for old unchanged premises, apportionment based on 1940 rent is valid in absence of evidence for higher land value in 1948.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 2(1)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 11(1)(e)
doctrines: Principle of apportionment in rent control
Statutory interpretation with regard to context and object
Prevention of fraud on statute
Deference to factual findings of lower courts under Article 136

card.dispute: The appellant, Rukmani Bai Gupta, challenged the rejection of her application for renewal of a quarrying lease for 'limestone for burning' and the grant of a fresh lease to another party, arguing that her application was for a minor mineral and should have been considered.
issues_decided: Whether the quarrying lease for 'limestone for burning' was validly granted for a minor mineral after the 1961 notification.
Whether the appellant's application for renewal was proper despite describing the mineral as 'limestone for burning as a minor mineral'.
Whether the State Government could grant a lease to another applicant without considering the appellant's competing application for a fresh lease.
Whether the Deputy Secretary had authority to extend the time for execution of the lease under the Rules of Business.
holdings: The lease for 'limestone for burning' was valid as it referred to 'limestone used in kilns for manufacture of lime used as building material', which was a minor mineral under the 1961 notification.

The application for renewal was proper because the description 'limestone for burning as a minor mineral' sufficiently identified the mineral as a minor mineral, despite not using the full statutory phrase.

The appellant could not raise for the first time in the Supreme Court the contention that her application should have been considered alongside another’s; the issue was not raised before the authorities or High Court and hence could not be entertained.
The Deputy Secretary had authority to extend the time for lease execution by acting under the State Government's power via the Rules of Business, even without formal delegation of power.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 3(e)
Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961, Rule 12(2)
Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961, Form V
doctrines: Strict construction of applications disfavored; substance over form
New contentions not raised before lower authorities cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court
Validity of administrative action under Rules of Business in absence of formal delegation

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent disputed whether their partnership continued after the lease term ended and if the suit for rendition of accounts was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the partnership subsisted after the expiry of the fixed term of five years
Whether the suit for rendition of accounts was barred by limitation
Whether implied agreement to continue the partnership could be inferred from conduct or correspondence
Whether post-dissolution acts by a partner indicated continuation of the firm
holdings: A firm constituted for a fixed term dissolves automatically upon expiry of that term unless there is an express or implied contract to continue.
The suit for rendition of accounts was barred by limitation as it was filed more than three years after the partnership ended on August 30, 1957.
No implied agreement to continue the partnership could be inferred from the conduct or correspondence of the parties.
Acts after dissolution, such as settling arbitration, were within the scope of winding up and did not indicate continuation of the partnership.
doctrines: Automatic dissolution of firm on expiry of fixed term
Continuation of partner authority for winding up after dissolution
Limitation period for suit for rendition of accounts

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of agricultural land by adverse possession and later sought to amend his written statement after the death of the original owner to assert reversionary rights, while the respondent claimed possession based on a gift deed.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant acquired ownership of the land by adverse possession?
Whether the appellate court can allow amendment of the written statement during the pendency of an appeal due to a change in circumstances (death of a party)?
holdings: The appellant failed to prove adverse possession as he did not challenge the revenue records or cease paying rent on behalf of the owner, indicating acknowledgment of her title.
The court can allow amendment of the written statement during appeal to account for changed circumstances, such as the death of a party, to do complete justice and avoid multiplicity of litigation.
