Whether the proviso to Section 14(2) applies to consecutive rent defaults in the same proceeding.
holdings: The Rent Controller has the discretion to extend time for deposit of future rent under Section 15(1), especially if the default was due to circumstances beyond the tenant's control.

Failure to comply with a Section 15(1) order does not automatically entitle the landlord to eviction; the tenant retains the right to claim protection under Section 14(2) if there is substantial compliance.
The proviso to Section 14(2) applies only if the tenant had previously availed protection under Section 14(2) in an earlier eviction proceeding, not for consecutive defaults in the same case.
doctrines: Substantial compliance
Judicial discretion in rent control matters
Rejection of indefeasible right to eviction
Binding effect of larger bench decisions

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of provisos to Section 7(1)(e) of the Resettlement of Displaced Persons (Land Acquisition) Act, 1948, arguing they violated fundamental rights under the Government of India Act, 1935, and resulted in illusory compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the provisos to Section 7(1)(e) of the 1948 Act are constitutionally invalid for violating Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935?
Whether the 1948 Act, being in the Ninth Schedule, is protected from challenges based on fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution?
Whether the decision in N.B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector affects the validity of earlier rulings upholding laws in the Ninth Schedule?
holdings: The provisos to Section 7(1)(e) of the 1948 Act are protected under Article 31B and immune from challenges based on inconsistency with fundamental rights, including those derived from Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935.
Article 31B grants absolute protection to laws in the Ninth Schedule from being declared void on grounds of violating fundamental rights, regardless of whether the rights were pre-existing or new.

The decision in Jeejeebhoy’s case does not overrule earlier Constitution Bench rulings as it involved a statute not in the Ninth Schedule, and thus does not undermine the protection afforded by Article 31B.
provisions: Resettlement of Displaced Persons (Land Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 3
Resettlement of Displaced Persons (Land Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 7(1)(e)
doctrines: Doctrine of Immunity under Article 31B
Doctrine of Continuity of Fundamental Rights from Government of India Act, 1935 to Constitution
Doctrine of Prospective Overruling (implied in treatment of Ninth Schedule laws)

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a right to purchase property in court receivership, while respondents 1 to 4, in possession of the property, challenged the sale and sought to buy it instead.
issues_decided: Whether a concluded contract of sale existed between the appellant and the court-appointed receiver
Whether respondents 1 to 4, despite unauthorized possession, could be considered eligible to purchase the property
Whether the court could direct the receiver to sell the property to someone other than the appellant in the interest of social justice
holdings: No concluded contract of sale was formed in favor of the appellant, as acceptance and full terms were not finalized.
Unauthorized possession does not disqualify persons from participating in a competitive purchase of property in custodia legis, especially when they seek rehabilitation.
Courts may consider social justice and human welfare in deciding sales of property under receivership, prioritizing practical justice over technicalities.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order XL
doctrines: Custodia legis
Social justice in judicial administration
Procedural rules as handmaids of justice
Human dignity and welfare in property disputes

card.dispute: A retired armed forces member sought to evict a tenant from a flat he inherited during service, claiming bona fide personal need, but the tenant resisted, arguing the law did not allow such eviction when the tenancy predated his ownership.
issues_decided: Whether a retired member of the armed forces can seek eviction under Section 13 A-1 of the Bombay Rents Act if he inherited the property while in service and the tenancy existed before he became landlord?
Whether the phrase 'regain possession' in the Statement of Objects and Reasons limits the benefit of Section 13 A-1 only to those who originally let out the premises during service?
holdings: Section 13 A-1 of the Bombay Rents Act applies to a member or retired member of the armed forces who inherited the property during service, even if the tenancy began before he became the landlord.
The phrase 'regain possession' does not restrict the benefit of Section 13 A-1 to cases where the landlord originally let out the premises; it simply means obtaining possession for bona fide use.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13 A-1
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(2)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent derived from statutory language and statement of objects and reasons
Beneficial construction for members of armed forces due to special service conditions

card.dispute: Landlords sought eviction of tenants to regain possession of premises, claiming they were already in occupation of part of the building and needed the entire unit for bona fide reasons under the Uttar Pradesh Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the premises constituted a single unit or separate units for the purpose of eviction under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972.
Whether the word 'occupation' in Explanation (iv) to Section 21(1)(b) of the 1972 Act requires actual physical residence by the landlord.
holdings: Where a building constitutes one single unit and the landlord is in occupation of a portion, they are entitled to seek release of the entire premises from the tenant.

The term 'occupation' includes constructive possession; actual physical residence is not necessary—retaining control, such as keeping household effects or making casual visits, suffices for the landlord to be deemed in occupation.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(b), Explanation (iv)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 22(1)(b), Explanation (iv)
doctrines: Constructive possession
Substantive right vs. rule of evidence
Bona fide requirement of landlord
Principle of vested rights in property law

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the state in 1957, arguing that the valuation was inadequate and that the High Court wrongly revived a judgment previously set aside by the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could legally revive a judgment that had been set aside by the Supreme Court on appeal.
What compensation should be awarded for a large tract of land acquired in Aurangabad in 1957, having regard to its location and development potential.
holdings: The High Court had no authority to resurrect a judgment nullified by the Supreme Court; such action rendered the revived judgment a legal nullity.

Compensation for large acquired tracts in developed areas must reflect potential value and not rely solely on small-property transactions; a rate of Rs. 1.50 per square yard was fixed with 15% solatium and interest.
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent (Article 141)
Principle of solatium in compulsory acquisition
Rule against reliance on small-property sales for valuing large acquisitions

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Raj Rani, challenged the exclusion of her name and that of other daughters and the widow from being recognized as legal heirs of Nanak Chand, who disappeared in 1954, after a death certificate issued by local respectable persons was used to substitute only his three sons in a land claim proceeding.
issues_decided: Whether a death certificate issued by 'respectable persons' of a place where the deceased once resided is admissible in evidence under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Whether the authorities below violated principles of natural justice by not affording the appellant an opportunity to be heard before allowing substitution of legal heirs
Whether Nanak Chand died before or after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, for the purpose of determining the succession rights of daughters
holdings: A death certificate issued by non-official 'respectable persons' is not admissible under Section 35 of the Evidence Act as it does not qualify as an official entry made in discharge of a statutory duty.

The authorities committed a procedural error by failing to afford the appellant an opportunity to be heard, violating the principles of natural justice under Section 5(2) of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954.

In the absence of legally admissible evidence of death before 1956, Nanak Chand is deemed to have died after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, entitling his daughters and widow to equal shares in his interest in the coparcenary property.
provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 6 (including Explanation I)
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Presumption of death under Indian law
Rule of admissibility of public documents under Section 35 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The appellants (hospital proprietors) and respondent (a doctor) disputed whether the doctor was a protected licensee under the Bombay Rent Act, entitled to continued occupation of a hospital cabin, or merely permitted to use it as an attached Honorary Surgeon.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was a 'protected licensee' under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947, as amended in 1973.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts regarding the nature of the respondent's occupation.
Whether the document Exh. No. 1, signed by the respondent, accurately reflected the true nature of the arrangement between the parties.
holdings: The respondent was not a licensee or tenant but was permitted to use the cabin solely due to his attachment as an Honorary Surgeon to the hospital, as clearly stated in Exh. No. 1 which he admitted understanding and signing.

The High Court erred in overturning the concurrent factual findings of the lower courts, which were supported by evidence, including the lack of independent payment for services and use of hospital facilities.
Oral testimony contradicting a clear documentary admission against interest is inadmissible unless the document is proven to be obtained by fraud or misrepresentation, which was not shown here.
provisions: Maharashtra Act XVII of 1973 (amending the Bombay Rent Act)
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact rule
Article 227 judicial review limits
Documentary evidence prevails over oral testimony when it contains an admission against interest

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra challenged the constitutional validity of the Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, 1975, which allowed for the summary eviction of unauthorized occupants, while landowners argued it violated their rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, 1975 violates Article 14 due to unguided and arbitrary conferment of power on the State Government.
Whether the Act infringes Article 19(1)(f) (right to acquire, hold and dispose of property) as it stood before its deletion by the 44th Amendment.
Whether the Act amounts to a requisition or acquisition of private property under Article 31, requiring compensation and Presidential assent.
Whether the State Legislature had the competence to enact the law under Entries 18, 64, and 65 of List II of the Seventh Schedule.
holdings: The Act violates Article 14 because it grants unguided and uncanalised discretion to the State Government to declare any land as 'vacant' without objective criteria or procedural safeguards.
The Act infringed Article 19(1)(f) at the time of its enactment, but this issue became moot after the deletion of that provision by the 44th Amendment; the doctrine of eclipse was not applied.
The Act does not amount to acquisition or requisition of property under Article 31, as it does not transfer possession or ownership to the State, hence Articles 31(2) and 31(3) do not apply.
The State Legislature had the legislative competence to enact the law under Entries 18 (public health), 64 (lands), and 65 (town and country planning) of List II of the Seventh Schedule.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entries 18, 64, 65
Maharashtra Vacant Lands (Prohibition of Unauthorised Occupation and Summary Eviction) Act, 1975, Sections 2(f), 3, 4, 4A, 4B
Maharashtra Vacant Lands (Service of Notice) Rules, 1975
doctrines: Doctrine of Arbitrary State Action (under Article 14)
Doctrine of Eclipse (not applied due to post-amendment context)
Principle of Legislative Competence (Seventh Schedule classification)
Test of Reasonable Classification (applied to invalidate unguided discretion)

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision that had invalidated the Central Government's revisionary order cancelling land allotments made to Avtar Singh and others, based on an alleged oral partition of land in Pakistan.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government had previously exercised its revisional power under Section 33 of the Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948, thereby precluding a second revision
Whether the letter dated May 31, 1963 from a Joint Secretary constituted a valid exercise of revisional power under Section 33
Whether the Central Government's 1965 order was without jurisdiction due to lack of prior revision
holdings: The Central Government had not previously exercised its revisional power under Section 33, so the 1965 order was validly made for the first time.
A mere expression of opinion or administrative suggestion in a letter does not amount to a decision under Section 33; there must be a clear exercise of revisional authority.
The power under Section 33 can only be exercised once per order, but the 1963 letter did not constitute such an exercise, so the 1965 revision was valid.
provisions: Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948, Section 33
doctrines: Finality of revisional jurisdiction
Doctrine of exhaustion of remedies
Principle against unjust enrichment

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant under the Delhi Rent Control Act, claiming the premises were let for residential use only, while the tenant argued the inclusion of 'personal office' in the lease made it a composite use tenancy, excluding it from residential eviction provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the use of the term 'personal office' in the lease deed changes the nature of the tenancy from residential to composite or commercial use?
Whether a tenancy permitting a 'personal office' falls outside the scope of 'residential premises' under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
What is the correct principle for interpreting the true meaning of a lease clause regarding permitted use of premises?
holdings: The term 'office' is not inherently non-residential; its meaning depends on context, and 'personal office' does not imply commercial use or alter the residential character of the tenancy.
A lease permitting a 'personal office' remains a residential tenancy if the parties intended to restrict use to residence and prohibited commercial use, as expressly stated in the lease.
Courts must interpret lease terms based on the document as a whole, giving natural meaning to the words used, without relying on extrinsic evidence when the language is clear.
doctrines: Literal Rule of Construction
Interpretation of Contracts as a Whole
Presumption Against Absurdity in Interpretation
Rejection of Extrinsic Evidence When Document is Clear

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether a settlement deed conferred an absolute estate or only a life estate on the mother-in-law, determining who inherited the property after her death.
issues_decided: Whether Padmavathi Ammal acquired an absolute or life estate under the settlement deed
Whether V. Sreenivasa Pai acquired a vested remainder interest in the property
Whether the respondent, as his widow, was entitled to the property after the life estate ended
holdings: In construing a document, the court must ascertain the intention from the language used, read as a whole, and not render any part meaningless.
The settlement deed created a life estate in favor of Padmavathi Ammal and conferred an absolute, vested remainder interest in favor of V. Sreenivasa Pai.
The respondent, as the sole heir of V. Sreenivasa Pai, was entitled to the property upon termination of the life estate, even though he predeceased Padmavathi Ammal.
provisions: Principles of construction of documents and wills
doctrines: Rule against repugnancy in testamentary dispositions
Vested remainder interest
Construction of documents to give effect to all provisions

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction and arrears of rent, while the tenant claimed protection under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, which became applicable when the building completed ten years during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applies to a building that completed ten years of construction during the pendency of eviction proceedings?
Whether a tenant can claim the benefit of amended statutory protections that arise after the institution of a suit but during its pendency?
Whether allowing the tenant to claim protection under the new Rent Act amounts to a change in cause of action?
holdings: A building becomes subject to the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings Act, 1972 once it completes ten years from the date of completion, even if this occurs during the pendency of litigation.
Courts may consider subsequent events during litigation that fundamentally affect the relief claimed, to ensure substantial justice, provided fairness to both parties is maintained.
Claiming protection under a newly applicable statute during litigation does not constitute a new cause of action but is an update of facts, allowing amendment of pleadings under equitable principles.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 40
doctrines: Subsequent events doctrine
Substantial justice doctrine
Equitable amendment of pleadings
Continuing cause of action

card.dispute: Members of a Hindu joint family fought over the character and division of family property, including shares in a company, cash, and jewellery, and whether income from a managing agency agreement was joint or personal property.
issues_decided: Whether commission and remuneration received under a managing agency agreement by co-sharers from joint family funds are joint family property
Whether one co-sharer could unilaterally claim such income as his personal property
What properties constituted joint family property and how they should be divided
Whether a final decree without reference to accounts could be passed to end prolonged litigation
holdings: Commission and remuneration received by co-sharers under a managing agency agreement, where the firm was formed from joint family funds, are joint family property.
A single co-sharer cannot unilaterally convert joint family property or income into his personal property by a mere letter or claim.

408 shares acquired using joint family funds are joint family property and must be equally divided among the three branches; other shares and personal possessions like jewellery are not joint family property.
A final decree may be passed without a formal account of transactions where litigation has been prolonged and parties agree, to prevent further delay.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family Property (customary law, not codified statute)
doctrines: Unity of joint family property
No unilateral alienation of joint family property
Finality of decree to prevent multiplicity of litigation

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the denial of enhanced solatium and interest in compensation for land acquired by the Union Territory of Chandigarh, claiming entitlement under the amended Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the enhanced solatium of 30% under amended Section 23(2) and interest rate of 9% under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act apply to appeals decided between April 30, 1982, and the commencement of the 1984 Amendment Act.
Whether the amended provisions apply to orders passed by the High Court or Supreme Court in appeals against awards made before April 30, 1982, if the appellate order was passed after that date.
holdings: The enhanced solatium and interest rates apply to any award or appellate order made after April 30, 1982, and before the 1984 Amendment Act commenced, regardless of when the original award was made.
Section 30(2) of the 1984 Amendment Act extends the benefit of enhanced compensation to pending appellate proceedings as of April 30, 1982, if the appellate order is passed after that date.
doctrines: Prospective operation of amendments
Literal interpretation of statutory language
Deemed application of amended provisions

card.dispute: The reversioners of a Hindu joint estate contested the validity of alienations made by three daughters (limited owners) of the original owner, challenging whether such alienations without mutual consent were binding and whether transferees could claim protection under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether alienations made by one of the three daughters (limited owners) of a joint Hindu estate without the consent of the others were binding on the reversioners.
Whether the transferees of properties under sale deeds from 1901, 1914, and 1915 could claim protection under Sections 43 and 51 of the Transfer of Property Act.

Whether the plaintiffs' acceptance of compensation determined by the trial court amounted to an election under Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, barring them from seeking remand for a fresh choice.
holdings: A limited owner in a joint Hindu estate can alienate her share during her lifetime, but such alienation does not bind the reversioners unless made with consent of all co-owners or for legal necessity with concurrence.

Transferees of a 1901 sale deed are protected under Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act due to subsequent deemed consent and exclusive possession by the last surviving limited owner, invoking the doctrine of 'feeding the grant by estoppel'.

Acceptance of compensation fixed by the trial court amounts to an election under Section 51, and it would be inequitable to allow reversioners to later demand market value, especially after valuable constructions by the transferee trust.
doctrines: Feeding the grant by estoppel
Deemed consent
Right of survivorship in Hindu joint estates
Alienation by limited owners for legal necessity

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification on the ground that public notice of the notification was not given within 40 days of its publication in the Official Gazette.
issues_decided: Whether public notice of the substance of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 must be given within 40 days of its publication in the Official Gazette.
Whether the High Court was correct in quashing the notification based on the delay in giving public notice.
holdings: A notification issued under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on or after 12th September 1975 is invalid if public notice of its substance is not given in the locality within 40 days of its publication in the Official Gazette.
The High Court rightly concluded that public notice was given on 18th December 1979, resulting in a delay of over 40 days, rendering the notification invalid.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983
doctrines: Doctrine of mandatory compliance with procedural requirements in land acquisition
Retrospective validation of amendments subject to procedural conditions

card.dispute: Landlords sought eviction of a tenant for default in rent payment and non-compliance with court orders to deposit arrears, leading to a dispute over whether the tenant's defence should be struck off under Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'shall' in Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 is mandatory or directory
Whether a tenant's defence must be struck off automatically upon failure to comply with a court order to deposit rent under Section 11A
Whether a court retains discretion to extend time for deposit of rent even after initial deadlines have passed
holdings: The word 'shall' in Section 11A is directory, not mandatory, as the beneficial purpose of the Act requires protection of tenants and preservation of judicial discretion.
Failure to comply strictly with a deposit order does not automatically result in striking off a tenant's defence; courts retain discretion to prevent miscarriage of justice.
Courts have inherent power to extend time for deposit of rent, consistent with Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the protective nature of rent control legislation.
provisions: The Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11A
doctrines: Mandatory vs. directory interpretation of statutory language
Beneficial construction of tenant protection laws
Judicial discretion in procedural compliance under rent control statutes

card.dispute: The Express Newspapers challenged executive actions affecting their construction project in Delhi, alleging violations of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 19(1)(g), while the Municipal Corporation of Delhi later disputed the accuracy of statements attributed to its counsel regarding compounding of building deviations.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition is maintainable to challenge executive action on grounds of violation of fundamental rights arising from a contractual or administrative decision affecting civil rights?
Whether the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes freedom of the press and can be invoked in matters of construction permissions for a press building?
Whether statements made by counsel during court proceedings can be disowned after judgment, and whether such disavowal warrants a review?
Whether the Lt. Governor of Delhi has the authority to deal with land allotment and leases under the Government of Part C States Act, 1951, and related rules?
holdings: Writ petitions under Articles 32 and 226 are maintainable when executive action infringes fundamental rights, even if the dispute arises from administrative or quasi-contractual dealings affecting civil rights.

Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) encompasses freedom of the press, and state actions that indirectly restrict press operations may be subject to judicial scrutiny on grounds of reasonableness and equality.

Statements made by counsel in open court, especially those recorded in court minutes and relied upon in judgment, cannot be disowned post-decision; attempts to do so constitute abuse of process and may amount to contempt.

The Lt. Governor of Delhi, as successor to the Chief Commissioner, possesses executive authority over land administration in the Union Territory, including powers related to lease and allotment under delegated statutes and rules.
provisions: Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 21, Proviso
Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961
doctrines: Doctrine of maintainability of writ petitions for enforcement of fundamental rights
Freedom of press as part of freedom of speech and expression
Doctrine of judicial propriety and sanctity of court records
Doctrine of abuse of process in review petitions
Doctrine of representation by counsel binding on parties

card.dispute: Fomento Resorts challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, after the government failed to conduct a mandatory enquiry under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 before issuing the notification under Section 4.
issues_decided: Whether compliance with Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 is mandatory before issuing a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for land acquisition for a company
Whether the High Court erred in quashing the notifications solely on the ground of non-compliance with Rule 4 without deciding other grounds of challenge
holdings: Compliance with Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 is not mandatory before issuing a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; such an enquiry may be conducted before or after the notification, depending on the circumstances.

When multiple legal and factual grounds are raised in a challenge to acquisition, the High Court should decide all grounds instead of relying on a single point, especially where an appeal lies, to avoid protracted litigation.
doctrines: Mandatory vs. directory procedural requirements
Obiter dicta
Principle of avoiding piecemeal adjudication

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, a registered firm running a rice and oil mill, sued to prevent the defendants from alienating the leased property and interfering with their possession, seeking permanent injunction and a direction to sell the property to them under tenancy protection law.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to protection under the Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1921 (as extended to Erode) on account of constructions they had raised on the leased property.
Whether the plaintiffs had a right to claim purchase of the leased property under Section 9 of the Act.
What equitable relief could be granted in view of the long-standing possession of the plaintiffs and the ownership rights of the defendants.
holdings: The lease primarily concerned a large vacant site behind a small standing structure, and the plaintiffs' purpose was to use the land for constructing and operating mills, which they lawfully did with the landlords’ knowledge.

The plaintiffs were not entitled to statutory protection under Section 3 or Section 9 of the Madras City Tenants Protection Act because the lease was not of a building as required by the Act, and the statutory remedy for purchase was not available.

Equitable relief was granted by partitioning the property: the front portion with the original structure was restored to the landlords, while the plaintiffs were allotted the remaining land (about 10,060 sq. ft.) upon payment of Rs. 7.5 lakhs, with provisions for shifting structures and access.
provisions: Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1921 (Tamil Nadu Act 3 of 1922), Section 3
Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1921 (Tamil Nadu Act 3 of 1922), Section 9
doctrines: Equitable partition in landlord-tenant disputes
Doctrine of substantial performance of lease purpose
Principle of fair compensation in de facto long-term possession

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of a property after a limited tenancy expired, but the tenant challenged the warrant of possession, claiming lack of notice and fraud in obtaining permission for the tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether a notice must be served on the tenant before issuing a warrant of possession under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the Rent Controller must inquire into allegations of fraud or collusion at the time of issuing the warrant
What remedy is available to a tenant who claims the original permission for limited tenancy was obtained fraudulently or collusively
holdings: No prior notice is required to be served on the tenant before issuing a warrant of possession under Section 21 if the limited tenancy has lawfully expired.
The Rent Controller is not obligated to hold an inquiry into allegations of fraud or collusion at the time of issuing the warrant; such pleas must be raised by the tenant during the tenancy period.

A tenant who alleges fraud, collusion, or mechanical grant of permission must approach the Rent Controller promptly upon discovering such facts, not wait until after the landlord applies for possession.
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in statutory orders
Harmonization of competing interests in special possession procedures
Timely adjudication of tenancy disputes to prevent abuse of process

card.dispute: Two or more trustees of a registered public trust, with the Charity Commissioner's written consent, sued to declare that certain property belonged to the temple trust and to recover possession from respondents who were holding it adversely after their services were terminated.
issues_decided: Whether two or more persons having interest in a public trust can file a suit under Section 50 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, with the written consent of the Charity Commissioner, for declaration of title and possession of trust property from a person holding it adversely?
Whether the definition of 'person having interest in the trust' under Section 2(10) of the Act includes trustees and beneficiaries?
Whether Section 50 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, is in pari materia with Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and whether the latter's procedural requirements apply?
holdings: Two or more persons having interest in a public trust, including trustees, can file a suit under Section 50 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, for declaration and possession of trust property, provided they obtain the written consent of the Charity Commissioner under Section 51.
The term 'person having interest in the trust' under Section 2(10) includes both trustees and beneficiaries, as the definition is inclusive and intended to be broadly interpreted.

Section 50 of the Bombay Public Trust Act creates a distinct and wider remedy than Section 92 of the CPC, and suits under it are not representative in nature but aimed at protecting the trust’s property, thus not subject to the procedural restrictions of Section 92.
doctrines: Inclusive interpretation of statutory definitions
Distinction between representative and private rights suits
Statutory exclusion of CPC provisions in special enactments

card.dispute: The decree-holders challenged the Custodian of Evacuee Property's application to set aside a court-ordered auction sale of a judgment debtor's property on grounds of res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the subsequent application by the Custodian to set aside the court sale was barred by res judicata due to a prior dismissal of a similar application under a different statutory provision.
Whether the Custodian's application under Section 17(2) of Ordinance No. XXVII of 1949 was validly made and based on a new cause of action.
holdings: The subsequent application was not barred by res judicata because the cause of action under Section 17(2) of Ordinance No. XXVII of 1949 arose only after the ordinance came into force and was distinct from the earlier claim under the East Punjab Act.

The Custodian validly invoked Section 17(2) of Ordinance No. XXVII of 1949 in a fresh application, which provided a new statutory basis for setting aside the sale, thus constituting a separate cause of action.
provisions: East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, Section 8
Administration of Evacuee Property (Chief Commissioners Provinces) Ordinance, 1949 (Ordinance No. XII of 1949), Section 15
Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949 (Ordinance No. XXVII of 1949), Sections 2(f), 7, and 17
doctrines: Res judicata
Cause of action
Statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Slum and pavement dwellers in Madras challenged the state's eviction actions without alternative accommodation, claiming violations of their fundamental rights to life and livelihood under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood
Whether eviction of slum and pavement dwellers without alternative accommodation violates Articles 21 and 19(1)(e) and (g)
Whether the State's policy and actions in slum clearance are constitutionally valid
holdings: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, as the two are interdependent.
Eviction of slum and pavement dwellers without alternative accommodation may violate Article 21 if it deprives them of livelihood and basic means of survival.
The State's policy of providing alternative accommodation and improving slum conditions is constitutionally acceptable, and no writ is needed if the State adheres to its assurances.

The State must not evict pavement dwellers before December 31, 1985, and must provide alternative accommodation to those residing before June 30, 1977, unless land is needed for urgent public purpose.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971
Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning Act, 1971
doctrines: Right to livelihood as part of right to life
Balancing of fundamental rights with state welfare measures
Judicial restraint in light of state assurances
Procedural fairness in eviction of marginalized communities

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of various provisions of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, on grounds of violation of fundamental rights including Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.
issues_decided: Whether the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 is constitutionally valid under Articles 39(b) and (c) and does not violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
Whether Section 11(6) of the Act, which caps compensation at two lakhs, is illusory or confiscatory and violates Articles 14 and 31(2).
Whether Section 27(1) of the Act, which restricts transfer of urban land without permission, violates Article 19(1)(f) and is unreasonable.
Whether Sections 23(1) to (3) and related parts are protected under Articles 31B and 31C and validly serve public purpose.
holdings: The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 is valid as it advances Directive Principles under Articles 39(b) and (c) and does not violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
The cap on compensation under Section 11(6) is not illusory; post-25th Amendment, adequacy of 'amount' is non-justiciable and cannot be challenged under Article 31(2).
Section 27(1) is invalid to the extent it restricts transfer of land within ceiling limits, as it unreasonably infringes the right under Article 19(1)(f) without serving the Act’s purpose.
Sections 23(1) to (3) and the conditional phrase in 23(4) are ultra vires and not protected by Articles 31B and 31C as they fail the 'social good' test for disposal of excess land.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(g)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 11(6)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 23
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 27(1)
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine
Doctrine of reading down
Principle of social good in land redistribution
Non-justiciability of compensation amount post-25th Amendment
Reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the eviction order based on the deemed cessation of tenancy after his brother built another house in the same city.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy of all co-tenants terminates when one member of the tenant's family builds or acquires another residential building in the same city?
Whether the heirs of a deceased tenant who resided with him become joint tenants or separate statutory tenants under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings Act?
What is the correct interpretation of the phrase 'tenant or any member of his family' in Section 12(3) of the Act?
holdings: The tenancy of co-tenants does not cease merely because one family member acquires another house; only the tenancy of the person who acquired the house and their immediate family is affected.
Heirs of a deceased tenant who resided with him become individual statutory tenants, not joint tenants, and each holds tenancy independently under Section 3(a)(1) of the Act.
The phrase 'tenant or any member of his family' in Section 12(3) refers to each statutory tenant individually and their own family, not the entire group of co-tenants collectively.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(3)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(a)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(g)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Deemed vacancy
Cessation of tenancy
Individual vs. joint tenancy under rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant, Mohd. Azeem, challenged the termination of tenancy of his family's residential premises after his brother Nairn built another house, which led to a deemed vacancy under the U.P. Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy of all co-tenants terminates when one member of the family builds or acquires another residential building under Section 12(3) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972.
Whether the Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court interpreting co-tenants as joint tenants was consistent with the statutory definition of 'tenant' and 'family'.
holdings: The tenancy of co-tenants does not terminate merely because one family member builds another house; each heir who qualifies under the Act is a separate tenant, and the tenancy continues for others.

The concept of joint tenancy does not apply under the Act; the statutory definition of 'tenant' and 'family' supports individual tenancies, and Section 12(3) applies only to the defaulting tenant and their immediate family.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(3)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Deemed vacancy
Individual tenancy vs. joint tenancy

card.dispute: Pavement and slum dwellers challenged the Bombay Municipal Corporation's plan to forcibly evict them without providing alternative accommodation, arguing it violated their fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood
Whether the forced eviction of pavement and slum dwellers without notice or alternative shelter violates Article 21
Whether Section 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, allowing removal of encroachments without notice, is constitutional
Whether the government is obligated to provide alternative accommodation before evicting slum and pavement dwellers
holdings: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, as life cannot be sustained without means of earning a living.
Forcible eviction of pavement and slum dwellers without providing alternative accommodation infringes Article 21 if it deprives them of livelihood.
Section 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act is valid but must be exercised reasonably and in accordance with principles of natural justice.
Slum and pavement dwellers enumerated in the 1976 census must be provided alternative accommodation or sites before eviction, though not as a condition precedent to removal.
doctrines: Right to life includes right to livelihood
Principle of audi alteram partem (right to hearing)
No estoppel against enforcement of fundamental rights
Positive obligation of the state to protect marginalized groups

card.dispute: The heirs of a temple's settlor sued to recover properties alienated by the settlor after she purported to cancel a trust; the defendants claimed the suit was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was governed by Article 134-B of the Limitation Act, 1908
From when the limitation period commenced: the settlor's death or her deemed resignation as trustee?
Whether wrongful alienation or cancellation of a trust deed amounts to deemed resignation of a trustee?
holdings: The suit fell under Article 134-B of the Limitation Act, which applies to suits for trust property by a trustee.
The limitation period of 12 years commenced from the death of the settlor, not from any deemed resignation.
Wrongful alienation or cancellation of trust property does not result in deemed resignation of a trustee; the trustee remains liable until death or lawful removal.
doctrines: Deemed resignation of a trustee
Irrevocability of a valid trust once ownership is divested
Wrongful alienation does not extinguish trustee status

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of a town planning scheme under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, alleging violations of Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 of the Constitution, particularly due to lack of appeal mechanism and solatium.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, particularly Sections 32 and 53, violates Article 14 by not providing an appeal against certain orders while allowing it for others.
Whether the denial of solatium under the Act, unlike the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, renders it discriminatory and unconstitutional under Article 14.
Whether the absence of solatium and different compensation mechanism in town planning schemes violates the right to property under Article 31.
holdings: The absence of an appeal mechanism in some cases under the Act does not render it arbitrary or unconstitutional, as adequate remedies exist under Article 226 of the Constitution.

The denial of solatium under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, does not make it discriminatory, as the scheme operates as a comprehensive development plan distinct from land acquisition proceedings.

The compensation mechanism under the Act, though different from the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, does not violate Article 14 or Article 31, as it forms part of a 'package deal' for public benefit and does not result in illusory compensation.
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent and binding nature of Constitution Bench decisions
Doctrine of equality under Article 14 with permissible classification
Distinction between land acquisition and town planning schemes
Principle of adequate alternative remedy

card.dispute: Ram and Shyam Company (highest bidder in a mineral quarry auction) challenged the State of Haryana's decision to award the quarry rights to another party without giving it a chance to match the higher bid.
issues_decided: Whether the State can reject the highest bid in an auction and privately award the quarry rights without affording the highest bidder an opportunity to respond or improve its bid.
Whether principles of natural justice apply to administrative decisions involving the grant of public resources like mineral concessions.
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the writ petition on grounds of alternative remedies when no effective remedy existed.
holdings: When a higher private offer is received after an auction, the highest bidder must be given an opportunity to match or exceed it before the contract is awarded to another.
Principles of natural justice, including fair play and opportunity to be heard, apply to administrative decisions involving distribution of public resources.
The rejection of the highest bid without notice or opportunity to respond violates fairness and renders the grant of concession void, even if the State claims the bid was inadequate.
provisions: Haryana Minor Minerals (Vesting of Rights) Act, 1973
Punjab Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964, Rule 130(4)(2)
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Rule of fair procedure in administrative action
Public interest in transparent disposal of state resources

card.dispute: The sons of a vendor challenged the validity of a sale deed executed by their father on the same day he deposited money to acquire Bhumidari rights, but before receiving the certificate, claiming he had no title at the time of sale.
issues_decided: Whether the vendor had the right to execute the sale deed on the date of deposit of the amount under Section 134 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, prior to the issuance of the Bhumidari certificate under Section 137.
Whether the vendee was entitled to protection under Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act despite the vendor's lack of formal title at the time of sale.
holdings: The vendor did not acquire Bhumidari rights until the certificate was issued on October 30, 1961, and thus had no valid title on October 28 when the sale deed was executed.

Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act applies where a vendor erroneously represents having title and later acquires it; the transferee is protected if they acted on the representation in good faith.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 134
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 137
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel under Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act
Feeding the grant doctrine

card.dispute: Landlords filed eviction petitions against tenants for wilful default in rent payment; tenants argued their default was not wilful under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's failure to pay rent constituted a wilful default under Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
Whether the Explanation to the proviso in Section 10(2)(i), deeming default as wilful after two months' notice, is mandatory or directory
holdings: A tenant's default in rent payment is not automatically wilful merely because it persisted after two months' notice; the Controller must examine the facts to determine if the default was intentional or due to genuine hardship.
The Explanation to Section 10(2)(i) is not a conclusive presumption; it creates a rebuttable presumption, allowing the tenant to prove that the default was not wilful despite the notice.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Proviso and Explanation to Section 10(2)(i)
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption
Literal vs. purposive interpretation of statutory provisions
Principle of fairness in rent control legislation

card.dispute: The appellant (Sant Lal Jain) sued the respondent (Avtar Singh) for a mandatory injunction to vacate a shed after the licence period ended, while the respondent claimed ownership of the property and resisted eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for mandatory injunction to evict a licensee is maintainable after the licence has been revoked.
Whether a licensee who purchases the property from the original owner after the grant of licence can resist eviction.
Whether delay in filing the suit for mandatory injunction is fatal to the claim.
Whether the relationship between the parties was that of licensor-licensee or landlord-tenant.
holdings: A suit for mandatory injunction to evict a licensee after revocation of licence is maintainable if filed within a reasonable time.
A licensee who acquires title to the property from the original owner after the licence is granted cannot use that title to resist eviction; possession remains that of a licensee until surrendered.
Delay in filing the suit does not defeat the claim if it is not inordinate and the court should avoid multiplicity of suits.
The absence of rent and rent receipts confirms the relationship is that of licensor and licensee, not landlord and tenant.
provisions: East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
doctrines: Once a licensee, always a licensee
Mandatory injunction for recovery of possession from a licensee
No merger of lease or licence upon subsequent sale to licensee
Maintainability of suit for possession disguised as mandatory injunction

card.dispute: The landlady sued to evict the tenant for arrears of rent, while the tenant contested the suit on grounds of the applicability of rent control law and the quantum of rent.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for eviction was maintainable under the Uttar Pradesh Buildings Act given the property's location within the jurisdiction of the Act
Whether the tenant's deposit of rent at the rate claimed by the landlord was unconditional despite disputing the quantum of rent in the written statement
Whether the tenant was entitled to relief from eviction under Section 20(4) of the Act despite failing to prove the lower rent
holdings: The suit for eviction was not maintainable under Section 20(1) of the Act as none of the grounds under Section 20(2) were pleaded or established.
A deposit under Section 20(4) is not rendered conditional merely because the tenant disputes the rent amount in the written statement.
The tenant is entitled to discretionary relief under Section 20(4) if the deposit is made within the stipulated time, even if he fails to prove the lower rent claimed.
provisions: The Uttar Pradesh Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(1)
The Uttar Pradesh Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)
The Uttar Pradesh Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
The Uttar Pradesh Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
doctrines: Social legislation doctrine
Unconditional deposit under rent control law
Discretionary relief in eviction cases

card.dispute: Somatya Organics (India) Ltd. challenged the levy of stamp duty on a sale deed, arguing that the consideration should exclude a contingent liability under an equitable mortgage in favor of a bank.
issues_decided: Whether a contingent liability under an equitable mortgage forms part of the consideration for stamp duty under Section 24 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 when a property is sold subject to such mortgage.
Whether the sale in question was free from encumbrances or subject to an equitable mortgage affecting the computation of stamp duty.
holdings: A contingent liability that may become payable under an equitable mortgage is part of the consideration for the sale of immovable property and must be included for stamp duty under Section 24 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.

Where a sale is subject to an equitable mortgage and the purchaser assumes responsibility for the contingent liability, the maximum possible liability under the guarantee forms part of the true consideration for stamp duty purposes.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Article 23, Schedule I-B
doctrines: True consideration doctrine in stamp duty
Inclusion of contingent liabilities in valuation
Doctrine of substance over form in fiscal statutes

card.dispute: The dispute was between Satya Pal Gopal Das, who propounded a will, and Panchu Bala Dasi and others, who contested its validity, over the inheritance of Nrisingha Prosad Das's estate.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated June 21, 1946, executed by Nrisingha Prosad Das was validly executed and attested.
Whether the signatures of the attesting witnesses, Kali Dasi and Panchu Bala Dasi, on the will were genuine.
Whether the will was executed with the knowledge and approval of the testator.
holdings: The will was validly executed and registered, and the testator had full knowledge of its contents as he signed every page and admitted execution before the Sub-Registrar.
The signatures of Kali Dasi and Panchu Bala Dasi as attesting witnesses were genuine, despite contrary expert opinion, given the family's conduct and documentary evidence.
The long survival of the testator after execution without revocation, along with the consistent family conduct, supports the will's authenticity and dispels suspicion of forgery.
doctrines: Testamentary capacity and due execution
Presumption of validity of registered wills
Rejection of handwriting expert opinion in light of cogent circumstantial evidence

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant's heirs from a commercial shop after the tenant's death, arguing they were not entitled to protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the heirs of a deceased commercial tenant are entitled to protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 after the tenant's death.
Whether commercial tenancy rights are heritable in the absence of specific statutory restrictions.
holdings: The status of a tenant continues even after termination of contractual tenancy, and such tenant retains an estate or interest in the premises until eviction.
In the absence of any statutory restriction, tenancy rights in commercial premises are heritable and devolve on heirs under the ordinary law of succession.
doctrines: Heritability of tenancy rights
Statutory tenancy protection
Legislative competence to regulate inheritance of tenancy rights

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Special Land Acquisition Officer and landowners over the quantum of compensation payable for land acquired for railway and industrial purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the compensation for agricultural and non-agricultural converted land?
Whether the High Court erred in relying on a prior judgment that was subsequently altered while determining compensation for land acquired for industrial expansion?
Whether the compensation awarded for land used for industrial expansion was excessive given its location and market conditions?
holdings: The High Court's reduction of compensation to Rs. 15,000 per acre for agricultural land and Rs. 22,000 per acre for non-agricultural converted land was upheld as reasonable and based on proper assessment.
The High Court's reliance on a prior trial court judgment—later modified on appeal—as a basis for compensation was misplaced, as that judgment did not remain final.

Given that the acquired land was the only available plot for industrial expansion in the area, a compensation rate of Rs. 12.50 per square yard was just, though lower than the Rs. 20 per square yard awarded by the High Court.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Doctrine of finality of judgments in appellate review
Special advantage doctrine for land with unique locational value

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat fought against the tenants (respondents) over the validity of land acquisition proceedings, which the tenants challenged due to lack of individual notice under Section 4 and Section 9(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether individual notice under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 read with Rule 1 of the Bombay Rules (adopted by Gujarat) is mandatory for valid acquisition proceedings.
Whether failure to serve individual notice under Section 9(3) of the Act invalidates the acquisition proceedings, especially when the affected parties had actual knowledge.
holdings: Section 4(1) read with Rule 1 does not require personal notice to each interested party; publication in the Official Gazette and public notice at convenient places in the locality suffice to comply with the notice requirement.

The absence of individual notice under Section 9(3) does not invalidate acquisition proceedings if the affected parties had actual knowledge and the statutory public notice requirements were otherwise fulfilled.
provisions: Bombay Land Acquisition Rules, Rule 1 (adopted by Gujarat)
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Notice and opportunity to be heard (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan and others challenged the Calcutta High Court's jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition filed by Swaika Properties, a company based in Calcutta, against the acquisition of its land in Jaipur under the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959.
issues_decided: Whether the Calcutta High Court had territorial jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to entertain the writ petition when the cause of action arose in Rajasthan.
Whether the mere service of notice at the company's registered office in Calcutta constitutes a cause of action within the territorial limits of the Calcutta High Court.
Whether the ad-interim ex parte order passed by the Calcutta High Court was justified in the absence of territorial jurisdiction.
holdings: The cause of action for challenging land acquisition arises where the land is situated, not where notice is served; thus, the Calcutta High Court lacked territorial jurisdiction.
Service of notice is not an integral part of the cause of action unless the impugned action itself depends on such service; here, it did not.
Ad-interim ex parte orders should not be passed without first determining territorial jurisdiction, especially when they obstruct public development schemes.
provisions: Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act 1959, Section 52(1), Section 52(2), Section 52(5), Section 52(6), Section 55(2)
doctrines: Territorial jurisdiction under Article 226
Cause of action in writ petitions
Judicial restraint in granting ad-interim ex parte orders

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu and others contested whether the civil court had jurisdiction to determine the nature of land when a religious math sought a Ryotwari Patta under the Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, after the Settlement Officer denied the patta on grounds the land was communal (poromboke).
issues_decided: Whether the civil court's jurisdiction is barred under Section 64-C of the Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, when a ryot challenges the nature of land in a suit after being denied a Ryotwari Patta under Section 11 of the Act.
Whether the finality of a Settlement Officer's order under Section 64-C excludes civil court jurisdiction to determine title or nature of land based on long possession.
Whether Section 64-C, read with Section 3(16), ousts civil court jurisdiction in cases where the Settlement Officer decides the land is not ryoti but poromboke.
holdings: The civil court retains jurisdiction to adjudicate on the true nature and character of land even after a Settlement Officer refuses a Ryotwari Patta under Section 11, as such a decision is incidental and summary, not conclusive on title.

Section 64-C does not bar civil court jurisdiction because the Settlement Officer lacks power to grant full reliefs like injunctions or declarations based on possessory title, which a civil court can provide.

The finality given to a Settlement Officer’s order under Section 64-C does not imply ouster of civil court jurisdiction where the statute does not provide the officer with authority to resolve disputes about the nature of land in a manner equivalent to civil court remedies.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 11
Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 64-C
Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 3(16)(a), (b), (c)
Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 15
Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Proviso to Section 3(d)
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction requires clear statutory language and adequate alternative remedies.
Finality of administrative orders does not automatically exclude civil court jurisdiction if remedies are incomplete.
Incidental and summary determinations by revenue authorities are not binding in civil suits involving title and possession.

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra contested whether three members of a joint Hindu family—Narayan Rao, his mother Gangabai, and his wife Sulochanabai—were entitled to separate ceiling area units under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, after the death of a male coparcener whose share they inherited.
issues_decided: Whether a female heir automatically ceases to be a member of a Hindu joint family upon inheriting a share under Section 6 of the Ceiling Act
Whether members of a joint family who inherit shares due to a coparcener's death are entitled to separate ceiling area units
The correct interpretation of the proviso to Section 6 of the Ceiling Act regarding separate landholding and family membership
holdings: A female heir does not automatically cease to be a member of a joint Hindu family merely by inheriting a share in the coparcenary property; separation requires her volition.
Inheritance of a definite share in joint family property does not entitle a member to a separate ceiling area unit if the family continues to live jointly.
The proviso to Section 6 of the Ceiling Act excludes a member from family count only for the purpose of increasing the ceiling area, not for treating them as a separate unit altogether.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 2(11)
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 2(22)
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 6
doctrines: Legal fiction under Explanation I to Section 6 of the Ceiling Act
Continuity of joint family status despite fixed shares
Mitakshara coparcenary and inheritance principles

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan and Associated Stone Industries (Kotah) Limited disputed the validity of a mining monopoly agreement and whether the company had to compensate the state for stone excavated after the agreement was cancelled, versus whether the state had to refund royalties collected.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement granting monopoly quarrying rights was void and, if so, what compensation was due under Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act
Whether the High Court erred in directing a full refund of royalties without adjusting for the state's entitlement to compensation
Whether the claim for adjustment of royalties for the years 1948–49 and 1949–50 was barred by limitation
holdings: A void contract under Section 65 of the Contract Act requires mutual restitution: the company must compensate the state for stone excavated, and the state may claim reasonable royalty, not the company's net profits.

The High Court erred in ordering a full refund of royalties without deducting compensation due to the state; a reasonable royalty of Rs. 2 per 100 sq. ft. and compensation for monopoly rights must be set off.
The claim for adjustment of royalties for 1948–49 and 1949–50 was barred by limitation as the suit was filed after the cause of action arose on April 1, 1950.
doctrines: Doctrine of restitution under void contracts
Mutual restitution under Section 65
Limitation of legal claims

card.dispute: The State of Orissa and others fought with The Titaghur Paper Mills Company Ltd. and another over the validity of notifications imposing purchase tax on standing trees and bamboos agreed to be severed, and whether such transactions were taxable under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications imposing purchase tax on standing trees and bamboos agreed to be severed are ultra vires the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947 and Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution
Whether the impugned tax provisions amount to a tax on immovable property rather than on goods
Whether the use of the term 'supersession' in the notifications wipes out tax liabilities under previous notifications
Whether the bamboo and timber contracts constitute sale of goods or creation of an interest in immovable property
holdings: The notifications imposing purchase tax on standing trees and bamboos agreed to be severed are valid under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, as the taxable event is the purchase of goods, not an agreement to sever.
The tax is on the sale of goods (timber/bamboos after severance), not on immovable property, and thus within the state's taxing power under Entry 54, List II.
The term 'supersession' in the notifications means repeal and replacement, not erasure of past tax liabilities; prior obligations remain enforceable.
Bamboo contracts create a profit à prendre, an interest in immovable property, and thus cannot be taxed as sale of goods; such taxation would be ultra vires the state's power.
doctrines: Doctrine of permissible classification under Article 14
Doctrine of severability
Doctrine of precedent (larger bench prevails under Article 141)
Doctrine of complete justice under Article 142
Principle of statutory interpretation based on transactional reality

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal levied cess on the sale price of percolated water sold by Ghusick & Muslia Collieries Ltd; the company challenged the levy claiming it was not part of mine profits.
issues_decided: Whether the sale price of water pumped out from a coal mine constitutes 'annual net profit derived from the mine' under Section 6 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880.
Whether casual income from the sale of mine water can be excluded from cess assessment.
holdings: Income from the sale of water pumped out of a coal mine is part of the annual net profit from the mine and is liable to cess under Section 6 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880.
The nature of income as 'casual' does not exempt it from cess; Section 6 does not distinguish between regular and casual income if derived from mine operations.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Inclusion of ancillary income in mining profits

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer challenged the High Court's decision invalidating land acquisition notifications due to delayed public notice in the locality compared to gazette publication.
issues_decided: Whether the delay of over 40 days between publication of the Section 4(1) notification in the Official Gazette and public notice in the locality invalidates the notification under the amended law.
Whether the Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, particularly Section 2, applies retrospectively to notifications issued before its enactment.
Whether a retrospective amendment that invalidates otherwise valid acquisitions can be sustained.
holdings: A public notice under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act must be given within 40 days of gazette publication in Andhra Pradesh, as mandated by the 1983 Amendment Act deemed effective from 12 September 1975.
The retrospective application of the amended Section 4(1) is valid and binding, regardless of whether it invalidates prior acquisitions that were lawful at the time.
The amendment in Section 4(1) clarifies the time limit for public notice and does not conflict with the judicial principle in Deepak Pahwa’s case, as it presumes a break in continuity beyond 40 days.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, Section 2
Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, Section 3(1)
Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, Section 1(3)
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes
Presumption of continuity in administrative action
Doctrine of legislative validation with retrospective effect

card.dispute: The Collector and District Magistrate challenged the High Court's decision invalidating a land acquisition notification, which was sought by the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan to acquire land where a cinema theatre was proposed, allegedly to prevent the theatre's construction rather than for a genuine public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition proceedings were vitiated by legal mala fides due to extraneous considerations
Whether non-publication of the notification and corrigendum in the locality invalidated the acquisition proceedings under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the acquisition required compliance with Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, as the land was being acquired for a company/society
holdings: Acquisition of land for a public purpose is invalid if the real motive is extraneous or irrelevant, such as preventing a cinema theatre's construction, even if cloaked as a public purpose; this constitutes legal mala fides.

Non-publication of the notification and its corrigendum in the locality does not automatically vitiate proceedings if no prejudice is shown, but the court need not decide this as the acquisition was already invalid due to mala fides.
The court declined to rule on the applicability of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, as the acquisition was already invalidated on grounds of mala fides.
provisions: U.P. Cinematograph Rules, 1951, Rule 3 and Rule 7(2)
doctrines: Legal mala fides
Colourable exercise of power
Fraud on power
Public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the inclusion of land held by his minor sons and wife in the calculation of his landholding for ceiling purposes under the Pondicherry Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the statutory definition of 'family' under the Pondicherry Land Reforms Act includes minor sons and wife regardless of a prior partition under Hindu law.
Whether property held by a wife from Sridhanam income and property allotted to minor sons in a pre-act partition can be included in the family's holding for ceiling limits.
holdings: The term 'family' in the Act refers to a statutory unit comprising a person, their spouse, and minor sons and unmarried daughters, irrespective of partition or joint ownership under Hindu law.
Properties held separately by minor sons and a wife using Sridhanam income must be included in the family's total holding for determining ceiling limits under the Act.
provisions: The Pondicherry Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1973, Section 2(10)
The Pondicherry Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1973, Section 4
The Pondicherry Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1973, Section 7 Explanation IV
The Pondicherry Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1973, Section 22(1)
doctrines: Statutory definition prevails over personal law concepts
Pooling of family holdings for land ceiling purposes

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds including non-user of the rented land for over six months; the tenant resisted, citing payment of rent and prior sub-letting.
issues_decided: Whether non-use of the premises for any purpose for over six months without reasonable cause makes a tenant liable to eviction under Section 13(1)(k) of the Bombay Rents Act, even if rent is paid as per a contractual stipulation.
Whether construction of superstructures on the land before the tenancy constitutes continued 'user' of the premises.
Whether a tenant can contract out of statutory eviction provisions through a private agreement.
holdings: Non-user of the premises for any purpose for more than six months without reasonable cause renders a tenant liable to eviction under Section 13(1)(k), regardless of rent payment as per contract.
The mere existence of pre-existing superstructures does not constitute 'user' of the land during the tenancy if no active use is made for the purpose for which it was let.
Parties cannot contract out of statutory tenancy control laws; private agreements cannot override public policy underlying rent control legislation.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(k)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to effectuate legislative intent
Public policy against contracting out of rent control laws
Non-user as ground for eviction in rent control statutes

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bonafide personal necessity, but the tenant argued that the landlord had other suitable accommodation and disentitled herself by letting it out for higher rent during the proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fide personal necessity for eviction under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 must continue to exist until the final disposal of the case.
Whether the landlord can be said to have 'no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation' if she chose not to occupy vacant premises in her own building during the eviction proceedings.
holdings: The landlord’s bona fide need for accommodation must exist not only at the time of filing the petition but also at the time of final disposal by the appellate court; otherwise, the eviction cannot be granted.

A landlord who has reasonably suitable accommodation available and chooses not to occupy it, but instead lets it out for higher income, is disentitled to evict the tenant on grounds of personal necessity.
doctrines: Subsequent events rule in eviction cases
Harmonious construction of rent control laws
Bona fide requirement vs. self-induced disentitlement
Balancing of landlord and tenant rights under beneficial legislation

card.dispute: The dispute was between two widows of Bhikhabhai over partition and possession of his immovable properties, with the second wife claiming adverse possession to bar the first wife's claim.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by Bai Jadav was barred by limitation
Whether Bai Reva had acquired title by adverse possession for a period of twelve years
holdings: The suit was not barred by limitation as Bai Reva did not prove continuous and hostile possession excluding Bai Jadav for twelve years prior to the suit.
Mere acts such as mutation, insurance of property, or payment of maintenance do not constitute adverse possession or ouster of co-heirs in a joint property.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Ouster by clear and hostile acts
Burden of proof in adverse possession claims

card.dispute: The landlord sued to recover possession of a non-residential property, challenging the petitioner's claim of tenancy through a will bequeathed by the original tenant, who was not a family member carrying on business with her.
issues_decided: Whether a statutory tenancy right under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 can be bequeathed by will to a person not belonging to the tenant's family and not engaged in the business with the tenant.
Whether section 15(1) of the Act prohibits testamentary disposition of tenancy rights.
holdings: A tenancy right protected under section 5(11)(c)(ii) of the Bombay Rent Control Act cannot be bequeathed by will to a person who is not a member of the tenant’s family carrying on business, trade, or storage in the premises at the time of death.

Section 15(1) of the Act, which prohibits tenants from assigning or transferring their interest in the premises, includes and prohibits testamentary dispositions such as bequests to strangers not contemplated by the Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(c)(ii)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15(1)
doctrines: Statutory tenancy is personal and not heritable beyond statutory exceptions
