holdings: The market value of land for compensation must reflect what a willing buyer would pay to a willing seller; concessional government rates to promote industry do not represent market value.
Past purchase price of land is irrelevant when current market value has appreciably increased due to development in the vicinity, especially near industrial areas.
Where identical or similar land in the same area was awarded higher compensation, denying the same rate to adjacent landowners creates an anomaly and is unjustified without material distinction.
doctrines: Market value determination in land acquisition
Principle of equal treatment for similarly situated landowners
Rejection of concessional pricing as benchmark for market value

card.dispute: The tenants, heirs of a lessee, fought to purchase the leased land from the landlords after being sued for ejectment, claiming rights under the Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, 1921.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants were entitled to the benefit of Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, 1921, to compel the landlord to sell the demised land.
Whether the tenants were in occupation of the land and required it for 'convenient enjoyment' as required under Section 9 of the Act.
Whether the statutory right under Section 9 is an absolute right or a discretionary equitable privilege.
holdings: Section 9 of the Act grants a statutory but not absolute right to purchase land, which is equitable in nature and depends on the tenant's need for convenient enjoyment of the property.
A tenant must be in actual occupation of the land or using the superstructure for residence or business to claim the benefit of Section 9.
If a tenant does not require the land for convenient enjoyment, the court may reject the application and allow ejectment with compensation for structures.
The court must determine the minimum extent of land necessary for convenient enjoyment before directing a sale.
provisions: Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, 1921, Section 3
Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, 1921, Section 9
doctrines: Equitable privilege doctrine
Convenient enjoyment test
Statutory right versus property interest

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased allottee challenged the cancellation of an allotment of excess land, claiming entitlement after depositing payment, while the government argued the land had already been transferred to Punjab under a package deal and could not be sold by the Central Government.
issues_decided: Whether the Managing Officer had jurisdiction to allow purchase of excess land after it was transferred to the Punjab Government under the package deal.
Whether the Chief Settlement Commissioner was competent to cancel the allotment of excess land under Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
Whether the allotment could be validated despite the land having vested in the Punjab Government prior to the sale.
holdings: The Managing Officer lacked jurisdiction to permit purchase of the excess land because it had already been transferred to the Punjab Government under the package deal and was no longer in the Central Government's compensation pool.

The Chief Settlement Commissioner is empowered under Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, to cancel allotments of excess land, even after proprietary rights were conferred.
An allotment of package deal land made after vesting in the State Government is void ab initio and cannot be validated, as only the Punjab Government could deal with such land after April 1, 1961.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 33
Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Rules, 1976, Rule 4
Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Rules, 1976, Clause 8
doctrines: Jurisdictional limitation of administrative authorities
Vesting of property and its legal consequences
Doctrine of competence of appellate and revisional authorities
Void ab initio transactions

card.dispute: The former ruler of Patadi State contested whether two temples he managed were public religious trusts subject to state regulation or private family properties.
issues_decided: Whether the temples of Shri Dwarakadhishji and Shri Trikamrayji are 'public temples' under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950
Whether the properties attached to the temples constitute a public religious trust
Whether the burden of proof lies on the Charity Commissioner to establish a public endowment
holdings: A temple is public if there is evidence of dedication to public worship, indicated by long-standing public access, participation in rituals, and offerings accepted as a right.
Properties attached to a temple form a public religious trust if temple income is separately managed and used for upkeep and public benefit, not merged with private funds.
The burden is on the party claiming private status to disprove public character; continuous public use and state support indicate a public trust.
doctrines: Dedication by conduct
Mixed question of fact and law
Presumption of public character from long-standing public use
Management control not determinative of private character

card.dispute: Landlords sought eviction of tenants under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, for demolition and reconstruction, while tenants challenged the constitutional validity of key provisions.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, permitting eviction for demolition and reconstruction, violates Article 14 or 19(1)(f) of the Constitution
Whether Section 16(2) of the Act, granting exemption from rent control for five years after reconstruction, is arbitrary and discriminatory
Whether the absence of a right for tenants to be re-inducted into reconstructed premises renders the provisions unreasonable
holdings: Section 14(1)(b) is constitutionally valid as it requires a bona fide need for reconstruction, and courts must assess the totality of facts to prevent misuse.
Section 16(2) is not arbitrary or discriminatory; the five-year exemption incentivizes construction and balances landlord and tenant interests.
The lack of a statutory right to re-induction of tenants after reconstruction does not make the law unreasonable, as the provision serves public interest by encouraging new housing.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(1)(b)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 16(2)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 30(ii)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement doctrine
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Balancing of private rights and public interest in rent control laws
Incentive-based regulatory framework

card.dispute: Mathew and Kuruvila disputed over the ownership of Kadalat Estate, with Varghese claiming specific performance of an earlier sale agreement assigned to him.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in decreeing specific performance of the agreement Ex. A1 in favour of Varghese?
Whether Chettiar had waived his rights under the agreement Ex. A1, thereby affecting the assignee’s right to enforce it?
Whether the execution of lease and sale agreements in Mathew's name (Ex. B43 and B44) was with the consent of Chettiar and intended to facilitate, not defeat, the transaction under Ex. A1?
holdings: The High Court erred in granting specific performance because Chettiar had waived his rights under Ex. A1, and Varghese, as assignee, could not enforce a right that no longer existed.

The conduct and pleadings of the parties, especially Varghese and Kuruvila, implied that Ex. B43 and Ex. B44 were executed with Chettiar’s consent to facilitate closing the Ex. A1 transaction, not to defraud him.
Courts must consider the plaintiff’s motive and equitable principles under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and not grant specific performance where it would be unjust or oppressive.
doctrines: Waiver of contractual rights
Equitable discretion in specific performance
Assignee cannot have better title than assignor

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Ram Sarup Gupta, who purchased the property, sued to recover possession from a school that had been using it under a claimed irrevocable license, while the school argued the property was permanently donated for educational purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the license granted by the property owner to the school was irrevocable despite being oral and undocumented.
Whether the construction of permanent structures by the school on the property rendered the license irrevocable under the Indian Easement Act.
Whether the karta of a joint Hindu family could validly grant such a license without consent of other co-sharers, particularly minor sons.
holdings: An oral license to use property for running a school becomes irrevocable if the licensee acts upon it by constructing permanent buildings, as per Section 60(b) of the Indian Easement Act.
The conduct of the parties and surrounding circumstances, including the donor's letter and the school's reliance, can establish an implied irrevocable license even without a written agreement.

The karta of a joint family may grant a permanent license for pious or charitable purposes benefiting the family’s legacy, and such act is not voidable for lack of consent of co-sharers, especially with their acquiescence.
doctrines: Doctrine of irrevocable license under Section 60(b) of the Indian Easement Act
Doctrine of implied license from conduct and circumstances
Doctrine of equitable estoppel in property licensing
Doctrine of family benefit in joint Hindu family property management

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the West Bengal government's decision to allot land from a zoological garden to the Taj Group for constructing a Five-Star Hotel, alleging ecological harm and procedural impropriety.
issues_decided: Whether the government's decision to allot land for a Five-Star Hotel violated environmental protection principles under the Constitution.
Whether the decision was arbitrary or unreasonable under Article 14 and violated public interest.
Whether the principles of natural justice were violated by not hearing interested parties before the allotment.
Whether the documents relied upon by the courts below were admissible despite objections to authenticity.
holdings: The Supreme Court held that the government's policy decision to promote tourism through the hotel project did not violate environmental principles, especially since adequate safeguards for ecology were provided.
The allotment was not arbitrary or unreasonable, as it followed a transparent process and served public interest by boosting tourism without compromising the zoo's integrity.
The principles of natural justice were not violated, as no statutory requirement existed to hear interested parties before such policy decisions, and no malafides were alleged.

Documents relied upon by the High Court, including cabinet memoranda, were admissible in appeal under Article 136, and objections to their authenticity could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
provisions: The Bengal Public Parks Act, 1904, Sections 3 and 4
West Bengal Land Management Manual, 1977, Paragraphs 165, 166, 167
doctrines: Public Interest Litigation
Principle of Natural Justice
Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness (Article 14)
Judicial Restraint in Policy Matters
Evidentiary Admissibility in Appeals under Article 136

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for sub-letting the premises without written consent, while the tenant argued there was no sub-letting or that it was done with implied permission.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant sub-let the premises without the landlord's written consent under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether mere permission or acquiescence by the landlord amounts to valid consent for sub-letting
Whether the tenant parted with legal possession, thereby constituting sub-letting
holdings: Sub-letting without the landlord's written consent violates Sections 14(1) proviso (b) and 16(2) and (3) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, making the tenant liable to eviction.
Consent to sub-letting must be in writing and specific; mere permission or acquiescence does not satisfy the statutory requirement.
Legal possession was transferred to the sub-lessee, evidenced by the company’s exclusive use and the official liquidator taking possession, amounting to sub-letting.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1) proviso (b)
doctrines: Requirement of written consent for sub-letting
Parting with legal possession as essential for sub-letting
Waiver of statutory rights not permitted
Distinction between licence and lease

card.dispute: The appellant wife and her husband were estranged, and he allegedly gave her land in lieu of maintenance; later, he sold the land to respondents, leading to a dispute over whether she had become its absolute owner under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant became the absolute owner of the land given to her by her husband in lieu of maintenance under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether Section 14(2) of the Act excludes property allotted in lieu of maintenance from becoming full ownership
holdings: A Hindu woman who is given property in lieu of maintenance acquires a limited interest in it, which under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, ripens into full ownership.

Section 14(2) does not apply where property is allotted in recognition of a pre-existing right like maintenance, as the instrument merely recognizes that right and does not create a restricted estate anew.
doctrines: Ripening of limited interest into full ownership under Section 14(1)
Recognition of pre-existing rights in property allocation
Statutory abolition of limited ownership for Hindu females

card.dispute: Landlords sought eviction of a tenant for rent default and bona fide need, which the High Court reversed in second appeal, prompting a challenge in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact on rent default in second appeal
Whether the High Court could overturn concurrent findings on the landlord's bona fide need for eviction
Whether the tenant's remittance to an old address constituted valid tender of rent
Whether the landlord's need was vitiated by the alleged availability of other vacant premises
holdings: The High Court could not interfere in second appeal on factual findings of rent default supported by concurrent judgments below.
Concurrent findings on the landlord's bona fide need, based on business disruption and family requirements, cannot be overturned without legal error.
Remittance to an address known to be incorrect does not constitute valid tender of rent, especially when the tenant had knowledge of the change.
The defense that the landlord had other vacant premises to meet the need fails where no evidence supports such availability.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1977, Section 12(1)(c)
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule in second appeal
Bona fide need for personal occupation under rent control law
Valid tender of rent requires proper knowledge and address
Judicial restraint in overturning findings of fact in second appeal

card.dispute: The landlords sought to enforce a decree for possession against the tenant based on a compromise and arbitration agreement where the tenant had allegedly surrendered tenancy, but the tenant resisted on the grounds that the surrender was invalid and the decree violated rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether a tenancy can be validly surrendered even if physical possession is not handed over, through mutual agreement and conduct.
Whether a tenant is estopped from challenging a decree based on an arbitration award if no objection was raised at the time of decree, particularly on grounds of violation of rent control law.
Whether the arbitration award and subsequent decree circumvented the provisions of Clause 13 of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949.
holdings: A tenancy can be surrendered by mutual agreement and conduct, even without physical delivery of possession, if the parties intend to end the tenancy and create a new arrangement.

A tenant who fails to object to a decree based on an arbitration award at the time of its confirmation, especially on jurisdictional grounds, is estopped from raising such objections later during execution.

An arbitration award that recognizes surrender of tenancy and provides for continued possession on new terms does not violate rent control laws, as the original tenancy has ended and no new tenancy is created.
provisions: C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13
doctrines: Surrender of lease by operation of law
Constructive res judicata
Estoppel by conduct

card.dispute: The State Government withdrew land acquisition proceedings after a long delay, and the landowner challenged the withdrawal as mala fide, seeking mandatory direction to complete the acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government can unilaterally withdraw acquisition proceedings under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act after issuing a notification under Section 4.
Whether the withdrawal of acquisition proceedings after a long lapse of time and after encroachments had occurred is mala fide or arbitrary.
Whether the landowner is entitled to a hearing before the withdrawal of acquisition proceedings.
Whether the State can be compelled to acquire land despite the land becoming unsuitable for the intended purpose due to encroachments.
holdings: The State Government has the unfettered power under Section 48 to withdraw acquisition proceedings at any stage before possession, without assigning reasons or affording a hearing.
The withdrawal of acquisition proceedings is valid even after a long delay and does not become mala fide merely because it was done after a writ petition was filed.
The landowner does not acquire any vested right upon issuance of a Section 4 notification, and the State is not obligated to protect the land from encroachments.

The State cannot be compelled to acquire land if the purpose of acquisition has become unfeasible due to large-scale encroachments, especially where eviction would pose serious social and administrative challenges.
doctrines: No vested right arises on issuance of notification under Section 4
Power of withdrawal under Section 48 is unilateral and discretionary
Principle of feasibility of acquisition purpose
Mala fide not presumed from delay or subsequent action

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant challenged the eviction order granted to the landlord-respondent under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, arguing that the landlord ceased to be the 'owner' after the lease of the land was cancelled by the DDA.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord remained an 'owner' under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act despite the cancellation of the lease by the DDA?
Whether the landlord was entitled to seek eviction for bona fide personal use when the property was built on leased land?
holdings: The term 'owner' in Section 14(1)(e) does not require absolute ownership; a person with leasehold rights and possession, especially where lease restoration is pending, qualifies as an owner.

The landlord did not cease to be an owner merely because of a procedural cancellation of lease, especially when proceedings were stayed and restoration was contemplated upon fulfillment of formalities.
doctrines: Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Doctrine of possession and beneficial ownership in leasehold properties
Principle that procedural cancellation without actual dispossession does not extinguish ownership for statutory purposes

card.dispute: The eldest son, who succeeded as ruler, challenged the validity of his father's gift and will in favor of a younger son, claiming the father lacked power to alienate properties of an impartible estate governed by primogeniture.
issues_decided: Whether the holder of an impartible estate governed by primogeniture can alienate estate properties by gift or will.
Whether a family custom existed that prohibited the ruler from alienating the estate by gift or will.
holdings: The holder of an impartible estate can alienate it by gift or will, even if such disposition defeats the right of survivorship of junior family members, unless restricted by family custom or tenure conditions.
Mere absence of prior alienations does not prove a custom of inalienability; positive evidence is required, and correspondence over quantum of maintenance does not establish such a custom.
doctrines: Rule of primogeniture in impartible estates
Right of survivorship under Hindu law
Doctrine of family custom requiring positive proof
Alienability of impartible estates by will or gift

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of the tenant for constructing permanent unauthorized structures and changing the use of the premises, which the tenant contested.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere under Article 227 with concurrent factual findings of lower courts regarding the permanency of structures erected by a tenant.

Whether the structures erected by the tenant were permanent in nature within the meaning of clause (p) of Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 13(1)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1974.
Whether the tenant had changed the user of the premises in violation of the tenancy agreement and the Rent Act.
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere under Article 227 with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless the findings are perverse, based on no evidence, or involve a legal error apparent on record.

Structures erected by a tenant, including lofts and rooms with pillars sunk into the floor, can be deemed permanent depending on the degree of annexation, removability, and purpose, and such a finding by the lower courts is sustainable if plausible.
A change in the user of the premises, such as allowing another company to operate from the premises while the original tenant ceased operations, constitutes unauthorized use justifying eviction.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 108(clause p)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1974, Section 13(1)(b)
doctrines: Limited scope of High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Doctrine of perversity in factual findings
Doctrine of change of user in landlord-tenant law
Test of permanency of structures under tenancy law

card.dispute: The Union Bank of India appealed against a High Court order directing it to first exhaust remedies against the mortgaged property and principal debtor before executing a decree against the guarantor, Manku Narayana.
issues_decided: Whether the bank could execute the decree against the guarantor without first proceeding against the mortgaged property and the principal debtor.
Whether the High Court was justified in directing the bank to exhaust remedies against the principal debtor and mortgaged property before proceeding against the guarantor.
holdings: Since a portion of the decreed amount was secured by mortgage, the bank must first proceed against the mortgaged property before executing the decree against the guarantor.

The appeal was dismissed initially due to lack of evidence that remedies against the mortgaged property and principal debtor were pursued, but the matter was remanded to the High Court to allow the bank to prove such steps were taken.
doctrines: Exhaustion of remedies
Independent liability of a guarantor
Priority of security in mortgage enforcement

card.dispute: The landlord, Smt. Surjit Kaur, sought eviction of tenant Vinod Kumar Arora from a hall in her house, alleging bona fide need for residence and unauthorized change of user to non-residential use, which the tenant contested.
issues_decided: Whether the concurrent findings of the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority dismissing the eviction petition were binding on the revisional court under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether the tenant could resist eviction on the ground that the premises were being used solely for a clinic, thus falling outside the scope of residential eviction under Section 13(3)(a)(i)(a).
Whether the landlord was precluded from seeking eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement after obtaining an earlier eviction order against another tenant in the same property.
holdings: Concurrent findings of statutory authorities are not binding on a revisional court if they are based on non-existent or fictitious material and suffer from errors of law and fact.

A tenant cannot rely on findings of non-residential use to resist eviction when those findings are vitiated, and the premises were originally let for residential use, especially where the tenant changed the user without the Rent Controller’s consent.
The second proviso to Section 13(3)(a) does not bar a landlord from seeking eviction of multiple tenants on the same ground of bona fide need, especially when proceedings are initiated concurrently.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 11
East Punjab Rent Restriction (Chandigarh Amendment) Act, 1982
doctrines: Binding nature of concurrent findings of fact
Doctrine of change of user without statutory consent
Revisional jurisdiction and error of law apparent on record
Mixed questions of law and fact not being pure questions of law

card.dispute: The Fairfield Cooperative Housing Society sued licensees A.V.R. & Co. to recover possession of a flat allegedly occupied without the society's consent and in breach of its bye-laws, while the licensees challenged the jurisdiction of the cooperative court and the constitutional validity of Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute over possession of a flat falls within the jurisdiction of the cooperative court under Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960
Whether Section 91(b) of the Act is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution
holdings: A dispute concerning possession of a flat by non-members claiming through a member, in violation of society bye-laws, pertains to the business and management of the cooperative society and falls within Section 91(1)(b) of the Act.
Section 91(b) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act does not violate Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution as it creates a reasonable classification with nexus to the object of the Act.
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Harmonious construction of statutes

card.dispute: The Administrator General of West Bengal challenged the inadequate compensation awarded for land, building, tree growth, and change of residence in a land acquisition case initiated in 1959.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of the building was correctly assessed by the Land Acquisition Officer.
Whether the tree growth on the acquired land could be valued separately on horticultural or timber value grounds.
Whether the appellant was entitled to enhanced solatium and interest under the U.P. Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1972 and the Central Amendment Act, 1984.
Whether a new plea for compensation for change of residence under Section 23(1)(fifthly) could be raised for the first time in appeal before the Supreme Court.
holdings: The market value of the building must reflect its quality and replacement cost; a rough estimate of Rs.2,00,000 was awarded after considering depreciation and construction costs as of 1959.
Tree growth cannot be valued on horticultural yield when land is valued for building potential, but timber or salvage value may be awarded; Rs.7,500 was granted as lumpsum compensation.
The question of applicability of enhanced solatium and interest under the 1972 and 1984 amendments was left open pending the decision in Bhag Singh v. U.T. Chandigarh.
A new ground of compensation for change of residence under Section 23(1)(fifthly) cannot be raised for the first time in a Special Leave Petition without being urged before the High Court.
doctrines: Principle of market value determination based on comparable sales and replacement cost
Rule against independent valuation of tree growth where land is valued for development potential
Doctrine of prospective versus retrospective application of remedial statutes
Prohibition on raising new grounds for the first time in Supreme Court under Article 136

card.dispute: Shareholders of Swadeshi Cotton Mills challenged the constitutional validity of the Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd. (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, alleging it confiscated shares and violated their rights under Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) without public purpose or compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of shares in subsidiary companies under the Act violated Article 14 by lacking public purpose and being arbitrary
Whether the acquisition infringed Article 19(1)(g) by restricting the right to carry on trade without reasonable restriction
Whether the Act amounted to confiscation due to non-payment of separate compensation for the shares
Whether the petitioners could re-agitate issues already decided by the Supreme Court in a prior judgment
holdings: The acquisition served a public purpose as mandated by Article 39(b) and (c), and the Act's preamble and scheme confirm this, negating any arbitrariness under Article 14.
The restriction on the right to carry on business was reasonable and justified by the State's duty to secure equitable distribution of resources under the Directive Principles.
No separate compensation was required for the shares as they were encumbered by liabilities, and the overall compensation framework under Section 8 satisfied constitutional requirements.
The petitioners were bound by the earlier Supreme Court decision in Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd., and could not collaterally challenge issues already decided, under Article 141.
provisions: Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd. (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 3
Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd. (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 4
Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd. (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 8
doctrines: Doctrine of Public Purpose in property acquisition
Doctrine of Res Judicata under Article 141
Doctrine of Binding Precedent (stare decisis)
Doctrine of Reasonable Restriction under Article 19(1)(g)
Doctrine of Non-confiscation with compensation

card.dispute: A tenant challenged the eviction order passed in favor of a landlord who sought possession of a tenanted property for his own use, claiming that the second application for eviction was barred under procedural rules.
issues_decided: Whether the second application for eviction under the 1972 Rent Act was barred by Rule 18(1) due to a prior rejection under the 1947 Rent Act within six months of the new Act's commencement
Whether two applications for eviction on the ground of personal requirement, made under different rent control laws, constitute the same ground for invoking Rule 18(1)
Whether partial eviction is permissible under Section 21(1) of the 1972 Rent Act
Whether the tenant could resist eviction on grounds of hardship or unsuitability of alternative accommodation
holdings: Rule 18(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Rules, 1972 is directory, not mandatory, and does not automatically bar a second application if material changes in circumstances have occurred.
Even if two applications under different rent laws are based on the same ground of personal need, Rule 18(1) does not apply where there is a significant time gap and changed conditions.
Section 21(1) of the 1972 Rent Act permits partial eviction, allowing the landlord to recover a specified part of the tenanted premises.
The tenant’s hardship is outweighed by the landlord’s greater hardship when alternative accommodation is available for the tenant’s business, and access to essential facilities can be arranged.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 18(1)
doctrines: Directory vs mandatory interpretation of statutory rules
Presumption as to prior findings under procedural rules
Principle of changed circumstances overriding prior determinations
Balancing of hardship in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of their land by the Haryana government through HUDA for industrial development, alleging procedural defects, profiteering, and discrimination.
issues_decided: Whether the substance of the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was adequately published in the locality.
Whether the acquisition for industrial development served a public purpose or was a profiteering venture.
Whether the government failed to apply its mind to its policy of restraint in acquiring agricultural land.
Whether the landowners were discriminated against by selective acquisition of their land.
holdings: Publication of the substance of the notification under Section 4(1) is a question of fact, and the affidavit evidence confirmed it was published, as shown by filed objections.
Development and industrialisation constitute a public purpose; mere possibility of profit does not invalidate acquisition if public purpose exists.
The government is not precluded from acquiring agricultural land for development; balancing agricultural and industrial needs is a policy decision within executive discretion.
Selective acquisition of land suitable for public purpose does not amount to discrimination against landowners whose land was acquired.
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Distinction between pleadings in civil suits and writ petitions regarding evidence
Judicial non-interference in policy decisions involving development and land use
Requirement to substantiate legal points with factual pleadings in writ proceedings

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the landlord's unilateral cancellation of a deed assigning rent benefits to his grandsons and their mother, arguing that the suit involved a question of title beyond the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court.
issues_decided: Whether the deed dated 8th December 1966 transferred a right in immovable property or merely permitted the collection of rent.
Whether the subsequent unilateral cancellation of the deed by the landlord was valid.
Whether the suit involved a question of title such that the Small Causes Court was required to return the plaint under Section 23 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act.
Whether the relationship of landlord and tenant continued after the alleged transfer and cancellation of rent rights.
holdings: A deed granting someone the right to collect rent does not amount to a transfer of immovable property if it only permits the use of rent for maintenance.
Where a plea about the transfer of rent rights affects the landlord's title to sue for rent or eviction, the issue goes to the root of title and is not merely incidental.
Section 23 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act requires the court to return the plaint when the resolution of title is necessary for complete justice between the parties.
If the alleged transfer of rent rights is upheld, the landlord-tenant relationship may be severed, making the suit non-cognizable by a Small Causes Court.
provisions: Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, Section 23
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1977, Section 30(2)
doctrines: Jurisdictional bar of Small Causes Courts in title disputes
Res judicata in relation to findings on title by courts of limited jurisdiction
Doctrine of complete justice requiring appropriate forum for title determination

card.dispute: The Calcutta Youth Front and others alleged that state authorities and lessees committed contempt of court by constructing structures above an underground market in violation of Supreme Court orders meant to preserve Satyanarayan Park.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of covered staircases (bunkers) and a four-storeyed service block above the underground market violated the terms of the Court's order.
Whether the alleged encroachment covered a substantial portion of the park, thereby breaching the Court's directive to maintain it as a green space.
Whether the actions of the respondents amounted to criminal contempt of court under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
holdings: The construction of bunkers over staircases leading to the underground market was necessary for the functioning of the central air-conditioning system and was in accordance with the sanctioned plan and court-anticipated structures.

The four-storeyed service block for staff quarters occupied less area than the previous structure and was permitted under the licensing agreement and court-approved plans, thus not violating any court order.

There was no contempt of court as the constructions were authorized, within the sanctioned plan, and did not substantially encroach upon the park area; the petition was dismissed as unfounded and vexatious.
doctrines: Judicial notice
Contempt by breach of court order
Doctrine of good faith implementation of court-sanctioned development projects

card.dispute: The lessor sought to eject the sub-lessee (petitioner) after terminating the lease with the lessee, without issuing a separate notice to the sub-lessee.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy continued for a further five years after the original term or became a month-to-month lease in absence of a registered instrument?
Whether a notice terminating the lease served only on the lessee is valid for ejecting the sub-lessee?
Whether the sub-lessee must be made a party to the ejectment suit when the lease is validly terminated with the lessee?
holdings: In absence of a registered instrument, a lease cannot be extended for a fixed term; it continues as a month-to-month tenancy under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act.
A notice of termination served on the lessee is sufficient to end the sub-lessee’s right to possession; no separate notice to the sub-lessee is required.
A sub-lessee can be evicted in execution of a decree against the lessee if the lease is validly terminated, even if not impleaded in the suit.
doctrines: Notice to quit must be construed contextually based on the parties' knowledge and facts
Doctrine of holding over
Principle of harmonious construction of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant, Dharma Shamrao Agalawe, challenged the right of Pandurang, adopted by his deceased brother's widow, to claim a share in the joint family property that had devolved on him as the sole surviving coparcener.
issues_decided: Whether joint family property ceases to be joint when it devolves on a sole surviving coparcener.

Whether a person adopted by a widow after the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 came into force can claim a share in joint family property that had devolved on a sole coparcener prior to adoption.
Whether clause (c) of the proviso to Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 bars a suit for partition by such an adoptee.
holdings: Joint family property does not cease to be joint family property merely because it comes into the hands of a sole surviving coparcener; it retains its character as long as the coparcenary structure can be revived.

An adopted son by a widow becomes a coparcener in the joint family and is entitled to claim a share in the joint family property, even if the property had devolved on a sole coparcener before adoption.
Clause (c) of the proviso to Section 12 does not apply because no 'vesting' of property in the sole coparcener occurs by survivorship that could be 'divested' by a subsequent adoption.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 14
doctrines: Survivorship in Mitakshara coparcenary
Continuity of joint family property
Effect of adoption by a widow under Hindu law
No divestment doctrine under Section 12(c) proviso

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant from a shop on grounds of personal necessity, but the tenant contested the landlord's ownership, which was central to the claim.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could reverse a concurrent finding of fact by lower courts in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code.
Whether the plaintiff established ownership of the property as required under Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
holdings: The High Court can interfere with a finding of fact if the lower courts' failure to consider material evidence gives rise to a substantial question of law, even though it cannot re-appreciate evidence.

Ownership under Section 12(1)(f) must be proven, and though the partition deed was not produced, the tenant’s admission in a legal notice reply and rent receipts describing the plaintiff as owner constitute relevant evidence that must be considered.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Concurrent finding of fact not binding if based on failure to consider material evidence

card.dispute: Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. and others fought the Union of India over whether equity shares in two companies and immovable properties held by Swadeshi Cotton Mills vested in the Central Government under the Swadeshi Cotton Mills (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986.
issues_decided: Whether equity shares in Swadeshi Polytex Limited and Swadeshi Mining and Manufacturing Company Limited held by Swadeshi Cotton Mills vested in the Central Government under Section 3 of the Act.
Whether immovable properties, namely Bungalow No. 1 and Administrative Block in Kanpur, vested in the Central Government under the Act.
Whether the National Textile Corporation (NTC) was entitled to be recognised as the shareholder and to vote in the annual general meeting of Swadeshi Polytex Limited.
holdings: Equity shares held by Swadeshi Cotton Mills in other companies vested in the Central Government under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act as they were 'in relation to' the textile undertaking.
Immovable properties owned by the company and used in connection with the textile undertaking vested in the Central Government due to the expansive language of Sections 3 and 4.

NTC is the rightful owner of the shares and entitled to recognition in the register of members and to vote in the company’s meetings by operation of law, without need for rectification under Section 108 of the Companies Act.
provisions: Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 3
Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 4
Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 7
Swadeshi Cotton Mills Company Limited (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1986, Section 8
doctrines: Deeming fiction
Inclusive definition ('includes' as expansive)
Acquisition under Article 39(b) and (c) of the Constitution
Vesting by operation of law
Principle of constitutional purposive interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord (N. Shankar Reddy) sought eviction of the tenant (Gangaram) from an adjacent building for additional business space, claiming it was part of the same building under the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether two adjoining buildings with separate municipal door numbers but owned by the same person can be treated as one building under Section 10(3)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960.
Whether a landlord occupying one building can evict a tenant from a separate adjoining building under Section 10(3)(c) for bona fide need of additional accommodation.
holdings: Section 10(3)(c) applies only when the landlord and tenant occupy different portions of the same building, not separate buildings, regardless of common ownership.
The oneness of a building is determined by physical and functional integration, not ownership; separate municipal numbers and independent saleability confirm separate buildings.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(c)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 2(iii)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Statutory limitation on judicial remedy
Oneness of building doctrine

card.dispute: The landlord, an advocate, sought eviction of the tenant from residential premises for his personal use, including part of the premises for an office, but the High Court restricted possession to only a portion, leading to a dispute over tenancy structure and permissible use under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether two separate tenancies were created in respect of the premises due to rent payments made partly in the name of a trust
Whether the landlord, being an advocate, could claim possession for bona fide residential requirement if part of the premises was to be used as an office or library
holdings: The payment of rent by two cheques, one in the tenant's name and one in the name of a trust, does not create two tenancies; there was only one tenancy in favour of the respondent.

A landlord who is an advocate may use a part of the residential premises for an office or library as incidental to his residential need, and such use does not disqualify him from claiming possession under proviso (e) to Section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction limited to jurisdictional errors, not reappreciation of facts
Bona fide residential requirement includes incidental professional use in residential premises
Substance over form in interpreting pleadings and tenancy arrangements

card.dispute: The widow and legal heirs of the original plaintiff fought with the original defendant over the enforcement of an agreement to re-convey a property allegedly sold as security, where the defendant refused to execute the sale deed despite a prior agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction between the parties was a genuine sale or a mortgage by conditional sale
Whether the plaintiff fulfilled the conditions necessary to enforce the agreement for specific performance
Whether the defendant was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract on the stipulated date
holdings: The transaction was in the nature of a mortgage by conditional sale, not an outright sale, as possession remained with the plaintiff and the defendant agreed to re-convey the property within ten years.
The plaintiff made sufficient efforts to perform his obligations, including sending notice and remaining present at the Sub-Registrar's office, thus entitling him to specific performance.
The defendant was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, as his evidence was inconsistent and false, and he failed to appear at the Sub-Registrar's office despite notice.
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Credibility of oral evidence and adverse inference

card.dispute: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. and its employee fought against Shyam Co-operative Housing Society over eviction from a flat, claiming protected tenancy under the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a subsisting leave and licence agreement as on 1 February 1973 entitled the licensee to deemed tenancy under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act?
Whether the rights under the leave and licence agreement were transferred to Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. after the acquisition of Esso Eastern Inc. by the Central Government?
Whether the Appellate Court erred in holding that no renewal of the licence occurred and that the petitioner had no protected status?
holdings: A person in lawful occupation under a subsisting leave and licence agreement as on 1 February 1973 acquires the status of a deemed tenant entitled to protection under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act.

The tenancy or occupancy rights of Esso Eastern Inc. vested in the Central Government under the Esso (Acquisition of Undertakings in India) Act, 1974, and subsequently in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd., carrying forward the deemed tenancy status.

Admissions in correspondence, particularly the letter dated 24 March 1980, prove the continued existence of a subsisting licence, making the Appellate Court’s finding of no renewal manifestly erroneous.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
Esso (Acquisition of Undertakings in India) Act, 1974, Sections 3, 5, and 19
doctrines: Deemed tenancy under rent control legislation
Succession of rights upon statutory acquisition
Admission against interest in documentary evidence
Continuity of tenancy rights upon corporate succession

card.dispute: The landlord (B. Mohan Lal Sowcar) sought eviction of the tenant (Hameedia Hardware Stores) from non-residential premises under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, claiming the premises were needed for his wife's business, while the tenant argued the requirement was not bona fide.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord filing a petition under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 must prove the bona fides of his requirement for eviction.
Whether the term 'claim' in Section 10(3)(e) of the Act includes the genuineness of the landlord's need for the premises.
holdings: A landlord seeking eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) must prove not only the statutory conditions but also that his requirement for the non-residential premises is bona fide.
The word 'claim' in Section 10(3)(e) implies a genuine and justifiable need; thus, the landlord must establish deservedness for possession, not merely a formal claim.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(e)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement doctrine in rent control laws
Principle of harmonious construction
Judicial interpretation to avoid absurdity in statutory construction

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants for non-payment of rent arrears for over six months, while the tenants claimed they were willing to pay but the landlord refused receipts and acted mala fide.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can resist eviction under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act without disputing standard rent within one month of notice?
Whether a tenant's failure to pay rent due to alleged mala fide conduct by the landlord prevents a decree for eviction?
Whether the court must pass a decree for eviction if the conditions under Section 12(3)(a) are satisfied?
holdings: Under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act, if there is no dispute about standard rent and the tenant is in arrears for six months or more without payment after notice, the court must pass a decree for eviction.
A tenant cannot avoid eviction by alleging the landlord’s refusal to issue receipts or mala fide conduct if the statutory conditions for eviction under Section 12(3)(a) are met.
The mandatory language 'shall pass a decree' in Section 12(3)(a) leaves no discretion to the court when the prescribed conditions are fulfilled.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 26(2)
doctrines: Mandatory statutory interpretation
Doctrine of strict compliance with rent payment conditions
No equitable relief against statutory eviction when conditions are met

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant's legal heirs on grounds of subletting or parting with possession of the premises to the tenant's sons who ran a business there.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant had 'parted with possession' of the premises within the meaning of Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 by allowing his sons to run a business in the premises?
Whether the proposed amendment to plead that the tenancy was in the name of the partnership firm should have been allowed?
Whether user of the premises by family members in a joint Hindu family setup amounts to parting with possession?
holdings: Parting with possession requires the tenant to divest himself of both physical and legal possession; mere user by family members does not amount to parting with possession if the tenant retains control.
An amendment to introduce a new case that contradicts prior admissions and prejudices the other side cannot be allowed under Order 6 Rule 17 of the CPC.
In a joint Hindu family, a father allowing sons to manage the business in rented premises does not constitute parting with possession if he retains the right to control the premises.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Parting with possession requires legal and physical divestment
Amendment not allowed if it introduces a new case or contradicts prior admissions
Presumption against eviction in absence of clear divestment of possession in family use cases

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of sub-letting after the tenant transferred management of the hotel business to another person.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the tenant and the second respondent amounted to sub-letting of the leased premises under the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Whether the transfer was merely of managing rights or of the business along with tenancy rights
Whether the courts below were justified in concluding that the transaction was camouflaged to conceal sub-letting
holdings: The transfer of the hotel business along with control over the premises and financial responsibilities constituted a de facto assignment of tenancy, amounting to sub-letting.
The dominant intention of the parties, as revealed by the agreement and conduct, was to transfer the business in toto with the right to occupy the premises, not merely managing rights.

Courts are justified in looking beyond the form of an agreement to its substance when determining if sub-letting has occurred, especially where there is an attempt to camouflage the true nature of the transaction.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10
doctrines: Substance over form
Dominant intention test
Camouflaging of transactions to avoid statutory restrictions

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired for the Lower Manair Dam Reservoir project, seeking higher compensation based on comparable awards and market value.
issues_decided: Whether Award Ex. A.5, granting Rs.70,000 per acre for similar lands, should be excluded from consideration due to lack of comparability.
Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the case for fresh disposal instead of determining compensation based on existing evidence.
holdings: Award Ex. A.5 should not be excluded outright; it is relevant for determining compensation if the lands are comparable in nature and potential use, regardless of slight differences in location.

The appellate power to remand should not be exercised lightly; where sufficient evidence exists, the court should decide compensation to avoid undue delay, especially when claimants are small farmers suffering hardship.
doctrines: Principle of just and timely compensation in land acquisition
Appellate discretion against remand in presence of adequate evidence
Use of comparable sale deeds and awards in determining market value

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the arbitrator's award that denied them protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act after they stopped paying monthly instalments and repudiated a reconveyance agreement, while the respondent sought specific performance of the contract.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator committed an error of law in holding that the appellants were not absolved from performing their contractual obligations after the respondent's alleged anticipatory breach.
Whether the failure to refer to certain documents in the award amounts to an error of law or legal misconduct.
Whether the award is liable to be set aside on the ground of mistake of fact or error of law under the Arbitration Act, 1940.
holdings: A party claiming specific performance after an anticipatory breach must show readiness and willingness to perform their own obligations, even if the other party repudiated first.
An award cannot be set aside merely because the arbitrator did not discuss all documents; there must be a demonstrable error of law on the face of the award.
Courts cannot interfere with an arbitral award for alleged mistakes of fact; only a clear error of law forming the basis of the award is justiciable.
doctrines: Error of law on the face of the award
Anticipatory breach of contract
Readiness and willingness to perform in specific performance claims
Limited judicial review of arbitral awards

card.dispute: The landlord sought to strike out the tenant's defence in an eviction suit for failure to deposit rent as ordered under the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982.
issues_decided: Whether the court has discretion to excuse a tenant's delay in depositing rent under Section 13 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982.
Whether the word 'shall' in Section 13 is mandatory or directory when a tenant fails to deposit rent within the stipulated time.
Whether the tenant's explanation for non-payment of rent was sufficient to justify not striking out the defence.
holdings: The court must assess whether a delay in rent deposit has been properly explained; if so, it may excuse the delay, but if not, it must strike out the defence.
The word 'shall' in Section 13 is not absolutely mandatory; the court has discretion where the delay is justified or technical in nature.
The tenant's delay was properly explained and all arrears were eventually deposited, so striking out the defence caused a miscarriage of justice.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982, Section 13
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Directory vs. mandatory interpretation
Discretion in the interest of justice
Prevention of unreasonable eviction

card.dispute: Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti challenged the High Court's quashing of land acquisition notifications for plot No. 289, while landowners Ratan Prakash Mangal and others argued the entire notification should have been quashed due to improper invocation of urgency provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the invocation of Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was justified in the notification under Section 4(1) for acquiring plot No. 289
Whether the subsequent notification under Section 6 was validly issued
Whether there was a lack of application of mind by authorities in reissuing the notification including already acquired land
holdings: The invocation of Section 17(4) was justified due to a material change in circumstances requiring urgent land acquisition for market yard facilities beyond just shops.
The Section 6 notification was valid as it followed a lawful Section 4(1) notification and procedural requirements were met.
The inclusion of already acquired land in the notification was due to clerical error, not lack of application of mind, and did not invalidate the acquisition for plot No. 289.
provisions: U.P. Agricultural Produce Marketing Act, 1964, Section 19(3)(vii)
doctrines: Doctrine of material change in circumstances justifying urgency under Section 17(4)
Doctrine of clerical error not invalidating administrative action
Doctrine of compensation based on date of fresh notification

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of a land acquisition award on grounds of delay, arguing it was made beyond the two-year period mandated by Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the award was made within the two-year period prescribed under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when the notice was served after the two-year deadline but the award was signed before it expired.
Whether inordinate delay in making the award, within the statutory two-year period, renders the acquisition proceeding invalid.
holdings: The phrase 'make an award' in Section 11-A means the Collector must sign the award within two years from the date of the Section 6 declaration or the commencement of the 1984 Amendment Act, whichever applies; service of notice thereafter does not invalidate the award.

Delay in making the award within the two-year statutory period, without exceeding it, does not invalidate the acquisition proceeding, as the statute itself sets the outer time limit and does not require earlier completion.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between limitation for administrative action and limitation for filing appeals
Presumption against invalidity of statutory proceedings within prescribed time limits

card.dispute: Larsen & Toubro Ltd. (lessee) fought the Trustees of Dharmamurthy, Rao Bahadur C. Cunnan Chetty (lessor) over whether the company was entitled to protection under Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, in eviction proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant company was entitled to protection under Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922
Whether the lease deed created a composite lease of building with appurtenant land or two separate leases (one for land and one for building)
Whether the lessee could claim rights under the Act based on clauses permitting construction and right of pre-emption in the lease
holdings: The Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922 applies only to tenants in specified areas where tenancy was created before a prescribed date and primarily protects small tenants who constructed buildings on leased land.
The lease deed constituted a single, composite lease of a building with appurtenant land, not two separate leases, and therefore the lessee was not entitled to protection under Section 9 of the Act.

Clauses allowing construction, subletting, and right of pre-emption are standard lease provisions and do not indicate an intention to create separate leases or confer rights under Section 9 of the Act.
provisions: Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, Section 9
Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, Section 3
Transfer of Property Act, general lease principles
doctrines: Composite lease doctrine
Statutory interpretation
Lessee's right to compensation and purchase under protective tenancy laws

card.dispute: The landlord sued for possession of premises after the tenant's defence was struck out for non-deposit of rent; the tenant challenged the complete denial of his right to contest the suit.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant whose defence is struck out under Section 17(4) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 is entirely precluded from contesting the suit.
Whether such a tenant can be allowed to cross-examine the plaintiff's witnesses and make arguments on the plaintiff's evidence.
holdings: Striking out a defence under Section 17(4) is a penal measure to be used with great restraint and does not render the tenant completely helpless or strip him of all procedural rights.

A tenant whose defence is struck out is still entitled to cross-examine the plaintiff's witnesses and address arguments on the plaintiff's case, but cannot lead his own evidence or use cross-examination to present a defence.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(4)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII, Rules 1, 5, and 10
doctrines: Strict construction of penal provisions in tenancy laws
Principle that plaintiff must prove his case even in absence of defence
Judicial discretion in procedural matters under CPC

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent arrears and bona fide need, while the tenant claimed protection under the Bombay Rent Act due to regular rent deposits.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's deposit of rent in court was 'regular' within the meaning of Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
Whether the tenant could be evicted for default in rent payment despite depositing arrears and ongoing rent in court.
holdings: The term 'regularly' in Section 12(3)(b) requires reasonable punctuality, not clock-like precision; deposits made at intervals of two or three months in advance can constitute regular payment.
A tenant who deposits rent with substantial regularity in court during the pendency of a suit is protected from eviction under Section 12(3)(b), even if payments are not made exactly on the due date.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(1)
doctrines: Substantial compliance with statutory conditions for tenant protection
Mandatory nature of Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act

card.dispute: The appellant, as assignee of one shop from a partition of co-owned leased property, sought eviction of the tenant from that shop, but the tenant resisted, claiming the unity of the tenancy could not be split without consent.
issues_decided: Whether a partition of reversionary interest allows an allottee to seek eviction from a part of jointly leased premises without splitting the tenancy's unity?
Whether Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to partition, not just transfer?
Whether tenant's consent is required for severance of reversionary interest in part of leased premises?
holdings: An assignee of a part of reversionary interest can exercise full landlord rights over that portion, including eviction, without violating the unity of tenancy.
Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act enables the assignee of part of the reversion to act as landlord for that part, even if the original lease was unified.
No consent of the tenant is required for severance of reversion or assignment of part thereof; attornment occurs by operation of law.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21
doctrines: Unity and integrity of tenancy
Statutory exception under Section 109 TPA
Operation of law attornment
Partition as effective severance of reversionary interest

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi fought Gurnam Kaur over the right to pitch a stall on public pavement, after the High Court restrained the Corporation from removing her encroachment.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could restrain the Municipal Corporation from removing an encroachment on public land in view of statutory powers under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957
Whether a prior judicial order based on consent and without full argument could bind the court as precedent
Whether the right to livelihood under Article 21 overrides the statutory power to remove illegal encroachments on public streets
holdings: The High Court erred in issuing a direction contrary to the statutory powers under Sections 320 and 322 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, which authorize removal of encroachments on public land.
A judicial order passed without argument, sub silentio, and without considering statutory provisions does not constitute binding precedent and may be disregarded.

The right to livelihood under Article 21 does not entitle pavement squatters to continue illegal encroachments, especially where public streets are obstructed and statutory powers are exercised reasonably.
doctrines: Ratio decidendi vs. obiter dicta
Precedent sub silentio
Binding nature of consent orders
Principle of per incuriam
Balancing of fundamental rights with statutory duties

card.dispute: The tenant claimed a right to purchase the leased site under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, while the landlord argued that a new tenancy had been created, disentitling the tenant to such benefits.
issues_decided: Whether a reduction in rent and change in payment terms amounted to a surrender of the original lease and creation of a new tenancy
Whether the tenant was entitled to the benefits of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act despite the alleged new tenancy
Whether the tenant could claim a sale of the entire leased site, including the portion used for non-residential purposes
holdings: A mere variation in rent and mode of payment does not, without more, amount to a surrender of the original lease and creation of a new tenancy.
The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act is a beneficial legislation, and courts must scrutinize claims of new tenancies strictly to prevent circumvention of tenant protections.
The tenant is entitled to purchase the entire leased site, including non-residential portions, as the government extended the Act’s benefits to such structures during the appeal.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, Section 12
Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent) Control Act, 1960
doctrines: Beneficial construction of tenant protection laws
Surrender and re-grant of tenancy
Strict scrutiny of contractual changes to avoid defeating statutory rights

card.dispute: The mortgagors' heirs sought to redeem a long-term mortgage and evict tenants inducted by the mortgagee, while the tenants claimed statutory protection under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether a 99-year mortgage term operates as a clog on the equity of redemption under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether tenants inducted by a mortgagee in possession are entitled to statutory protection under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 after redemption of the mortgage
Whether a mortgagee can create a tenancy binding on the mortgagor beyond the term of the mortgage without the mortgagor's concurrence
holdings: A long-term mortgage does not automatically become a clog on redemption if it is not unconscionable or oppressive under the circumstances.
Tenants inducted by a mortgagee without the mortgagor's concurrence do not acquire tenancy rights enforceable against the mortgagor after redemption.
The Bombay Rent Act does not enlarge tenancy rights of persons who were not tenants of the mortgagor and whose lease was not approved by the mortgagor.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Clog on redemption
Prudent management rule
Statutory tenancy protection limited to valid tenancies

card.dispute: The landlords (Rakesh Kumar & Shri Shakti Kumar) sought eviction of the tenant (Hindustan Everest Tool Ltd) for non-payment of rent, but the High Court set aside the eviction order, leading to an appeal before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the notices issued by the landlords amounted to a valid notice of demand for arrears of rent under the proviso to Section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the eviction order passed by the Rent Controller and affirmed by the Rent Control Tribunal
holdings: A notice of demand for arrears of rent under Section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act must be understood as an ordinary person would interpret it, and can be implied from conduct or a series of communications.

When read together, the two notices issued by the landlords clearly conveyed a demand for unpaid rent and an intimation that failure to pay would lead to eviction, satisfying the statutory requirement under the proviso to Section 14(1)(a).
doctrines: Notice must be construed from the perspective of a common man
Implied demand for rent can satisfy statutory notice requirements

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, belonging to two branches of a joint family, disputed over ownership and possession of a plot of land following a claimed partition of ancestral properties in 1955 and a later settlement in 1971.
issues_decided: Whether the memorandum of partition (Exh. P-12) dated August 3, 1955, required compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the unregistered document could be admitted in evidence under the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act for collateral purposes
Whether the document Exh. P-12 was an instrument of partition or a mere record of a past partition or family arrangement
holdings: A document that merely records a past partition or family arrangement and does not itself create or declare new rights in immovable property does not require registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.

An unregistered document, though inadmissible to prove the creation of a right in property, may be used under the proviso to Section 49 to prove a collateral fact such as the nature of possession or a prior severance of status.
A family arrangement that adjusts competing claims among members of a joint family and recognizes pre-existing titles does not create new interests and hence does not require registration.
A mere list of properties allotted after partition, which is a recital of past events, is not an instrument of partition and is admissible to prove the factum of partition.
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement
Doctrine of severance of joint status
Collateral use of unregistered documents
Test for determining instrument of partition vs. mere record of partition

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent default and personal requirement, leading to a dispute over whether the tenant's deposits cured the default and entitled him to protection under the tenancy law.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant committed default in payment of rent for January 1966 and subsequent months
Whether the tenant's deposits with the Rent Controller under the amended law entitled him to protection under Section 17(4) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act
holdings: The tenant failed to prove valid tender of rent for January 1966, and the money order and subsequent deposit did not cure the initial default under the Act.

To claim relief under Section 17(4), the tenant must deposit arrears in compliance with Section 17(1), including amounts previously invalidly deposited; mere prior deposits with the Rent Controller are insufficient.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(ff)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(1)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(4)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 22(3)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 4
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact
Strict compliance with statutory conditions precedent
No waiver of default by landlord accepting invalid deposits

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether occupants of homesteads or huts without initial permission from the owner could be recognized as Kudikidappukarans and entitled to rights under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964, as amended.
issues_decided: Whether Explanation II-A to clause (25) of Section 2 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act grants Kudikidappu rights to occupants without proof of initial permission from the owner.
Whether the occupation under Explanation II-A must be lawful or can include occupation without permission.
Whether the decision in Palayi Kizhakkekara Mathai's case limits the scope of Explanation II-A to lawful occupation.
holdings: Explanation II-A to Section 2(25) grants Kudikidappu rights to any person in continuous occupation of a homestead or hut from 16.8.1968 to 1.1.1970, irrespective of whether initial permission was granted.
The legislature intended to override prior judicial requirements of lawful or permissive occupation; actual occupation during the stipulated period is sufficient.
There is no conflict with Palayi Kizhakkekara Mathai's case, as Section 7D dealt with different provisions requiring lawful origin, whereas Explanation II-A does not impose such a condition.
provisions: Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, Section 2(25) with Explanation II-A
doctrines: Non obstante clause interpretation
Legislative override of judicial decisions
Validation of occupation by statutory recognition

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition process, arguing that withdrawal of a declaration under Section 6 invalidated the initial notification under Section 4.
issues_decided: Whether a withdrawal of a declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act renders the prior notification under Section 4 ineffective and infructuous
Whether there is a legal distinction between a court declaring a Section 6 declaration invalid and the government withdrawing it voluntarily due to illegality
holdings: A valid declaration under Section 6 exhausts the notification under Section 4, but this principle does not apply if the declaration is invalid, ineffective, or withdrawn due to illegality.
There is no distinction in law between a Section 6 declaration declared invalid by a court and one withdrawn by the government when an obvious illegality exists.
doctrines: Exhaustion of notification under Section 4 upon valid declaration under Section 6
Validity and consequences of withdrawal of acquisition proceedings
Principle of supersession of earlier notification by a subsequent one

card.dispute: The dispute was between the appellants (Krishna Rajpal Bhatia & Ors) and respondents (Leela H. Advani & Ors) over whether the agreement for occupation of a flat in a cooperative housing society was a lease or a licence, and whether the eviction proceedings under Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act were maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the parties was one of lease or licence.
Whether the dispute fell within the jurisdiction of the Cooperative Court under Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960.
Whether the society was a tenant co-partnership society or a mixed-type society including tenant owner members.
holdings: The agreement between the parties was one of licence, not lease, and the relationship was not that of landlord and tenant.
The dispute pertained to the business of the cooperative society and was therefore within the jurisdiction of the Cooperative Court under Section 91 of the Act.

The society was a tenant co-partnership society, and the respondent was a tenant co-partner member, not a tenant owner member, as confirmed by the corrected bye-laws and the Registrar’s classification.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact
Jurisdiction of cooperative courts under special statutes
Doctrine of rectification of legal status by amendment of bye-laws
