card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi challenged the tax exemption granted to Children Book Trust, a society running a private unaided school, arguing it did not meet the conditions for charitable use under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act.
issues_decided: Whether the society running the school qualifies as engaged in 'charitable purpose' under Section 115(4)(a) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957
Whether the society is 'supported wholly or in part by voluntary contributions' as required for exemption
Whether a trade or business is carried on in the property, disentitling it to tax exemption under Section 115(5) and (6)
Whether part of the property used for non-charitable purposes can still allow exemption for the rest
holdings: Running a school constitutes a 'charitable purpose' under the Act, including education as a valid form of charity.
The society is not entitled to exemption unless it is supported wholly or in part by genuine voluntary contributions; forced donations or internal transfers from school to society do not qualify.
If a trade or business is carried on in the property and its profits are not applied to charitable purposes, that portion of the property is liable to tax.
A part of the property used for charitable purposes may be exempt if separate from the portion used for trade or business, which remains taxable.
provisions: Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, Section 115(4)(a), proviso and explanation
doctrines: Doctrine of charitable purpose
Doctrine of voluntary contributions
Doctrine of severability of property for tax exemption
Doctrine of non-distribution of profits in charitable institutions

card.dispute: Mahesh Chandra challenged the U.P. Financial Corporation's sale of his mortgaged property after loan default, claiming violation of natural justice and unfair sale procedures.
issues_decided: Whether the Corporation's sale of mortgaged property without notice or opportunity to the debtor violated principles of natural justice?
Whether the State Financial Corporation, as an instrumentality of the State, is bound to act fairly and reasonably in recovering dues?
Whether the mode of sale by invitation of tenders without public auction was valid under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951?
holdings: The sale of mortgaged property by the Corporation without notice or opportunity to the debtor violated principles of natural justice and was vitiated.
State Financial Corporations are instrumentalities of the State and must act fairly, reasonably, and in the manner of a prudent owner when disposing of debtor's property.
Public auction is the preferred method of sale; sale by tender or private negotiation must follow strict guidelines and afford the debtor opportunity to participate or object.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Doctrine of fair procedure in administrative action
Doctrine of lis pendens
Prudent owner rule

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, members of the royal family of Jaipur, fought over whether certain properties belonged to the Hindu Undivided Family or were the personal property of the eldest son, and whether a receiver should be appointed to manage the properties due to alleged violations of a court injunction.
issues_decided: Whether a prima facie case exists that the properties in dispute belong to the Hindu Undivided Family rather than being the personal property of the eldest son
Whether the eldest son violated a court injunction by disposing of properties included in the suit schedules
Whether it is just and convenient to appoint an Administrator to manage and preserve the suit properties
holdings: A prima facie case exists that the properties may belong to the Hindu Undivided Family, especially since the eldest son declared them as such in tax returns for many years.
The eldest son disposed of over 2,000 shares that were part of the suit properties, violating the court's injunction against alienation.
It is just and convenient to appoint an Administrator to take control of the suit properties to prevent dissipation and preserve the status quo pending final adjudication.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 40 Rule 1
doctrines: Prima facie case
Injunction violation
Appointment of Receiver/Administrator to preserve subject matter of litigation

card.dispute: The Madhya Pradesh Housing Board challenged the High Court's decision quashing land acquisition proceedings initiated for constructing buildings and shops, on grounds of vagueness in the notification and lack of clear public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was valid despite lacking precise details of the land and locality.
Whether the public purpose stated in the notification was sufficiently clear and specific to satisfy legal requirements.
Whether defects in the Section 4(1) notification could be cured by detailed particulars in the Section 6(1) declaration.
holdings: A notification under Section 4(1) must specify the locality of the land with sufficient clarity; mere mention of a large town without khasra numbers or ward details is invalid.
The public purpose must be clearly and specifically stated; stating only 'residential' or 'housing scheme' without details renders the notification void for vagueness.
Defects in the Section 4(1) notification cannot be cured by providing detailed particulars in the subsequent Section 6(1) declaration.
doctrines: Doctrine of Strict Compliance with Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act
Doctrine of Non-Curative Defects in Land Acquisition Notifications
Requirement of Clear and Specific Public Purpose in Acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed over possession of property, specifically whether the respondents had impliedly surrendered their leasehold rights, making their suit for recovery of possession maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents had impliedly surrendered their leasehold interest in the property under Section 111(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
Whether the suit for recovery of possession was maintainable given the alleged surrender of leasehold rights.
holdings: Execution of an agreement allowing a third party to take over management, pay rent, and conduct business constitutes implied surrender of leasehold rights under Section 111(f).

A lessee who ceases to pay rent and authorizes another to enter into a rental agreement with the landlord is deemed to have surrendered the lease; thus, a suit for possession based on leasehold rights is not maintainable.
doctrines: Implied surrender of lease
Doctrine of merger of judgments

card.dispute: The Ramjas Foundation challenged the land acquisition notifications issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing that its land, used for educational and charitable purposes, should have been excluded like wakf property and that the notifications were invalid due to lack of personal hearing and delay.
issues_decided: Whether the delay and laches in challenging the notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, justified dismissal of the writ petition?
Whether the exclusion of wakf property from acquisition while not extending the same benefit to Hindu or non-Muslim charitable institutions violated Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the rejection of objections under Section 5A without a personal hearing invalidated the acquisition proceedings?
holdings: A challenge to acquisition notifications under Sections 4 and 6 must be made promptly; undue delay and laches, especially when grounds were available at the time of notification, warrant dismissal of the challenge.
The failure to extend exemption from acquisition to non-Muslim charitable institutions does not, by itself, violate Article 14 if the classification is reasonable and based on policy considerations.
The denial of personal hearing in disposal of objections under Section 5A does not automatically invalidate the acquisition process if the objections were otherwise considered.
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Doctrine of Delay and Acquiescence
Principle of Equal Protection under Article 14
Doctrine of Proper Opportunity of Hearing in Administrative Proceedings

card.dispute: The State Bank of India sought to execute a composite decree against a guarantor without first realizing the decretal amount from the mortgaged property, which the guarantor objected to.
issues_decided: Whether a decree-holder can execute a composite decree first against a guarantor without proceeding against the mortgaged property.
Whether a guarantor can be proceeded against in execution without first exhausting remedies against the principal debtor or the mortgaged security.
Whether the executing court can interpret or add conditions to a decree not present in its original terms.
holdings: A decree-holder is entitled to execute a personal decree against a guarantor independently, even if a portion of the debt is secured by mortgage, unless the decree itself imposes a condition to proceed against the security first.

The liability of a guarantor is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, and the creditor may choose to proceed against either without being compelled to first exhaust remedies against the mortgaged property.
An executing court cannot go beyond the terms of a final decree; any limitations on execution must be part of the decree itself and cannot be introduced during execution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 30, 46, 46A, 46B, 46F, 50, 72A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rules 4 and 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Sections 47 and 151
doctrines: Co-extensive liability of guarantor
Finality of decree
Execution within the four corners of the decree
No implied condition to exhaust security first

card.dispute: The dispute was between service holders and the Shri Patteswaraswami Devasthanam over whether the service holders or the temple were entitled to ryotwari pattas for lands granted as service inams.
issues_decided: Whether the inam grant was absolute and in favour of the Devasthanam or the service holders
Whether the grant was of both melvaram and keelvaram or only melvaram
Whether service holders could claim individual title to the inam lands based on possession
Whether entries in the Inam Fair Register and title deeds could determine the nature of the grant
holdings: The grant was in favour of the Devasthanam, not the service holders, as the documents and entries indicate dedication to the temple.
The use of terms like 'Devadayam' and 'permanent' in official records supports that the grant was to the temple for religious purposes.
Service holders, even if in possession, are derivative holders and cannot claim individual title against the Devasthanam.
Entries in the Inam Fair Register, when read with other contemporaneous documents, confirm the Devasthanam as the grantee.
provisions: Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, Section 8
Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, Section 21
doctrines: Presumption against lost grants
Use of contemporaneous documents to interpret nature of grants
Derivative possession does not confer independent title
Entries in revenue records are not conclusive when contradicted by other evidence

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged whether Section 8(3)(a) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, which denies solatium, violates Article 14 of the Constitution, and landowners claimed additional compensation and interest.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8(3)(a) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the inclusion of the Act in the Ninth Schedule via the 39th Constitutional Amendment protects it from constitutional challenge
Whether solatium and interest can be awarded despite the statutory scheme excluding them
holdings: Section 8(3)(a) does not violate Article 14 as the classification it creates is reasonable and based on intelligible differentia.

The Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, having been included in the Ninth Schedule by the 39th Amendment, is protected under Article 31-B and immune from challenge on grounds of fundamental rights, with retrospective effect.
Solatium and interest beyond statutory limits cannot be awarded unless the case falls under exceptional circumstances justifying equitable relief due to inordinate delay in arbitration.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 8(3)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of Basic Structure
Doctrine of Retrospective Validation under Article 31-B
Principle of Equitable Relief in Cases of Administrative Delay

card.dispute: The petitioners, landowners in Pune Cantonment, challenged the Cantonment Board's refusal to sanction their building plans unless they converted their land to freehold and complied with new building restrictions limiting height and floor space index.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners had a legal right to sanction of building plans under the old bye-laws despite non-payment of conversion charges and non-compliance with new building restrictions
Whether the new Pune Cantonment (Building) Bye-Laws, 1988, which imposed stricter building restrictions, were valid and applicable to pending plans
Whether the petitioners could rely on a previous Supreme Court order in Shoriar Baharam Irani to claim similar relief
holdings: No legal right accrues to a building plan until final sanction is granted; therefore, petitioners had no vested right to approval under earlier, more lenient regulations.

The new building bye-laws and schemes of restriction, introduced in public interest to prevent overcrowding and environmental degradation, validly apply to all unsanctioned plans, even those submitted earlier.
The earlier Supreme Court order in Shoriar Baharam Irani did not set a binding precedent as it did not express any opinion on the merits and was limited to the parties involved.
doctrines: No vested right in administrative approval until final sanction
Public interest justification for regulatory changes
Distinction between binding precedent and per incuriam or limited orders

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent default and bona fide need, while the tenant claimed he had overpaid rent due to an illegal enhancement and that the excess should be automatically adjusted against arrears.
issues_decided: Whether excess rent paid due to an illegal, mutually agreed enhancement can be automatically adjusted against subsequent rent defaults under the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947
Whether a tenant can resist eviction for rent default by claiming adjustment of excess rent without a specific agreement or demand for such adjustment
holdings: Excess rent paid due to an illegal enhancement does not automatically adjust against future rent arrears under the Bihar Act; an express agreement or specific request for adjustment is required.
A tenant cannot claim automatic adjustment of excess rent to avoid eviction; adjustment must be specifically claimed as a set-off within the legal procedure and time limits.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 4
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 5
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11
doctrines: No automatic adjustment of illegal excess rent
Set-off must be specifically pleaded and not presumed
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with in second appeal

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for using leased land for selling cloth instead of the permitted sugarcane crushing business, as originally agreed.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant used the premises for a purpose other than that specified in the lease agreement.
Whether the tenant was entitled to change the use of the premises to any business of his choice.
Whether the landlord had acquiesced to the change in the use of the premises.
holdings: A tenant cannot use leased property for a purpose other than that specified in the lease, as per Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act.
The right to carry on 'business' does not allow a tenant to alter the specific nature of the business for which the premises were leased.
Mere continuation of tenancy during off-season does not constitute landlord’s acquiescence to a change in the primary use of the premises.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of permissible user of leased property
Doctrine of change of user as ground for eviction
Doctrine of acquiescence in lease disputes

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from a non-residential building claiming bona fide need for business, while the tenant argued the claim was not genuine and motivated by rent enhancement.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord can seek eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, if he already occupies another non-residential building in the same locality?
Whether the landlord's requirement of the demised premises for business was bona fide?
holdings: A landlord already in occupation of a non-residential building in the same city, town, or village is not entitled to evict a tenant from another such building, regardless of suitability or convenience of the existing premises.
The landlord’s claim of bona fide requirement for business was not genuine, especially given his possession of multiple shops and offices and the context of a disputed rent hike.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 122
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Strict interpretation of statutory eviction grounds
Finality of appellate findings on facts

card.dispute: The appellant tenant challenged the execution and sale of his property to recover a small decretal amount, claiming the sale was unjust and caused substantial injury.
issues_decided: Whether the execution court had jurisdiction to order the sale of the judgment-debtor's property despite prior rent deposit in another proceeding.
Whether the sale of the entire property for a small decretal amount without considering partial sale constituted a material irregularity.
Whether inadequacy of sale price alone could justify setting aside a court-confirmed auction sale.
Whether the auction-purchaser was a bona fide buyer entitled to protection despite potential collusion.
holdings: The execution court has exclusive jurisdiction under Section 47 CPC to decide questions relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree, including prior deposits.
Selling an entire large commercial property to recover a small amount without considering partial sale causes substantial injury and amounts to material irregularity under Order 21 Rule 90 CPC.
Mere inadequacy of price does not vitiate a court sale; however, when combined with material irregularity and substantial injury, the sale can be set aside.
A stranger purchaser is not automatically protected if there is evidence of collusion or knowledge of pending litigation; bona fides must be established.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 54
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 66
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 90
doctrines: Material irregularity in court sale
Substantial injury to judgment-debtor
Bona fide purchaser for value
Exclusive jurisdiction of executing court under Section 47 CPC

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of land acquisition by the State of Rajasthan, arguing that the public purpose was not sufficiently specified and that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed due to delay.
issues_decided: Whether the period during which acquisition proceedings were stayed by court orders should be excluded in computing the two-year period for making an award under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

Whether the notification under Section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, specifying the purpose of acquisition as 'development plan and construction of residential, commercial and administrative buildings', was sufficiently clear and valid.
holdings: The period during which acquisition proceedings were stayed by court orders must be excluded when computing the two-year period for making an award under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as per the Explanation to that section.

A notification specifying acquisition for 'development plan and construction of residential, commercial and administrative buildings' is sufficiently specific, especially when large areas of land are involved, and does not render the acquisition void for vagueness.
doctrines: Exclusion of stay period in limitation computation
Sufficiency of public purpose specification in acquisition notices

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the State of Punjab, claiming it was below market value.
issues_decided: Whether sale deeds of small land extents can be relied upon to determine market value for large-scale land acquisition
Whether the highest sale price in the neighborhood should be adopted as the market value
Whether 'belting' (differential pricing based on proximity to roads) is justified in this case
Whether and to what extent deduction for development charges should be made from market value
holdings: Sale deeds of small land extents reflect retail prices and are not comparable for determining compensation in large-scale acquisitions; they must be excluded unless supported by proper evidence.
The highest sale price in the vicinity cannot automatically be adopted; market value must be based on a reasoned average of comparable and proximate sales.
Belting is legally valid but not justified here since the acquired land has road access on three sides and is surrounded by habitation, making uniform valuation appropriate.
A deduction of one-third from the market value is warranted to account for development charges in undeveloped land, consistent with prior rulings.
doctrines: Principle of average market value in land acquisition
Distinction between wholesale and retail land prices
Deduction for development charges in undeveloped land
Belting doctrine for differential land valuation based on accessibility

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings by U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad on grounds of delay beyond the three-year limitation period prescribed under the proviso to Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, limiting declaration under Section 6 to three years from notification under Section 4, applies to acquisitions under the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965?
Whether the acquisition proceedings became invalid due to delay in issuing the declaration beyond three years?
Whether the petitioners could raise issues beyond limitation after special leave was granted only on the limitation question?
holdings: The proviso to Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act applies to acquisitions under the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, as the beneficial limitation provision is applicable unless expressly excluded.
Though the acquisition lapsed due to delay, the Court refused to quash proceedings in view of public interest and equitable considerations arising from constructed housing colonies.
Petitioners invoking Article 32 are not strictly bound by the limited leave order in connected SLPs and may raise other issues, though relief here is confined to compensation adjustment.
provisions: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965 (Act 1 of 1966), Section 28(1), Section 32(1), Section 32(4)
doctrines: Benign construction of statutes in favour of social justice
Delay destroys remedy but not right
Equitable relief in public interest
Fictional revival of lapsed proceedings for compensation purposes

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of the acquisition of 86 villages for New Bombay, alleging inordinate delay, malafide intent to peg land prices, and non-implementation of policies for alternative sites.
issues_decided: Whether inordinate delay in completing land acquisition proceedings invalidates the acquisition and awards made under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the acquisition was a colourable exercise of power aimed solely at pegging land prices from 1968–1970.
Whether the acquisition of Gaothan and hamlet areas violated the government’s policy decision not to acquire such lands.
Whether affected landowners must be provided alternative sites at subsidised rates to prevent hardship.
holdings: Acquisition proceedings completed within the time frame under Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act cannot be invalidated solely due to delay, as the statute provides a reasonable time limit for completion.
The acquisition was not vitiated by malafide or colourable exercise of power merely because notifications were issued early; the purpose was lawful planned development.
The claim that Gaothan and hamlet areas were acquired in violation of policy is a disputed factual issue not determinable in these proceedings and was not accepted by the High Court.
Affected landowners must be offered alternative sites at a price covering only acquisition and development costs, not commercial rates, to prevent illusory compensation due to long delays.
doctrines: Colourable legislation doctrine
Malafide exercise of power
Statutory time limits as validation of administrative action
Principle of equitable relief in land acquisition for urban development

card.dispute: The dispute was between Maharaja Pratap Singh and Maharani Sarojini Devi over ownership of properties allegedly purchased by the former ruler Ripudaman Singh, specifically whether they were private family properties or state properties.
issues_decided: Whether the property at 34, Alipore Road, Delhi, and Sterling Castle in Simla were private properties of the royal family or properties of the Nabha State
Whether the benami purchase of property by a ruler during British rule indicates private ownership or state ownership
Whether the covenant under Article 12 of the Instrument of Accession entitles the ruler to claim private property distinct from state property
Whether prior inconsistent pleadings by a party bar subsequent claims to property
holdings: Properties purchased benami by a ruler during British rule due to restrictions on acquisition are presumed to be state properties unless proven otherwise by clear user and enjoyment as private property.
The restriction imposed by the British on rulers acquiring property in British territory explains benami purchases and does not automatically make such properties private family assets.

Under Article 12 of the Covenant, only properties genuinely owned, used, and enjoyed by the ruler as private can be claimed as such; mere inclusion in an inventory does not convert state property into private property.

A party’s earlier admission in a legal proceeding that a property was purchased from another family member contradicts and bars a later claim that the same property is joint family or private royal family property.
provisions: Covenant for the Formation of the Patiala and East Punjab States Union, Article 6 and Article 12
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 86 read with Section 87-B
doctrines: Benami Transaction Doctrine
Act of State Doctrine
Doctrine of Estoppel by Conduct
Rule of Primogeniture

card.dispute: The landlord sought execution of a compromise decree for possession of premises, while the tenant challenged it as a nullity, claiming no statutory grounds for eviction were established.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise decree in an eviction suit is a nullity if the court's satisfaction about statutory grounds for eviction is not explicitly recorded
Whether the executing court can permit a tenant to lead fresh evidence to challenge the validity of a compromise decree
Whether an implied admission in a compromise agreement suffices to establish statutory grounds for eviction under the Bombay Rents Act
holdings: A compromise decree is not a nullity if there is some material, including an implied admission, on which the court could be prima facie satisfied about the existence of statutory grounds for eviction.

The executing court cannot allow fresh evidence to challenge the validity of a compromise decree; it may only examine the existing record to determine if there was material supporting jurisdictional facts.

An express or implied admission by the tenant in the compromise, pleadings, or judicial conduct is sufficient to establish statutory grounds for eviction and binds the tenant in execution proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 3
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(2)
doctrines: Prima facie satisfaction doctrine
Binding nature of judicial admissions
Execution court's limited jurisdiction under Section 47
Presumption of lawfulness of compromise under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC

card.dispute: The appellants (husband and mother-in-law) were accused of murdering the deceased (young bride) by setting her on fire, allegedly due to dowry-related harassment, and challenged their conviction in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt based on circumstantial evidence?
Whether the dying declarations and other pieces of evidence were reliable and sufficient to sustain the conviction?
Whether the appellants' absconding after the incident was a relevant circumstance pointing towards guilt?
Whether the trial court erred in acquitting the accused while the High Court reversed the acquittal?
holdings: The prosecution successfully established all circumstances pointing to the appellants' guilt by clear, cogent, and reliable circumstantial evidence, forming a complete and unbroken chain.
The dying declarations, medical evidence, and conduct of the accused collectively inspired confidence and were trustworthy enough to base conviction upon.
The appellants' unexplained absconding after the incident, though not conclusive by itself, became significant when considered with other incriminating circumstances.

The High Court was justified in reversing the trial court’s acquittal, which was based on conjectures and failure to appreciate key evidence; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction under Section 302/34 IPC.
doctrines: Principle of appreciation of circumstantial evidence in criminal trials
Reliability test for dying declarations
Conduct of accused as a relevant fact under Section 8 of the Evidence Act
Presumption against accused in dowry death and bride-burning cases
Courts' duty to be sensitive in crimes against women

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Union of India for brick kilns, claiming higher market value based on potential for residential and commercial development.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in confirming the market value of acquired land without considering potential for future development.
Whether mutation records showing higher sale prices could be relied upon without proof of genuine sale transactions.
Whether different categories of land (Abi, Barani, Ghair Munkin) should be valued uniformly based on potential use.
holdings: Land situated near Chandigarh and within a development-restricted zone possesses potential value for residential and commercial use, justifying higher compensation despite current use for agriculture.
Mutation entries alone are inadmissible to prove market value; sale transactions must be proved by examining witnesses with personal knowledge to establish comparability and genuineness.
Abi and Barani lands, though differing in quality, can be valued differently based on location and potential, while Ghair Munkin (waste) land cannot be equated with cultivated land.
doctrines: Principle of just and reasonable compensation
Comparable sales doctrine
Potential value doctrine
Solatium for compulsory acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant and Shantilal Malik disputed over the right to purchase a plot of land in Delhi during the winding up of India Electric Works Ltd., after multiple rounds of bidding and court interventions.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could reopen an auction after accepting a bid and direct a fresh auction.
Whether a court-confirmed sale in a winding up proceeding becomes final and binding even if higher offers emerge.
Whether the conditions of sale allowing the court to set aside a sale even after confirmation are valid and binding.
holdings: A court in winding up proceedings may reopen an auction and reject an accepted bid if it serves the interest of creditors and the property can fetch a higher price.
A sale in court proceedings is not final until confirmed by the court, and the court retains discretion to set aside the sale for the benefit of creditors, even after deposit of consideration.
Conditions of sale that empower the court to modify terms or set aside a sale even after confirmation are valid and do not violate fairness, provided they are disclosed in advance.
provisions: Companies Act, 1956, Section 447 (Power of Court in winding up)
Companies Act, 1956, Section 529 (Application of assets in winding up)
doctrines: Judicial discretion in court-supervised sales
Finality of auction subject to court confirmation
Public interest and creditor protection in insolvency proceedings

card.dispute: Whether statutory development authorities like the Lucknow Development Authority are subject to the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 for housing-related complaints such as delayed possession or defective construction.
issues_decided: Whether statutory development authorities fall within the definition of 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
Whether housing activities of development authorities were covered by the Act even before its 1993 amendment.
holdings: Statutory development authorities providing housing services are 'service providers' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and are amenable to complaints for deficiencies in service.
The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 covered housing activities of statutory authorities even prior to the 1993 amendment, as such activities constituted 'service' under Section 2(1)(o) of the Act.
doctrines: Principle of strict liability for deficiency in service by public authorities
Liberal interpretation of consumer protection legislation to serve social welfare objectives

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee, Bhatinda fought with landowners over whether land acquisition proceedings for a public park had lapsed due to delay in taking possession.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Committee had locus standi to challenge the order quashing the acquisition proceedings.
Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed due to non-taking of possession within one year of the Section 6 declaration.
holdings: The Municipal Committee had locus standi to file the writ petition as it was directly affected by the order quashing the acquisition it had initiated for a public park.

Acquisition proceedings do not automatically lapse if possession is not taken within one year of the Section 6 declaration, especially when delay was due to judicial proceedings and no formal abandonment was made under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
doctrines: Locus standi of a public body benefiting from acquisition
Automatic lapse of acquisition proceedings
Doctrine of state competence to abandon acquisition

card.dispute: The heirs of Wazira Singh (respondents) sued the daughters Parsinni and Chinto (appellants) for declaration of title and possession over 53 kanals 12 marlas of land, claiming ownership, while the appellants claimed adverse possession over the property for more than 30 years.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants perfected their title by adverse possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
Whether the possession of the appellants was adverse to the co-heirs after the marriage of the daughters?
Whether the suit was barred by limitation?
holdings: Possession that is open, continuous, and exclusive for over 12 years, with entries in revenue records showing ownership, can mature into title by adverse possession even against co-heirs.
Initial permissive possession until marriage becomes adverse after marriage if continued without consent and to the exclusion of other heirs.
A suit for declaration of title is barred by limitation under Article 65 when the defendant's adverse possession has continued for more than 12 years.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Permissive possession turning adverse
Prima facie title from possession and revenue entries

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a sale of minors' property by their mother without court permission, arguing it was voidable and time-barred, while the respondents claimed it was void and sought possession.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of a minor's immovable property by the mother without court permission is void or voidable under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956
Whether the attestation of the sale deed by the father amounts to a sale by the natural guardian satisfying the requirements of Section 8
Whether the suit for possession was barred by limitation
holdings: A sale of a minor's immovable property by a parent without court permission under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 is void, not voidable, as the provision is designed to fully protect the minor's property from parental depredations.

The attestation of a sale deed by the father does not make the mother's unauthorized sale a valid act by the natural guardian, especially when the father was present and active but did not execute the sale.
The suit was not barred by limitation because the sale was void ab initio and could be challenged at any time after the minor attained majority.
provisions: The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8
doctrines: Void vs voidable transactions
Protection of minor's property under guardianship law
Legal necessity in alienation of minor's property

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased coparcener claimed to continue a partition suit, based on a gift deed and succession rights, which was contested over the validity of the gift and the claimant's status as a legal heir.
issues_decided: Whether a coparcener can validly gift his undivided interest in joint family property under Mitakshara law?
Whether the appellant, as a daughter, is a legal heir entitled to represent the deceased in a partition suit under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956?
Whether the gift deed executed by the deceased coparcener in favor of his daughter validly conferred succession rights under Order 22 Rule 10 of CPC?
holdings: A coparcener cannot make a valid gift of his undivided interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property without the consent of other coparceners or in exceptional circumstances; such a gift is void.

A daughter, as a Class I heir, is entitled to succeed to the interest of a deceased male coparcener in coparcenary property by intestate succession under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and can be substituted in a pending suit under Order 22 Rule 3 of CPC.
A gift of undivided coparcenary interest does not confer any succession rights under Order 22 Rule 10 of CPC, as it is not a testamentary disposition and is void under Hindu law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10
doctrines: Doctrine of survivorship in Mitakshara coparcenary
Statutory fiction of partition under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Voidness of gifts of undivided coparcenary interest without consent
Principle of testamentary disposition under Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act

card.dispute: The appellant-father sought possession of a portion of his ancestral house in New Delhi from which he was allegedly dispossessed by his son, the respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate could drop proceedings under Section 145 CrPC after dropping proceedings under Section 107 CrPC?
Whether the pendency of a civil suit for injunction bars the maintenance of criminal proceedings under Section 145 CrPC when there is no dispute over title?
Whether the appellant was wrongfully dispossessed and entitled to restoration of possession under Section 145 CrPC?
holdings: Dropping of proceedings under Section 107 CrPC, which pertains to public peace, does not automatically justify dropping proceedings under Section 145 CrPC, which deals with possession disputes.
The pendency of a civil suit does not bar proceedings under Section 145 CrPC when the dispute is solely about possession and not title, especially among co-owners.
The appellant was wrongfully dispossessed without lawful authority and is entitled to immediate restoration of possession under Section 145 CrPC.
doctrines: Preventive justice under Section 107 CrPC
Summary remedy for possession under Section 145 CrPC
No ouster of criminal jurisdiction in possession disputes merely because of parallel civil proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants, landowners in Delhi, challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, seeking higher market value, solatium, and interest.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of the acquired land should be enhanced beyond Rs. 6 per square yard based on price trends and location advantages?
Whether the appellants are entitled to solatium despite not being statutorily entitled, due to inordinate delay in appointing an arbitrator?
holdings: The appellants are entitled to an enhanced market value of Rs. 8 per square yard due to the land's proximity to developed roads and rising property prices, reduced to Rs. 750 per square yard after deducting one-third for development charges.
The appellants are entitled to solatium at 15% of the market value due to a five-year delay in appointing the arbitrator, and interest at 6% per annum as not challenged.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 23(2)
doctrines: Equitable solatium for administrative delay
Market value assessment based on locational advantages and price trends

card.dispute: Pratap Singh and his mother Sarojini Devi disputed ownership of properties, including Sterling Castle in Simla and a house at 34 Alipur Road, Delhi, allegedly purchased by or for the former Maharaja Ripudaman Singh.
issues_decided: Whether the property at Sterling Castle, Simla, was private family property or State property of Nabha
Whether the property at 34 Alipur Road, Delhi, was privately owned by Sarojini Devi or part of the joint family estate
Whether the covenant under Article XII of the Instrument of Accession allowed rulers to retain private properties distinct from State properties
holdings: Properties purchased by a ruler during British paramountcy in benami names due to restrictions were presumed to be State properties unless proven otherwise by clear user and enjoyment as private property.
An admission in a prior legal application that a property was purchased from Pratap Singh estopped Sarojini Devi from later claiming it as joint family property.

Article XII of the Covenant allowed rulers to retain only those properties they exclusively owned and enjoyed privately; mere inclusion in an inventory did not convert State property into private property.
doctrines: Doctrine of Benami Transactions
Doctrine of Estoppel
Act of State Doctrine
Rule of Primogeniture

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of sub-letting without written consent and rent default; the tenant argued waiver by acceptance of rent.
issues_decided: Whether sub-letting without the landlord's previous written consent constitutes a valid ground for eviction under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956
Whether acceptance of rent by the landlord after knowledge of sub-letting amounts to waiver of the right to evict
Whether a sub-tenancy created before the landlord's purchase of the property bars a subsequent eviction suit
holdings: Sub-letting without the landlord's prior written consent is a valid ground for eviction under Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
Mere acceptance of rent by the landlord does not constitute waiver of the right to evict for unauthorized sub-letting; conscious relinquishment must be proven.
A sub-tenancy created without written consent, even before the current landlord's ownership, does not bar an eviction suit under the Act.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 16
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 23
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 24
doctrines: Waiver by conduct
Statutory interpretation (mandatory vs directory provisions)
Public interest in rent control legislation

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased landowner fought the Union of India over the adequacy of compensation for land and a building requisitioned and acquired in 1967 under the Defence of India Act and the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of the acquired land was correctly determined by the High Court at Rs. 4 per sq. yard without considering the rising trend in land prices between 1961 and 1967.
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the Arbitrator’s valuation of the building at Rs. 2,50,000 and fixing it at Rs. 1,41,100 based on state engineering estimates.
Whether solatium should be awarded at 15% under the Central Land Acquisition law or 10% under the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act for property acquired under the Requisitioning Act.
holdings: When determining market value, the rising trend in land prices in the vicinity between a relevant prior sale and the acquisition date must be considered; an additional Re. 1 per sq. yard was added to account for price rise, fixing the value at Rs. 5 per sq. yard.

The High Court rightly rejected the Arbitrator’s valuation based on a non-testifying engineer’s estimate but should have included Rs. 5,720 for omitted items; the correct value of the building is Rs. 1,46,820.

Solatium for land acquired under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 must follow the rate under the applicable state law (Rajasthan Act), i.e., 10%, not the higher central rate of 15%.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Sections 7, 8
doctrines: Comparable Sales Method as a valid criterion for market valuation
Principle of just equivalent compensation in land acquisition
Doctrine of functus officio in arbitration
State-specific benefits apply when central acquisition laws are used in states

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the delay in land acquisition proceedings where awards were made 14–20 years after notifications, resulting in unfairly low compensation based on outdated market values.
issues_decided: Whether excessive delay in making awards after Section 6 declarations renders acquisition proceedings invalid or entitles claimants to additional compensation.
Whether the market value for compensation should be determined by the date of Section 4 notification despite long delays in award issuance.
Whether the courts can grant modified relief instead of quashing acquisition proceedings due to public interest and third-party interests.
holdings: Excessive and unexplained delay in making awards after Section 6 declarations violates the principles of fair compensation under the Land Acquisition Act and the Constitution.
Courts can modify compensation by awarding additional amounts at 12% interest from two years after a key judicial decision until the award date, to counteract undervaluation caused by delay.
Acquisition proceedings need not be quashed despite procedural arbitrariness if quashing would harm public interest and affect third parties; alternative relief is permissible under Article 142.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Principle of fair and just compensation
Doctrine of unreasonable delay
Arbitrariness in exercise of state power
Equitable relief under Article 142
Balance between public interest and individual rights

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the delay in land acquisition proceedings where awards were made 14–20 years after notifications, resulting in compensation based on outdated market values.
issues_decided: Whether excessive delay in making awards after Section 6 declarations renders acquisition proceedings invalid or entitles claimants to additional compensation.
Whether the courts can modify compensation to account for unjust enrichment due to prolonged inaction by authorities.
holdings: Excessive and unexplained delay in making awards after Section 6 declarations, especially beyond a reasonable period, violates the principles of fair compensation under the Land Acquisition Act and the Constitution.

Courts can grant additional compensation at 12% per annum from two years after the Aflatoon judgment (23.8.1974) until the award date, calculated on the original market value, to mitigate injustice caused by administrative inaction.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Principle of fair and just compensation
Doctrine of unreasonable delay
Power of judicial remedy under Article 142 for ends of justice
Balancing public interest with individual rights

card.dispute: The Rajasthan Housing Board challenged the de-acquisition of land previously acquired for a housing project, after the government tentatively decided to release the land back to a cooperative society.
issues_decided: Whether a tentative decision to de-acquire land under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, communicated via an administrative letter, amounts to a final decision permitting withdrawal from acquisition
Whether the government can withdraw from an acquisition under Section 48 after taking possession of the land
Whether the existence of superstructures on the land prevents the government from dispensing with inquiry under Section 17(4) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953
holdings: A communication of a tentative decision to de-acquire land does not constitute a final decision under Section 48; only a final, implemented decision can have legal effect.
Once possession of land is taken by the government in an acquisition, it is not open to withdraw from the acquisition under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The presence of some superstructures on part of the land does not bar the government from dispensing with inquiry under Section 17(4) if the majority of the land is waste or arable.
doctrines: Finality of administrative decisions
Possession as a bar to de-acquisition
Doctrine of colourable legislation (implied in scrutiny of procedural compliance)

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of the declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, arguing it was published beyond the statutory time limit.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration under Section 6(1) was invalid due to non-publication within the prescribed time under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the period of court-ordered stay of dispossession should be excluded in computing the time limit for publishing the declaration under Section 6(1).
holdings: The plea that the declaration under Section 6(1) was time-barred was barred by constructive res judicata under Section 11 of the CPC as it was not raised earlier.
The period during which a court order stayed dispossession must be excluded in computing the time limit for publishing a declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Exclusion of judicial stay period from limitation
Legality of administrative action during judicial proceedings

card.dispute: Private parties and the Municipal Corporation of Delhi contested over unauthorized constructions and the maintainability of civil suits challenging demolition orders, amid concerns about misuse of interim injunctions.
issues_decided: Whether the jurisdiction of civil courts is ousted in suits relating to demolition of unauthorized constructions under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957
Whether interim injunctions can be granted without notice to the opposite party in such matters
Whether courts must record reasons for granting ex parte injunctions under Order 39 Rule 3, proviso, of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
holdings: Section 347E of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 does not completely bar civil court jurisdiction; it only bars suits in respect of actions taken in good faith under Sections 343 and 347E.

Courts must record reasons before granting ex parte injunctions, as required by the proviso to Order 39 Rule 3 of the CPC, and failure to do so renders the order non-compliant with statutory procedure.
Ex parte injunctions in demolition cases should be granted sparingly, only when delay would defeat justice, and must be limited to two weeks unless extended after hearing the opposite party.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39, Rule 3 (proviso)
doctrines: Doctrine of ouster of jurisdiction
Doctrine of mandatory compliance with procedural requirements
Principle of ex parte injunctions in urgent cases
Rule of recording reasons for exceptional judicial orders

card.dispute: The appellant claimed declaration and possession over disputed land, asserting title through Ramaswamy, whose legitimacy and right to inherit were challenged by the respondents.
issues_decided: Whether a presumption of valid marriage arises from prolonged cohabitation between a man and woman as husband and wife
Whether the presumption of marriage was rebutted by evidence in this case
Whether Chinathambi had the right to execute a deed of settlement over ancestral coparcenary property in favour of his son Ramaswamy
holdings: Prolonged cohabitation as husband and wife raises a rebuttable presumption of valid marriage under law.
The circumstances relied upon by the High Court—omission in will, absence in compromise, and witness depositions—were insufficient to rebut the presumption of marriage.
A coparcener who obtains his share through partition becomes the absolute owner and can validly execute a deed of settlement in favour of his family.
doctrines: Presumption of marriage from cohabitation
Rebuttable presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act
Partition converting coparcenary interest into separate ownership

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a preliminary decree in a partition suit, claiming it was obtained by fraud as the plaintiff had no title to the property due to a prior release deed in favour of his employer.
issues_decided: Whether a preliminary decree obtained by non-disclosure of a material document (release deed) amounts to fraud on the court
Whether a plaintiff has a legal duty to disclose all material facts and documents, including those adverse to his case
Whether such fraud can vitiate a judicial decree even if the opposing party could have discovered the truth with due diligence
holdings: A decree obtained by deliberate non-disclosure of a material document, such as a release deed, constitutes fraud on the court and is a nullity.
A plaintiff has a legal duty to come to court with clean hands and disclose all material facts and documents, especially those executed by him that affect his title.
The principle of finality of litigation does not protect a decree obtained by fraud, even if the opposing party could have uncovered the truth through diligence.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates all judicial proceedings
Clean hands doctrine
Intrinsic vs. extrinsic fraud
Finality of litigation (interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium)

card.dispute: Members of a cooperative housing society challenged the quashing of a land acquisition declaration by the Patna High Court, which had remanded the matter due to procedural violations in the acquisition process.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the entire declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act due to procedural irregularities under Section 5A and Rule 4?
Whether a cooperative society qualifies as a 'company' under Chapter VII of the Land Acquisition Act, requiring compliance with Section 40?
Whether the High Court should have granted individualized relief instead of a blanket remand affecting non-petitioners?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the entire Section 6 declaration; the remand should have been limited to the interests of the actual writ petitioners and not extended to all acquired land.
A cooperative society seeking land acquisition under the Act must comply with Chapter VII, including Section 40, as it qualifies as a 'company' for the purposes of the Act.

Courts exercising powers under Article 226 must consider equitable factors and individual circumstances, tailoring relief to avoid unjust disruption where procedural defects do not nullify the overall fairness of the process.
doctrines: Procedural fairness in land acquisition
Doctrine of proportionality in judicial review
Equitable discretion under Article 226
Condition precedent in statutory compliance

card.dispute: Surjet Kaur, claiming to be the legally wedded wife of Gulaba Singh, fought with his alleged heirs over possession of his property after his death.
issues_decided: Whether Surjet Kaur's marriage to Gulaba Singh was validly solemnized under Hindu law or custom.
Whether mere cohabitation and a Karewa Nama are sufficient to establish a valid marriage.
Whether the plaintiffs, as alleged grandsons of Gulaba Singh's paternal uncle, were entitled to inherit the property in the absence of a valid will.
holdings: A valid marriage under Hindu law requires proof of essential customary ceremonies; mere execution of a Karewa Nama and distribution of gur are insufficient.
Cohabitation as husband and wife, without proof of valid marriage ceremonies, does not confer legal status of marriage.
The burden to prove a customary marriage lies on the party asserting it, and failure to plead or prove such custom results in the marriage not being recognized.
doctrines: Essential ceremonies doctrine in Hindu customary marriages
Doctrine of burden of proof in establishing custom
Legal irrelevance of cohabitation without valid marriage

card.dispute: The United Bank of India and the Official Liquidator disputed over the disclaimer of a leasehold property during company liquidation, and subsequent claims for payment of arrears, interest, and diminution in sale price by the purchaser, Triputi.
issues_decided: Whether the Official Liquidator was justified in disclaiming the leasehold property under Section 535 of the Companies Act, 1956, on grounds of onerous covenants?
Whether the purchaser, Triputi, was entitled to a reduction in the sale price due to defective title or non-possession of certain properties?
Whether Triputi was liable to pay interest at 15% per annum on the unpaid balance of the sale consideration?
holdings: The lease of land for 99 years at a nominal rent of Rs 1,200 per annum cannot be considered onerous; thus, the disclaimer under Section 535 was unjustified.
The sale was conducted on an 'as is where is' basis with no warranty from the Official Liquidator; hence, the purchaser cannot claim price reduction for title defects.
Triputi is liable to pay interest at 15% per annum from January 1, 1989, on the unpaid amount, as per its own undertaking to the Court.
doctrines: Doctrine of disclaimer of onerous property in liquidation
Principle of 'as is where is' sale in insolvency proceedings
Enforcement of court-accepted undertakings

card.dispute: The Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation and a borrower disputed whether the Corporation could invoke recovery proceedings under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act after obtaining a decree under Section 31 but not executing it.
issues_decided: Whether the Corporation can invoke Section 29 proceedings after obtaining a decree under Section 31 without executing it?
Whether the right under Section 29 is lost if the Corporation initially proceeds under Section 31?
holdings: The Corporation can abandon proceedings under Section 31 at any stage and invoke Section 29, even after obtaining a decree, if the decree remains unsatisfied.
The phrase 'without prejudice to the provisions of Section 29' in Section 31 preserves the Corporation's right to use Section 29, preventing defaulters from exploiting delays to evade recovery.
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Equity and good faith
Legal fraud prevention

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming hereditary management of temples on Pavagarh hill, contested the classification of Kalika Mataji temple as a public trust under the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, challenging the Charity Commissioner's registration of the temple as public property.
issues_decided: Whether the Kalika Mataji temple is a public trust within the meaning of Section 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950
Whether the temple qualifies as a public temple under Section 2(17) of the Act
Whether dedication to the public must be proved by express document or can be inferred from user and circumstances
holdings: A temple may be held to be a public trust even in the absence of express dedication, if longstanding public worship as of right is established through historical and circumstantial evidence.
The Kalika Mataji temple is a public temple as it has been used by the general Hindu public for centuries without hindrance, supported by state patronage, grants, and pilgrimage practices.
Internal management by a family does not make a temple private; public character is determined by public access, worship, and offerings, not merely by managerial control.
doctrines: Inference of dedication from public use
Presumption of public character from antiquity and continuous worship
Relevance of historical and official records in proving public trust
Distinction between private family temple and public temple

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the state's acquisition of their property for connecting two temples under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming it lacked a valid public purpose and was mala fide.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act was void for vagueness in specifying public purpose.
Whether the acquisition for connecting two temples served a public purpose.
Whether the exercise of power under Section 4(1) was mala fide due to prior failed private purchase attempts.
holdings: A notification under Section 4(1) is not invalid merely for lack of detailed public purpose if the purpose is evident from the record or subsequent clarification.
Providing access between two religious sites visited by thousands of pilgrims constitutes a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act.
Failure to acquire land by negotiation before resorting to compulsory acquisition does not make the process mala fide if a genuine public purpose exists.
doctrines: Colourable legislation doctrine
Judicial review of administrative action
Presumption of public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the rejection of their applications for enhanced compensation under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, seeking parity with a higher award granted to another landowner whose case was pending appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants are 'aggrieved persons' entitled to apply for reference under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the Special Land Acquisition Officer could proceed under Section 28-A while the original compensation award was under appeal
Whether applications under Section 28-A based on awards from pending appeals can be entertained
Whether the State or beneficiary can seek reference under Section 28-A(3) and what safeguards apply against fraudulent claims
holdings: Landowners are 'aggrieved persons' under Section 28-A(1) if they have an interest in land covered by the same notification and award, and seek enhanced compensation based on a higher court-awarded compensation.

The Collector must await the final decision in an appeal under Section 54 or Article 136 before deciding applications under Section 28-A, to prevent premature redetermination based on uncertain awards.

An award under Section 26 that forms the basis for a Section 28-A application must be genuine and not based on antedated or fraudulent Section 18 applications; the Collector may examine such claims before proceeding.

The State or beneficiary cannot unilaterally seek a reference under Section 28-A(3) unless permitted by local amendments; however, they may challenge an award under Article 226/227, but not after accepting its benefits.
doctrines: Principle of parity in compensation
Doctrine of ripeness of cause of action
Judicial review under Articles 226 and 227
Fraud vitiates proceedings
Aggrieved person test under statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord, Anar Devi, sought possession of a shop from tenant Nathu Ram under Section 23A(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, but the High Court rejected her application for failing to prove ownership; she appealed the decision.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord must plead and prove ownership of the accommodation in an application under Clause (b) of Section 23A of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 to succeed in recovering possession.
Whether the tenant can deny the landlord's title when he has previously acknowledged it.
holdings: The words 'if he is the owner thereof' in Clause (b) of Section 23A do not require the landlord to plead or prove ownership in the application; such proof is not a precondition for eviction if the tenant does not contest ownership or is estopped from doing so.

A tenant who has acknowledged the landlord's ownership in writing is estopped from later denying it, especially under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, and cannot resist eviction on grounds of disputed title.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 23A(b)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 23D(3)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 23E
doctrines: Estoppel against tenant denying landlord's title (Section 116, Evidence Act)
Presumption of bona fide requirement under Section 23D(3)
Statutory interpretation to effectuate legislative intent for expedited possession

card.dispute: The petitioner, owner of a coking coal mine, challenged the validity of the Coal Mines Nationalisation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1986, which retrospectively deemed compensation paid to include value for coal stock, thereby nullifying a prior Supreme Court judgment in his favor.
issues_decided: Whether the Coal Mines Nationalisation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1986, which retrospectively amended the compensation provisions, is valid despite nullifying a judicial decision?
Whether a legislative amendment that retrospectively deems compensation to include stock of coal violates the doctrine of separation of powers or judicial independence?
Whether the amendment effectively removes the legal defect identified in the earlier judicial decision, thereby validating the prior action?
holdings: A retrospective amendment that removes the legal defect identified by a court and alters the basis of a prior judgment is a valid exercise of legislative power and does not encroach on judicial authority.

A validating law is effective only if it removes the cause of invalidity; mere declaration to override a court decision is insufficient, but substantive correction with retrospective effect is permissible.

The deeming provision in the amendment, which treats compensation as including value for coal stock from the beginning, legally nullifies the need for additional payment or accounting, rendering the prior judgment inoperative.
provisions: Coking Coal Mines (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1971, Section 3
Coal Mines Nationalisation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1986, Section 10(2) and Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of Validating Legislation
Doctrine of Retrospective Operation of Laws
Separation of Powers
Deeming Provisions in Statutes

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether an arbitral award dividing joint family movable and immovable properties among six branches should be set aside due to alleged errors and misconduct.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitral award suffers from errors apparent on its face regarding property valuation and omission of movables from partition.
Whether the arbitrator failed to decide disputes about advances taken from joint family funds as required by the arbitration agreement.
Whether the unequal value of shares allotted renders the award invalid.
Whether the allotment of family deity worship and attached properties to one party alone is illegal.
holdings: The award does not suffer from errors apparent on the face of the record; valuation based on evidence before the arbitrator cannot be challenged by subsequent evidence not presented during arbitration.
The arbitrator considered disputes over advances and made a lump sum award, which is permissible; failure to itemize advances does not invalidate the award.
Unequal share values due to differential adjustments for advances do not invalidate the award, as arbitrators may distribute shares based on their judgment.
Allotting maintenance of the family deity to the party receiving the property where it is located is reasonable and does not invalidate the award, especially when worship rights remain joint.
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the award
Finality of arbitral awards
Presumption that award disposes of all matters unless shown otherwise
Lump sum award doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioners, owners of a coked coal mine, challenged the validity of the Coal Mines Nationalisation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1986, which retrospectively deemed compensation paid to include value of coal stock, thereby nullifying a prior Supreme Court judgment favoring them.
issues_decided: Whether the Coal Mines Nationalisation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1986, which retrospectively deems compensation to include stock of coal, is valid despite overriding a prior judicial decision?
Whether a legislative amendment that retrospectively validates action by removing the basis of judicial invalidity encroaches on judicial power?
holdings: A retrospective amendment that removes the legal defect identified by a court and alters the basis of the judgment does not encroach on judicial power and can render the prior judgment inoperative.

The deeming provision in the amended law, which treats compensation as including the value of coal stock from the beginning, is valid and binding, and courts must give effect to such legislative validation.
provisions: Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, Section 10 and Section 22(1)
Coal Mines Nationalisation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1986, Section 2 (amending Section 10) and Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective validation
Doctrine of separation of powers (legislative power to cure defects in law)
Deeming fiction in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Landlords and tenants contested the constitutional validity and applicability of Section 3(c) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which excluded premises with a monthly rent exceeding Rs. 3,500 from rent control protections.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(c) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an arbitrary classification?
Whether tenants in premises with rent above Rs. 3,500 had acquired a vested right to statutory protection against eviction?
Whether the term 'rent' in Section 3(c) refers to 'standard rent' or the actual rent being paid?
holdings: The classification under Section 3(c) based on rent threshold is reasonable and does not violate Article 14, as it serves the legitimate state purpose of excluding those who can afford higher rents from rent control benefits.
Tenants do not acquire a vested right in statutory protections under rent control laws; such protections are conditional and can be withdrawn by the legislature through valid amendments.
The term 'rent' in Section 3(c) refers to the actual monthly rent being paid, not 'standard rent', and no prior determination of standard rent is required for the provision to apply.
doctrines: Doctrine of Vested Rights
Principle of Prospective Operation of Repeal
Reasonable Classification under Article 14
Literal Rule of Statutory Interpretation

card.dispute: The legal heirs of statutory tenants of residential premises challenged the constitutional validity of Section 2(1)(iii) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which denied heritability of statutory tenancies in residential premises, claiming it violated Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 2(1)(iii) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which denies heritability of statutory tenancy in residential premises, is discriminatory under Article 14?
Whether the denial of heritability of residential statutory tenancy infringes the right to shelter under Article 21?
holdings: The classification between residential and commercial statutory tenants is valid as they are not similarly situated; commercial tenancies involve livelihood and business continuity, justifying differential treatment under Article 14.
The right to shelter under Article 21 does not mandate heritability of statutory tenancies; reasonable restrictions on residential tenancy succession do not violate Article 21.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Balancing of fundamental rights with legislative policy
Statutory creation of tenancy rights and their limitations

card.dispute: The Jaipur Development Authority challenged the executability of an award that allotted land in lieu of compensation to respondents who had purchased land later acquired by the state.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition Officer had jurisdiction to allot part of the acquired land in lieu of compensation under the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953
Whether the objection to the executability of such an award could be raised during execution proceedings
holdings: The Land Acquisition Officer has no jurisdiction under the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 to allot acquired land in lieu of compensation, as such power is not conferred by Section 11 or Section 31(3), which only allows exchange of other land for limited interest holders with government sanction.

An award directing allotment of acquired land in lieu of compensation is a nullity and can be challenged during execution, as only matters related to compensation, measurement, and apportionment are executable under Sections 11 and 18.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of jurisdictional limitation
Doctrine of executability of decrees

card.dispute: Tea estate owners challenged the validity of education and rural employment cess imposed by the West Bengal government on tea estates, arguing it was ultra vires and overlapped with central taxation.
issues_decided: Whether the West Bengal legislature had the competence to levy a cess on tea estates under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule
Whether the impugned cess was in reality an excise duty on tea, a subject under central jurisdiction (Entry 84, List I)
Whether the levy of cess on tea estates violated the principle of non-discrimination or was arbitrary
Whether the retrospective application of the impugned amendment was constitutionally valid
holdings: The West Bengal legislature had the power to levy a cess on tea estates as a tax on land under Entry 49 of List II, which covers taxes on land and buildings.
The cess was not an excise duty on tea production but a tax on land measured by tea output, and thus did not encroach upon central legislative power under Entry 84 of List I.
The classification of tea estates as a separate category for taxation was valid and did not violate equality, as it was based on intelligible differentia with rational nexus to the object.
The retrospective operation of the amendment was valid as it cured a defect in prior legislation struck down in an earlier judgment and restored continuity of lawful taxation.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 84
West Bengal Taxation Laws (Second Amendment) Act, 1989
West Bengal Rural Employment and Production Act, 1976, Section 4(2)
doctrines: Legislative competence based on entries in the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of pith and substance
Doctrine of occupied field
Principle of retrospective legislation curing invalidity

card.dispute: The owners of cashew factories challenged the validity of a government order that transferred their factories to state ownership, alleging violation of mandatory procedural requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the government complied with the mandatory procedural requirements under Section 3(1) of the Kerala Cashew Factories (Acquisition) Act, 1974 before issuing the acquisition order.
Whether the notice issued by the government was sufficient to justify acquisition under clause (c) of Section 3(1) on grounds of large scale unemployment.
Whether the satisfaction of the government for issuing the acquisition order was based on relevant material and subject to judicial review.
holdings: The government must strictly comply with the mandatory procedural requirement in the proviso to Section 3(1) of the Act, including providing specific grounds for acquisition and considering objections.
A notice that fails to specify which clause of Section 3(1) is invoked and lacks particulars about actual large scale unemployment does not meet statutory requirements.
The government's satisfaction for acquisition must be based on relevant material and is subject to judicial review; mere apprehension of future unemployment is insufficient for invoking clause (c).
doctrines: Procedural fairness in administrative action
Judicial review of executive satisfaction
Strict compliance with mandatory statutory procedure

card.dispute: The landowners and the State of Kerala disputed whether the benefit of enhanced solatium under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, applied to all pending acquisition proceedings on 24-9-1984 or only to those specified in the transitional provisions of the 1984 Amendment Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, applies to all references pending before the Court under Section 18 on 24-9-1984, or only to cases covered under Section 30(1)(a) and (b) of the 1984 Amendment Act.
Whether the enhanced solatium under Section 23(1-A) is payable in appeals pending before the High Court or Supreme Court after 24-9-1984.
