Whether the Collector is liable to pay additional compensation under Section 23(1-A).
holdings: Section 23(1-A) applies only to cases falling under Section 30(1)(a) and (b) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, and not to all references pending before the Court on 24-9-1984.
No additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) is payable in appeals pending before the High Court or Supreme Court on or after 24-9-1984.
The Collector is liable to pay additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) in cases covered by the transitional provisions.
doctrines: Prospective operation of amendments
Transitional provisions interpretation
Literal construction of statutory language

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Kenchegowda and Siddegowda fought over whether certain land was self-acquired or joint family property and whether a preliminary decree for partition could be granted in a suit originally for declaration and injunction.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for partial partition is maintainable without impleading all co-sharers and including all joint family properties?
Whether a court can grant a preliminary decree for partition in a suit originally filed for declaration of title and permanent injunction?
Whether the death of a party during appeal without bringing legal representatives on record leads to abatement of the appeal and finality of the trial court's findings?
holdings: A suit for partial partition is not maintainable if all joint family properties are not included and all co-sharers are not impleaded.
A preliminary decree for partition cannot be passed in a suit for declaration and injunction when the cause of action and reliefs are distinct and no proper pleadings or parties exist for partition.
When a party dies during appeal and legal representatives are not brought on record, the appeal abates and the trial court's findings become final and binding.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
Hindu Law of Joint Family and Partition
doctrines: Abatement of suit on death of party without substitution
Finality of findings when appeal abates
Non-maintainability of partial partition suits

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from a shop premises on grounds of bona fide requirement for expansion of a partnership pawn broking business, which the tenant resisted.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's failure to mention the ground of bona fide requirement in the eviction notice disentitles him from relying on it in the eviction petition.
Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the case for reassessment of the space requirement for the landlord's business.
Whether a prior dismissal of an eviction petition affects the maintainability of a subsequent petition based on changed circumstances.
holdings: Non-mention of a ground for eviction in the notice does not disentitle a landlord from relying on it if the ground is proved and legally valid.
The appellate authority must objectively assess the actual space required for the claimed business expansion, especially when the Rent Act requires bona fide need.
A landlord can file a fresh eviction petition based on a new or changed cause of action even if a previous petition was dismissed, provided the claim is supported by cogent evidence.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(1)(b)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Recurring cause of action
Beneficial legislation interpretation
Objective assessment of landlord's need

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer and the claimants fought over the market value of agricultural land acquired for housing sites near Eluru, Andhra Pradesh, and whether compensation should reflect potential building value.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of acquired agricultural land should be enhanced based on potential for residential use.
Whether sale deeds and prior awards relied upon by claimants were reliable indicators of market value.
Whether the High Court applied incorrect legal principles in determining compensation.
holdings: Market value must reflect actual demand and conditions as of the notification date; potential use alone, without evidence of market demand, cannot justify higher valuation.
Sale deeds and prior awards based on inflated or non-bona fide transactions cannot form the basis for determining market value.
The High Court erred in law by relying solely on unreliable documents and ignoring absence of development; compensation must be based on agricultural land value.
doctrines: Principle of market value on date of notification
Rejection of 'got-up' sales in valuation
Requirement of genuine market demand for potential use valuation
Error of law in application of wrong valuation principles

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the respondent, claiming she was a trespasser, while she claimed to be the daughter and heir of the deceased tenant entitled to inherit the tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was the daughter of the deceased tenant and thus eligible to inherit the tenancy
Whether the respondent was entitled to inherit the tenancy under Section 2(h) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, particularly in light of the 1965 amendment
holdings: The respondent, as the heir of a contractual tenant, inherited the tenancy upon the tenant's death, irrespective of whether she was residing with the tenant at the time of death.

The 1965 amendment to Section 2(h) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act applies only to statutory tenants, not contractual tenants, and thus does not limit inheritance rights of contractual tenants to those residing with them.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 2(h)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation with reference to Statement of Objects and Reasons
Distinction between contractual and statutory tenancy
Heritability of tenancy rights

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of a bungalow and recovery of rent arrears from the tenant, who contested the validity of the notice and claimed standard rent had already been fixed and paid.
issues_decided: Whether the notice demanding rent arrears was valid under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947
Whether the landlord could claim rent arrears that accrued before the assignment of leasehold interest
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution in interfering with lower court decisions
holdings: A valid notice under Section 12(3)(a) must demand legally recoverable arrears relating to the accommodation let; if standard rent is disputed or already paid, the notice is invalid.
A transferee of leasehold interest is not entitled to arrears of rent due before the transfer; such arrears are merely an actionable claim or debt, not recoverable as rent under the Act.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by acting as a court of appeal and re-evaluating factual findings, which is not permissible under the supervisory jurisdiction.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a) and (b)
doctrines: Doctrine of actionable claim
Doctrine of valid notice for eviction
Limits of supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Nataraja Iyer (plaintiffs) fought with R. Gopala Pathar (defendant) over ownership of a property, claiming title through a sale deed from Kasambu Ammal, who allegedly inherited it after her husband Govindaswamy's death.
issues_decided: Whether Govindaswamy was presumed dead under Section 108 of the Evidence Act after being unheard of for seven years?
Whether Kasambu Ammal acquired an undivided half-share in the property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937?
Whether the sale deed executed by Kasambu Ammal in 1970 was valid?
holdings: Section 108 of the Evidence Act creates a presumption of death after seven years of absence, but not of death at any particular time; the burden to prove death at a specific time lies on the party asserting it.
Kasambu Ammal did not prove that her husband died after 1937; thus, she did not acquire rights under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937.
Since Kasambu Ammal had no valid title, her sale deed was invalid; title passed by survivorship to Srinivasa, who lawfully sold it to the defendant.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937
doctrines: Presumption of death under Section 108
Burden of proof in cases of prolonged absence
Survivorship in joint family property

card.dispute: The Maharashtra State Financial Corporation sought to recover a defaulted loan by taking possession of Suvarna Board Mills' factory under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, which the High Court set aside for violating natural justice; the Corporation appealed.
issues_decided: Whether a separate show-cause notice is required before invoking action under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, to take possession of a defaulter's property.
Whether the principles of natural justice were violated by not considering the borrower's representation before taking possession.
holdings: The notice under Section 29, which clearly warned of possession if payment was not made by a specified date, satisfied the requirements of natural justice; a separate show-cause notice is not mandatory.

Although the borrower's representation should have been considered before taking drastic action, the failure to do so was cured by affording a post-decisional hearing, which met the ends of natural justice in this case.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Post-decisional hearing as a substitute for pre-action opportunity in certain cases
No straitjacket formula for fair procedure

card.dispute: The owner of a private colony challenged the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's condition requiring transfer of land reserved for parks and schools to the Corporation free of cost as a condition for sanctioning the layout plan.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Corporation of Delhi could lawfully require the owner to transfer land reserved for parks and schools to it free of cost under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.
Whether the reservation of land for public purposes in a layout plan results in vesting of ownership in the Corporation.
Whether the Corporation could claim ownership of the land without legal authority or payment of compensation.
holdings: The Corporation cannot claim ownership of land reserved for parks, schools, or open spaces merely by imposing conditions in a layout plan approval, as the Act does not authorize such a transfer of ownership.
Reservation of land for public use creates a trust-like obligation on the owner but does not automatically transfer ownership to the Corporation.
The Corporation may manage the reserved land for public benefit but cannot change its use or claim ownership without paying market value for it.
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of separation of ownership and management rights
Public trust doctrine

card.dispute: Premium Granites and others challenged the Madras High Court's declaration that Rule 39 of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, was unconstitutional, which had invalidated leases granted under it.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 39 of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, is ultra vires the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, and therefore invalid.
Whether Rule 39 confers arbitrary and unguided power on the executive, thereby violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
holdings: Rule 39 is valid as it forms part of an integrated scheme of the Mineral Concession Rules and does not violate the MMRD Act, as it allows for reasonable relaxation consistent with mineral development and public interest.

Rule 39 does not violate Article 14 because it permits objective classification and structured discretion; the power to grant exemptions is not arbitrary if exercised based on valid, non-discriminatory principles.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15(1)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 3
Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, Rule 39
Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, Rule 8(C)
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Reading down of statutes
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Structured discretion in executive action

card.dispute: The petitioners claimed to be successors in title to land acquired by the Union of India and sought injunction against interference with their possession, but the land had already been acquired and vested in the railways.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners had a valid title or interest in the land acquired by the government.
Whether the petitioners were entitled to a declaration that the acquisition was illegal and void.
Whether the petitioners could claim an injunction against the true owner (Union of India) despite lack of lawful possession or title.
holdings: The petitioners derived no title from the original owner or subsequent purchasers, as the land had already vested in the government free of encumbrances at the time of the sale.
The acquisition proceedings were final and binding, and the petitioners had abandoned their challenge to the validity of the award.
An injunction cannot be granted to a trespasser or a person without lawful possession or title, especially against the true owner of the property.
doctrines: Vesting of title in the state upon completion of acquisition
Finality of acquisition awards
Injunction as an equitable and discretionary remedy
No injunction in favour of a trespasser

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the validity of the acquisition of their land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, after the state government re-initiated acquisition proceedings following a prior acquisition completed under urgent provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the re-initiation of acquisition proceedings under Section 5-A and Section 6(1) after a prior acquisition under Section 17(1) was valid when the land had already vested in the state government?
Whether the declaration under Section 6(1) made after three years from the Section 4(1) notification was invalid under the first proviso to Section 6(1)?
Whether the High Court's judgment in 1982, which set aside only the non-application of Section 5-A, could revive the landowners' title after vesting under Section 17(1)?
holdings: Once land is taken possession of under Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, it vests absolutely in the state free from encumbrances, and subsequent re-acquisition proceedings are unnecessary and inconsequential.
A Section 6(1) declaration made beyond the three-year period under the first proviso is not automatically void if the land has already vested in the government through prior valid acquisition.
The High Court’s setting aside of only the order dispensing with Section 5-A did not restore ownership to the landowners, as vesting under Section 17(1) remained unaffected.
doctrines: Vesting of title by operation of law
Doctrine of finality of acquisition under urgent provisions
Laches in challenging acquisition proceedings
Conclusive declaration under Section 6(3)

card.dispute: The appellant Noorduddin claimed independent possession and title over Khasra No. 179, resisting execution of a decree by respondent Dr. K.L. Anand, who had purchased properties under Khasra Sakni Nos. 13 and 14 through auction of evacuee property.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court could dismiss the appellant's claim without adjudicating his independent right, title, or interest in the property under Order 21, Rule 97 of the CPC
Whether the dispute regarding possession and boundaries of Khasra No. 179 was conclusively decided in prior proceedings (RFA or writ petition)
Whether the executing court was required to determine if Khasra No. 179 formed part of the properties sold under the decree
holdings: The executing court must adjudicate claims of independent right, title, or interest under Order 21, Rules 97–101 CPC, and cannot dismiss such claims without inquiry.
A party not bound by a decree or adversely affected in prior litigation can raise an independent claim in execution proceedings.
The limited question for adjudication is whether Khasra No. 179 is part of Khasra Sakni Nos. 13 and 14; if not, the respondent cannot dispossess the appellant from it during execution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 97, 98, 99, 100, 101, 103, 104
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 20
doctrines: Finality of adjudication on title in execution proceedings
Protection of independent possession during execution
Parliamentary intent to shorten litigation through summary adjudication in execution

card.dispute: Ram Dular (appellant) fought against the Deputy Director of Consolidation over his claim to a half share in ancestral land as a co-khatadar in Khata Nos. 196 and 99, which the Deputy Director denied by relying on allegedly fabricated revenue records.
issues_decided: Whether the Deputy Director of Consolidation was legally justified in overturning the findings of the lower authorities that Ram Dular was a co-khatadar in ancestral property?
Whether the Deputy Director committed an error in disregarding the 1308 Fasli revenue entry showing Sampath as son of Angan, which was not challenged as forged?
holdings: The Deputy Director exceeded his revisional powers under Section 48 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 by reappreciating evidence de novo instead of correcting legal or procedural errors, thus committing a manifest error of law.

Where a revenue entry (1308 Fasli) showing lineage is not disputed as forged and is supported by continuous possession and revenue payments, it must be considered, and its disregard amounts to an error in law.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction limited to legality, not reappreciation of facts
Principle of manifest error in law when vital evidence is ignored
Continuity of possession and unchallenged documentary evidence as proof of co-ownership

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Ram Prasad (appellants) fought against the Assistant Director of Consolidation and Jwala Singh (respondent) over ownership and tenancy rights in Khata No. 66, specifically challenging Jwala Singh's claim of co-tenancy based on a decree obtained under Section 59 of the U.P. Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether the civil suit challenging the collusive and fraudulent decree under Section 59 of the U.P. Tenancy Act was maintainable despite abatement due to consolidation proceedings.
Whether the consolidation authorities had exclusive jurisdiction to decide tenancy disputes after notification under Section 5 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.

Whether Smt. Jivani, as a female heir and widow, acquired absolute ownership of the tenancy under the U.P. Abolition of Zamindari Act, and could thereby validly create a co-tenancy in favor of Jwala Singh.

Whether the decree under Section 59 of the U.P. Tenancy Act, obtained by Jwala Singh, bound the reversioners (appellants) in the absence of ratification by Smt. Jivani after she became an absolute owner.
holdings: A civil suit seeking declaration that a decree under Section 59 of the U.P. Tenancy Act was collusive and fraudulent is maintainable under Section 9 of the CPC, as such relief is outside the exclusive domain of revenue courts.

Upon publication of a notification under Section 5 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, civil court jurisdiction is ousted, and consolidation authorities have exclusive power to adjudicate tenancy disputes, rendering pending suits abated.

A widow inheriting tenancy rights becomes an absolute owner under the U.P. Abolition of Zamindari Act from the date of its notification, but any prior limited rights or privileges do not automatically confer power to create binding co-tenancy without ratification.

A decree under Section 59 of the U.P. Tenancy Act, found to be collusive and fraudulent, does not bind reversioners, especially when the alleged co-tenancy was not ratified by the widow after she attained absolute ownership.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 5
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 242
U.P. Abolition of Zamindari Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Privileges Act, Section 5 and Section 6
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Abatement of civil suits upon consolidation
Fraud vitiates all proceedings
Limited estate versus absolute ownership
Doctrine of res judicata not applicable to collusive decrees

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of multiple murders and other offences, challenged their convictions and death sentences, arguing mitigating circumstances including alleged influence of violent films.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' convictions and death sentences for murder were legally justified
Whether the influence of violent films on the accused could be a mitigating factor in sentencing
Whether the case falls within the 'rarest of rare' category warranting the death penalty
holdings: The convictions and death sentences for A-1 and A-2 were upheld as the case falls within the 'rarest of rare' category due to the brutal and diabolical nature of the crimes.
The alleged influence of violent films on the accused cannot be a mitigating factor, especially when the accused was already a hardened criminal with no regard for human life.
The death sentence for A-3 was commuted to life imprisonment, while the life sentences for other appellants were upheld.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Principle of mitigating circumstances in capital sentencing
Role of media influence on criminal behaviour

card.dispute: Sardar Singh challenged the decree of specific performance of a sale agreement for a house, claiming he owned half the property and had not consented to the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered arbitration award declaring Sardar Singh's half ownership in the property was compulsorily registrable under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the courts below were justified in decreeing specific performance of the sale agreement for the entire property despite Sardar Singh's non-consent and co-ownership
Whether partial specific performance of the contract could be granted in respect of the transferable portion of the property
holdings: An arbitration award that declares pre-existing rights in immovable property, without creating new title, is not compulsorily registrable under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908.

A decree for specific performance of a sale agreement for entire co-owned property is improper when one co-owner has not consented; such a decree defeats equitable rights of the non-consenting co-owner.

Where a contract relates to divisible property and one part is legally enforceable, courts may direct partial specific performance under Section 12(4) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, to meet the ends of justice.
doctrines: Doctrine of pre-existing rights in immovable property
Equitable discretion in specific performance
Partial enforcement of contracts
Benami transaction doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of multiple murders and related offences, challenged their convictions and death sentences, arguing mitigating circumstances including alleged influence of violent films.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' convictions and sentences for murder and other offences were legally justified
Whether the influence of violent and immoral films could be a mitigating factor in sentencing
Whether the death penalty was appropriate in this case, particularly for accused A-3
holdings: The convictions of all appellants for murder and other charges were upheld, with death sentences confirmed for A-1 and A-2 as the case fell within the 'rarest of rare' category.
Exposure to violent films cannot be a mitigating circumstance in sentencing, especially when the accused is a hardened criminal who committed brutal murders.
The death sentence for A-3 (Shivaji) was commuted to life imprisonment, while all other sentences were confirmed.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Doctrine of joint liability under Section 34 IPC
Mitigating factors in capital sentencing

card.dispute: The State of Goa and others appealed against the Bombay High Court's decision to quash the government's order rejecting A. H. Jaffar and Sons' mining lease application and restoring the Minister's earlier order in their favor.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain the petition under Article 226 when an alternative remedy under Section 30 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 was available
Whether the delay in filing a revision under Rule 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 could be condoned
holdings: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition when an effective alternative remedy under Section 30 of the Mines and Minerals Act was available.
Delay in filing revision can be condoned if sufficient cause is shown, and bona fide pursuit of remedy in the High Court constitutes sufficient cause.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 30
doctrines: Alternative remedy doctrine
Condonation of delay

card.dispute: The dispute was between a cooperative housing society and landowners over whether the acquisition of land for the society constituted a public purpose or was a colourable exercise of power benefiting private individuals.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition for a private cooperative housing society qualifies as a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the State's contribution of Rs 100 per acre constituted a genuine public purpose or a colourable exercise of power
Whether the procedural requirements under Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act were mandatory in cases of partial public funding
holdings: Acquisition for a company or society can serve a public purpose if public funds are used, wholly or partly, for the acquisition.
A token contribution from public funds does not automatically make an acquisition valid; the purpose must genuinely serve the public and not primarily benefit private individuals.

When a cooperative society consists of affluent members and the land is transferred to them individually, the acquisition cannot be deemed for public purpose and amounts to a colourable exercise of power under Section 6 of the Act.
doctrines: Colourable legislation doctrine
Public purpose doctrine in land acquisition
Presumption of constitutionality and burden of proof in mala fide allegations
Use of public funds as determinant of public purpose

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and Atur India Pvt. Ltd disputed whether the instrument between them was a reversionary lease or merely an agreement to lease, and whether stamp duty was payable on it.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the parties constituted a lease or an agreement to lease under the Indian Stamp Act and the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the agreement created a present demise or merely contractual rights
Whether the benefit of an agreement to lease can be assigned to a third party
holdings: An agreement that does not create a present and immediate demise in possession is not a lease but an agreement to lease, and does not require registration or attract stamp duty under Section 2(n) of the Indian Stamp Act.
A reversionary lease creates an estate in land, whereas an agreement to lease creates only contractual obligations; the instrument in question was merely an agreement to lease.
The benefit of an executory agreement to lease can be assigned to a third party, such as a cooperative housing society, even if the lessee is acting as a promoter.
provisions: Maharashtra Ownership Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963
doctrines: Distinction between lease and agreement to lease
Doctrine of reversionary lease
Equity of Walsh v. Lonsdale not applicable in India
Assignability of benefits under an agreement to lease

card.dispute: Suresh Chandra Bahri, Gurbachan Singh, and Raj Pal Sharma appealed their convictions and death sentences for the murder and criminal conspiracy to kill Bahri's wife and two children, and for destruction of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence awarded to Suresh Chandra Bahri was justified in light of the 'rarest of rare' doctrine.
Whether the death sentences awarded to Gurbachan Singh and Raj Pal Sharma were appropriate given their roles in the murders and conspiracy.
Whether the trial and High Court correctly applied the law in confirming the convictions and sentences.
holdings: Suresh Chandra Bahri's actions fell within the 'rarest of rare' category due to the brutal, premeditated murder of his wife and children for property-related motives, warranting the death penalty.
Gurbachan Singh, though part of the conspiracy, did not participate in the actual killings and thus deserved life imprisonment instead of death.
Raj Pal Sharma, despite active involvement, lacked evidence showing he played a leading or particularly cruel role, so his death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Principle of proportionality in sentencing
Balancing of aggravating and mitigating circumstances in capital punishment

card.dispute: The U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad (a local authority) challenged its exclusion from land acquisition proceedings and sought to be impleaded in appeals filed by landowners over compensation.
issues_decided: Whether a local authority for whom land is being acquired has a right to be impleaded and heard in acquisition and reference proceedings under Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the local authority has a right to receive notice of proceedings for determining compensation.
Whether the local authority can file an appeal against enhancement of compensation if the government does not appeal.
Whether the High Court’s determination of compensation was arbitrary and required remittal.
holdings: Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act grants a local authority the right to appear and adduce evidence in compensation proceedings before the Collector and reference court.
The right under Section 50(2) includes the right to adequate notice from the Collector and reference court about hearings on compensation.
A local authority may file an appeal in the High Court against enhanced compensation after obtaining leave, even if the government does not appeal.
The High Court’s compensation determination was arbitrary and unsupported by evidence; the matter is remitted for fresh decision in accordance with law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 3
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 15
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 16
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 17
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 28
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 30
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 31
U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 32
doctrines: Right to be heard as a statutory authority in acquisition proceedings
Judicial review under Article 226 for denial of statutory rights
Suo motu powers under Article 142 for ends of justice
Principle of impleadment of necessary parties in appeals affecting public interest

card.dispute: The appellant claimed adverse possession over 0.56 acres of land leased to the respondent, who sued for possession, asserting title under a lease deed executed before the land vested in the State under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the lease deed executed on 5-12-1949 but registered on 3-4-1950 could confer title despite the land vesting in the State on 31-3-1950 under Section 6 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950?
Whether the lease was valid in absence of the lessee's signature, and whether the Transfer of Property Act applied to agricultural leases?
Whether the appellant had acquired title by adverse possession after initially entering as a licensee?
holdings: A registered document takes effect from the date of its execution, not registration; thus, the lease conferred title from 5-12-1949, prior to vesting, and the land did not vest in the State.
Agricultural leases are excluded from the Transfer of Property Act under Section 117; hence, requirements like a written lease under Section 107 do not apply, and state tenancy law governs validity.
Permissive possession does not become adverse merely by passage of time; there must be clear evidence of hostile animus and knowledge by the true owner, which was not established here.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, Section 6
doctrines: Doctrine of relation back of registered documents
Exclusion of agricultural leases from Transfer of Property Act
Requirement of hostile animus for adverse possession
Burden of proof in adverse possession by licensee

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant bank for allegedly subletting the premises to its employees' trade union without consent; the tenant claimed the union's use was part of its business and under its control.
issues_decided: Whether Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 applies to non-residential premises
Whether the tenant bank sublet the premises to the trade union without the landlord's consent
holdings: Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act applies to both residential and non-residential premises, as the provision does not distinguish between them and aims to protect landlords' rights uniformly.

There was no subletting under Section 13(1)(a) because the bank retained control over the premises, received no monetary consideration, and allowed the union to use the space as part of its business activities under its authority.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(a)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 14
doctrines: Exclusive possession with consideration is essential to establish subletting
Constructive possession may be retained by a tenant even if another entity occupies the premises
Burden of proof in subletting cases lies on the landlord, and inferences must align with human conduct and evidence

card.dispute: Residents challenged the state government's lease of open land reserved under a town planning scheme to a private trust for constructing a dharamshala, alleging violation of public purpose and environmental safeguards.
issues_decided: Whether the state government had the power to lease out land reserved for open spaces under a town planning scheme to a private trust.
Whether the municipality could lawfully permit construction on land vested in it for public amenities like open spaces.
Whether the delay in challenging the allotment and ongoing construction warranted upholding the impugned action as a fait accompli.
holdings: The state government cannot lease land reserved for open spaces under a town planning scheme to a private entity, as it defeats the statutory purpose of preserving public amenities and environmental health.
Land vested in a municipality under a town planning scheme must be used only for the purposes specified in the scheme, and any deviation requires a compelling public interest not present here.
Construction begun during pending litigation cannot create a fait accompli; courts will not validate illegal actions merely because they have progressed.
doctrines: Fait accompli
Colourable exercise of power
Prospective overruling
Public trust doctrine
Statutory purpose and legislative intent

card.dispute: Tenants of buildings challenged the assessment of property tax by the Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, arguing they had standing to appeal and that the method of determining annual letting value was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant is entitled to file and maintain an appeal against a property tax assessment under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 as applicable in Gujarat
Whether proviso (aa) to sub-clause (ii) of clause (1A) of Section 2 of the Act, which deems actual rent as annual letting value where standard rent is not fixed, is valid and effective
holdings: A tenant is entitled to maintain an appeal against a property tax assessment if the tax burden falls on them under the lease agreement and they comply with the procedural requirements under Sections 406 and 407 of the Act.

Proviso (aa) to Section 2(1A) is valid and must be applied where standard rent is not fixed; the actual rent received by the owner is deemed the annual letting value for property tax, overriding any contrary provisions in rent control laws.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 2(1A) proviso (aa)
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Sections 406 and 407
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1944, Section 11
doctrines: Doctrine of standing (locus standi) in tax appeals
Doctrine of non-obstante clause
Principle of actual rent as basis for property tax where standard rent is not fixed

card.dispute: Bhoop Singh claimed entitlement to possession of suit land based on a prior declaratory decree, while Ram Singh Major and others contested its validity due to non-registration and alleged collusion.
issues_decided: Whether a decree passed without registration can confer rights in immovable property valued at Rs.100 or more under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether a compromise decree that creates new rights in immovable property must be registered
Whether the decree in Suit No.215 of 1973 was a valid declaration of pre-existing rights or an unregistered instrument creating new rights
holdings: A decree that creates new rights in immovable property worth Rs.100 or more must be registered under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, even if passed by a court.
A compromise decree that does not declare pre-existing rights but instead creates new rights in immovable property is compulsorily registrable.
The decree in Suit No.215 of 1973 was not a declaration of pre-existing rights but created new rights and thus required registration; its non-registration rendered it ineffective.
doctrines: Doctrine of compulsory registration of instruments creating rights in immovable property
Doctrine of pre-existing rights versus creation of new rights in property
Doctrine of collusive or sham decrees defeating third-party rights

card.dispute: Landowners and encroachers challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings and resisted the implementation of a court-directed award for the construction of a Buddha temple, while the Society sought enforcement of prior judicial directions to complete the acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the proceedings dated 31.7.1984 constitute a valid award under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 despite not being in Form 15
Whether the High Court could entertain a writ petition under Article 226 when alternate remedies were available under the Bihar Public Land Encroachment Act, 1956 and in a civil title suit
Whether the State could be directed to complete land acquisition proceedings after a long delay and inaction
holdings: A document not in Form 15 can still be treated as a valid award under Section 12 of the Land Acquisition Act if it contains all essential requisites and reflects substantial compliance with the law and court directions.
The High Court can exercise its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 despite alternate remedies when the enforcement of prior judicial orders is at stake and there is a risk of thwarting justice.
Courts can direct executive authorities to complete long-pending land acquisition proceedings, especially when delays are due to inaction or malafide conduct, to give effect to judicial orders.
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Judicial enforcement of court orders
Discretionary nature of writ jurisdiction
Vesting of property upon possession

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the validity of the land acquisition for housing Dalits, arguing that the urgency clause used to bypass inquiry was unjustified and violated their right to livelihood under Article 21.
issues_decided: Whether the invocation of Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to dispense with Section 5-A inquiry was valid in the absence of genuine urgency.
Whether pre- and post-notification delays undermine the claim of urgency for land acquisition.
Whether acquisition of land that is the sole source of livelihood violates Article 21 of the Constitution.
holdings: The State can invoke Section 17(4) to dispense with Section 5-A inquiry if there is a subjective satisfaction of urgency, especially for housing for marginalized communities, and such satisfaction is entitled to judicial deference.
Delays in the acquisition process, even if substantial, do not negate the existence of urgency at the time of notification, and administrative lethargy does not invalidate the urgency clause.

Acquisition for public purpose with compensation and solatium does not amount to deprivation of livelihood under Article 21, as constitutional safeguards are fulfilled through payment and recompense mechanisms.
doctrines: Subjective satisfaction in urgency cases
Deference to executive satisfaction in land acquisition
Right to livelihood under Article 21 with compensation safeguards
Public purpose overriding individual property rights

card.dispute: The Chandigarh Administration challenged the High Court's decision to allow Jagjit Singh's writ petition, which restored his plot allotment after a long delay, based on alleged discrimination and precedent from another case.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in allowing the writ petition on grounds of discrimination by comparing the respondent's case with that of another person (Prakash Rani)?
Whether the principle from Jaswant Singh v. Chandigarh Administration applied to the facts of the present case?
Whether the respondent's inordinate delay of 17 years in challenging the cancellation of lease affected the maintainability of the writ petition?
holdings: The High Court cannot issue a writ based on alleged discrimination by relying on another person's case unless it first determines that the order in that case was lawful and the cases are factually similar in material respects.
The decision in Jaswant Singh does not apply to this case as the facts are materially different, and thus cannot be a basis for granting relief.

A delay of 17 years in filing a writ petition, without satisfactory explanation, renders the petition unjusticiable and indicates an attempt to benefit from changed circumstances rather than enforce a legal right.
provisions: Punjab and Haryana High Court Rules, 1978 (for writ jurisdiction)
Chandigarh Rent Control and Housing Act, 1956 (implied by context of lease and forfeiture powers)
doctrines: Rule of law and non-discrimination in administrative action
Principle of factual similarity for applying precedent
Laches and inordinate delay in invoking writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax challenged whether the Kamla Town Trust was entitled to tax exemption under charitable trust provisions for assessment years 1949-50 to 1965-66.
issues_decided: Whether the Kamla Town Trust was entitled to exemption under Section 4(3)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 for the years 1949-50 to 1955-56;
Whether the trust qualified for exemption under the same provision for the years 1956-57 to 1961-62;
Whether the trust was eligible for exemption under Section 11 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for the years 1962-63 to 1965-66;
Whether the trust's objects, particularly providing residential quarters for company employees, constituted 'charitable purpose' under the law.
holdings: The trust was not entitled to exemption under Section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act for 1949-50 to 1955-56 as the 1945 rectified deed did not show trust property was held wholly for charitable purposes.
The trust was entitled to exemption under Section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act for 1956-57 to 1961-62 as the 1955 rectified deed established wholly charitable objects.
The trust is entitled to exemption under Section 11 of the 1961 Act for 1962-63 to 1965-66, subject to compliance with conditions including the 25% accumulation limit.
Providing residential quarters for employees of a specific company, regardless of need, does not constitute a charitable purpose or an object of general public utility.
doctrines: Test for charitable purpose under Indian tax law
Principle of 'wholly for charitable purposes'
Doctrine of public benefit in charitable trusts
Interpretation of trust deeds in tax exemption cases

card.dispute: The Chandigarh Administration challenged High Court orders restoring lease rights to two respondents who had defaulted on payments after winning plots in auctions, arguing that the restoration was unjustified and discriminatory.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could direct the restoration of lease rights based on alleged discriminatory treatment compared to another beneficiary (Prakash Rani).
Whether the High Court could rely on a previous decision (Jaswant Singh) to allow a writ petition filed after a 17-year delay by a defaulted allottee.
holdings: The High Court cannot compel an authority to repeat an action based on alleged discrimination unless it first determines that the action in favor of the other person was lawful and that the cases are factually similar; mere disparity in treatment does not entitle a defaulted allottee to restoration of lease rights.

A writ petition filed after a 17-year delay, without explanation or pending proceedings, cannot be allowed merely by relying on a prior decision with distinguishable facts; laches and inaction bar equitable relief.
provisions: Punjab Urban Rent Control and Eviction Act, 1949 (if applicable by context)
Chandigarh Rent Control Act, 1951 (implied by context)
doctrines: Rule of law and non-repetition of illegality
Principle of lawful discrimination and equal treatment under administrative law
Laches and delay in seeking equitable relief
Separate adjudication of cases on individual merits

card.dispute: Displaced villagers and their descendants sought employment or preferential treatment in the Rourkela Steel Plant, claiming a government assurance after land acquisition for the plant.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents were constitutionally obligated to provide employment to all adult members and descendants of families displaced by the acquisition of land for Rourkela Steel Plant.
Whether the failure to provide employment to more than one person per displaced family violated Article 21 of the Constitution.
Whether the principle of promissory estoppel required the State to provide preferential employment to displaced persons and their future generations.
holdings: The State is not constitutionally obligated to provide employment to every adult member or descendant of displaced families; providing one job per family satisfies the fair and equitable treatment standard.
Payment of compensation under the Land Acquisition Act and providing one job per displaced family does not violate Article 21, as no deprivation occurred without due process.
The principle of promissory estoppel does not extend to creating perpetual employment rights for future generations or multiple members of displaced families beyond the original assurance.
doctrines: Promissory Estoppel
Right to Livelihood under Article 21
Balancing of Fundamental Rights with Public Interest

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over possession and ownership of 34.9 bighas of land in Himachal Pradesh, with the appellants claiming title by adverse possession and the respondents seeking recovery of possession based on an alleged sale agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of res judicata applies to bar the appellants from denying tenancy status based on a finding in a previous suit?
Whether an adverse finding against a party who succeeded in the previous suit can operate as res judicata in a subsequent proceeding?
Whether the appellants were entitled to retain part of the land in equity despite lack of legal title?
holdings: Res judicata does not apply where the issue of tenancy was not raised, framed or decided in the subsequent suit due to different pleadings and causes of action.
An adverse finding against a party who obtained a favorable decree cannot be used as res judicata against them in a later suit since they had no right to appeal that finding.
Equity permits the appellants to retain 10 bighas of the disputed land as protected tenants, with the balance to be restored to the respondents, to meet the ends of justice.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, Section 91
doctrines: Res judicata
Conclusiveness of judicial findings
Equitable relief in property disputes

card.dispute: The H.M.T. House Building Co-operative Society challenged the High Court's decision quashing land acquisition proceedings initiated for its housing scheme, arguing the acquisition was for public purpose and legally sanctioned.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition for a co-operative society's housing scheme was for a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether prior approval by the State Government under Section 3(f)(vi) of the Land Acquisition Act was validly obtained.
Whether the involvement of agents in securing land acquisition vitiated the process.
holdings: Acquisition of land for a co-operative society of government employees does not serve a public purpose if the land is primarily for private benefit of society members.
An order dated 9.8.1984 could not be valid under Section 3(f)(vi) as the amended definition of 'public purpose' came into force only on 24.9.1984.
The use of agents who undertook to 'manage all concerned at all levels' in acquiring land indicates mala fide and renders the acquisition process illegal.
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine in land acquisition
Mala fide use of agents in administrative process
Prospective operation of statutory amendments

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the constitutional validity of an amendment that removed his right to evict a tenant from non-residential premises for bona fide personal use, claiming it violated Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1956, which denied landlords the right to evict tenants from non-residential premises for bona fide personal use, violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the classification between residential and non-residential tenants under the amendment has a reasonable nexus with the object of the Act?
holdings: The amendment creating a distinction between residential and non-residential premises by denying eviction for bona fide need in non-residential cases violates Article 14 as it lacks a reasonable nexus with the Act's object.
The right to evict for bona fide personal use is equally valid for both residential and non-residential premises, and denying it for non-residential units is arbitrary and unjust.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1956 (Punjab Act 29 of 1956)
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Arbitrariness in state action
Principle of equal protection of laws

card.dispute: The plaintiff, a daughter of the deceased Ram Nath Dewan, challenged the validity of a sale deed executed by her brother's power of attorney in favor of third-party defendants, seeking partition and possession of her share in a house property.
issues_decided: Whether the 1942 Will of Ram Nath Dewan was valid and operated to vest ownership of the property in the first defendant (son) upon his father's death.
Whether the first defendant or his alienees acquired the property by adverse possession, thereby barring the plaintiff's claim by limitation.
Whether the sale deed executed by the second defendant (as General Power of Attorney of the first defendant) in favor of defendants 3 to 5 was valid.
Whether the plaintiff’s suit for partition and possession was within time, particularly in relation to the first floor of the property.
holdings: The 1942 Will was upheld as valid, and the first defendant became full owner of the ground floor of the property upon Ram Nath Dewan's death.
The plea of adverse possession failed because it was not properly pleaded or established, and possession under a claimed title does not become adverse unless explicitly renounced.
The sale deed in favor of defendants 3 to 5 was valid concerning the ground floor, as the first defendant had lawful title and his legal representatives did not challenge the sale.

The first floor became absolute property of the widow Satyawati under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and on her death, it devolved equally among her five children; thus, the plaintiff was entitled to 1/5th share in the first floor.
doctrines: Adverse possession must be clearly pleaded and proven with specific facts about commencement and nature of possession.
Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, confers absolute ownership on Hindu female heirs, removing prior limited estate (stridhan) restrictions.

card.dispute: Two widows and daughters of Lachiram fought with the second wife and her descendants over partition of family property, validity of an adoption, and authenticity of a will in favor of the grandson.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of defendant No. 3 (Purshottam) was valid under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956?
Whether the will in favor of Purshottam was validly executed and proved under the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and the Evidence Act?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of fact in second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure?
holdings: An adoption by a Hindu male during the lifetime of his wife is invalid without her consent under Section 7 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, and absence of the first wife’s consent renders the adoption void.

A will required to be attested under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act must be proved by at least one attesting witness; mere assumption of execution without evidence of attestation fails to satisfy Section 68 of the Evidence Act.
The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or reverse concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is formulated and involved, as mandated by Section 100 CPC.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 7
doctrines: Consent requirement for valid adoption under Hindu law
Strict proof of attestation for wills
Substantial question of law doctrine in second appeals

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of their land in Nilothi, Delhi, for a sewage treatment plant, arguing the process was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition notifications under Sections 4, 6, and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, were validly issued without a Section 5-A inquiry due to urgency
Whether the land could be acquired for a public purpose despite its existing use under the Master Plan
holdings: The invocation of Section 17(4) to dispense with the Section 5-A inquiry was valid due to the urgent public need for sewage treatment to combat severe pollution in Delhi.
Land can be acquired for a public purpose like environmental protection even if it is designated for other uses under urban planning schemes.
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine
Urgency exception in land acquisition
Judicial notice of environmental degradation
Doctrine of necessity in administrative action

card.dispute: The Indore Development Authority and allottees of flats in a housing scheme disputed over the escalation in the cost of flats and the payment of interest on the balance amount after possession was given.
issues_decided: Whether the Development Authority could lawfully increase the cost of flats beyond the initially advertised estimated cost?
Whether the allottees could be required to pay interest on the unpaid balance amount after taking possession of the flats?
holdings: A development authority may revise the cost of flats if the original terms stated the cost was only an estimate subject to change, provided the escalation is not arbitrary and is justified by factors like increased area or construction costs.
Allottees in possession of flats must pay the balance amount with simple interest at 6% per annum from the date of possession, as it is inequitable to enjoy possession without payment.
provisions: M.P. Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973
doctrines: Principle of non-arbitrariness in administrative action
Equity and good conscience
Promissory estoppel (implied)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired for a bus stand, claiming it was undervalued compared to similar lands.
issues_decided: What is the reasonable market value of agricultural land with potential for non-agricultural use at the time of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether deductions for developmental charges (53% for layout and 33 1/3% for development costs) are justified when land is acquired for a bus stand?
Whether prior sale deeds, stamp duty circulars, or commissioner’s valuation can reliably determine compensation?
holdings: The market value of land must reflect its potential use but cannot assume immediate development; Rs. 20 per sq. yd. was just given the land's location and undeveloped state.
Deductions for developmental charges are permissible based on building rules and actual development needs, even if land is acquired for public purposes like a bus stand.
Government stamp duty circulars and commissioner’s assessments are not reliable proxies for market value without corroborative evidence of actual transactions.
doctrines: Potential market value doctrine
Deduction for development charges doctrine
Rule of comparable sales with caution for small or isolated transactions

card.dispute: K.Raheja Constructions Ltd. fought with Alliance Ministers over whether they could amend their plaint to seek specific performance of a property sale contract after initially only seeking an injunction.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners were entitled to amend their plaint to seek specific performance of a contract of sale after a lapse of seven years from the original suit.
Whether the amendment sought was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963.
holdings: A party seeking specific performance must claim it within the period of limitation; delay of seven years in seeking amendment to claim such relief defeats the opposing party's right accrued under limitation.
Permission from the Charity Commissioner for alienation of trust property is not a condition precedent to filing a suit for specific performance, but the decree would be subject to such permission.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 6, Rule 17
doctrines: Condition precedent
Amendment of pleadings
Limitation bar

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal heirs of Sukh Devi and other family members over whether Sukh Devi had full ownership of property she received in lieu of maintenance, allowing her to sell it.
issues_decided: Whether property allotted to a Hindu widow in lieu of maintenance attracts Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, thereby converting her limited interest into full ownership.
Whether the right to residence forms an essential component of maintenance under Hindu law.
holdings: A Hindu widow who receives property in lieu of her pre-existing right to maintenance acquires limited ownership, which under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, becomes full ownership upon the Act's commencement.

Maintenance under Hindu law necessarily includes provision for residence, and such provision—whether through money or life interest in property—is sufficient to trigger the application of Section 14(1).
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1959, Section 3(d)
doctrines: Doctrine of full ownership conversion under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act
Doctrine of maintenance including residence in Hindu personal law

card.dispute: The appellants, successors of Mohan Lal, fought against Mirza Abdul Gaffar over possession of land after an earlier agreement for sale was not specifically enforced and the land was later sold to the respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could retain possession of the suit property based on adverse possession
Whether the appellant could retain possession under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the appellant pleaded and proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract under the agreement
holdings: The plea of adverse possession is not available where possession was originally obtained under a contract of sale, as such possession is not hostile or independent but permissive.

Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act allows a transferee to retain possession only as a defense, not as a claim for title, and only if he remains ready and willing to perform his contractual obligations.
A transferee relying on Section 53-A must expressly plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract; mere denial of unwillingness is insufficient.
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53-A
Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Possession nec vi nec clam nec precario
Equity requires mutual fairness in equitable defenses

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee challenged the award of uniform compensation to all acquired agricultural land, arguing that a belting system (different rates based on proximity to roads) should apply instead.
issues_decided: Whether the acquired agricultural land possessed potential value for residential or commercial use despite no formal sanction for such use.
Whether the principle of 'belting'—different compensation rates based on proximity to roads—could be applied in determining market value.
Whether the Division Bench erred in awarding a uniform flat rate of compensation to the entire land.
holdings: Land within municipal limits and near developed areas possesses potential value for non-agricultural purposes, justifying higher compensation even if used for agriculture at the time of acquisition.
The principle of belting is legally permissible when supported by evidence showing price differentials between land abutting roads and interior land.
Awarding a flat compensation rate across the entire acquired land, ignoring proven value differences, constitutes a patent error of law and is arbitrary.
doctrines: Principle of potential market value
Belting principle in land compensation
Error of law in ignoring factual evidence in favor of legal generalization

card.dispute: The dispute was between Mahboob Sahab (appellant) and Syed Ismail & others (respondents) over ownership and possession of land allegedly gifted to the respondents by their father, which the appellant purchased through sale deeds.
issues_decided: Whether the oral gifts of property by the father and mother to the sons were valid and proved?
Whether the decree in OS No. 3/1/1951 operated as res judicata in the subsequent suit?
Whether the father, as a natural guardian, could validly alienate the minors' property without appointment of a guardian?
holdings: The oral gifts by the father and mother to the sons were not proved, as there was no evidence of delivery of possession or acceptance, and thus the gifts were incomplete and invalid.

The doctrine of res judicata does not apply between co-defendants unless there was a conflict of interest, necessary adjudication, final decision, and proper party alignment, none of which existed in OS No. 3/1/1951.
A natural guardian cannot alienate minor's property without legal necessity or court permission; no such necessity was proved, but the son's conduct in attesting the sale deed amounted to estoppel.
doctrines: Res judicata between co-defendants
Estoppel by conduct
Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings
Requirements for valid gift under Muslim law

card.dispute: The Pleasant Stay Hotel fought the Palani Hills Conservation Council over whether the hotel could legally construct more than two floors in violation of the sanctioned building plan and Master Plan Rules.
issues_decided: Whether the construction by the hotel was in accordance with the sanctioned plan.
Whether the revised plan proposing additional floors was lawfully rejected by the authorities.
Whether the High Court erred in directing demolition of structures beyond the sanctioned two floors.
Whether the High Court's observations against government officials were justified.
holdings: The hotel's construction deviated from the sanctioned plan and was not justified, as the claim of structural necessity was found to be false.
The rejection of the revised plan was valid because constructing more than two floors violated clause 8.6.1 of the Master Plan Rules.
The High Court's direction for demolition was upheld, though clarification was needed on which portions of the structure were to be demolished.
The High Court's observations criticizing lack of application of mind by the Minister and Chief Minister were factually correct and necessary for disposal.
doctrines: Principle of compliance with sanctioned building plans
Doctrine of fait accompli rejected in environmental and regulatory violations
Requirement of application of mind by statutory authorities

card.dispute: The petitioner claimed ownership and sought to prevent the sale of land attached to recover dues owed by the judgment debtor, arguing he had purchased the land under an unregistered sale agreement and was protected by Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act; the respondents contested the validity of the agreement and asserted their right to execute the award.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner could invoke Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act to resist the attachment and sale of the land in execution of an award?
Whether the unregistered agreement of sale dated June 29, 1969, was valid, genuine, and enforceable under Section 53-A?
Whether the petitioner had come to court with clean hands and was entitled to equitable relief?
holdings: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act provides a statutory shield to a transferee in possession under a contract for sale but does not confer title or a right to seek declaratory relief.
The petitioner failed to prove the genuineness of the agreement and the payment of consideration; the agreement was found to be a sham document created to defeat the rights of creditors.
A person seeking protection under Section 53-A must come to court with clean hands; the petitioner, being a party to fraud, was not entitled to equitable relief.
provisions: Gujarat Stamp Act (local amendment making agreement of sale registerable)
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance (Section 53-A)
Clean hands doctrine
Equitable relief as a shield, not a sword

card.dispute: The Oxford English School challenged the Government of Tamil Nadu's land acquisition proceedings, arguing that a fresh declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act after the expiry of three years from the Section 4(1) notification was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether a fresh declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be made after the expiry of three years from the publication of the Section 4(1) notification, despite a court-ordered stay.
Whether the period of stay granted by the court in proceedings related to adjacent land can be excluded in computing the three-year period under the proviso to Section 6.
holdings: A fresh declaration under Section 6 cannot be made after the expiry of three years from the publication of the Section 4(1) notification, even if a court stay was granted, because the proviso creates an absolute bar.
The period of court-ordered stay in proceedings concerning adjacent land cannot be excluded from the three-year period for making a Section 6 declaration regarding the appellant’s land.
provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Rule 3(b) (framed under Section 55(1))
doctrines: Strict compliance with mandatory timelines in land acquisition
Exclusion of court-ordered stay periods under proviso to Section 6 is limited to proceedings directly concerning the land in question

card.dispute: The petitioners, who purchased land after the publication of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, claimed title by adverse possession against the Rural Institute, which had been handed possession of the acquired land by the State.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of land after the publication of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act is valid?
Whether the petitioners could acquire title by adverse possession over land already acquired by the State?
Whether the State and the Rural Institute became absolute owners of the acquired land free from encumbrances?
holdings: A sale of land after the publication of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act is void and does not bind the State.
Adverse possession cannot be claimed over acquired land unless the claimants assert their possession openly against the possessor and there is acquiescence, which was not proved here.
Upon acquisition, the State acquires absolute title under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, free from all encumbrances, and possession taken is conclusive against prior owners and transferees.
doctrines: Doctrine of extinguishment of title upon acquisition
Doctrine of voidness of transactions after Section 4(1) notification
Requirements for adverse possession: nec vi, nec clam, nec precario

card.dispute: Two branches of a family fought over whether self-acquired property of a common ancestor and its accretions constituted joint Hindu family property eligible for partition as such, or were inherited as tenants-in-common.
issues_decided: Whether self-acquired property of a father devolves on sons as joint Hindu family property or by inheritance as tenants-in-common in the absence of grandsons.
Whether property acquired from the income of such inherited property can be treated as joint Hindu family property.
Whether the defendants were in adverse possession of the accreted properties.
holdings: Self-acquired property of a father, upon his death, passes by inheritance to his sons as tenants-in-common and not as joint Hindu family property, especially in the absence of grandsons.
Accretions made from the income of inherited self-acquired property do not become joint Hindu family property but remain joint properties subject to accounting between co-owners.
The defendants failed to prove adverse possession, and thus could not claim exclusive ownership over the disputed accreted properties.
doctrines: Tenancy-in-common under Hindu law
Distinction between joint Hindu family property and coparcenary
Adverse possession
Spes successionis

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired by HUDA for an inner ring road, seeking higher compensation based on market value.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the sale and gift deeds and Basic Valuation Register extract as evidence of market value?
Whether the High Court was correct in doubling the sale deed rate and fixing compensation at Rs. 32 per square yard?
What is the proper method to determine the wholesale market value of acquired land with building potential based on retail sale prices in the vicinity?
holdings: The High Court's rejection of sale deeds, gift deeds, and Basic Valuation Register extract as unreliable for market value determination is upheld due to proper appreciation of evidence.
The High Court erred in deducting only 20% from the retail price to arrive at wholesale value; a deduction of one-third is required to account for layout costs and development potential.
The market value of acquired land with building potential must be determined by deducting one-third from the retail price of plots in nearby undeveloped layouts to reflect wholesale value.
doctrines: Appreciation of evidence by High Court not interfered with by Supreme Court in absence of perversity
Wholesale value deduction principle for undeveloped acquired land
Use of comparable sales in determining market value of acquired land

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over the validity of a will that excluded certain properties from a partition suit.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to the death of some respondents and non-substitution of their legal representatives
Whether the registered will (Ex.B-12) executed by Lakshmi Amma was validly proven and free from suspicious circumstances
holdings: The appeal did not abate because the deceased respondents had transferred their interests before death, and under Order 22 Rule 10 CPC, their legal representatives need not be brought on record.

A registered will, once propounded, benefits from a presumption of validity; mere suspicion without evidentiary basis cannot override the propounder's proof, especially when no pleading or evidence challenged coercion or lack of testamentary capacity.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22 Rule 10
Indian Succession Act, 1925 (implied by context of will validity)
doctrines: Presumption of validity of registered wills
Requirement to prove suspicious circumstances as real and not conjectural
Principle of transmission of interest by operation of law under CPC

card.dispute: The appellant, a former lessee of a cinema theatre, sought renewal of his cinema licence after the lease expired, but the landlady objected, claiming he was no longer in lawful possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was required to prove lawful possession for renewal of a cinema licence under Rule 12(B) of the A.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1970, after the lease had expired.
Whether the appellant’s continued possession of the theatre after expiry of the lease was lawful or juridical.
holdings: The omission of the requirement of lawful possession in Rule 12(B) does not imply that unlawful possession suffices for renewal; the licensing authority may still consider possession status as relevant.

A lessee whose lease has expired and who remains in possession is in unlawful, not juridical, possession, and must vacate unless lawfully permitted to stay; such possession is not protected as settled or lawful under the law.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1970, Rule 11(B) and Rule 12(B)
doctrines: Lawful possession required for licensing
Possession at sufferance after lease expiry is unlawful
No self-help in eviction: protection of possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act
Interpretation of lease covenants to determine nature of post-lease possession

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased plaintiff sued for specific performance of a contract to reconvey property sold in 1959, claiming a prior agreement for reconveyance upon repayment within three years, which the defendants denied.
issues_decided: Whether a 'gentleman's understanding' recorded in writing amounted to an enforceable contract for reconveyance of property
Whether the relief of specific performance should be denied due to inordinate delay and rise in property value
Whether assignment of the plaintiff's rights during litigation renders the claim champertous and bars specific performance
holdings: A written 'gentleman's understanding' with clear terms for reconveyance, executed by agents of both parties, created an enforceable contract as it showed intention to create legal relations.
Delay in disposal and rise in property value during litigation, not caused by the plaintiff, do not render specific performance inequitable or bar the relief.
Assignment of rights during litigation does not amount to champerty if done transparently and for valid consideration; assignees can seek specific performance as representatives-in-interest.
doctrines: Intention to create legal relations
Discretionary nature of specific performance
Champerty and maintenance
Actus curiae neminem gravabit

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a deceased defaulter challenged the validity of an auction sale of his land, arguing that the purchaser's payment of 25% of the bid amount by cheque did not constitute a valid tender under the rules.
issues_decided: Whether the deposit of 25% of the auction sale amount by cheque constitutes a valid tender under Rule 285-D of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952
Whether non-compliance with the requirement of immediate deposit of 25% of the bid amount renders the auction sale a nullity
holdings: A deposit of 25% of the bid amount by cheque, not encashed on the day of the auction, does not constitute a valid tender under Rule 285-D, which requires immediate payment in cash.
Non-compliance with the mandatory requirement of immediate deposit of 25% of the bid amount renders the auction sale a complete nullity, and the purchaser acquires no rights.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rule 285-D
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rule 285-E
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rule 25-G
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 84
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 85
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 86
doctrines: Mandatory nature of procedural rules in auction sales
Nullity of sale for non-compliance with mandatory deposit requirements
Literal interpretation of statutory terms like 'immediately' and 'forthwith'

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the land acquisition process, claiming violation of his right to a personal hearing under Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act and that the declaration under Section 6 was issued beyond the one-year time limit.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to provide a separate notice fixing a date for hearing violated Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act when the initial notice stated that hearing would be given at the time of filing objections.
Whether the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was invalid for being issued beyond one year from the publication of the notification under Section 4(1).
holdings: The requirement of Section 5A(2) was satisfied because the notice explicitly informed the petitioner that he would be heard at the time of producing objections, and since he chose to submit objections by post without appearing, no further hearing was required.
The declaration under Section 6 was valid as it was issued within one year of the last publication date under Section 4(1), excluding periods during which proceedings were stayed by court orders.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (right to be heard)
Compliance with mandatory procedural requirements in statutory interpretation
Doctrine of substantial compliance
