Doctrine of pious dedication under Muslim law for wakf creation

card.dispute: The appellants (developers) failed to provide a flat to the respondents as promised under a 1987 agreement, leading to a consumer complaint for deficiency in service, compensation, and interest.
issues_decided: Whether the consumer complaint was barred by limitation under Section 24A of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Whether the 1991 agreement substituted the 1987 agreement, thereby ousting the jurisdiction of the Consumer Commission
Whether the appellants were guilty of 'deficiency in service' under the Consumer Protection Act
holdings: The cause of action was continuing due to the preservation of rights under the 1987 agreement, so the complaint was not time-barred.
The 1991 agreement did not amount to novation because the original contract remained enforceable until full payment, so the Consumer Commission had jurisdiction.
The failure to deliver the flat despite repeated demands constituted 'deficiency in service' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
doctrines: Continuing cause of action
Novation of contract

card.dispute: The appellant, a decree-holder for eviction, fought the respondent, who claimed tenancy rights, over possession of the property and payment of mesne profits.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent should be directed to deliver possession to the appellant despite a pending declaratory suit on tenancy?
What interim measures should be adopted to protect the decree-holder's interest during prolonged execution proceedings?
holdings: The Court declined to direct immediate possession as the respondent's declaratory suit on tenancy was still pending.

The respondent must pay mesne profits at Rs.10 per sq. ft. from 1984 until the date of the order and Rs.20 per sq. ft. thereafter until the suit's disposal, with arrears payable in 12 monthly instalments.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 22
doctrines: Protection of judgment creditor's interest during execution delays
Interim compensation through mesne profits equivalent to market rent

card.dispute: Shopkeepers in Chandigarh's Sector 17 challenged the Union Territory's enhancement of their shop rents from Rs.2,671 to Rs.14,000 per month as arbitrary and discriminatory, seeking relief under Article 14 and contesting liability for interest during stay orders.
issues_decided: Whether the rent enhancement during the lease term violated the terms of the lease agreement
Whether the appellants were entitled to exemption from paying interest on arrears during the period of court-ordered stay
Whether the failure to enhance rent for some lessees created a valid claim of discrimination under Article 14
Whether the High Court erred in directing interest at 18% per annum on arrears
holdings: The rent could not be enhanced during the initial fixed term of the lease, and any such enhancement was invalid until the renewal period, when the government had authority to fix a new rent.
A party benefiting from a stay order remains liable to pay interest on statutory dues withheld during the stay, as the stay does not nullify the obligation.

No discrimination arises under Article 14 unless the favourable treatment of others is legally valid and the cases are comparable; mere administrative inaction does not create a right to equal treatment.
Interest at 18% per annum was excessive; 15% per annum was held to be just and appropriate in the circumstances, considering the public nature of the respondent authority.
provisions: Punjab Urban Rent Control and Eviction Act, 1949, Section 3
Punjab Urban Rent Control and Eviction Act, 1949, Section 22
doctrines: Rule of law and non-repetition of illegality
Interest liability during stay orders
Principle of equal protection under Article 14
Lease terms binding on lessor and lessee

card.dispute: M.I. Builders Pvt. Ltd. challenged the High Court's decision to quash its construction of an underground shopping complex in a public park in Lucknow, which was deemed illegal and unconstitutional.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of an underground commercial complex in a public park by a private builder with municipal permission was legal and in public interest.
Whether judicial discretion could be exercised to allow continuation of an unauthorized construction on grounds of equity or investment.
Whether the municipal body fulfilled its statutory duties in preserving public spaces and managing urban infrastructure.
holdings: Construction in a public park for commercial purposes without lawful authority is illegal and cannot be validated by municipal resolution; public trust doctrine protects parks as essential environmental and recreational assets.
Judicial discretion in granting relief must conform to law and cannot perpetuate illegality; substantial investment or completion of construction does not justify permitting unauthorized projects.

Municipal bodies have a statutory duty to provide parking and public amenities; part of an unauthorized structure may be repurposed for public use if it serves a civic need and aligns with statutory obligations.
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Judicial Discretion Bound by Law
Statutory Duty of Municipal Authorities

card.dispute: The developers of Perpetual Apartments refused to execute a sale deed in favor of the buyer (on behalf of her minor daughter) despite full payment and delivery of possession, leading to a consumer dispute over specific performance and repairs for sub-standard construction.
issues_decided: Whether the complaint filed under the Consumer Protection Act was barred by limitation?
Whether the Consumer Commissions were justified in directing specific performance of the agreement?
Whether the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply to complaints under the Consumer Protection Act prior to the insertion of Section 24A?
holdings: Prior to the insertion of Section 24A, the Consumer Protection Act did not prescribe any period of limitation, and courts could not imply limitation from the Limitation Act, 1963.
Even assuming applicability of the Limitation Act, the cause of action arose only when the appellants denied performance in August 1991, making the 1992 complaint timely under Article 54.
The Consumer Commissions acted within jurisdiction in directing specific performance and condoning delay, given the ongoing acknowledgments of liability by the developers.
doctrines: Doctrine of acknowledgment of liability under limitation law
Remedial nature of the Consumer Protection Act
Cessation of remedy, not right, upon limitation

card.dispute: Olympus Superstructures Pvt. Ltd. challenged the enforcement of arbitral awards in favor of Meena Vijay Khetan and others, who sought specific performance of agreements for sale of flats, over disputes regarding overlapping arbitration clauses and the arbitrator's competence to grant specific performance.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration clause in the main agreement governs disputes arising under both the main agreement and the Interior Design Agreement.
Whether conflicting arbitral awards can be made on overlapping claims under two agreements.
Whether an arbitrator can grant specific performance of a contract relating to immovable property.
Whether the arbitral award could be set aside on merits under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
holdings: The arbitration clause in the main agreement governs disputes arising under both agreements where claims overlap, as the parties intended a unified dispute resolution mechanism for interconnected disputes.
Conflicting awards on overlapping claims under two agreements are impermissible; a single arbitration clause must govern such interconnected disputes.

An arbitrator can grant specific performance of a contract for immovable property, as there is no statutory prohibition under the Specific Relief Act, 1963 or the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
Courts cannot interfere with an arbitral award on merits unless it falls under Section 34(2)(b); mere dissatisfaction with factual findings does not justify setting aside the award.
doctrines: Competence-competence of arbitrators to decide on their own jurisdiction
Separability of arbitration clauses
Public policy exception under Indian arbitration law
Finality of arbitral awards on factual findings

card.dispute: The landlord, Pawan Kumar Gupta, sued tenant Rochiram Nagdeo for eviction; the tenant challenged Gupta's title, claiming the property was held benami for his father, Pyarelal.
issues_decided: Whether the finding of title in the first suit operated as res judicata in the second suit?
Whether the sale deed in favor of the appellant was a benami transaction under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988?
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the trial and appellate courts?
holdings: A final finding on title in a prior suit operates as res judicata even if the suit was dismissed on procedural grounds, provided the issue was directly and substantially decided.

A transaction is not benami merely because the purchase money was funded by a relative; 'consideration provided' under Section 2(a) of the Benami Act refers to cases where payment is not made, not the source of funds.
The High Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of fact without sufficient reason, especially when no substantial question of law was involved.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)
Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, Section 2(a) and Section 3(1)
Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Section 91, Section 92, and Section 106
doctrines: Res judicata
Burden of proof in challenging documentary title
Presumption of validity of registered sale deed
Prospective operation of Benami Act

card.dispute: The Municipal Council, Ahmednagar appealed against a Bombay High Court order directing it to hand over possession of acquired land to the respondents, who had challenged the acquisition after a long delay.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could quash the acquisition notification under Section 126(4) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, after a long delay and after acceptance of compensation.
Whether the respondents, having participated in the acquisition process and accepted benefits, could later challenge the validity of the acquisition.
holdings: Once an award is made and compensation accepted, a challenge to the acquisition notice cannot be permitted, especially after inordinate delay.
A party cannot approbate and reprobate—accept benefits under a proceeding and later challenge its validity—thus the respondents were estopped from challenging the acquisition.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 126(4)
doctrines: Approbation and reprobation
Laches (inordinate delay)
Finality of acquisition proceedings after award and possession

card.dispute: The heirs of a deceased landlord appealed for possession of a non-residential property from a tenant, claiming bona fide need to start a grocery business after job loss due to a company lock-out.
issues_decided: Whether the suit abated upon the death of the original landlord who sought possession for personal use
Whether the amendment of the plaint to reflect the heirs' own requirement for the premises was legally permissible
Whether the requirement of the legal representative for starting a grocery business was bona fide
holdings: The suit did not abate as the cause of action for bona fide requirement survived to the heirs, especially after amendment of the plaint and full evidence on the new plea.
Amendment of the plaint to include the heirs' personal requirement was valid and did not prejudice the tenant, who had full opportunity to contest it.
A landlord need not resign employment or prove destitution to establish bona fide need; temporary measures for livelihood do not negate the reasonableness of the requirement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Bona fide requirement of landlord
Survival of cause of action upon death
Liberal amendment of pleadings under CPC
Discretionary interference under Article 136

card.dispute: The dispute was between Ram Kumar Agarwal and Thawar Das (through his legal heirs) over whether Thawar Das was entitled to specific performance of an agreement to purchase land from Phool Chand, and whether the High Court erred in decreeing that relief.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court committed an error in allowing a second appeal on a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC?
Whether the plaintiff (Thawar Das) was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract for specific performance?
Whether the plea under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act could be raised for the first time in second appeal?
Whether the suit for specific performance was barred by delay and laches?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC by reappreciating evidence and reversing findings of fact without framing a substantial question of law.
A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform; this was not established where a false claim of partial payment was made.
A plea under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, being a mixed question of law and fact, cannot be raised for the first time in second appeal if not pleaded or argued earlier.
A suit for specific performance filed nearly nine years after the stipulated period is barred by laches, even if limitation is not formally decided.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform in specific performance
Part performance under Section 53A
Substantial question of law in second appeal
Laches in equitable relief

card.dispute: The tenant, S. Thangappan, refused to pay rent to the landlord, P. Padmavathy, claiming she was not the true owner, and sought protection from eviction under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's denial of the landlord's title was bona fide under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act
Whether the non-payment of rent amounted to wilful default
Whether the premises were legitimately required for demolition and reconstruction
holdings: A tenant cannot deny the landlord's title at the beginning of the tenancy under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, even if the title is defective.
Non-payment of rent is wilful when the denial of landlord's title is not bona fide and is contrary to the estoppel principle under Section 116.
The landlord's requirement of the premises for demolition and reconstruction was legitimate and sufficient ground for eviction.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
doctrines: Estoppel against tenant denying landlord's title (Section 116, Indian Evidence Act)
Wilful default in rent payment due to mala fide denial of title

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant challenged the High Court's order allowing the landlord to evict him from a residential property in Delhi on grounds of bona fide need.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord established a bona fide need for the tenanted premises?
Whether the availability of another property with the landlord negates his claim for possession?
Whether the High Court committed a jurisdictional error in admitting evidence without proper procedure?
holdings: A landlord’s need for possession must be genuine, honest, and reasonable, and courts must consider all relevant circumstances including family size and living conditions.
The mere existence of another property with the landlord does not defeat the claim for possession unless that property is suitable and legally available for the landlord’s use.
The High Court erred in considering a will without formally admitting it into evidence, but the error was inconsequential as the ultimate finding on bona fide need was supported by existing record.
doctrines: Bona fide need of landlord
Reasonableness in landlord's requirement
Presumption of bonafide requirement
Irrelevance of alternative accommodation without legal right or suitability

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the decree in a summary suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, where the respondent claimed possession of a tuck shop and sought injunction against dispossession, which the lower courts granted despite legal and factual errors.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was in exclusive possession as a tenant within six months prior to filing the suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act?
Whether the Trial Court and High Court erred in granting relief beyond the plaint and outside the scope of Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act?
Whether the presumption of tenancy can arise solely from exclusive possession?
Whether the respondent's suit was barred by limitation and whether he approached the court with clean hands?
holdings: Exclusive possession alone does not create a presumption of tenancy; the respondent failed to prove tenancy or recent dispossession within six months, as required under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act.

The Trial Court exceeded its jurisdiction by granting relief not prayed for in the plaint and beyond what is permissible under Section 6, which only allows recovery of possession in cases of recent unlawful dispossession.
The lower courts wrongly relied on an erroneous legal presumption and ignored material contradictions in the respondent’s pleadings and evidence, rendering their decisions perverse.
The respondent failed to establish equitable relief eligibility due to inconsistent pleadings, delay, and abuse of process, disentitling him to relief under the Specific Relief Act.
doctrines: Presumption of tenancy from exclusive possession
Equitable relief and clean hands doctrine
Limitation and recent dispossession under Section 6
Scope of relief in summary suits

card.dispute: The legal representative of a deceased landlord sued for possession of property after a prior eviction decree based on tenancy was not executed; the tenant resisted, claiming the second suit was barred by Section 47 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether a second suit for possession based on title is barred by Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure when a prior decree for eviction on tenancy grounds remained unexecuted and became time-barred.
Whether the second suit was barred by res judicata under Section 11 CPC.
Whether non-execution of the earlier decree extinguished the plaintiff's title to the property.
holdings: A suit for possession based on title is not barred by Section 47 CPC if the earlier decree was based on tenancy and its execution lapsed, provided the title has not been extinguished.
A second suit on a different cause of action—title instead of tenancy—is not barred by res judicata under Section 11 CPC.

Mere failure to execute a decree for eviction does not extinguish the plaintiff's title; unless title is lost by adverse possession, statute, or decree, a fresh suit on title is maintainable within limitation.
doctrines: Res judicata
Cause of action estoppel
Continuity of title despite lapsed execution
Distinction between tenancy-based and title-based eviction suits

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased landlady fought the tenants over recovery of possession of rented premises on grounds including bona fide personal requirement for setting up a family business.
issues_decided: Whether the landlady had a bona fide requirement of the suit premises for setting up a Kirana shop for her son under Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents Act?
Whether the appellate courts erred in rejecting the claim of bona fide requirement based on the landlady's non-appearance as a witness and other circumstantial factors?
Whether the requirement under Section 13(2) of the Act regarding hardship was satisfied?
holdings: A landlord can establish bona fide personal requirement under Section 13(1)(g) through a family member, such as a son and GPA holder, even if the landlord does not personally appear as a witness.
The fact that the intended occupant took up alternate employment during prolonged litigation does not negate the bona fide intention to start a family business in the future.

The court must consider hardship to both parties under Section 13(2), and if the landlord would suffer greater hardship, eviction may be granted; such a finding, once established, supports the grant of relief.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Hardship test in eviction cases
Judicial review of findings on subjective satisfaction

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased tenant challenged the eviction decree passed due to non-deposit of arrears of rent by the 'first hearing' under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972.
issues_decided: Whether the date fixed for filing the written statement constitutes the 'first hearing' for the purpose of depositing rent arrears under Section 20(4) of the UP Act?
Whether the actual date of hearing or the date fixed in the summons for final hearing determines the due date for deposit of arrears?
holdings: The 'first hearing' under Section 20(4) means the date on which the court proposes to apply its mind to determine the controversy and frame issues, not the date fixed for filing the written statement.
The due date for deposit of rent arrears is the date fixed in the summons for the first or final hearing, not the actual date on which the hearing takes place.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order V, Rule 1(1)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Binding precedent on interpretation of 'first hearing'
Waiver of service of summons when party appears voluntarily

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Taherakhatoon sued Salambin Mohammad for possession of a 25' x 11' strip of land and demolition of two rooms built by the defendant, alleging encroachment on her property.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in interfering with findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC?
Whether the appellant's delay in filing suit affected the relief granted?
Whether the Supreme Court should exercise its discretion under Article 136 to grant relief despite legal error?
holdings: The High Court erred in interfering with a pure question of fact in a second appeal, as Section 100 CPC permits review only on substantial questions of law.
Despite the legal error, the long delay of over seven years in filing the suit and the 30-year existence of the construction make it inequitable to grant demolition.
Under Article 136, the Court may refrain from interfering on merits even after granting special leave, and can instead mould relief equitably, such as awarding compensation instead of possession.
doctrines: Principle of limitation of second appeal to substantial questions of law
Discretionary power under Article 136 to refuse relief despite legal error
Equitable relief and power to mould decrees under Article 142

card.dispute: The appellant (vendor) and respondents (vendees) fought over whether the vendees were entitled to specific performance of two sale agreements despite delayed or non-payment of the balance consideration beyond the time stipulated in the decrees.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court could grant extension of time for depositing the balance consideration under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act after a significant delay of five years from the decree and three years from the dismissal of appeal.
Whether the vendees remained ready and willing to perform their part of the contract, a condition precedent for specific performance.
Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the matter to the executing court to consider applications for extension of time, despite imposing constraints on the court's discretion.
holdings: A court may extend time for depositing balance consideration under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, but such discretion must be exercised equitably and not arbitrarily, especially after undue delay without sufficient explanation.

Continuous readiness and willingness of the plaintiff to perform is a condition precedent for specific performance; failure to deposit balance consideration within the stipulated time without valid reason negates this requirement.

The High Court erred in remanding the matter with observations that restricted the executing court’s discretion, but the overall circumstances, including long delay and lack of justification, warranted denial of extension of time.
doctrines: Condition precedent of readiness and willingness in specific performance
Equitable discretion in granting specific performance
Doctrine of delay and laches
Finality of decrees and enforcement within reasonable time

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's order setting aside the SDM's decision to discontinue proceedings under Section 145 CrPC in a land dispute already pending before a civil court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in setting aside the SDM's order discontinuing proceedings under Section 145 CrPC on the ground that earlier interim orders had become final and binding.
Whether proceedings under Section 145 CrPC should continue when a civil suit involving the same property and parties is already pending with a status quo order in place.
holdings: Interim orders in criminal revision, even if confirmed by higher courts, do not bind the magistrate at the final stage of Section 145 proceedings and cannot prevent a contrary decision based on fresh evidence or admissions.

When a civil suit concerning the same property and parties is pending and the civil court has passed a status quo order, continuation of parallel Section 145 CrPC proceedings is unjustified to avoid multiplicity of litigation and waste of public time.
doctrines: Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings
Finality of interim orders
Binding effect of civil court decrees on criminal proceedings

card.dispute: Two nationalised banks, Allahabad Bank and Canara Bank, disputed over the distribution of sale proceeds from a debtor-company's assets, with Allahabad Bank seeking to enforce its decree under the RDB Act and Canara Bank claiming a share based on its secured creditor status despite not participating in winding up proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the Company Court has jurisdiction to stay recovery proceedings under the RDB Act under Sections 442 and 537 of the Companies Act, 1956
Whether a secured creditor like Canara Bank can claim a share in sale proceeds realised by another creditor under the RDB Act without participating in winding up
Whether Section 529A of the Companies Act allows a secured creditor to claim priority over proceeds realised by other creditors when workmen's dues have impacted their security
Whether workmen's dues must be satisfied before any distribution of recovery proceeds to secured or unsecured creditors
holdings: The RDB Act ousts the jurisdiction of the Company Court under Sections 442 and 537 of the Companies Act; thus, the High Court could not stay recovery proceedings before the Recovery Officer.

A secured creditor not participating in winding up cannot claim distribution of proceeds realised by another creditor under Section 19(19) of the RDB Act unless it has suffered a loss of security due to workmen's dues being enforced rateably.

Section 529A(1)(b) allows a secured creditor to claim priority only to the extent of the lesser of the amount lost from security for workmen's dues or the unpaid secured debt, and only if such loss occurred during winding up.
Workmen's dues have overriding priority over all creditors; no distribution of recovery proceeds can be made until the Tribunal confirms such dues are satisfied.
provisions: Recovery of Debts due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 19(19)
doctrines: Priority of workmen's dues over secured and unsecured creditors
Doctrine of lis pendens in winding up proceedings
Principle of rateable contribution by secured creditors towards workmen's dues
Jurisdictional primacy of Debt Recovery Tribunal under the RDB Act

card.dispute: The appellant Anthony challenged his eviction from a building, claiming tenant protection under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1965, despite an unregistered lease deed.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered lease deed, required to be registered, can create a valid lease under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the appellant can be considered a tenant entitled to protection under the Rent Control Act despite the unregistered instrument
Whether possession coupled with payment and acceptance of rent can establish a lease in the absence of a validly registered deed
holdings: An unregistered lease deed for more than one year is void and cannot be used as evidence to create a lease under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act.

Despite the invalidity of the unregistered deed, a lease for a term not exceeding one year can be created by oral agreement accompanied by delivery of possession under the second paragraph of Section 107.
Where possession is delivered and rent is paid and accepted, a jural relationship of landlord and tenant arises by implication, entitling the lessee to protection under rent control legislation.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act
Doctrine of implied lease
Doctrine of statutory tenancy

card.dispute: The widowed daughter of a testator claimed full ownership of a 1/3rd share in her father's property under a will and Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, while other heirs claimed she only had a life interest.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant widowed daughter acquired full ownership or only a life interest in the suit property under the will dated 21st August 1959.
Whether Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to convert a life interest into full ownership when the female beneficiary has a pre-existing right to maintenance.
holdings: A female Hindu acquires full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if she has a pre-existing right to maintenance, even if the will grants only a life interest.
Section 14(2) does not apply to override Section 14(1) when the property is granted under a will that recognizes a pre-existing right, such as maintenance, in favor of a female heir.
doctrines: Strict construction of exceptions to ameliorative statutes
Pre-existing right doctrine under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act

card.dispute: The Delhi Administration and DDA sought to acquire land in village Chatrapur; the landowners challenged the acquisition, and later sought de-notification under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act after a representation by DDA that proceedings were quashed.
issues_decided: Whether the representation by DDA that acquisition proceedings were quashed gives rise to estoppel in favour of the landowner?
Whether the landowner is entitled to de-notification under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether the DDA's order dated 7.12.99 to take possession of land is valid after the Supreme Court's decision in the civil appeals?
Whether an application for 'recall' of the judgment can be entertained when a review petition is pending?
holdings: A clear representation by DDA that acquisition proceedings were quashed, relied upon by the landowner, gives rise to a prima facie case of estoppel under Section 115 of the Evidence Act.

The government shall consider the application for de-notification under Section 48 sympathetically, subject to conditions including original ownership, compliance with building plans, and non-payment of compensation.
The DDA's order to take possession is not warranted as the Supreme Court gave no such direction; the writ petition is dismissed with liberty to approach the High Court.

An application for 'recall' cannot be used to circumvent the review process or obtain an oral hearing on issues pending in a review petition; such applications are rejected to prevent abuse of process.
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel
Principle of Legitimate Expectation
Abuse of Process of Court
Finality of Judicial Orders

card.dispute: The landlords (widow and two sons of the deceased owner) sought eviction of two tenants from shops in Indore, claiming bona fide need for the sons' businesses, leading to a dispute over jurisdiction and validity of the eviction claim.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controlling Authority had jurisdiction to hear the eviction petition when co-owner landlords included one falling under Section 23-J and others not, and the claim was for bona fide business need.
Whether the landlords proved bona fide requirement of the premises under Section 23-A(b) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
holdings: When co-owner landlords include at least one eligible under Section 23-J and the claim falls under Section 23-A(b), they may jointly choose to file before the Rent Controlling Authority or a Civil Court; the choice of forum lies with them.
The landlords proved bona fide requirement for the shops for their sons' businesses; absence of owned alternative suitable accommodation upholds the eviction claim under Section 23-A(b).
doctrines: Plaintiff is dominus litis
Every right must have a remedy (ubi jus ibi remedium)
Objective and subjective standards in determining bona fide requirement
Joint right of co-owners to choose forum when cause of action is common

card.dispute: Divya Manufacturing Co. and workers' union fought with Union Bank of India and other bidders over the confirmation and setting aside of a court-ordered sale of assets of a sick company in liquidation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had the power to set aside a confirmed sale of company assets in liquidation despite acceptance of the highest bid at that stage.
Whether the adequacy of the sale price, in absence of fraud or irregularity, is a valid ground for judicial intervention in a court-supervised auction.
Whether the court could reopen sale proceedings when a significantly higher bid emerged after confirmation of sale.
holdings: A court confirming a sale in liquidation must ensure the price is adequate and in the best interest of creditors, even if there is no fraud or irregularity.
The court retains jurisdiction to set aside a confirmed sale if it results in an inadequate price, as it acts as custodian of the company and creditors’ interests.
A confirmed sale can be reopened if a substantially higher bid emerges, to prevent underbidding and ensure fair market value is achieved.
doctrines: Judicial discretion in confirming sales during liquidation
Custodianship of court over company assets in winding up
Adequacy of price as a ground for setting aside a confirmed sale
Open auction principle to prevent underbidding and syndication

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent brothers disputed the ownership and possession of a MHADA flat in Mumbai, culminating in a challenge to a court-confirmed settlement agreement arising from conciliation proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the conciliator acted in accordance with the procedure laid down under Part III of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Whether a settlement agreement drawn up by a conciliator without the signatures of the parties and kept confidential from them is valid and binding
Whether the High Court erred in confirming the settlement agreement without ensuring compliance with statutory requirements
holdings: A conciliator must follow the procedure in Section 73 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and cannot unilaterally draft a binding settlement without party input or signatures.
A settlement agreement under Section 73 becomes final and binding only when signed by the parties; a document prepared in secrecy and not signed does not have legal sanctity.
The High Court cannot confirm a settlement agreement that violates the mandatory procedures of the Act, as such action undermines the distinction between conciliation and arbitration.
doctrines: Procedural compliance doctrine
Confidentiality in conciliation
Distinction between arbitration and conciliation
Binding nature of settlement agreements under statute

card.dispute: The appellant, Gautam Paul, challenged the High Court's decision allowing co-sharers to exercise pre-emption under Section 4 of the Partition Act after he purchased a 1/9th share in a family dwelling house, despite not suing for partition.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of a share in a dwelling house to the appellant constituted a transfer to a stranger within the meaning of Section 4 of the Partition Act.
Whether the right of pre-emption under Section 4 of the Partition Act can be exercised when the transferee has not sued for partition.
holdings: The appellant, though related by blood to the original family, was not a member of the undivided family of Nirode Baran Paul, which owned the dwelling house, and thus was a stranger under Section 4 of the Partition Act.

The right of pre-emption under Section 4 arises only when the transferee initiates a suit for partition or claims partition in execution; mere ownership of a share without seeking division or possession does not trigger the right.
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of statutes
Legislative intent in conferring pre-emption rights
Distinction between asserting ownership and claiming partition

card.dispute: The Ghaziabad Development Authority appealed against orders directing it to refund amounts with interest and pay compensation for mental agony to allottees due to delays or failure in executing housing schemes.
issues_decided: Whether compensation for mental agony can be awarded against a development authority for delay or failure in executing housing schemes?
Whether interest can be awarded on amounts refunded by a development authority in consumer or MRTP proceedings, and at what rate?
Whether a no-interest clause in the authority's brochure is enforceable when the delay is attributable to the authority?
holdings: Compensation for mental agony cannot be awarded in ordinary contractual disputes; such relief is only available under administrative law if mala fide or capricious exercise of power is proven, which was not established here.
Interest can be awarded on equitable grounds in consumer and MRTP cases even without a contractual or statutory basis, guided by justice, equity, and good conscience.
A no-interest clause in a development authority’s brochure is unenforceable when the authority is at fault for the delay; refund with interest is mandatory in such cases.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, Section 4
Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969
doctrines: Principle of equity, justice and good conscience
Administrative law doctrine of liability for mala fide exercise of power
Contractual liability for breach of promise in public development schemes

card.dispute: The appellants, brothers and co-owners of a property, sold land to a cooperative society but were accused of cheating for not disclosing a pending partition suit; they challenged the criminal proceedings as an abuse of process.
issues_decided: Whether the allegations in the complaint, if taken as true, make out a prima facie case of cheating under Section 420 IPC?
Whether the failure to disclose a pending partition suit amounts to dishonest or fraudulent inducement under Section 415 IPC?
Whether the criminal proceedings should be quashed under Section 482 CrPC as an abuse of process of court?
holdings: Mere non-disclosure of a pending partition suit, without allegations of dishonest or fraudulent intention at the time of the transaction, does not constitute cheating under Section 420 IPC.
A breach of contract or failure to perform a promise does not automatically amount to cheating; there must be evidence of fraudulent or dishonest intent at the inception of the agreement.
Criminal proceedings based on allegations that do not disclose a cognizable offence or make out a case for cheating constitute an abuse of process and can be quashed under Section 482 CrPC.
doctrines: Distinction between civil breach of contract and criminal cheating
Abuse of process of court
Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 CrPC
Principle of quashing criminal proceedings in the rarest of rare cases

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for using the rented shop for a business purpose different from that specified in the rent agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's use of the shop for selling provisions, contrary to the agreed business of radios, cycles, fans, clocks, and steel furniture, constitutes a change of user under Section 10(2)(ii)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
Whether a specific restriction in the rent agreement on the type of business to be conducted binds the tenant, even if the change remains commercial in nature.
Whether a change of user requires the substantial portion of the premises to be used for the unauthorized purpose to attract eviction.
holdings: A tenant who uses the premises for a business purpose other than the one specifically permitted in the rent agreement is liable for eviction under Section 10(2)(ii)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.

Specific contractual terms restricting the use of leased premises must be given full effect, and such restrictions are not overridden by general provisions of the Transfer of Property Act where the contract explicitly prohibits other businesses.

For eviction under Section 10(2)(ii)(b), it is sufficient that there is a change in user of the building; it need not be of a substantial portion, as the statutory criterion is significance of user, not quantum of space used.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(ii)(b)
doctrines: Contractual freedom in lease agreements
Specific performance of lease terms
Change of user as a ground for eviction

card.dispute: Lalmuni Devi filed a criminal complaint alleging that respondents fraudulently induced her father to execute a gift deed; the respondents got the complaint quashed on the grounds it was a civil wrong, and the appellant challenged that quashing.
issues_decided: Whether a criminal complaint can be quashed under Section 482 CrPC on the ground that the dispute is essentially civil in nature?
Whether the High Court can exercise inherent powers to quash criminal proceedings if allegations disclose a possible criminal offence?
holdings: A criminal complaint cannot be quashed merely because it involves a civil dispute; if allegations prima facie disclose a criminal offence, prosecution may proceed.
The High Court erred in quashing the complaint without finding that no offence was disclosed; the possibility of a civil remedy does not bar criminal prosecution when criminal elements are present.
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Inherent powers of High Court
Dual liability in civil and criminal law

card.dispute: The Marwari Kumhar Community sued to declare their title to a temple and dharamshala, previously managed by a pujari, against the pujari's son and widow who claimed ownership after his death.
issues_decided: Whether secondary evidence of a lost certified copy of a prior final judgment could be admitted under the Evidence Act
Whether the prior judgment in favor of the appellants created res judicata binding the respondents
Whether the respondents had acquired title by adverse possession
holdings: Secondary evidence of a public document is admissible if the original is lost, even if a certified copy is normally required, provided the loss is not due to the party's default.
A final judgment affirming the appellants' title binds the parties and their representatives, creating res judicata on the issue of title.
The respondents failed to prove adverse possession as there was no pleading or evidence that their possession became hostile after the 1948 judgment.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11 (res judicata)
doctrines: Res judicata
Adverse possession
Secondary evidence

card.dispute: The appellant (Motilal Jain) sued for specific performance of a contract to purchase property from the defendant, who denied the contract's validity; the High Court set aside the trial court’s decree, prompting this appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing the suit justified denial of specific performance.
Whether the plaint sufficiently averred the plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.
Whether claiming damages as an alternative relief bars the claim for specific performance.
holdings: Delay in filing the suit, within limitation and without prejudice to third-party rights, does not justify refusal of specific performance.
Averments of readiness and willingness need not follow exact wording of CPC Forms 47 and 48; substance over form governs, and the plaint here sufficiently showed readiness.
Claiming damages in the alternative does not disentitle a plaintiff to specific performance under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, First Schedule, Forms 47 and 48
doctrines: Substance over form in pleadings
Readiness and willingness as a factual determination from conduct and context
Discretionary nature of specific performance relief

card.dispute: The landlord, Kay Iron Works, sought eviction of tenant Molar Mal from rented land for personal use, but the tenant argued the eviction was not bona fide as the landlord had already obtained possession of other tenanted premises for similar use.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 13(3)(b)(i) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 bars a landlord from seeking eviction after obtaining possession of another tenanted premises of the same class
Whether the proviso applies only at the stage of filing the petition or extends to the stage of actual eviction
Whether the High Court's prior interpretation of the proviso, allowing multiple evictions from parts of the same premises, is correct
Whether the proviso can be applied in the absence of a framed issue and evidence on the nature of the premises
holdings: The proviso to Section 13(3)(b)(i) bars a landlord from seeking eviction if they have already obtained possession of a tenanted premises of the same class that can reasonably meet their needs.
The restriction in the proviso applies not only at the filing stage but continues until the court decides on eviction, to prevent circumvention of the law.
The High Court's interpretation allowing eviction of multiple parts of the same premises is incorrect, as the proviso does not distinguish between separate buildings or parts of the same premises.
Since no issue was framed and no evidence recorded on the nature of the premises, the matter must be remanded to the trial court to determine if the premises are of the same class.
provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(3)(b)(i) proviso
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation with exception for absurdity
Purpose-based interpretation of rent control legislation
Courts' duty to correct erroneous legal interpretations even if long-standing

card.dispute: The Narmada Bachao Andolan challenged the construction of the Sardar Sarovar Dam, raising concerns about environmental impact, displacement of people, and adequacy of rehabilitation measures.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of the Sardar Sarovar Dam at a full reservoir level of 455 ft. violates environmental and rehabilitation safeguards under Article 21 of the Constitution
Whether the project should be halted due to inadequate relief and rehabilitation of displaced persons
Whether the environmental clearances and monitoring mechanisms are sufficient to protect ecological and human rights
holdings: The construction of the dam at 455 ft. FRL is valid and consistent with constitutional and environmental safeguards, provided rehabilitation and environmental conditions are strictly followed.

Further raising of the dam height beyond 90 meters must be pari passu with completion of relief and rehabilitation, and subject to clearance by the Relief and Rehabilitation Sub-group and the Narmada Control Authority.
Environmental clearance must be obtained at each stage by the Environment Sub-group, and continuous monitoring is required to protect rights under Article 21.
doctrines: Pari passu principle in rehabilitation and construction
Right to life includes right to livelihood and environment under Article 21
Judicial deference to expert tribunals in inter-state water disputes

card.dispute: The erstwhile landowners and vegetarianism advocates challenged the state's decision to lease surplus acquired land to a company for an integrated food processing unit with an abattoir, alleging deviation from public purpose and arbitrariness.
issues_decided: Whether the State's action in leasing the surplus land by negotiation instead of public auction was arbitrary, illegal, or violative of Article 14
Whether the change in land use from railway project to abattoir violated the original public purpose of acquisition
Whether the lease at a negotiated rate was mala fide or against public interest
holdings: Leasing surplus land by negotiation is constitutionally permissible if rationally connected to a public purpose and not arbitrary.
The State may repurpose surplus land for industrial development generating employment and export, which constitutes a valid public purpose.
The absence of public auction does not invalidate a lease if the State demonstrates rationality, bona fides, and economic benefit in the transaction.
doctrines: Principle of reasonableness in state action
Non-arbitrariness as a core constitutional value
Public purpose doctrine in property utilisation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the tenant (Ram Niwas's legal heirs) and subsequent purchasers (Smt. Bano & Ors) over whether the tenant was entitled to specific performance of an earlier agreement to sell a shop, against the purchasers who bought it later.
issues_decided: Whether the subsequent purchasers had notice of the earlier agreement to sell under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963?
Whether the trial court's finding on the validity of the earlier agreement (Ext.1) should be accepted without independent scrutiny by the appellate court?
Whether the purchasers could be deemed to have notice under Explanation II to Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act despite lack of actual knowledge?
holdings: Subsequent purchasers claiming under a vendor are bound by an earlier contract for specific performance unless they are bona fide purchasers for value without notice; mere lack of actual knowledge does not suffice if they failed to make due enquiry under Explanation II to Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act.
An appellate court must independently assess the validity of an earlier agreement for sale rather than merely assuming the trial court's finding as correct when deciding specific performance.

A person may be deemed to have notice under Explanation II to Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act if, in the circumstances, they had reason to make further enquiry about a tenant’s interest, especially where the possession was inconsistent with a mere landlord-tenant relationship.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 3, Explanation II
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive notice
Equity behind specific performance as a discretionary remedy
Priority of equitable rights over subsequent legal rights in absence of bona fide purchase for value without notice

card.dispute: The heirs of Roop Singh sued the heirs of Ram Singh to recover possession of 15.32 acres of agricultural land, claiming Ram Singh was a trespasser, while Ram Singh's heirs claimed ownership via sale agreement and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the defendant acquired the suit land by a valid sale agreement protected under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act?
Whether the defendant acquired title to the suit land by adverse possession?
Whether the High Court erred in interfering with concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC?
holdings: To claim protection under Section 53A, a defendant must plead and prove a written agreement, payment of consideration, and possession in pursuance of the agreement; failure to produce any document or plead loss of it bars such protection.

Permissive possession, such as under a batai (tenancy) arrangement, does not ripen into adverse possession unless there is clear evidence of hostile animus and open assertion of ownership against the true owner.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC by re-appreciating evidence and overturning concurrent factual findings without identifying any substantial question of law.
doctrines: Adverse possession requires hostile, continuous, and uninterrupted possession with animus to possess as owner, distinct from permissive possession.
Section 53A protection requires strict compliance with conditions: written contract, part performance, and possession in furtherance of the contract.
Concurrent findings of fact by two courts below are binding in second appeal unless perverse or illegal.

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of a property held in the name of his brother's tenant, arguing it was a benami transaction, while the respondents claimed the property was lawfully theirs and the suit was barred by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by Section 281-A of the Income Tax Act or Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 due to retrospective operation?
Whether the appellant proved his title and possession over the suit property?
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by re-appreciating evidence in the second appeal?
holdings: The suit was not barred by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, as Section 4 is not retrospective, following R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan.
The appellant failed to prove ownership, possession, or that the transaction was a benami one; the decree by the first appellate court was perverse and based on no evidence.
The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction in a second appeal by drawing adverse inferences from non-examination of a key witness and evaluating the entire evidence.
doctrines: Doctrine of perversity in appellate review
Adverse inference from non-examination of a material witness
Non-retrospectivity of procedural or curative statutes

card.dispute: The brother of a murder victim and the State of Maharashtra challenged the acquittal of 17 accused, including gang members and police officers, in a case involving the murder of Suresh Dube and alleged terrorist activities under TADA.
issues_decided: Whether the accused A-1 to A-6 could be convicted for the murder of Suresh Dube based on confessional statements and eyewitness testimony.
Whether the acts of the accused amounted to 'terrorist acts' under Section 3 of the TADA Act.
Whether the police officers A-14 to A-17 could be convicted solely on the basis of co-accused confessions for conspiring to screen the offenders.
holdings: A-1 was convicted for murder under Section 302 IPC based on corroboration of his confession by two eyewitnesses; A-2 to A-6 were convicted under Section 302 read with Sections 120-B and 149 IPC as part of an unlawful assembly and common object.
The confessional statements of A-1 to A-6, supported by witness evidence, established that the gangs created terror and committed terrorist acts under Section 3(3) of the TADA Act.
Conviction of police officers A-14 to A-17 solely on co-accused confessions is unsafe; strong suspicion of collusion is not sufficient for conviction without independent evidence.
provisions: Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3(3)
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3(4)
doctrines: Corroboration of confessional statements
Common object of unlawful assembly
Standard of proof in conspiracy cases
Insufficiency of suspicion in criminal conviction
Use of confessions as substantive evidence under TADA

card.dispute: The legal heirs of S. Saktivel contested the right of M. Venugopal Pillai to claim a share in property under a registered settlement deed, alleging a subsequent oral arrangement had modified the deed.
issues_decided: Whether parol evidence can be admitted to prove a subsequent oral agreement that modifies or rescinds a registered settlement deed?
Whether proviso (4) to Section 92 of the Evidence Act allows oral evidence to alter a registered disposition of property?
holdings: Parol evidence cannot be admitted to prove a subsequent oral agreement that modifies or rescinds a registered settlement deed, as such deeds can only be altered by another registered document.
Proviso (4) to Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act does not permit oral evidence to modify a disposition of property that is required by law to be in writing or is registered.
doctrines: Exclusion of oral evidence to vary written contracts
Requirement of writing and registration for disposition of property

card.dispute: Tenants challenged eviction orders on grounds that the landlord's lease was not validly cancelled and that commercial use of the premises should be permitted under urban planning laws.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could be evicted under Section 14(1)(k) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for using the premises for commercial purposes contrary to the lease terms
Whether the absence of a zonal development plan specifying land use or unframed regulations under Section 57(1)(f) of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 barred eviction
Whether prior statements or suspensions by DDA regarding action on misuse estopped it from later insisting on lease compliance
holdings: A tenant can be evicted under Section 14(1)(k) of the Delhi Rent Control Act if they use premises contrary to conditions imposed by DDA, especially when the lessor insists on compliance and has not waived the breach.
The absence of a zonal plan or unframed regulations under the Delhi Development Act does not override lease terms or prevent enforcement of lease covenants by the paramount lessor.
Temporary suspensions or statements by DDA in other cases do not bind it permanently; DDA may lawfully insist on lease compliance later if no formal regularization has been approved.
doctrines: Condition precedent for eviction under Section 14(1)(k): threat of lease cancellation by DDA
Primacy of lease terms over general planning provisions
No estoppel against statutory authorities based on temporary administrative inaction

card.dispute: The landlady, Shamim Akhtar, fought to evict tenant Iqbal Ahmad over denial of her title and rent default, while the tenant challenged the suit's maintainability citing jurisdictional issues related to evacuee and enemy property laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Small Causes Court could decide an eviction petition under Section 20 of the UP Rent Act without finally determining title to the property?
Whether the objection regarding evacuee or enemy property status could bar the eviction proceeding in the absence of a formal declaration under the relevant Acts?
Whether the Trial Court was justified in returning the plaint under Section 23 of the Small Causes Courts Act?
holdings: A Small Causes Court can adjudicate eviction petitions under Section 20 of the UP Rent Act by examining title incidentally without finally deciding ownership.
Objections under the Evacuee Property Act, 1950 or Enemy Property Act, 1968 are irrelevant unless the property has been officially declared as such by a competent authority.
The Trial Court erred in returning the plaint under Section 23 of the Small Causes Courts Act as the relief did not depend on final determination of title.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)(f)
doctrines: Incidental determination of title
Final determination of title not prerequisite for eviction
Judicial discretion under Section 23 of the Small Causes Courts Act

card.dispute: The Shriomani Gurudwara Prabandhak Committee contested the ownership of certain land with Shri Som Nath Dass and others, who claimed rights over property originally gifted for a dharamshala managed in the name of Guru Granth Sahib.
issues_decided: Whether Guru Granth Sahib can be recognized as a juristic person under Indian law.
Whether the mutation of land in the name of Guru Granth Sahib Birajman Dharamshala Deh was legally valid.
Whether the respondents could claim ownership over the disputed land originally entrusted to their ancestors for charitable use.
holdings: Guru Granth Sahib is a juristic person capable of holding property, as it was declared the living Guru by Guru Gobind Singh and is treated as such by Sikhs.
The mutation in favor of Guru Granth Sahib was valid, based on a proper revenue enquiry and not merely on the Faraman-i-Shahi, which was only a protective directive.
The respondents, as mere trustees, could not claim ownership over the endowed land, especially after failing to fulfill the charitable purpose for which it was entrusted.
provisions: Sikh Gurdwaras and Shrines Act, 1922 (VI of 1922)
doctrines: Juristic personhood of religious idols and texts
Perpetuity of religious endowments
Trustee's fiduciary duty in religious trusts

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Smt. Dilboo challenged the ownership claims of Smt. Dhanraji and others over property originally mortgaged in 1902, asserting title based on adverse possession and subsequent sales.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the High Court erred in shifting the burden of proof regarding knowledge of the adverse transactions
Whether the purchasers in 1942 and 1954 acquired valid title under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act
holdings: A suit challenging an adverse transaction must be filed within 12 years of the plaintiff's or their predecessor's knowledge of the transaction; failure to plead or prove timely knowledge bars the suit.
The burden of proving lack of knowledge within 12 years lies on the plaintiff; it cannot be shifted to the defendant in absence of such pleading or evidence.
Purchasers for valuable consideration under absolute sale deeds in 1942 and 1954 acquired valid title protected under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, irrespective of bona fides.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Once a mortgagee always a mortgagee
Protection of bona fide purchasers for value without notice

card.dispute: The State Government Houseless Harijan Employees Association challenged the withdrawal of land acquisition proceedings initiated for providing house sites to its members, claiming the withdrawal was illegal.
issues_decided: Whether the beneficiary of a land acquisition can resist the withdrawal of acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the acquisition was validly carried out under Part II (public purpose) rather than Part VII (acquisition for companies) of the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the State Government could rely on prior material to justify a fresh notification under Section 4(1) after delays caused the lapse of earlier notifications.
Whether the withdrawal of acquisition under Section 48(1) was valid without hearing the appellant and based on incorrect grounds.
holdings: A beneficiary of land acquisition has a legitimate interest and must be heard before withdrawal of proceedings under Section 48(1).
The acquisition was validly initiated and continued under Part II for public purpose, not Part VII, as evidenced by the notifications and government approvals.
The State Government may rely on previously collected material to support a fresh notification if it is relevant, sufficient, and genuine, despite administrative delays.
Withdrawal under Section 48(1) is invalid if based on incorrect grounds and without affording the affected party an opportunity to be heard.
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Doctrine of legitimate expectation
Rule against arbitrary administrative action
Doctrine of continuity of administrative proceedings despite delay

card.dispute: The appellants claimed ownership of a bungalow and land previously owned by a coal company, but the respondent (BCCL) challenged the sale as sham to prevent vesting of property in the Central Government under the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973.
issues_decided: Whether the sale transaction between the company and the appellants was bona fide and genuine or a sham to avoid vesting of property under the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973
Whether the suit property vested in the Central Government free of encumbrances under Section 3(1) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973
holdings: The sale transaction was not bona fide or genuine, as it was between directors and their wives, lacked consistency in documents, and showed no exercise of ownership rights before vesting; thus, it conferred no valid title on the appellants.
Since the transaction was invalid, the property remained with the company and vested in the Central Government under Section 3(1) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, free of encumbrances.
provisions: Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, Schedule, Serial No. 133
doctrines: Piercing the corporate veil
Burden of proof in sham transaction cases
Vesting of property free of encumbrances under nationalisation laws

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan challenged the lower courts' recognition of Harphool Singh's claim to ownership of a public plot of land through adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide a title dispute involving public land under the relevant revenue law.
Whether the plaintiff acquired title to the public land by adverse possession.
holdings: The civil court retains jurisdiction to decide disputes over title to immovable property, even if possession is in question under a special revenue law, as long as the statute does not provide machinery to resolve title disputes.

A claim of adverse possession against public property requires clear and unequivocal proof of open, continuous, hostile possession with the necessary animus for the statutory period; mere assertions and insufficient evidence do not suffice.
provisions: Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Urban Properties Act, Section 22
doctrines: Adverse possession
Jurisdiction of civil courts not ousted by special statutes without clear exclusion
Nec vi, nec clam, nec precario

card.dispute: The appellant (Surjit Kaur) and respondent (Naurata Singh) disputed whether the respondent could claim part performance of a sale agreement after refusing to accept partial performance when the appellant failed to deliver possession.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was entitled to claim specific performance of the sale agreement in part after refusing to accept part performance on the stipulated date?
Whether the conditions under Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 were satisfied for enforcing part performance?
Whether the trial court was justified in awarding only Rs. 8,800 as damages instead of double the advance as stipulated in the agreement?
holdings: A party who unambiguously refuses to accept part performance of a contract on the date fixed for performance cannot later resile from that election and claim part performance.

To claim specific performance in part under Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, the party must have paid or tendered the full consideration and relinquished all claims to performance of the remainder; this was not done here.

Where a contract fails due to the vendee's refusal to accept part performance, and the agreement provides for double the advance as compensation, the vendee is entitled to such compensation if the vendor defaults on full performance.
doctrines: Election theory in contract law
Part performance under specific relief
Readiness and willingness to perform contract

card.dispute: The appellants (children of Hiri Thimmaiah's first wife) fought with the respondents (his second wife and her daughter) over the share in coparcenary properties after Hiri's death, challenging gifts he made and claiming rights under personal law.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in question were ancestral or self-acquired and part of the coparcenary estate
Whether the gifts made by Hiri Thimmaiah to the respondents were valid or void
Whether the respondents were entitled to shares in the coparcenary property under the Mysore Hindu Succession Act or the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
How the shares of the parties should be determined upon partition of the coparcenary property
holdings: Items 1 to 6 were part of the coparcenary property; the gifts made by Hiri were invalid as he could not alienate coparcenary property without consent of coparceners.
Section 8(1)(d) of the Mysore Hindu Succession Act is superseded by the proviso to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, when Class I heirs exist.
The unmarried daughter (respondent No. 2) was entitled to a share under Section 8(1)(a) of the Mysore Act as a female coparcener, in addition to her share as a Class I heir under the 1956 Act.

The shares of the parties shall be determined by notional partition under Explanation I to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, with the son getting 1/2, and the daughter 1/4 of the coparcenary share, plus equal inheritance of Hiri’s interest as Class I heirs.
doctrines: Notional partition under Explanation I to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Supersession of state succession laws by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 where inconsistent
Survivorship vs. testamentary/intestate succession in coparcenary property
Entitlement of female members to coparcenary shares under pre-1956 regional laws in addition to inheritance rights

card.dispute: The Consumer Action Group challenged the constitutional validity of Section 113 of the Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning Act, 1971, and the government's practice of granting arbitrary exemptions for unauthorized constructions, arguing it violated Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 113 of the Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning Act, 1971, amounts to excessive delegation of legislative power and is ultra vires Articles 14 and 21
Whether the 62 government orders granting exemptions for unauthorized constructions under Section 113 are valid
Whether Section 113-A, introduced as a one-time regularization measure, is constitutionally valid
Whether the public must be given notice before regularization of unauthorized constructions affecting public interest
holdings: Section 113 is valid as it does not involve excessive delegation; the Act provides sufficient policy and guidelines to the executive.
The 62 government orders granting exemptions under Section 113 are arbitrary and unsustainable, and are quashed.
Section 113-A, as a one-time regularization measure, is valid and within the legislative competence of the State.
While public notice for each regularization may not be practicable in large-scale cases, the State should consider providing public hearing or appeal mechanisms in future to protect public rights.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning Act, 1971, Section 113
Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning (Amendment) Act, 1998, Section 113-A
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Doctrine of separation of powers
Public interest litigation
Principle of procedural fairness

card.dispute: Union Bank of India challenged the confirmation of an auction sale of a company's mortgaged property during liquidation, arguing the sale price was inadequately low and the court failed to properly scrutinize it.
issues_decided: Whether the court below properly exercised its discretion in confirming the auction sale of the company's assets at an allegedly inadequate price.
Whether the failure to consider market value and other material factors in confirming a court-ordered sale constitutes a material irregularity.
Whether the auction purchaser is entitled to interest on the refunded sale amount when the sale is set aside on appeal.
holdings: A court confirming a sale in liquidation must actively assess whether the bid price is reasonable in relation to the market value, as confirmation acts as a safeguard against inadequate pricing.
Mechanical or routine approval of a sale without evaluating the adequacy of the price amounts to a material irregularity, even in the absence of fraud.
An auction purchaser is not entitled to interest on the refunded sale amount when the sale is set aside, especially where the purchaser incurred expenses at their own risk during pending appeals.
doctrines: Adequacy of price in court-confirmed sales
Judicial discretion in confirming auction sales
Material irregularity in sale proceedings
Equity of redemption

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed over the right to possession and sale of a mortgaged property, with the respondents claiming ownership via auction purchase from Bihar State Finance Corporation, while the appellant sought its sale in another proceeding involving United Bank of India.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents had a prima facie right to the property based on the sale certificate and record of rights?
Whether the grant of temporary injunction in favour of the respondents was justified at the interlocutory stage?
holdings: A validly issued sale certificate creates a presumption of ownership and possession, which cannot be disregarded merely because it was amended later; it must be challenged in a proper legal proceeding.
Where a party shows prima facie title and possession through official records like the record of rights, a temporary injunction in their favour can be granted even if competing claims exist.
doctrines: Prima facie title and possession
Presumption of validity of sale certificate
Interlocutory injunction in property disputes

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming tenancy rights under the Bombay Rent Act, 1947, challenged the execution of a decree for possession obtained by the landlord against another family member who had been recognized as the tenant.
issues_decided: Whether a decree passed against one member of a deceased tenant's family, who was recognized as the tenant, is binding on other family members claiming tenancy rights under Section 5(11)(c) of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947.
Whether the appellants, who claimed to be members of the original tenant's family, were entitled to resist execution of the compromise decree.
Whether the tenancy devolved jointly on the heirs of the deceased tenant or was separate and individual.
holdings: A decree passed against one member of a deceased tenant's family, who was accepted by the landlord as the tenant, is binding on all other family members where the tenancy is joint and undivided.
The compromise decree was valid and executable against all members of the tenant's family, including those not impleaded, as the tenancy devolved jointly on the heirs.

The appellants failed to prove continued residence with the original tenant at the time of death and had effectively waived or surrendered their tenancy rights by relocating and acquiring other premises.
doctrines: Joint tenancy succession upon death of original tenant
Binding effect of decree on co-tenants in joint tenancy
Waiver of tenancy rights by conduct and non-residence

card.dispute: The Balco Employees Union challenged the Union of India's decision to disinvest 51% of its shares in Bharat Aluminium Company Limited (BALCO), arguing it violated public interest and legal principles.
issues_decided: Whether the disinvestment of 51% shares of BALCO by the Union of India is legally valid and subject to judicial review?
Whether the policy decision of disinvestment can be challenged through Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?
Whether the State of Chhattisgarh can challenge the validity of land transfers made to BALCO years earlier?
Whether the courts can interfere with economic policy decisions based on allegations of lack of transparency or procedural haste?
holdings: The disinvestment decision by the Union of India in BALCO is a valid exercise of economic policy and does not violate any constitutional or statutory provision.
Public Interest Litigation is not maintainable to challenge economic or administrative policy decisions unless there is a violation of fundamental rights or statutory illegality.
The State of Chhattisgarh cannot now challenge the legality of land transfers to BALCO that were validly made years ago under its own prior actions.
Courts should not interfere with policy decisions involving economic matters unless there is mala fide, arbitrariness, or clear illegality; valuation and policy wisdom are not judicially reviewable.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 165(6)
doctrines: Principle of separation of powers
Judicial restraint in economic policy matters
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) limitations
Non-justiciability of policy decisions absent illegality or mala fide
Finality of past administrative acts (legitimate expectation and estoppel)

card.dispute: The appellant, Ghulam Qadir, claimed rights to evacuee property in Jammu after the death of Sardar Begum, who had previously claimed the same property, leading to a dispute over entitlement under the Jammu and Kashmir State Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to claim the evacuee property as a legal heir after the death of Sardar Begum who had already been denied the claim during her lifetime.
Whether the Custodian and allottees had locus standi to challenge the order of the Special Tribunal restoring the property to the appellant.
Whether rights under Section 8 of the Act can be claimed by legal heirs after the original claimant's death, and whether Section 8 remains operative.
Whether the revisional authority could examine factual questions regarding title and succession under the Act.
holdings: A legal heir cannot prefer a claim under Section 8 of the Act for property already denied to the original claimant during her lifetime, as Section 8 does not confer succession rights.
Allottees and the Custodian General have locus standi to challenge orders affecting evacuee property, given their direct interest and the custodian’s dual administrative and adjudicatory role.
Section 8 of the Act has become redundant and no further claims can be entertained under it; it does not allow claims by heirs after the original claimant's death.

The revisional authority under the Act can examine factual issues to determine the legality of orders, including whether a claimant has established title, but cannot adjudicate title, which requires a civil court decree.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir State Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Section 2(c)
Jammu and Kashmir State Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Section 8
