Jammu and Kashmir State Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Section 14
Jammu and Kashmir State Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Rule 14
Jammu and Kashmir State Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Rule 15(4)
doctrines: Locus standi of affected parties in administrative proceedings
Separation of jurisdiction between civil courts and administrative authorities on title adjudication
Doctrine of redundancy of statutory provisions due to lapse of time
Revisional jurisdiction allowing examination of facts for legality and propriety

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Maharani and Savjibhai Haribhai Patel over the specific performance of an agreement concerning land development under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, after the Act was repealed.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement for development of land under the ULC Act was specifically enforceable after the repeal of the Act
Whether the contract involved continuous duties that the court could not supervise
Whether it would be inequitable to enforce specific performance of the agreement
Whether clauses in the agreement allowed for its termination before possession
holdings: An agreement tied to a statutory scheme that has been repealed cannot be specifically enforced if the scheme is no longer operational.
A contract requiring continuous supervision that the court cannot effectively monitor is not specifically enforceable under Section 14(d) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
It would be inequitable to enforce specific performance where the public purpose of the law (housing for weaker sections) cannot be fulfilled and the decree would result in unjust enrichment.
A contract terminable at will by one party before performance is complete is not specifically enforceable under Section 14(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 21
doctrines: Doctrine of specific performance as discretionary relief
Doctrine of supervisability in specific performance
Doctrine of inequity in enforcement of contracts
Doctrine of harmonious construction of contract clauses

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of Kewal Chand Mimani and S.K. Sem & Ors over who was entitled to regain possession of requisitioned premises after termination of requisition — the former tenant or the owner.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government is obligated to restore possession of requisitioned premises to the former tenant or to the owner after termination of requisition
Whether a lessee whose lease expired and who remained in possession without consent became a tenant holding over or a tenant at sufferance
Whether the Mimanis had a legal right to claim possession of the property at the time of judgment
holdings: The State Government must conduct an inquiry under Section 6 of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 to determine who is entitled to possession; it is not bound to restore possession to the person from whom it was taken.

A lessee who remains in possession after the lease expires without the landlord’s consent is a tenant at sufferance, not a tenant holding over, and does not have a legal right to continued possession.
The Mimanis had no legal right to possession at the time of judgment as the lease had expired and they were dispossessed, so they could not claim restoration of possession.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 6
doctrines: Tenant at sufferance
Juridical possession vs. lawful possession
Statutory inquiry for determination of entitlement to possession

card.dispute: The appellants (Krishna Gopal Chawla & Ors.) fought the State of U.P. and U.P. Jal Nigam over possession of leased property, claiming entitlement to eviction and rent after the lease expired, while the respondents contested ownership and refused to vacate despite a decree for eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in quashing the eviction decree and requiring a fresh execution petition after the Supreme Court had affirmed the decree?
Whether the respondents could raise the issue of ownership of the property for the first time in execution proceedings under Section 47 CPC?
Whether the undertaking given by the respondents to vacate the premises was bona fide and consistent with the Supreme Court's order?
holdings: The High Court committed a manifest error in holding that a fresh execution petition was required; the original execution petition remained maintainable after the Supreme Court affirmed the decree without modification.
Ownership of the property could not be re-agitated in execution proceedings under Section 47 CPC, especially when the respondents had not raised it as a defense in earlier proceedings.
The respondents' undertaking to vacate was not bona fide and was designed to frustrate the decree, as it introduced new conditions not consistent with the Supreme Court's order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 11(2)(d)
doctrines: Merger of decree
Res judicata in execution
Bona fides of undertaking in decree execution

card.dispute: The landlord's son (Respondent) sought eviction of the tenant (Appellant) for bonafide personal requirement under the Delhi Rent Control Act, which the tenant opposed by alleging suppression of alternative accommodations.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord had a bonafide requirement for the tenanted premises.
Whether the existence of other residential properties in the family disqualified the landlord's claim for eviction.
Whether the High Court was justified in relying on unproven wills while assessing property ownership.
holdings: A landlord's need is bonafide if it is natural, sincere, and honest, and must be assessed based on the totality of circumstances including family size, lifestyle, and profession.

The mere existence of other family-owned properties does not negate a landlord’s bonafide need if those properties are not under the landlord's ownership or control or are unsuitable due to location or use.

Courts should not rely on unproven documents like unauthenticated wills without affording parties an opportunity to contest them, though such error was not fatal where ownership still did not vest in the landlord.
doctrines: Bonafide requirement for personal use
Prativa Devi doctrine on alternative accommodation
Principle of judicial notice and evidence admissibility

card.dispute: The landlord and tenant disputed whether the Rent Controller or the Civil Court had jurisdiction to decide an eviction petition after the repeal of the applicable Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether the repeal of the Delhi Rent Control Act deprived the Rent Controller of jurisdiction over a pending eviction petition.
Whether the landlord's right to evict the tenant for illegal subletting survived the repeal of the Rent Act.
Whether parallel proceedings before the Rent Controller and the Civil Court could be maintained.
holdings: The repeal of a rent law does not extinguish pending eviction proceedings if the right to evict had accrued; such rights are preserved under Section 6(c) of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
A right to evict for illegal subletting is not a vested right but an accrued right under Section 6(c) of the General Clauses Act, sufficient to sustain pending proceedings.
A landlord cannot maintain parallel proceedings in both the Rent Controller court and the Civil Court; one must be withdrawn.
doctrines: Doctrine of accrued rights under repeal
Doctrine of saving of rights and proceedings upon repeal
Doctrine of jurisdictional exclusivity in rent control matters

card.dispute: The nephew (tenant) challenged the eviction order granted to his uncle (landlord) on grounds of bona fide requirement, claiming no landlord-tenant relationship existed due to an agreement to sell the property.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Rent Controller was justified in rejecting the tenant's application for leave to contest the eviction petition under Section 25(B) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the tenant had admitted the landlord-tenant relationship and the landlord's claim of bona fide requirement.
holdings: The rejection of leave to contest under Section 25(B) is invalid if the tenant raises a triable issue; the Controller must examine the petition and affidavit to determine if a prima facie case exists.

The Additional Rent Controller erred in assuming admission of landlord-tenant relationship when the tenant explicitly denied it and claimed possession under an agreement to sell, which constitutes a triable issue.
doctrines: Strict interpretation of tenant protection statutes
Deemed admission under special eviction procedures requires proper factual basis
Judicial review of rent controller orders for manifest error

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether a will was validly executed, specifically whether the required attesting witnesses had signed with the intent to attest as mandated by law.
issues_decided: Whether a person who signed a will as 'writer' or 'scribe' can be considered an attesting witness under the Transfer of Property Act and the Indian Succession Act.
Whether the statutory requirement of attestation was satisfied in the absence of proper evidence from attesting witnesses.
Whether oral evidence can prove the intent to attest when the document itself shows the person signed only as a scribe.
holdings: A person who signs a document only as a scribe or writer, without clear intent to attest, does not qualify as an attesting witness under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act.
The statutory requirement of attestation requires that witnesses sign with the animo attestandi—intent to attest—and mere presence or description as writer is insufficient.
Oral evidence attempting to show intent to attest cannot override the clear designation of a person as 'writer' on the document, especially when no attesting witness is examined.
doctrines: Animo attestandi
Onus probandi
Rule of exclusion of oral evidence to contradict documentary designation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of Madhegowda and Ankegowda over ownership and possession of property originally belonging to Ninge Gowda, specifically concerning the validity of a sale of a minor's share by her sister as de facto guardian.
issues_decided: Whether the sister of a minor Hindu female could validly sell the minor's share in ancestral property as a de facto guardian
Whether Section 11 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 applies to such a transfer
Whether the transfer of the minor's property by a de facto guardian without court permission is void or voidable
Whether the minor, upon attaining majority, ratified the sale or effectively repudiated it by subsequent conduct
holdings: A sister of a minor is not a natural guardian under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, and can at best be considered a de facto manager, not a de facto guardian with power to transfer immovable property.

Section 11 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 bars any person from disposing of a Hindu minor's property merely on the ground of being a de facto guardian, and such a transfer is per se invalid.

A transfer made by a de facto guardian in violation of Section 11 is invalid ab initio and does not require a separate suit for cancellation; it can be repudiated by the minor upon attaining majority.
The subsequent sale of her share by the minor after attaining majority, without affirming the earlier sale, constituted repudiation of the earlier invalid transfer.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 4(b)
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 11
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 12
doctrines: De facto manager doctrine
Rule in Hanoomanpersaud Pandays case
Repudiation of voidable/invalid transactions by a minor upon majority
Legislative intent behind protective provisions for minors under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956

card.dispute: The landlord sought to recover possession of rented premises on grounds of bona fide requirement, but the tenant resisted, arguing the suit was barred due to a prior withdrawn eviction petition.
issues_decided: Whether a second eviction suit on grounds of bona fide requirement is maintainable after withdrawal of a prior similar suit without court permission under Order XXIII Rule 1(4)(b) of CPC
Whether Section 45 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 bars a fresh eviction application when the previous application was withdrawn without decision
holdings: A landlord is not barred by Order XXIII Rule 1(4)(b) CPC from filing a fresh eviction suit on bona fide requirement if the cause of action arises anew based on current need, even if the prior suit was withdrawn.
Section 45 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 does not bar a fresh application where the previous proceeding was withdrawn without final decision on the merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 1(4)(b)
doctrines: Res judicata
Recurring cause of action

card.dispute: The plaintiff appealed against the High Court's reversal of a decree for specific performance of part of a land sale agreement, after the seller's title to a portion of the land was found defective.
issues_decided: Whether the relief under Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 can be claimed at the appellate stage by amending the plaint.
Whether a plaintiff can relinquish a part of the claim and seek specific performance of the remaining part when the defendant is unable to perform the entire contract.
holdings: A plaintiff may seek relief under Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 at the appellate stage by amending the plaint, provided the right existed at the time of filing the suit and new facts justifying the amendment arise later.

Where a defendant cannot perform part of a contract, the court may decree specific performance of the performable part if the plaintiff pays the full consideration and relinquishes claims regarding the unperformed part and any compensation.
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings at appellate stage
Relinquishment of part performance under Section 12(3)
Continuation of suit in appeal

card.dispute: Punjab National Bank appealed against a High Court order that set aside a Debts Recovery Tribunal's direction to sell mortgaged property, on grounds of territorial jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution when an alternative remedy under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 was available?
Whether the Debts Recovery Tribunal had territorial jurisdiction to direct sale of mortgaged property situated in a different location?
holdings: The High Court should not have entertained a petition under Article 227 when an appeal lay under Section 20 of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, as the statutory remedy must be exhausted first.
The question of the Tribunal’s territorial jurisdiction over mortgaged property need not be decided by this Court, as the proper course was to pursue the statutory appeal mechanism under the Act.
provisions: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 20
doctrines: Exhaustion of statutory remedies
Limitation on writ jurisdiction when alternative remedy exists
Hierarchy of appellate remedies in special recovery law

card.dispute: Prakash Dhawal Khairnar and his son Sandeep were convicted for multiple murders and related offences; Prakash challenged the death sentence, while the state appealed Sandeep's acquittal in the murder charges.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence imposed on Prakash Dhawal Khairnar under Section 302 IPC was justified in the facts of the case?
Whether the confessional statement of Sandeep could be used to corroborate circumstantial evidence against him?
Whether Sandeep had common intention or conspiracy to commit murder under Section 34 IPC?
holdings: The death sentence was set aside as the case did not fall within the 'rarest of rare' category; life imprisonment with a minimum of 20 years without remission was imposed.
A confessional statement, even if not fully relied upon as substantive evidence, can be used to lend assurance to circumstantial evidence if it contains inculpatory details that are corroborated.
Sandeep was not guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC with common intention, but was liable under Section 201 IPC for destroying evidence to protect his father.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Use of confession to lend assurance to circumstantial evidence
Principle of common intention under Section 34 IPC
Doctrine of constructive use of confessional statements in joint trials

card.dispute: The tenant's heirs challenged the eviction order on the grounds that the rent demand notice was not validly served.
issues_decided: Whether the service of rent demand notice was valid despite the tenant's alleged refusal to receive it.
Whether the proceedings based on presumed service of notice are illegal in the absence of proof of actual service.
holdings: Service of notice is valid if the postman testifies that the tenant refused to accept it, even if the tenant denies service.
Failure to cross-examine the postman on his availability during delivery days prevents challenging the veracity of his testimony.
doctrines: Browne v. Dunn rule
Principle of fair opportunity to explain during cross-examination

card.dispute: The sons of Indira Bai appealed against the High Court's decision invalidating her will, which had been challenged by their sister who claimed a share in the estate.
issues_decided: Whether the will of Indira Bai was duly executed and proved despite uneven distribution of assets?
Whether the non-registration of the will and non-disclosure in family correspondence raise suspicion about its validity?
Whether the High Court was justified in holding the will to be 'unnatural' and reversing the trial court's finding?
holdings: A will cannot be declared invalid solely on the ground of uneven distribution of property among heirs, as testamentary discretion allows unequal dispositions.
The non-registration of a will and its non-disclosure in family correspondence do not, by themselves, create suspicion about its due execution if properly attested.
The finding that a will is 'unnatural' cannot be based on the executant's choice to disinherit certain family members, especially when supported by attesting witnesses and not challenged by them.
doctrines: Testamentary discretion
Presumption of validity of wills with proper attestation
No presumption of fraud or undue influence from unnatural disposition without supporting evidence

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a deceased property owner challenged the validity of a tax recovery sale of the property, arguing that no valid demand notice was served and the tax demand had ceased to exist.
issues_decided: Whether the recovery proceedings and subsequent sale of property were valid in the absence of service of a notice of demand under Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 1961
Whether a sale in recovery proceedings can be sustained when the underlying tax demand had ceased to exist
holdings: Service of a notice of demand under Section 156 of the Income-tax Act is mandatory, and non-service vitiates the entire recovery process, rendering any sale null and void.
A recovery sale based on a non-existent tax demand is invalid, as the authority lacks jurisdiction to proceed with recovery once the demand is extinguished.
doctrines: Jurisdictional defect doctrine
Nullity doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, partners in a hotel business, disputed over the dissolution of the partnership, appointment of a receiver, and whether court proceedings should be stayed in favor of arbitration.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to refer the dispute to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, after the appellants had withdrawn their earlier application under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
Whether the plea of estoppel could prevent the appellants from invoking Section 8 of the 1996 Act after withdrawing their earlier application under the 1940 Act.
Whether the appointment of a receiver and injunctive orders by the High Court were justified, given the existence of an arbitration agreement.
holdings: The High Court erred in refusing to refer the matter to arbitration under Section 8 of the 1996 Act merely because the earlier application under Section 34 of the 1940 Act was withdrawn; the repeal of the 1940 Act made the new remedy under the 1996 Act available.
The doctrine of estoppel does not apply to bar invocation of Section 8 of the 1996 Act, as the provisions of the two Acts differ in scope, purpose, and legal effect.
The appointment of a receiver and prohibitory orders by the High Court were premature and failed to balance the interests of the parties, especially when disputes fell under an arbitration agreement.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel
Mandatory referral to arbitration
Balance of convenience
Continuity of arbitral rights despite procedural withdrawal

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra appealed against the acquittal of several accused, including Bharat Chaganlal Raghani, Subhash Bind, and Shekhar Kadam, in a case involving contract killing, criminal conspiracy, and illegal possession of arms under TADA.
issues_decided: Whether the recovery of weapons from the accused was legally valid despite contradictions in confessional statements and a police press conference.
Whether the test identification parade was vitally flawed to render the identification of the accused unreliable.
Whether the confessional statements of the accused were voluntary and sufficiently corroborated to sustain conviction.
Whether the trial court erred in acquitting the accused by applying an overly technical approach to the evidence.
holdings: Recovery of weapons from the accused was validly proved through panchanamas and witness testimony, and minor contradictions in confessional statements do not invalidate the recovery.
The failure to properly conduct a test identification parade is not fatal when confessional statements are voluntary and corroborated.
Confessional statements, if proved voluntary and legally recorded, can form the basis of conviction when corroborated by independent evidence.
The trial court erred in adopting a hyper-technical approach and disregarding reliable evidence; the prosecution case was sufficient to sustain conviction under IPC, Arms Act, and TADA.
provisions: Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3(2)(i)
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3(2)(ii)
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3(3)
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3(5)
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 5
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 6
doctrines: Corroboration of confessional statements
Principle of deeming confession reliable if voluntary and corroborated
Judicial caution against hyper-technical evaluation of evidence in serious criminal cases
Use of panchanama as substantive evidence of recovery

card.dispute: The Dental Council of India challenged the High Court's order directing it and the Central Government to approve a dental college's admission of 100 students annually instead of 60.
issues_decided: Whether the Dental Council of India was justified in limiting student intake to 60 despite the college meeting infrastructure requirements for 100 students.
Whether admissions of 100 students per batch, granted in compliance with the High Court's mandamus, should be recognized despite lack of prior approval from DCI.
Whether the college could continue operating and permit students admitted beyond sanctioned strength to appear in examinations.
holdings: The Dental Council and Central Government must grant permission for 100 students if the college meets all prescribed infrastructure and teaching staff requirements.
Admissions of 100 students were upheld due to the High Court's mandamus and absence of a stay, making it unjust to invalidate those admissions.
Students admitted in excess of sanctioned strength may appear in examinations if they meet eligibility criteria and have attended the minimum required classes.
provisions: Dental Council of India (Recognition of Dental Qualifications) Regulations
doctrines: Doctrine of legitimate expectation
Principle of non-arbitrariness in administrative action
Judicial non-interference in academic matters when standards are met

card.dispute: The dispute was between the sons of a deceased Hindu man over whether their mother's sale of ancestral property as their guardian was void or voidable, and whether they could reclaim their shares after attaining majority.
issues_decided: Whether the alienation of minor's immovable property by a natural guardian without court permission is void or voidable under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956
Whether the suit for setting aside such alienation was barred by limitation under Article 60 of the Limitation Act
Whether the amendment of the plaint to include a prayer to set aside the sale deeds could relate back to the original filing date
holdings: Alienation of a minor's immovable property by a natural guardian without prior court permission is voidable, not void, and can only be set aside by a suit filed within three years of the minor attaining majority.
A suit to set aside such alienation is governed by Article 60 of the Limitation Act, and the limitation period begins when the minor attains majority.

An amendment to the plaint introducing a new cause of action to set aside alienation takes effect from the date of amendment, not the original filing date, if the original plaint lacked necessary averments.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8
doctrines: Voidable transfer by guardian
Relation back of amendment to plaint
Legal necessity in guardianship alienations

card.dispute: Tenants appealed against their eviction, claiming the property belonged to a religious trust and that the landlord's title was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 applies to a property held under a religious charitable trust
Whether there was a valid landlord-tenant relationship between the parties
Whether the tenants' denial of the landlord's title was bona fide, depriving the Rent Controller of jurisdiction under Section 10(2)(vii) of the Act
holdings: Properties covered by a religious endowment under the Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act may be exempt from the Rent Control Act, and a prima facie case for such exemption limits the Rent Controller's jurisdiction.

A landlord-tenant relationship exists only if the landlord has valid title; where tenants were inducted by a trust, subsequent claimants must prove lawful derivation of title to enforce tenancy rights.

A tenant's denial of a landlord's derivative title is bona fide if it challenges the validity of the transfer from the original owner; such a dispute must be decided by a civil court, not a Rent Controller.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(vii)
Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act
doctrines: Res judicata
Estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act
Limited jurisdiction of Rent Controller
Derivative title and bona fide dispute

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for alleged wilful default in paying rent and property tax, which the tenant argued did not constitute part of the rent under the lease control law.
issues_decided: Whether the amount agreed to be paid by the tenant towards property tax forms part of 'rent' under Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960?
Whether the tenant committed a wilful default in payment of rent, justifying eviction under the Act?
holdings: Payments agreed by a tenant to pay the landlord for property tax, as part of the lease, constitute 'rent' under the Act, based on the broad judicial understanding of rent including all agreed payments for use and occupation.

A tenant commits wilful default under Section 10(2)(i) if, after a two-month notice demanding arrears, the rent (including agreed tax) is not paid, unless incapacity due to unavoidable circumstances is proved, which the tenant failed to do.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Explanation to Section 10(2)
doctrines: Wilful default doctrine in rent control cases
Broad interpretation of 'rent' to include agreed payments for taxes and amenities

card.dispute: Abdul Rahman (appellant) fought against Prasony Bai and another (respondents) over the right to possess and claim title to land originally allotted to Mangal Singh, a displaced person, after escheat proceedings were initiated following his alleged death intestate without heirs.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to withdraw and dispose of the civil suit on preliminary issues such as res judicata and maintainability?
Whether the appellant could challenge the relationship of the first respondent with Mangal Singh after having failed to raise the issue before revenue authorities?
Whether the appellant could claim adverse possession over the land while having previously acknowledged Mangal Singh's title as a tenant?
Whether the principles of constructive res judicata and abuse of process barred the appellant's suit?
holdings: The High Court had the jurisdiction under Order XIV Rule 1 of the CPC to withdraw and dispose of the suit on preliminary issues, including res judicata and maintainability, especially when facts were admitted.

The appellant was estopped from challenging the first respondent's status as heir of Mangal Singh, as he failed to raise the issue before revenue authorities despite having the opportunity, and the revenue orders attained finality.
A tenant cannot claim adverse possession against the landlord's title; the appellant, having acknowledged Mangal Singh's title, could not later assert ownership by adverse possession.
The appellant's suit amounted to an abuse of process, as he allowed final adjudication in earlier proceedings and later sought to re-litigate the same issues, undermining finality in litigation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XIV Rule 1
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Res judicata
Abuse of process of court
Estoppel by record
Adverse possession

card.dispute: The petitioner filed a public interest litigation alleging that former Prime Minister Chandra Shekhar, through a trust, illegally usurped about 600 acres of common and forest land in Village Bhondsi, Haryana, by manipulating Gram Panchayat resolutions and violating land and forest laws.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of village common land to a private trust via Gram Panchayat resolutions was lawful under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961 and its Rules
Whether the State Government's approval of the land transfer was valid and in compliance with statutory mandates
Whether the petitioner was entitled to a direction for the return of the land to the Gram Panchayat and for penal action against the respondents
Whether the respondent could retain possession of the land due to constructions made in good faith
holdings: Transfers of village common lands must strictly comply with the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961; any deviation renders the transfer void ab initio.
Resolutions and government orders permitting land transfer for unauthorized purposes are legally invalid and do not affect the rights of the Gram Panchayat or villagers.
The Court can direct restitution of illegally transferred land to the Gram Panchayat even if structures have been built, balancing public interest and private investment.
Cost of constructions by a wrongful possessor may be reimbursed by the state, but this does not confer any right over the land.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961, Sections 5A and 5B
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Void ab initio
Principle of restitution in public interest litigation
Judicial review of administrative and panchayat actions violating statutory mandates

card.dispute: The landlord, Atma S. Berar, sought eviction of tenant Mukhtiar Singh from a residential property in Moga for personal occupation, which the High Court reversed in revision; the landlord appealed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority on the landlord's bona fide need for self-occupation?
Whether the High Court, in exercise of revisional jurisdiction, could reappreciate evidence regarding the landlord’s residential requirement?
Whether subsequent events during litigation affected the landlord’s bona fide requirement for self-occupation?
holdings: The High Court cannot overturn concurrent findings of fact on bona fide need for self-occupation unless the findings are perverse, illegal, or based on no evidence.
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 does not permit reappreciation of evidence or substitution of a different factual view.
Subsequent events during litigation, if not properly brought on record and lacking material bearing, do not undermine a landlord’s established bona fide need for self-occupation.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(5)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for self-occupation
Limits of revisional jurisdiction
Concurrent findings of fact not easily disturbed
Subsequent events in pending proceedings

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Collector appealed against the Calcutta High Court's decision quashing the acquisition of two premises in Calcutta, which were needed for students of Calcutta National Medical College, over whether the invocation of emergency powers under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act was valid and mala fide.
issues_decided: Whether the invocation of emergency powers under Section 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act was justified given the continued occupation of the premises by the medical college students.
Whether the failure to deliver physical possession as per earlier court directions rendered the acquisition mala fide.
Whether the landowners' right under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act to object to acquisition could be dispensed with despite the acquiring authority already being in possession.
holdings: The invocation of emergency powers under Section 17(1) and 17(4) is based on subjective satisfaction of the government, which cannot be challenged unless there is non-application of mind or mala fides, both of which were absent here.
The failure to comply with prior court orders to deliver possession does not, by itself, render the acquisition mala fide, especially when the public purpose remains genuine and urgent.
The right to object under Section 5A can be dispensed with under Section 17 even if the land is occupied, provided the occupation is not lawful and urgency exists for formal acquisition.
provisions: West Bengal Requisition and Control (Temporary Provision) Act, 1947, Section 10B
doctrines: Subjective satisfaction doctrine under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act
Mala fide exercise of power
Doctrine of non-application of mind
Public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The landlords (widow and two sons of the deceased owner) sought eviction of two tenants from shops in Indore, claiming bona fide need for the sons to start/continue businesses, leading to a dispute over jurisdiction and validity of the eviction claim.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controlling Authority had jurisdiction to entertain the eviction application when co-owner landlords included one falling under Section 23-J and others not?
Whether the requirement of the landlords for the premises was bona fide and not defeated by alleged alternative accommodations?
holdings: When co-owner landlords, some falling under Section 23-J and others not, jointly file for eviction based on a common cause of action under Section 23-A(b), they may choose to file before the Rent Controlling Authority or in a Civil Court; the choice of forum lies with them.

The bona fide requirement of landlords for non-residential premises cannot be defeated by pointing to rented or less suitable accommodations; alternative accommodation must be owned and reasonably suitable compared to the suit premises.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 23-A(b)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 23-E
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 23-J
doctrines: Plaintiff is dominus litis
Every right must have a remedy (ubi jus ibi remedium)
Bona fide requirement with objective and subjective standards
Reasonable suitability of alternative accommodation

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority challenged the manner in which responsibility was assigned for administrative and banking irregularities in a land transaction involving Skipper Construction Co., particularly concerning the issuance of a bank guarantee and alleged malfeasance by bank officials.
issues_decided: Whether the administrative action in assigning blame solely to one individual (Mr. Suneja) for a multi-official banking decision was arbitrary under Article 14
Whether the court should apply the proportionality test or Wednesbury reasonableness in reviewing administrative punishment decisions
Whether the Central Vigilance Commission should re-examine the quantum of loss and responsibility in the matter, independent of prior reports
holdings: When administrative action is challenged as arbitrary under Article 14 in disciplinary matters, courts must apply the Wednesbury test of reasonableness, not proportionality, and generally remit the matter for fresh consideration.

Assigning full responsibility to a single official for a collective banking decision violates principles of fairness and administrative reasonableness, especially when others involved were exonerated without justification.
The Central Vigilance Commission must independently investigate the extent of loss and official accountability,不受 prior reports or technicalities, and submit a fresh report within 18 months.
doctrines: Wednesbury unreasonableness
Proportionality in administrative law
Arbitrariness under Article 14
Primary vs. secondary judicial review

card.dispute: The owners of a property in Chandigarh fought with occupants (Raj Kumar Aneja and others) over whether the occupants were sub-tenants or direct tenants, and whether the occupants could amend their pleadings in court to challenge their status.
issues_decided: Whether the occupants were entitled to amend their written statements in the trial court to assert a new legal position regarding their tenancy status
Whether the High Court, in revision, could validly allow amendments to the pleadings without following proper procedural requirements
Whether the trial court and appellate authorities correctly decided the tenancy status of the occupants
holdings: An application for amendment of pleadings must clearly specify the proposed changes and comply with Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC, especially in jurisdictions with local rules requiring detailed formulation.
The High Court, in revision, should not casually allow amendments to pleadings without considering procedural safeguards and the possibility of prejudice to the opposite party.
Even if pleadings are amended, if the trial proceeds on the amended pleadings and the party still fails on merits, the appellate court may uphold the original judgment without remanding.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 7
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings must be precise and not cause surprise
Consequential amendment doctrine
Liberal amendment policy subject to procedural compliance

card.dispute: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. and a dealer disputed over the validity of termination of a dealership agreement and the grant of an interim mandatory injunction to restore possession of a petrol pump.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in granting an interim mandatory injunction to restore the dealer's possession of the petrol pump?
Whether the dealer had a strong prima facie case entitling him to interim relief?
Whether the balance of convenience and risk of irreparable injury favored the grant of mandatory injunction?
holdings: An interim mandatory injunction should not be granted unless the plaintiff shows a strong prima facie case, risk of irreparable injury, and that the balance of convenience favors such relief.
The High Court erred in granting the injunction without properly evaluating the Trial Court's findings on possession and the contractual breach by the dealer.
Mandatory injunctions are exceptional and should not be granted when damages would be an adequate remedy; the Court must not decide the final merits at the interim stage.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39 Rules 1 & 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1(r)
doctrines: Balance of convenience
Prima facie case for interim relief
Irreparable injury
Status quo in interim injunctions
Equitable discretion in granting mandatory injunctions

card.dispute: The Haryana Financial Corporation sought to auction the property of Jagdamba Oil Mills for defaulting on a loan, while the Mills sought an injunction to stop the auction.
issues_decided: Whether the Financial Corporation must consult the defaulting borrower at every stage of asset disposal under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951?
Whether the guidelines laid down in Mahesh Chandra v. Haryana Financial Corporation regarding sale procedures are binding?
Whether the High Court was justified in upholding the injunction against the Corporation's auction?
holdings: The Financial Corporation is not required to consult or associate the defaulting borrower in the sale process under Section 29; doing so would cause undue delay and hinder recovery.
The guidelines in Mahesh Chandra’s case imposing mandatory consultation with the borrower are incorrect and inconsistent with Section 29; the decision is overruled.
Courts must not mechanically rely on precedents without considering factual distinctions; the appeal is allowed with directions to repay within six months or face lawful disposal of assets.
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis with contextual application)
Principle of effective recovery and legislative intent in financial statutes
Judicial restraint in interpreting judicial observations as statutory mandates

card.dispute: The owner of a commercial building challenged the Calcutta Municipal Corporation's assessment of annual valuation for property tax, which included rent received by the tenant from sub-tenants, rather than the rent actually received by the owner.
issues_decided: Whether the annual valuation under Section 174 of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 can include rent received by a tenant from sub-tenants when determining the rateable value of the property.
Whether the municipal authority is bound to fix the annual value only up to the standard rent determined under the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950.
Whether the actual rent received by the owner must be the sole basis for determining annual value in the absence of fraud or collusion.
holdings: The municipal authority may consider the rent received by a tenant from sub-tenants as one of the relevant factors in determining the gross annual rent under Section 174 of the 1980 Act, provided all circumstances are considered.
The standard rent under the Rent Control Act is a relevant guideline but not a binding ceiling where the municipal law contains a non obstante clause and allows broader assessment powers.

The actual rent received by the owner is not the sole criterion for annual valuation; the authority must assess what the property might reasonably be expected to fetch, considering all relevant factors including local rental trends and sub-lease income.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 2(1)(b)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 9
doctrines: Reasonable expectation of rent
Non obstante clause overriding rent control restrictions
Statutory interpretation of municipal taxation powers
Principle of fairness in property tax assessment

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant-school under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, for demolition and reconstruction, which the tenant opposed claiming lack of bona fides.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fides under Section 14(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, can be denied solely because they did not rely on the building's condition for demolition?
Whether the High Court could interfere in revision with the Appellate Authority's finding of fact on eviction?
Whether public interest in continuing a private unrecognized school outweighs the landlord's right to redevelop the property?
holdings: Bona fides under Section 14(1)(b) depend on multiple factors including financial capacity, utility of reconstruction, and intent, not solely on the building’s condition; non-reliance on condition does not negate bona fides.

The High Court, in revision, can interfere with findings of fact if there is an error in law or failure to apply binding legal principles, as occurred when the Appellate Authority relied on overruled precedent.

Eviction under Section 14(1)(b) is not barred by public interest where the tenant runs an unrecognized private school for profit; redevelopment serves greater public good by enabling better use of urban space.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(1)(b)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(2)(b)
doctrines: Bona fides in landlord's need for demolition and reconstruction
Judicial review in revisional jurisdiction
Balancing private property rights and public interest

card.dispute: The landlord-respondents sought eviction of tenant-appellants for alleged rent default, while tenants contested the claim, disputing the rent amount and service of notice.
issues_decided: Whether the denial of title by the tenant was not bona fide and could ground eviction
Whether the tenants committed wilful default in payment of rent justifying eviction under Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
Whether the Municipal Corporation or Hemlata Mohan should be impleaded in the eviction proceedings
holdings: Denial of title by the tenant was not shown to be mala fide, and thus cannot sustain an eviction petition.

Non-payment of rent for one or two months does not constitute wilful default when there is a dispute over rent rate, prior conduct of accepting rent bi-monthly, and uncertainty over to whom rent should be paid.
The Municipal Corporation and Hemlata Mohan are not necessary parties in a landlord-tenant eviction dispute and their impleadment is rightly denied.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
doctrines: Wilful default requires intentional, deliberate, and conscious non-payment with knowledge of consequences
Doctrine of necessary and proper parties in civil litigation
Principle of res judicata and party autonomy in separate proceedings for title and rent fixation

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from non-residential premises for use as an office for his chartered accountant son, leading to a legal dispute over whether this qualified as 'requirement for his own use' under the rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement of a landlord for 'his own use' under Section 13(3)(a)(ii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 includes use by a family member such as a son?
Whether the literal meaning of 'own use' should be interpreted narrowly or in a manner consistent with social and familial realities?
holdings: The phrase 'for his own use' in Section 13(3)(a)(ii) must be given a wide, liberal, and purposive interpretation, not limited to personal physical occupation by the landlord.
The requirement of a landlord’s son, especially when economically or socially interdependent, can constitute 'own use' if the claim is genuine and not a ruse to evict the tenant.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)(ii)
doctrines: Purposive interpretation of statutes
Contextual and beneficial construction
Rule against literalism in statutory interpretation
Balancing tenant protection with landlord rights

card.dispute: Environmental activists and a trustee challenged the continuation of mining activities by Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd. in the ecologically sensitive Kudremukh National Park, alleging violations of forest and wildlife protection laws.
issues_decided: Whether mining activities in a national park require prior approval under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, even for lease renewal
Whether the absence of an Environment Impact Assessment report invalidates temporary working permission for mining
Whether the Forest Advisory Committee's recommendation on time-bound mining should be upheld
holdings: Renewal of a mining lease in forest land requires prior approval under Section 2 of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, as it constitutes a non-forest activity, regardless of prior lease status.
Mining cannot proceed lawfully without a completed Environment Impact Assessment, especially in ecologically sensitive areas like the Western Ghats.
Mining in the already disturbed area may continue until the end of 2005, subject to ecological safeguards, based on the Forest Advisory Committee’s expert assessment and recommendations.
doctrines: Precautionary Principle
Sustainable Development
Public Trust Doctrine
Principle of Harmonious Construction with International Environmental Norms

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the quantum of compensation awarded for 84.23 acres of land acquired by the State of Haryana for developing residential and commercial sectors, contesting a 20% deduction for development charges.
issues_decided: Whether a deduction for development charges is justified in determining compensation for large tracts of undeveloped land acquired for urban development.
Whether the market value of acquired land should be based on sale deeds of developed plots without adjustment for development costs.
Whether the decision in Bhagwathula Samanna (supra) applies to undeveloped land lacking civic amenities.
holdings: A deduction for development charges is justified when land is acquired in bulk for development and lacks existing infrastructure, even if it has potential for development.
Market value of large, undeveloped tracts cannot be determined solely by sale prices of small, developed plots; a deduction must be made to account for development costs.
The Bhagwathula Samanna case does not apply where the acquired land is not fully developed with civic amenities, and thus does not bar deduction for development purposes.
doctrines: Deduction for development charges in land acquisition compensation
Principle of just and fair market value for large tracts of land
Distinction between developed and undeveloped land in valuation

card.dispute: The appellant, Konda Lakshmana Bapuji, challenged the declaration that he was a land grabber under the A.P. Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, and the consequent order to restore possession of disputed land to the State of Andhra Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a land grabber within the meaning of the A.P. Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982
Whether the allegations in the petition were sufficient to invoke the provisions of the Act despite not using the exact statutory language
Whether permissive possession negates a finding of land grabbing under the Act
holdings: A person who occupies government land under an invalid perpetual lease from someone without title does so with the intention of illegally taking possession, satisfying the definition of 'land grabber'.
It is not necessary to use the exact words of the statute; if the pleadings, issues, and evidence address the ingredients of land grabbing, the finding can be sustained.
An averment of permissive possession does not automatically negate land grabbing if the possession lacks lawful entitlement and is based on an invalid title.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 2(2)(d) and (e)
Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 7(1)
Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 8(1)
doctrines: Necessary implication in inferring mens rea for land grabbing
Substantial compliance with pleading requirements
Constructive understanding of issues by parties despite technical deficiencies

card.dispute: The appellants, owners of a property, sued to recover possession from respondents who claimed to be in possession under an oral agreement to purchase, invoking Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a person can claim protection under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act based on an oral agreement to sell not reduced to writing.
Whether letters admitting an agreement to sell can constitute a written agreement under Section 53-A.
Whether possession can be protected under Section 53-A without a written agreement containing essential terms of the sale.
holdings: Section 53-A requires a written agreement signed by the transferor containing terms ascertainable with reasonable certainty; an oral agreement does not suffice.

Letters admitting an oral agreement to sell do not constitute a written agreement under Section 53-A if they lack essential terms like time for execution of sale deed or payment of registration charges.
Possession in part performance cannot be protected under Section 53-A unless the transferee was put in possession pursuant to a written agreement meeting statutory requirements.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Equitable protection under Section 53-A
Requirement of writing and certainty of terms in part performance

card.dispute: The plaintiff claimed ownership of a property through a will and sale deed, while the defendant, a former tenant, claimed title by adverse possession and denied the will's validity.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated 22nd September 1963 was validly executed by Bhagubai and could be relied upon to establish title
Whether the earlier judicial findings upholding the will in a previous suit between the same parties had evidentiary value in the present suit
Whether the courts below erred in disbelieving the will based on speculative and irrelevant grounds
holdings: A registered will, supported by attesting witnesses and accepted in prior litigation between the same parties, must be given due weight unless there is strong evidence to disprove it.
Findings in a former suit between the same parties on the validity of a will are relevant and admissible under Sections 11, 13, and 35 of the Evidence Act, even if not strictly res judicata.
Courts cannot reject a will based on mere suspicion, absence of medical evidence, or conjectures about the testator’s capacity without concrete contradictory evidence.
doctrines: Res judicata (discussed but not applied)
Evidentiary value of previous judicial findings
Presumption of validity of registered wills

card.dispute: The appellant, Mahesh Chand, filed a second criminal complaint against B. Janardhan Reddy for forgery and trespass after his first complaint was dismissed, and challenged the High Court's refusal to allow the second complaint.
issues_decided: Whether a second criminal complaint on the same facts is maintainable after dismissal of a prior complaint under Section 203 of the Cr.P.C.
Whether a Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence based on a protest petition after a police final report has been accepted.
holdings: A second criminal complaint on the same facts is not statutorily barred and may be entertained in exceptional circumstances such as manifest error, miscarriage of justice, or emergence of new facts not previously available.
A Magistrate may take cognizance under Section 204 Cr.P.C. upon a protest petition or second complaint if there is sufficient ground for proceeding, even after acceptance of a police final report.
doctrines: Manifest error or miscarriage of justice doctrine
Exceptional circumstances doctrine for second complaints
Continuity of complaint via protest petition

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the rejection of his writ petition to quash land acquisition proceedings and award under the B.D.A. Act, claiming delay and inapplicability of time limits from the amended Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether amendments to the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (especially Sections 6 and 11-A) apply to acquisition proceedings under the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1973?
Whether the delay in passing the award under the B.D.A. Act renders the acquisition proceedings liable to be quashed?
holdings: The amendments to the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including Sections 6 and 11-A, do not apply to the B.D.A. Act because the latter is a special, self-contained law not supplemental or in pari materia with the Central Act.
The acquisition proceedings under the B.D.A. Act are not invalidated by delay in passing the award, especially when the delay was partly caused by the landowner's own litigation and injunctions.
doctrines: Legislation by incorporation
In pari materia
Self-contained special statute
Necessary intendment

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether the High Court was justified in remanding the case for fresh trial on a contract for sale of immovable property, after the contract allegedly became inoperative due to non-receipt of Urban Land Ceiling permission.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the case for trial on additional issues despite adequate material on record to decide the appeal?
Whether the absence of a specific issue framing on readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, warranted remand?
Whether the parties were prejudiced by the trial court's failure to frame specific issues when evidence on those points was led and considered?
holdings: An appellate court should not remand a case unless expressly permitted under Order 41 Rules 23, 23A, or 25 CPC, and remand is unwarranted when findings can be made on existing record.

Where parties have led evidence and argued on an issue despite no specific framing, and no prejudice is shown, the appellate court can decide the issue without remand, following the principle in Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao.
Remand is not necessary when both parties indicate no desire to adduce further evidence and subsequent events are documented and admitted.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rules 23, 23A, 25, and 27
doctrines: Nagubai Ammal doctrine on substantial justice over technical pleading
Principle of constructive res judicata
Doctrine against unnecessary remand in appellate proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, Nirmala Anand, sued for specific performance of an agreement to purchase a flat, which remained incomplete due to cancellation of the land lease, while the respondents sought additional payment before execution of the sale deed.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant is entitled to specific performance of the agreement despite the flat remaining incomplete for decades.
Whether the court can impose a condition requiring the appellant to pay an additional amount beyond the agreed sale consideration.
What equitable conditions, if any, should be attached to the grant of specific performance in light of the long pendency and changed circumstances.
holdings: The appellant is entitled to specific performance as she was ready and willing to perform her part and the breach was committed by the respondents.
The court may impose reasonable conditions while granting specific performance, including payment of an additional amount, to balance equities between the parties.
The appellant must pay Rs.6,25,000 (including interest) instead of the original balance of Rs.25,000, but not the Rs.40 lakh sought, to avoid rewarding the defaulting party.
doctrines: Discretionary nature of specific performance
Equitable balancing of interests in specific performance
No unjust enrichment of defaulting party

card.dispute: The appellant, Nirmala Anand, sought specific performance of a flat purchase agreement, while the respondents resisted, citing delays and changed circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant is entitled to specific performance of the flat purchase agreement despite long delay and partial payment?
Whether equitable conditions can be imposed while granting specific performance?
Whether the appellant must contribute to renewal and revalidation efforts undertaken by others for the benefit of the entire property?
holdings: Specific performance may be granted conditionally where balance of equities favours it, even if the plaintiff has delayed and not fully performed.
Courts may impose compensatory conditions, such as additional payment, to prevent unjust enrichment and balance hardships between parties.
A plaintiff seeking benefit from collective efforts like lease renewal must contribute proportionately to expenses incurred for the common good.
doctrines: Balance of equities
Conditional specific performance
Fiduciary relationship in flat allotment schemes

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether the High Court was justified in remanding the case for fresh trial on additional issues despite sufficient material on record to decide the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in remanding the case for trial of additional issues when the pleadings and evidence were sufficient to decide the matter?
Whether the absence of a specifically framed issue on readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act barred the High Court from deciding the issue?
Whether the High Court could consider subsequent events, such as the property being within ceiling limits and the plaintiff being declared a sick company, in deciding the appeal?
holdings: The High Court should not have remanded the case as the trial court had already adjudicated on the issues and the parties had full opportunity to present their case; remand was unwarranted under CPC Rules 23, 23A, and 25.

Even if no specific issue was framed on readiness and willingness, the parties had notice of the issue, adduced evidence, and argued it, so the High Court could decide it without remand, following the principle in Nagubai Ammal.
The High Court may consider subsequent events supported by public documents, such as the ceiling limit determination and sick company status, without requiring additional evidence or remand.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 23
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 23A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 25
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Nagubai Ammal doctrine on substantial justice over technical pleading defects
Principle against unwarranted remand under CPC
Appellate court's power to consider subsequent events and mould relief

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant company for sub-letting the premises without consent, while the tenant claimed implied consent due to the landlord's long inaction.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could be evicted for sub-letting without the landlord's consent under Section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965
Whether the landlord's inaction over several years amounted to implied consent or acquiescence to sub-letting
holdings: A tenant can be evicted for sub-letting without the landlord's consent if the lease does not confer a right to sub-let, as required under Section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Act.
Implied consent cannot be inferred from mere inaction or prolonged silence by the landlord; consent must be a positive, clear act amounting to conferral of right.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(4)(i)
doctrines: Implied consent
Acquiescence vs. Consent
Positive act requirement for conferral of rights

card.dispute: The appellants, whose land was acquired for urban development, challenged the High Court's decision setting aside a 1971 compromise that had granted them residential plots in lieu of enhanced compensation, seeking enforcement of the original allotment.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court should exercise its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 to interfere in the matter of the compromise-based allotment of residential plots in a land acquisition case.
Whether the tripartite compromise, which included allotment of residential plots in the acquired land, was valid and in the interest of justice.
Whether the appellants are entitled to retain or be re-allotted residential plots as part of compensation, despite irregularities in the original allotment process.
holdings: The Supreme Court declined to exercise jurisdiction under Article 136, holding that the facts did not warrant interference due to concerns over misuse of public office and inequitable allotments.
The compromise allotting large plots in the acquired land was vitiated and could not be upheld, as it undermined the public purpose of acquisition and showed signs of abuse.
To ensure justice and consistency, the appellants are entitled to a residential plot of 250 square yards in another JDA scheme at 1971 rates, but not from the originally acquired land.
provisions: Rajasthan Lokayukta and Up-Lokayukta Act, 1973, Section 10
doctrines: Discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136
Doctrine of public purpose in land acquisition
Principle of consistency and equitable rehabilitation
Power under Article 142 to do complete justice

card.dispute: Nirmala Anand (appellant) sued Advent Corporation Pvt. Ltd. and others for specific performance of an agreement to sell Flat No. 71 in the Divya Prabha building, while the respondents resisted, citing price escalation and delay.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant is entitled to specific performance of the agreement to sell despite the long delay in execution?
Whether the appellant must pay an additional sum of Rs. 40 lakhs as compensation for price escalation as a condition for specific performance?
Whether the court can impose equitable terms while decreeing specific performance under the Specific Relief Act, 1963?
holdings: The appellant is entitled to specific performance as she remained ready and willing to perform her part and did not cause inordinate delay.
The appellant is not required to pay an additional Rs. 40 lakhs as a condition for specific performance, as such a requirement would frustrate the relief and is not justified on equity.

Courts have discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 to grant specific performance, but must exercise it fairly and not impose unfair financial burdens absent mutual agreement or concession.
doctrines: Discretion in granting specific performance
Equitable relief under specific performance
No unjust enrichment or benefit from one's own wrong

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the bulk sale of land by CIDCO to certain respondents on grounds of procedural illegality and violation of public interest.
issues_decided: Whether the bulk sale of land by CIDCO was conducted in violation of statutory and procedural norms
Whether third-party interests created after the impugned allotments should be protected
Whether the High Court acted within its jurisdiction in entertaining a public interest litigation against the land allotments
holdings: The impugned land sales by CIDCO in favor of certain respondents were vitiated due to procedural illegality and are not binding on CIDCO.

Despite invalidity of allotment, third-party purchasers who made substantial construction and created bona fide interests must pay the difference between the amount paid and the reserve price, but can retain the land.
The High Court had jurisdiction to act in public interest to scrutinize CIDCO's land allotments, even beyond the specific reliefs sought in the petition.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 113(3A)
doctrines: Public interest litigation
Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Principle of equitable restitution

card.dispute: The appellants (vendees) fought the respondents (vendors) over the enforcement of an agreement for sale of land, which the vendors claimed was rendered unenforceable due to material alterations in the document by adding two marginal witnesses.
issues_decided: Whether the alteration in the agreement of sale by adding two marginal witnesses amounted to a material alteration invalidating the document?
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of the lower courts based on this alleged alteration?
holdings: An alteration in a deed is not material if it does not change the legal effect of the original document, express implied terms, or prejudice the party bound, and thus does not invalidate the agreement.
The High Court erred in setting aside concurrent findings of lower courts on a ground not substantially raised in the appeal, violating the limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC.
doctrines: Material alteration doctrine
Concurrent finding rule in second appeals
Principle of implied terms in contracts

card.dispute: Ranbir Singh (appellant) and Dalbir Singh (respondent) fought over the attachment of disputed land under Section 145 Cr.P.C., following competing civil suits and allegations of dispossession and breach of peace.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court acted within its jurisdiction in quashing the orders under Sections 145(1) and 146(1) Cr.P.C.?
Whether the Sub-Divisional Magistrate’s preliminary order under Section 145(1) Cr.P.C. was valid?
Whether the High Court erred in directing restoration of possession to Dalbir Singh?
holdings: The High Court correctly quashed the orders under Sections 145(1) and 146(1) Cr.P.C. due to non-compliance with statutory requirements, particularly the lack of recorded satisfaction regarding apprehension of breach of peace.
Proceedings under Section 145 Cr.P.C. are limited to possession and do not allow determination of title or rights of possession, especially when civil suits are pending.
The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by acting like an appellate court and should not have directed restoration of possession; civil court must decide interim relief independently.
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
Separation of powers between criminal and civil proceedings in possession disputes
Doctrine of non-determination of title in Section 145 Cr.P.C. proceedings

card.dispute: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant who denied the landlord-tenant relationship and claimed ownership of the property, leading to a dispute over whether a triable issue existed for granting leave to defend.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent-tenant raised a triable issue warranting grant of leave to defend under Section 14(4) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982.
Whether the tenant is estopped from denying the landlord's title under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act.
holdings: The tenant failed to raise a triable issue as his claim of ownership was contrary to his prior judicial admission and documentary evidence, rendering the defence frivolous.
A tenant is estopped from denying the landlord's title during the continuance of tenancy under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, especially when inducted by the landlord and in possession.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982, Section 14(4) and (5)
doctrines: Estoppel of tenant under Section 116 of the Evidence Act
Triable issue in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The tenant, S.R. Ejaz, challenged the High Court's order remanding his suit for restoration of possession after being forcibly dispossessed by the landlord, the Tamil Nadu Handloom Weavers Co-operative Society Ltd.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 for fresh consideration of evidence after 15 years of dispossession.
Whether the appellant was dispossessed illegally and without consent, entitling him to restoration of possession under the Act.
holdings: The High Court's remand for fresh appreciation of evidence after 15 years frustrates the summary nature and purpose of Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
A tenant who is forcibly dispossessed without consent is entitled to restoration of possession if the dispossession was illegal and outside due process of law.
doctrines: Summary remedy under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act
Illegality of self-help and forcible dispossession
Juridical possession of a lessee
Rule of law over might

card.dispute: Legal representatives of deceased parties in land acquisition appeals fought over whether the appeals could continue after the death of some appellants and whether substitution of parties should be allowed.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal abates entirely when one of multiple appellants with separate rights dies without substitution.
Whether a decree in a consolidated proceeding with multiple claimants having distinct rights is joint and inseverable.
Whether delay in filing applications for substitution of legal representatives can be condoned.
Whether non-parties can be impleaded at a late stage to claim compensation in a land acquisition case.
holdings: An appeal does not abate entirely if one of several appellants with distinct, separate, and independent rights dies; the appeal can continue for the remaining parties.
A decree in a consolidated proceeding involving multiple claimants with separate rights is not joint and inseverable but a combination of severable decrees.
Courts may condone delay in substitution applications to ensure justice, especially when appeals are pending and rights would otherwise be rendered ineffective.
Persons whose predecessors were not parties at any stage of proceedings cannot be impleaded at a late stage, especially when it disrupts the finality of the process.
doctrines: ubi jus ibi remedium
severability of decrees in multi-party litigation
principle of effective adjudication of rights
avoidance of inconsistent or self-destructive decrees

card.dispute: Legal representatives of deceased claimants in land acquisition proceedings fought over whether the appeals could continue despite abatement due to death, and whether the decree was joint and inseverable.
issues_decided: Whether a decree passed in favour of multiple claimants with distinct and independent rights is joint and inseverable or severable.
Whether the abatement of an appeal by one party renders the entire appeal incompetent if other appellants have independent claims.
Whether the High Court erred in rejecting applications for substitution and condonation of delay.
holdings: A decree in favour of multiple claimants with distinct, separate, and independent rights is not joint and inseverable but a combination of several severable decrees.

An appeal does not abate in its entirety if one party dies; the appeal can proceed for the remaining parties if their rights are independent and enforcement of decrees would not be mutually destructive.
The High Court must adopt a liberal approach in condoning delay and allowing substitution to ensure effective adjudication of claims on merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII (Death of Parties)
doctrines: ubi jus ibi remedium
principle of severability of decrees
doctrine of inconsistent or contradictory decrees

card.dispute: The transferor sued to recover possession of agricultural land from the transferee who had taken possession under an agreement to sell, claiming the defence of part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act despite the limitation period for specific performance having expired.
issues_decided: Whether a defendant transferee can invoke Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act to protect possession obtained under part performance of an agreement to sell after the limitation period for filing a suit for specific performance has expired.
Whether the law of limitation bars a defence based on part performance under Section 53A even if the right to sue for specific performance is time-barred.
holdings: A transferee can defend possession under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act even if the limitation period for filing a suit for specific performance has expired, provided all conditions under Section 53A are satisfied.
The law of limitation bars remedies, not defences; thus, a time-barred right to sue does not prevent a defendant from relying on part performance as a shield to protect possession.
provisions: Limitation Act, Articles relating to suits for specific performance
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Equitable protection against fraud
Distinction between remedy and right under limitation law

card.dispute: The landlady Sushila sought eviction of tenant Baij Nath from a shop she owned, alleging bonafide need to settle her unemployed, technically trained son in business, while the tenant resisted on grounds of long tenancy and hardship.
issues_decided: Whether the landlady established a bonafide need for eviction under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972?
Whether the availability of alternative business premises to the tenant affects the weight given to his long tenancy?
Whether the comparative hardship between the parties favors the landlord or the tenant?
holdings: A landlord's bonafide need to provide self-employment to an unemployed, technically educated son qualifies as a valid ground for eviction under Section 21(1)(a) of the Act.
The length of tenancy loses significance when the tenant has alternative suitable business premises available to shift to.
Where the landlord has no other property to settle an unemployed son, while the tenant has multiple shops, the balance of hardship favors the landlord.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 16(2)
doctrines: Bonafide need
Comparative hardship
Judicial review of findings of fact in writ jurisdiction
