holdings: Land held under a government grant is not transferable without the State's permission, and any transfer in violation of grant conditions is invalid.
Transfers made after the cut-off date with intent to defeat the Ceiling Act are not in good faith and must be ignored in determining surplus land.
The High Court erred in imposing lump-sum costs as damages; such quantification must be done by ceiling authorities under Section 16 and Rule 18A.
Remand for hearing of transferees is unnecessary when the legal issue is settled and no prejudice arises due to prior opportunity before higher courts.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings (Amendment) Act, 1972, Section 16
doctrines: Doctrine of good faith in land transfers under ceiling laws
Doctrine of notice under Article 142 for doing complete justice
Principle of natural justice in administrative proceedings
Rule against colourable transactions to circumvent land reform laws

card.dispute: The Government of Andhra Pradesh appealed against orders directing reassignment of acquired land and a building to original owners who had received compensation, based on a revenue standing order and claims of non-utilization for public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the original owner is entitled to reassignment of acquired land unused for public purpose under a revenue standing order after compensation has been paid?
Whether Section 54-A of the Andhra Pradesh Act applies to allow reconveyance of land no longer needed for public benefit?
Whether a mere letter from an engineer stating land is no longer required amounts to formal relinquishment by competent authority?
Whether a standing order can override the statutory vesting of acquired land in the government under the Land Acquisition Act?
holdings: Once land is acquired under the Land Acquisition Act and compensation paid, it vests absolutely in the government and cannot be re-conveyed to the original owner by executive order.
Section 54-A applies only when land is formally relinquished by competent authority, not merely unused, and even then, reconveyance is not automatic.
A letter from a Resident Engineer stating land is no longer required does not constitute formal relinquishment; only a competent authority can make that decision.
Standing Order No. 90(32) has no statutory force and cannot override the Land Acquisition Act or permit reconveyance contrary to settled law.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, Section 54
Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, Section 54-A
doctrines: Absolute vesting of acquired land in the government
Public purpose doctrine in land acquisition
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (plain meaning rule)
Doctrine of executive orders lacking statutory force

card.dispute: The H.P. Housing Board appealed against the High Court's determination of compensation for land acquired for a housing colony, challenging the exclusion of certain sale instances and the method of calculating compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in excluding the sale instances relied upon by the appellants while determining compensation.
Whether the High Court correctly applied a 40% deduction for the largeness of the acquired land.
What is the proper method for determining market value of acquired land based on comparable sale instances?
holdings: The High Court erred in excluding the two sale instances cited by the appellants; all proved sale instances must be considered regardless of an unaccepted offer.
A deduction for largeness of holding is warranted, but 33-1/3% is appropriate instead of 40%, to account for development advantages in large acquisitions.
Market value must be based on averaging all reliable sale instances of comparable land, adjusted for size and purpose, even if land types differ slightly when acquired for the same use.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales in land valuation
Deduction for development cost in large acquisitions
Inadmissibility of ignoring relevant evidence of market value

card.dispute: Applicants for industrial plots in Chandigarh fought with the Union Territory administration over allotment of plots after a long delay and changes in policy and environmental norms.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's directions for allotment of industrial plots should be upheld or modified
Whether non-consentees and left-out applicants could be granted alternative plots in a new industrial area
Whether applicants who were not parties before the High Court could be allowed to claim allotment
What price and conditions should apply to fresh allotments in the new industrial area
holdings: The High Court's directions are partly upheld but modified to allow allotment by draw of lots to eligible consentees and one-kanal allottees from available plots in Phase I/II.
Non-consentees may be allotted plots in the new industrial area (Phase III at Mouli Jagran) at the prevailing price, with prior deposit adjusted, if they express willingness within one month.
Applicants who were not parties before the High Court cannot claim allotment due to laches and abandonment of rights.
Allotments in restricted zones near the airbase are conditional and may be cancelled without compensation if future restrictions apply, with only deposit refund due.
provisions: Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952
Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Principle of fairness in administrative allotment
Conditional allotment subject to environmental and statutory compliance

card.dispute: The Friends Colony Development Committee challenged the unauthorized construction of the Kalyani Apartment in excess of sanctioned plans, while the builder sought regularization of deviations.
issues_decided: Whether the unauthorized construction exceeding sanctioned building plans should be demolished or regularized.
Whether the High Court erred in directing only reconsideration of revised building plans without a comprehensive hearing.
What principles should govern compounding of building deviations, especially by professional builders.
holdings: Unauthorized constructions, particularly by professional builders, must be dealt with strictly to deter future violations, and compounding should be minimal and granted only in bona fide cases.

The High Court must jointly hear the builder's and the residents' writ petitions with a public interest focus, considering all relevant documents and ensuring rehabilitation and compensation for affected parties.
The case shall be decided under pre-2001 building regulations, and the builder must provisionally deposit compounding fees pending final determination.
provisions: Cuttack Development Authority (Planning and Building Standard) Regulations, 2001
doctrines: Public interest litigation
Judicial review of administrative discretion in regularization of building violations
Deterrence in urban planning enforcement
Principle of rehabilitation and compensation for displaced occupants

card.dispute: Gajraj Jain challenged the sale of assets by BICICO to Stichworth Exports, alleging malafide and violation of statutory duties under the State Financial Corporation Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether BICICO acted malafide and in breach of Section 29 of the State Financial Corporation Act, 1951 in transferring the mortgaged assets of Katihar Flour Mills to Stichworth Exports Pvt. Ltd.
Whether the agreement dated 26.4.2002 for the sale of assets was valid and lawful, particularly in light of the prior repayment of BICICO's dues by the appellant.
Whether the auction process was fair and transparent, and whether the corporation failed to protect the interests of the second charge holder and the mortgagor.
holdings: A financial corporation under the 1951 Act must act reasonably and in good faith to secure the best possible price for mortgaged assets, including obtaining a valuation and ensuring transparency.
The sale of mortgaged assets without a proper valuation, public auction, or consideration of competing offers violates Section 29 of the 1951 Act and is ultra vires.
The right of redemption of a borrower is not extinguished merely by initiating an auction; full repayment of dues entitles the borrower to return of assets.
An agreement to sell assets for a fraction of their value, especially when executed before the auction and without board approval, indicates collusion and is invalid.
doctrines: Principle of fair and reasonable exercise of statutory power
Equity of redemption under mortgage law
Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness in public authority action

card.dispute: Haryana Urban Development Authority appealed against orders directing it to provide alternate plots at original prices and pay high interest due to delayed possession.
issues_decided: Whether consumer commissions can award interest at 18% across the board without considering facts
Whether compensation can be awarded for mental agony and increased construction costs due to delayed possession
Whether the authority must offer an alternate plot at the original price if it fails to deliver possession
holdings: Consumer commissions cannot award interest at 18% as a standard rate; interest must be fact-based and justified.
Where possession is unreasonably delayed, compensation for mental agony and increased construction costs may be awarded.
If a development authority cannot deliver possession of an allotted plot, it must offer an alternate plot at the original price in the same or nearby sector.
doctrines: Deficiency in service
Misfeasance in public office
Compensation for mental agony
Principle of reasonable compensation

card.dispute: The Ghaziabad Development Authority appealed against orders directing it to refund amounts with interest to allottees due to non-delivery of plots or flats in housing schemes.
issues_decided: Whether a uniform interest rate of 18% can be awarded as compensation for deficiency of service by a development authority
Whether interest should be awarded during the period when a stay order was in operation
Whether consumer forums must provide detailed reasoning when awarding compensation or interest
holdings: Awarding flat 18% interest as compensation without considering facts is unjustified; interest must reflect actual deficiency, delay, and harassment, and be justified with reasons.
Interest is not payable during periods when a valid stay order prevented performance, if the authority was genuinely restrained from delivering possession.
Consumer commissions must assess compensation under separate heads with reasons, rather than awarding interest mechanically as a substitute for detailed assessment.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973
doctrines: Deficiency in service
Compensation for non-performance
Principle of reasoned orders
Effect of stay orders on liability

card.dispute: M.C. Mehta, a public interest petitioner, fought against the Union of India and others over whether mining activities in the Aravalli hills and within 5 km of the Delhi-Haryana border caused environmental degradation and should be restricted or banned.
issues_decided: Whether mining in the Aravalli hills and near the Delhi-Haryana border causes environmental degradation and warrants regulatory action
Whether areas in Haryana with mining activities qualify as 'forest' under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, requiring prior central approval for non-forestry use
Whether environmental impact assessment requirements apply to renewal of mining leases
Whether mining leases in ecologically sensitive areas can be permitted without compliance with sustainable development and expert recommendations
holdings: Mining activities in ecologically sensitive areas like the Aravalli hills and within 5 km of the Delhi-Haryana border cause significant environmental degradation and must comply with strict environmental safeguards.

Areas declared as forest in official records or affidavits must be treated as 'forest' under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and cannot be used for mining without prior central government approval.
The requirement of environmental clearance under the 27 January 1994 notification applies to renewal of mining leases, and such applications must be decided transparently within 10 weeks.
Mining can only proceed on the principles of sustainable development and strict compliance with expert recommendations; continued environmental harm may lead to total closure of mining operations.
provisions: Punjab Land Preservation Act, 1900, Section 4 and Section 5
doctrines: Sustainable development
Precautionary principle
Public trust doctrine
Principle of intergenerational equity

card.dispute: The appellants, Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani and another, claimed co-ownership in a property at Koregaon Park, Pune, which was attached by Indusind Bank under recovery proceedings, and challenged the Debt Recovery Tribunal's decision denying their interest in the property.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were co-owners of the property at 38, Koregaon Park, Pune, on the date the decrees were passed.
Whether the appellants contributed to the purchase of the property from their independent income.
Whether the burden of proof was discharged by the appellants to establish their share in the property.
holdings: The appellants failed to prove they were co-owners of the property at the relevant time.
Mere appearance in the sale deed or financial transactions linked to the property does not establish ownership without proof of contribution from independent income.
The burden of proving ownership interest lies on the party claiming it, and failure to disclose sources of foreign remittances or gifts undermines such claims.
doctrines: Burden of proof
Independent source of income for establishing ownership
Relevance of documentary evidence and admissibility of interpolated entries

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the apportionment of compensation for land acquired by the Allahabad Development Authority, claiming entitlement to the full amount, while the authority contested the valuation of buildings and trees and sought modification of the award.
issues_decided: Whether the lessee was entitled to the entire compensation after the lease expired prior to acquisition.
How compensation should be apportioned between the lessee and the State Government for leased land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the valuation of the building and trees in the award was correct.
holdings: A lessee whose lease has expired cannot claim ownership and is not entitled to full compensation; leasehold rights are distinct from ownership.
Compensation for acquired leased land must be apportioned based on the lessee's remaining interest; here, 20% to the lessee and 80% to the State Government was appropriate.
The valuation of the building at Rs. 60,000 and trees as determined by the High Court was correct and based on proper assessment.
doctrines: Eminent domain
Apportionment of compensation between lessor and lessee
Determination of lease termination by efflux of time
Valuation principles for leasehold property under acquisition

card.dispute: The dispute was between family branches over whether a prior partition of joint family property had occurred, affecting the plaintiffs' claim for partition and separate possession of half the suit properties.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered partition deed (Exh. D-101) could be used to prove a prior partition among Hindu joint family members.
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the lower courts’ findings based solely on the inadmissibility of the unregistered deed without addressing other evidence of partition.
Whether severance of status and separate enjoyment of properties could be established without a registered document.
holdings: An unregistered document intended to be a formal record of partition declaring exclusive titles must be registered under Section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Registration Act to be admissible as evidence of partition.
Even if a partition deed is inadmissible, oral and documentary evidence of separate possession, independent management, and enjoyment of properties can prove prior partition and severance of status.

The High Court erred in reversing the lower courts’ concurrent findings without addressing substantial evidence supporting prior partition, as its jurisdiction in second appeal is limited to substantial questions of law.
doctrines: Severance of status in a Hindu joint family
Partition by metes and bounds
Concurrent findings in second appeal

card.dispute: The landlady, Amar Kaur, sought eviction of tenant Mukand Singh and his son Joginder Singh for sub-letting a shop without consent, which the son contested claiming he was always the intended occupant.
issues_decided: Whether sub-letting occurred without the landlord's written consent under the East Punjab Urban Rent Control Act, 1949
Whether the relationship between tenant and occupant (father-son) negates a finding of sub-tenancy
Whether the landlord waived her right to object to sub-letting by accepting rent and allowing possession
holdings: Exclusive possession by a third party, coupled with an unsatisfactory explanation from the tenant, permits an inference of sub-letting even without direct proof of monetary consideration.
The familial relationship between tenant and occupant is irrelevant; a son can be a sub-tenant if he is in exclusive possession without the landlord’s consent.
Waiver of the right to evict on grounds of sub-letting must be expressly pleaded and proved; it cannot be inferred, especially when statutory prohibitions exist.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Control Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(ii)(a)
doctrines: Inference of sub-letting from exclusive possession and unsatisfactory explanation
No privity between landlord and sub-tenant
Statutory compliance overrides implied waiver

card.dispute: The dispute was between a market committee and landowners over the compensation amount for land acquired for public purposes.
issues_decided: Whether market value for land acquisition can be determined based on stamp duty valuation fixed by authorities.
Whether a party can claim market value higher than the price stated in their own registered sale deed.
What is the correct method to determine market value and enhancement for delay in acquisition proceedings.
holdings: Market value under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 cannot be based on stamp duty valuation fixed by revenue authorities.
A party cannot claim a market value higher than the price in their own registered sale deed due to Section 92 of the Evidence Act.
Enhancement in market value must be calculated on the actual sale price from comparable deeds, with reasonable annual appreciation applied over the correct time period.
doctrines: Section 92 of the Evidence Act barring proof contrary to terms of a written document
Prohibition on using stamp duty valuation for determining market value in land acquisition
Principle of reasonable annual appreciation for delay in acquisition process

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside a Rent Control Tribunal's condition requiring the tenant to deposit Rs.15,000 per month during appeal, over and above the controlled rent, after an eviction order was passed.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court can impose terms requiring payment of an amount higher than the contractual rent during the pendency of an appeal against eviction?
Whether a tenant remains a tenant or becomes an unauthorized occupant after an eviction decree, pending appeal?
Whether the doctrine of merger postpones the date of termination of tenancy to the date of the appellate decree?
holdings: An appellate court has the equitable power to impose reasonable terms, including payment of mesne profits equivalent to market rent, when staying an eviction decree, to compensate the landlord for delayed possession.

Under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a tenant's tenancy terminates upon the passing of an eviction decree, and the tenant becomes an unauthorized occupant liable to pay compensation at market rates, not controlled rent, from that date.
The doctrine of merger does not postpone the date of termination of tenancy; the tenancy ends on the date of the original eviction decree, not when the appellate court confirms it.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 5
doctrines: Doctrine of mesne profits
Doctrine of merger
Equitable jurisdiction of appellate courts in stay orders

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant, a sole proprietorship turned partnership, alleging unlawful subletting under the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution abates due to the repeal of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 by the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1999
Whether conversion of a sole proprietary business into a partnership amounts to sub-letting under Section 21(1)(f) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961
holdings: The repeal of the 1961 Act does not cause the appeal under Article 136 to abate, as the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136 is not affected by the repeal of the statute under which the proceedings originated.

Conversion of a sole proprietary business into a partnership does not amount to sub-letting if the tenant remains actively involved and retains control and possession of the premises, and there is no evidence of parting with possession to strangers or using partnership as a cloak for sub-tenancy.
doctrines: Burden of proof in eviction cases for sub-letting
Sub-letting requires parting with legal possession
Rejection of corporate fiction in partnership tenancy cases
Survival of appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 despite repeal of enabling statute

card.dispute: M/S S.J.S. Business Enterprises (P) Ltd. challenged the sale of its mortgaged hotel by BICICO to respondent No. 6, alleging unfair and improper conduct in the sale process under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of the mortgaged property by BICICO under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 was conducted fairly and in accordance with law?
Whether the borrower's repayment efforts entitled it to judicial relief against the sale?
Whether the conduct of BICICO and respondent No. 6 indicated collusion or abuse of statutory power?
holdings: A sale under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act must be fair, reasonable, and aimed at securing the best price through maximum participation, requiring adequate publicity and time for bidders.
The sale was invalid due to inadequate notice, precipitate action, and unexplained circumstances suggesting unfairness and possible collusion.
A borrower who has made substantial repayments and shown willingness to settle cannot be treated as a mere defaulter undeserving of equitable relief.
doctrines: Principle of fairness in exercise of statutory powers
Doctrine of reasonableness under Article 226
Presumption of bona fide official action rebuttable by suspicious circumstances

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Meenakshiammal contested the validity of a will executed by Siva, claiming it was forged and executed under suspicious circumstances, while the defendants (beneficiaries) propounded the will.
issues_decided: Whether the will was executed by Siva in a sound disposing state of mind and without undue influence or fraud
Whether the propounder of the will discharged the burden of proving its due execution under the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Whether the allegations of forgery and suspicious circumstances were sufficient to invalidate the will
holdings: A will must be proved to be executed voluntarily by a testator in a sound disposing state of mind, with the burden initially on the propounder to establish due execution.
Suspicious circumstances require closer scrutiny, but mere suspicion or conjecture cannot override legally admissible and convincing evidence of a will's validity.
Once the propounder proves the testator’s competence and proper execution, the burden shifts to the contestant to prove fraud, undue influence, or forgery with evidence, not mere allegation.
The execution, attestation, and genuineness of the will were proved, and the lower court erred in holding it forged without evidence of fraud or coercion.
doctrines: Burden of proof in will propounding
Sound disposing mind
Suspicious circumstances doctrine
Presumption of due execution of will

card.dispute: The tenant, Nathi Devi, challenged the eviction order passed in favor of the landlord, Radha Devi Gupta, who sought possession of the premises under Section 14D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, as a widow requiring the premises for her personal residence.
issues_decided: Whether a widow who acquired tenanted premises by transfer can invoke Section 14D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for eviction of a pre-existing tenant?
Whether the expression 'let out by her, or by her husband' in Section 14D limits the applicability of the provision only to premises originally let out by the widow or her husband?
Whether the High Court erred in upholding the eviction order without considering the requirement of who originally let out the premises?
holdings: Section 14D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 applies only to a widow who herself let out the premises or whose husband originally let them out; it does not apply to a widow who acquired the property by transfer.
The phrase 'let out by her, or by her husband' is a necessary condition under Section 14D and cannot be read as merely referring to ownership; it restricts the benefit to a specific class of widows.
A harmonious construction of Sections 14(6) and 14D shows that a transferee landlord, including a widow, cannot bypass the five-year restriction on eviction by invoking Section 14D.
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Principle against redundancy in statutory language

card.dispute: The landlord, Parvinder Singh, sought eviction of tenants Renu Gautam and others from a shop in Shimla, alleging subletting and rent default under the H.P. Urban Rent Control Act, 1987.
issues_decided: Whether the heirs of a deceased tenant can be evicted for subletting done by the original tenant?
Whether a partnership deed can mask a prohibited subletting under rent control law?
Whether the law laid down in A.S. Sulochana v. C. Dharmalingam applies to eviction proceedings under other rent control statutes?
holdings: Successors-in-interest of a tenant inherit both the rights and obligations of the deceased tenant and can be evicted for subletting done during the original tenancy.
A partnership deed does not automatically prevent a finding of subletting; courts may look beyond the document to determine if possession was effectively transferred.

The decision in A.S. Sulochana v. C. Dharmalingam is overruled to the extent it requires the subletting act to be committed by the current tenant, and it does not bind interpretation of other rent control laws.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, Section 14(2)(ii)(a)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(ii)(a)
doctrines: Strict construction of penal provisions in rent control laws
Successor-in-interest doctrine in tenancy law
Piercing the veil of partnership to uncover fraudulent subletting
Admissibility of oral evidence to prove the true nature of a transaction despite a written deed

card.dispute: The landowners and the Union of India disputed the fair market value of agricultural land acquired for public use, following a change in land use from agricultural to commercial in the master plan.
issues_decided: What was the fair market value of the acquired land as on the date of the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether the change in the master plan from agricultural to commercial use affected the market value of the land despite no actual commercial use?
Whether escalation in land value should be calculated progressively or at a flat rate over time?
holdings: The fair market value of the land must reflect its potential use as indicated in the master plan, even if no actual commercial development had occurred by the date of notification.
A change in land use classification from agricultural to commercial imparts commercial potentiality, justifying a higher market value than purely agricultural land.
Progressive annual escalation in land value at 10% from 1963 to 1973 and 12% thereafter is a reasonable method to determine fair market value in the absence of concrete market evidence.
provisions: Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, Sections 22 and 23
doctrines: Principle of fair market value in land acquisition
Escalation of land value over time based on potential use
Rejection of flat-rate escalation in favor of progressive appreciation
Consideration of master plan changes in valuation despite no physical change in land use

card.dispute: The dispute was between tenants and their landlord over eviction orders sought by the landlord on grounds of bona fide need to demolish and reconstruct the rented premises under the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to re-appreciate evidence in revision under the Karnataka Rent Control Act?
Whether the landlord proved bona fide requirement for demolition and reconstruction of the building?
Whether the tenants would suffer comparative hardship if evicted?
Whether the finding of the Rent Controller could be interfered with by the High Court in revision?
holdings: The High Court has wide revisional powers under Section 50 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act to re-appreciate evidence and examine the legality and correctness of orders, including findings of fact.

A landlord need not prove that the building is dilapidated or dangerous; the age, condition, financial capacity, and bona fides must be collectively assessed for demolition and reconstruction under Section 14(1)(b).
Eviction does not cause undue hardship to tenants when alternative accommodation is available and the landlord has no suitable alternative, especially in a developing urban area.
The High Court can interfere with findings of the Rent Controller if they are perverse, against the weight of evidence, or result in miscarriage of justice.
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for demolition and reconstruction
Comparative hardship in eviction cases
Revisional jurisdiction beyond error of law
Judicial review of rent control orders on factual findings

card.dispute: Palitana Sugar Mills and the State of Gujarat fought over the ownership and development rights of 952 acres of land in Vadva village, previously owned by the former ruler of Bhavnagar, involving agricultural and urban land ceiling laws.
issues_decided: Whether the land in question was excluded from the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act, 1960 as 'bid land'.
Whether the mutation and title entries in favour of the appellants were final and binding.
Whether the State could reopen concluded proceedings to challenge the validity of the sale deed and mutation.
Whether the appellants were entitled to non-agricultural permission and planning sanctions for development.
holdings: Pasture land (bid land) not fit for cultivation is excluded from the purview of the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act, 1960, and cannot be subjected to ceiling proceedings.
Mutation and title entries in favour of the appellants, confirmed by multiple judicial and revenue authorities, are final and cannot be reopened.
The State cannot initiate fresh proceedings to challenge matters already concluded by final orders of the Tribunal, High Court, and Supreme Court.
The appellants are entitled to non-agricultural permission and planning sanctions for the land, subject to payment of applicable charges as per the law at the time of application.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 21(1)
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976
doctrines: Finality of judicial and administrative orders
Res judicata in revenue and land matters
Doctrine of merger of orders
Principle against re-agitation of concluded litigation

card.dispute: The defendants appealed against the High Court's decision to remand the case for reconsideration of an application for stay under Section 10 CPC, after the trial court dismissed a suit for specific performance of a property sale agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court was obligated to decide the application under Section 10 CPC before deciding the merits of the suit?
Whether the suit for specific performance was barred by limitation?
Whether the plaintiff had averred and proved readiness and willingness to perform the contract as required under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act?
holdings: A court is not bound to decide an application under Section 10 CPC before adjudicating on the merits; it may proceed if the suit is clearly barred by limitation or lacks substantive merit.

The suit for specific performance was barred by limitation under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, as more than three years had elapsed and the plaintiff had notice of refusal long before filing the suit.

The plaintiff failed to establish readiness and willingness to perform the contract under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, especially after rescinding the agreement and suing for refund of advance.
doctrines: Res judicata and bar of limitation
Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Procedural vs. substantive justice
Court's discretion in case management under CPC

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the decree of specific performance of an agreement for sale of property, seeking to avoid transfer despite part performance and payments by the respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement for sale was enforceable despite the lapse of time and part performance?
Whether specific performance could be granted when the defendant accepted part payments and later sought to avoid the contract due to escalation in property value?
Whether the court could direct payment of additional compensation to the defendant while decreeing specific performance?
holdings: An agreement for sale can be specifically enforced if the plaintiff has performed or is ready to perform their part, and the defendant has accepted part payments without objection.
Mere escalation in property prices does not justify refusal of specific performance, especially when the defendant caused delay or accepted payments under the agreement.
Courts may, in equity, direct the plaintiff to pay additional compensation to balance hardships, but cannot condition specific performance on such payment if it effectively negates the decree.
doctrines: Balance of equities
Part performance under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act
No party can take advantage of their own wrong

card.dispute: The appellant and others challenged the state's action to remove unauthorized constructions on agricultural and common village land near scheduled roads, arguing lack of proper notice and invalidity of the controlled area declaration.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration of a controlled area under Section 4(1) of the Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction on Unregulated Development Act, 1963 becomes effective without publication in two non-English newspapers as required under Section 4(2)?
Whether the appellants were denied natural justice due to improper service of notices?
Whether unauthorized constructions on agricultural or village common land adjacent to scheduled roads could be lawfully removed under the Act?
holdings: The declaration of a controlled area under Section 4(1) becomes effective upon notification in the Gazette, and subsequent publication in two non-English newspapers under Section 4(2) is not mandatory for its enforceability.
The appellants were not denied natural justice, as they had knowledge of the notices and filed objections; alternative service by affixture was valid after attempts by post.

Unauthorized constructions in violation of Section 3(1) of the Act, especially on agricultural or common village land without permission, are illegal and subject to removal to protect public safety and orderly development.
provisions: Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction on Unregulated Development Act, 1963, Section 3(1)
Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction on Unregulated Development Act, 1963, Section 4(1)
Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction on Unregulated Development Act, 1963, Section 4(2)
Punjab Village Common Land (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 5
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Rules, 1964, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of effective notification
Doctrine of public interest over private interest
Principle of natural justice
Doctrine of statutory compliance for land use

card.dispute: The appellant claimed possession of agricultural land based on a chain of unregistered sale agreements, while the respondent, the original owner, sued for recovery of possession after being dispossessed.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of part performance under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act can be invoked by a person who has no direct agreement with the transferor?
Whether a purchaser from a transferee under an unregistered sale agreement can claim protection under Section 53-A against the original owner?
holdings: The doctrine of part performance under Section 53-A can only be invoked by a transferee who has a direct agreement with the transferor and cannot be extended to a subsequent purchaser from such transferee.
A person who is not a party to the agreement of sale and has no privity of contract with the transferor cannot claim protection under Section 53-A against the original owner, even if in possession.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Privity of contract
Equitable estoppel

card.dispute: The appellants, family members of the deceased's husband, were convicted of abetment to suicide and cruelty under IPC; they challenged the conviction, arguing lack of evidence and erroneous reliance on unproven circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the charge of abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC?
Whether the prosecution established cruelty under Section 498A IPC?
Whether the trial and appellate courts properly evaluated the evidence independently?
Whether the circumstances relied upon by the trial court were legally sufficient to sustain conviction?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove abetment of suicide as the alleged dowry demands and harassment were not substantiated by credible evidence.
The conviction under Section 498A IPC cannot be sustained due to lack of reliable evidence of cruelty or harassment by the accused.
The High Court failed to independently assess evidence, merely paraphrasing the trial court, thus not fulfilling its appellate duty.
Circumstances like non-attendance at funeral or prolonged stay at maternal home do not indicate guilt when explained by context and documentary evidence.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Independent evaluation of evidence by appellate courts
Corroboration of circumstantial evidence
Presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The legal heirs of R.L. Jain contested whether they were entitled to interest on compensation for a land acquisition where possession was taken before the issuance of the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether a claimant is entitled to interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act for the period prior to the notification under Section 4(1) when possession was taken earlier.
Whether the claimant is entitled to additional compensation at 12% per annum under Section 23(1A) for the period before the Section 4(1) notification when possession was taken earlier.
Whether equitable principles entitle the claimant to further compensation or interest despite prior receipt of compensation and successful challenge to earlier acquisition.
holdings: Interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act cannot be claimed for the period before the notification under Section 4(1); it runs only from when compensation becomes payable, typically from the date of award.

No additional amount at 12% per annum under Section 23(1A) is payable for the period prior to the Section 4(1) notification if possession was taken earlier; entitlement begins only from the date of notification or possession, whichever is earlier.
A landowner who received compensation, challenged prior acquisition successfully, and was later re-compensated is not entitled to further interest or compensation on equitable grounds.
doctrines: Equitable compensation
Interest on delayed compensation
Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Binding effect of decree

card.dispute: Tenants of a temple trust challenged the rejection of their suit seeking declaration of tenancy and injunction against eviction, while the trust argued the suit required prior consent under charity law.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint was liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC due to reliefs beyond the civil court's jurisdiction
Whether Sections 50 and 51 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act bar a tenant's suit for tenancy rights
Whether a tenant in unlawful possession can claim injunction against the trust
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the tenancy dispute
holdings: A plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC merely because some reliefs are not maintainable; separable reliefs within civil court jurisdiction must be allowed to proceed.
Sections 50 and 51 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act do not apply to tenancy disputes, as tenants are not 'persons interested in the trust' under the Act.
A person in unlawful possession cannot obtain an injunction against the rightful owner, as courts will not protect wrongful possession.
The civil court has jurisdiction to decide tenancy issues even when the property belongs to a public trust, unless the suit falls squarely under the Trust Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 1
doctrines: Separability of reliefs in a plaint
Jurisdictional bar under special statutes
Injunction not available to wrongful possessors
Protection of settled possession under Section 6, Specific Relief Act

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of Singer India Limited from rented premises, alleging unauthorized subletting by the original tenant, an American company, to an Indian company.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of possession from the American company to the Indian company amounted to subletting or parting with possession under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act
Whether the corporate veil could be lifted to show continuity of identity between the American and Indian companies
Whether the appellant could rely on its own corporate restructuring under FERA to deny liability under the Rent Control Act
holdings: The transfer of possession to the Indian company without landlord's consent constituted parting with possession under Section 14(1)(b), making eviction lawful.
The corporate veil cannot be lifted at the instance of a company to establish identity with another entity; the principle applies only to prevent fraud or injustice.
A company cannot claim to be non-existent for FERA purposes while asserting its separate legal existence under rent control law; such dual positions are inconsistent.
provisions: Esso (Acquisition of Undertakings in India) Act, 1974, Section 5
doctrines: Lifting of the corporate veil
Doctrine of separate legal entity
Prohibition against inconsistent legal positions (approbate and reprobate)

card.dispute: The Printers (Mysore) Ltd. challenged the High Court's decision to invalidate its 1985 allotment of land by the Bangalore Development Authority, which was contested by M.A. Rasheed in a public interest litigation on grounds of illegality and public policy.
issues_decided: Whether the allotment of 1 acre 20 guntas of land by the Bangalore Development Authority to the appellant was a 'bulk allotment' within the meaning of Section 38-B of the Bangalore Development Authority Act?
Whether the High Court erred in allowing a public interest litigation challenging the sale deed after a delay of three years?
Whether the High Court incorrectly applied the doctrine of separation of powers by interfering with executive functions of the Authority?
holdings: The allotment of 1 acre 20 guntas for industrial purposes does not constitute a bulk transfer under Section 38-B, and thus the transaction is valid under the Act.
The public interest litigation was barred by delay and laches, and the High Court should have dismissed it on those grounds.
Courts must exercise self-restraint in matters of policy and administration, intervening only when there is a violation of statutory or constitutional provisions or principles of natural justice.
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers
Judicial self-restraint in public interest litigation
Principle of delay and laches
Interpretation of 'subject to' in statutory provisions

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision quashing the land acquisition notification for 14 properties, arguing that the urgency clause under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act was validly invoked, while landowners and tenants contested the legality of the acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was vitiated due to non-mention of urgency and lack of material justifying urgency
Whether the High Court could appoint an arbitrator to determine compensation in a writ petition despite no agreement or specific prayer
Whether the acquisition notification could be partially sustained under Section 4 of the Act if invalid under Section 17
Whether tenants had locus standi to challenge the acquisition proceedings
holdings: A notification under Section 17 need not explicitly state the reason for urgency; however, there must be material on record showing genuine urgency arising from circumstances, not administrative delay.

The High Court has the power to appoint an arbitrator to determine compensation in writ petitions to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, especially when this Court has upheld such appointments in similar cases.
If a common acquisition notification is invalidated due to improper invocation of Section 17, it cannot be partially sustained under Section 4, as that would create an anomalous and unjust result.
A tenant with a subsisting interest in the land may challenge acquisition proceedings if entitled to claim compensation under Section 5A(3) of the Act.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
doctrines: Doctrine of Locus Standi in Public Interest Litigation
Doctrine of Consistency in Judicial Precedent
Doctrine against Partial Invalidity creating Anomalous Results
Doctrine of Urgency in Land Acquisition

card.dispute: The owner of a property in Lucknow fought against tenants who were allotted possession under rent control law after the property was declared vacant, challenging the validity of the allotment and seeking rent during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether an order declaring vacancy under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings Act can be challenged in revision against the final allotment order without a prior independent challenge?
Whether the failure to immediately challenge the vacancy order bars a later challenge to the allotment order?
What interim measures should be imposed on tenants occupying the property during prolonged litigation?
holdings: An order declaring vacancy under the UP Urban Buildings Act can be challenged in a revision petition against the final allotment order; a prior independent challenge is not mandatory.

The aggrieved party has two options: challenge the vacancy order immediately via writ or challenge it in revision against the allotment order; the failure to take the first route does not preclude the second.
Tenants occupying property during long-pending litigation must make provisional rent payments as a condition to continue contesting the case, to prevent unjust enrichment.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 8(2)
doctrines: Election of remedies
Mesne profits
Principles of natural justice in administrative orders

card.dispute: The appellants claimed ownership and possession of ancestral land against respondents who claimed title by adverse possession and contended the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants became owners of the suit land only upon the 1965 partition, thereby affecting the limitation period for adverse possession?
Whether the respondents established all necessary elements to prove adverse possession?
holdings: The appellants did not acquire a new title through the 1965 partition; their antecedent title as co-sharers meant adverse possession ran from when respondents' possession became hostile, not from the partition date.

The respondents proved adverse possession by demonstrating long, continuous, open, and exclusive possession since at least 1935 or 1941, supported by revenue payments, official records, and panchayat permission for construction.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Spes successionis
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with by higher courts
Partition as severance of joint enjoyment, not creation of new title

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against the Delhi High Court's decision that the Lt. Governor's order dispensing with the Section 5A inquiry in land acquisition for a festival was invalid due to non-application of mind.
issues_decided: Whether the appropriate government must independently apply its mind before dispensing with the inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, even if urgency exists under Section 17(1) or Section 17(2).
Whether the Lt. Governor applied his mind to the facts while ordering the dispensation of the Section 5A inquiry in this case.
holdings: The appropriate government must independently apply its mind to justify dispensing with the Section 5A inquiry; it is not automatic even if urgency under Section 17(1) or unforeseen emergency under Section 17(2) exists.

The Lt. Governor failed to apply his mind as he was not informed of relevant facts, including a prior lapsed acquisition for the same purpose, rendering the order to dispense with Section 5A inquiry invalid.
doctrines: Non-application of mind
Substantive due process
Statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The landlords sought an order directing the tenant to pay mesne profits during the stay of an eviction decree, based on current market rent rather than the contractual rent.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can be required to pay mesne profits at market rate during the stay of an eviction decree?
What is the appropriate rate of mesne profits to be paid during the pendency of an appeal against eviction?
holdings: A tenant liable under a decree for eviction may be required to pay mesne profits at a rate reflecting current market rent, not the old contractual rent, as a condition for staying execution of the decree.
The court may set a reasonable rate for mesne profits based on comparable rents in the locality, subject to final determination by a competent forum upon conclusion of the appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX, Rule 12
doctrines: Mesne profits during stay of eviction decree
Compensation for use and occupation of property
Court's power to impose conditions for stay

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement for sale of property, while the defendant claimed the agreement was only a security and that the plaintiff failed to plead readiness and willingness as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff's pleadings sufficiently averred readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Whether strict compliance with particular wording in the plaint is required to satisfy Section 16(c), or whether substance over form applies.
holdings: The plaint must aver readiness and willingness to perform the contract, but no specific phraseology is required; the substance of the averment is what matters.
Courts must examine the pith and substance of the pleadings as a whole to determine if the plaintiff has met the requirement of Section 16(c), not insist on mechanical use of statutory words.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, First Schedule, Forms 47 and 48
doctrines: Substance over form in pleadings
Personal bar under specific performance
Readiness and willingness as a continuous state

card.dispute: The heirs of Sir Datar Singh fought over whether a 1993 consent decree settling partition suits was valid, with some challenging the decree on grounds of non-registration, lack of procedural compliance, and alleged fraud.
issues_decided: Whether the consent decree dated 25th August 1993 was validly passed under Order XXIII Rule 3 of the CPC despite staggered recording of agreements.
Whether the agreements leading to the consent decree required registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908.
Whether the non-joinder of the appellants in the third agreement and non-application under Order 22 Rule 10 invalidated the decree.
Whether the decree could be set aside on grounds of fraud or non-payment of dues under the compromise.
holdings: A consent decree under Order XXIII Rule 3 is valid if the court records satisfaction and the compromise, even if agreements are recorded at different times.
Family arrangement and composition deeds, including those merged in a court decree, are exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(i) and (vi) of the Registration Act, 1908.
An assignee need not apply under Order 22 Rule 10 to continue a suit if the suit is being concluded by compromise, and the assignor is aware of the assignment.
Mere non-payment of compromise amounts does not amount to fraud or justify setting aside a decree, especially when parties have benefited under the arrangement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10
doctrines: Family arrangement doctrine
Doctrine of merger of agreement into decree
Presumption of judicial compliance with Order XXIII Rule 3
Judicial reluctance to disturb compromises on technical grounds

card.dispute: Tenants challenged eviction decrees granted to non-resident Indian landlords under Section 13-B of The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, claiming the evictions were not justified or maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord qualifies as a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) under Section 2(dd) of The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Whether a single ejectment petition for both residential and non-residential tenanted premises is maintainable
Whether the landlord's requirement of the premises for personal use or reconstruction is bona fide and sufficient under Section 13-B
Whether the landlord must personally file the petition or can do so through an attorney
holdings: A person born in India but residing abroad with foreign citizenship qualifies as an NRI under Section 2(dd) of the Act, even if holding a foreign passport.
A joint ejectment petition for residential and non-residential premises under a single tenancy is maintainable if the premises were let out as a composite unit.
The landlord's bona fide requirement for reoccupation or reconstruction of the building satisfies Section 13-B, provided statutory conditions are met.
An NRI landlord may file an ejectment petition through an attorney; personal presence is not mandatory under Section 13-B.
provisions: The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 2(dd)
The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13-B
doctrines: Burden of proof on tenant to rebut presumption of bona fide need
Statutory interpretation of 'Non-Resident Indian' in rent control laws
Maintainability of composite ejectment proceedings
Agency in filing legal proceedings by non-resident parties

card.dispute: A deserted wife contested eviction proceedings initiated against her husband, the tenant, seeking to protect her right to reside in the matrimonial home, which was a tenanted property.
issues_decided: Whether a deserted wife has the right to contest eviction proceedings against her husband in respect of the matrimonial home.
Whether a divorced wife can continue to claim residence in a tenanted matrimonial home after dissolution of marriage.
Whether the wife could be permitted to defend the eviction suit and appeal the matter despite no privity of contract with the landlord.
holdings: A deserted wife in occupation of the matrimonial home can contest eviction proceedings if the husband has abandoned the defence and her right to residence as part of maintenance is still intact.
A divorced wife’s right to reside in the tenanted premises ends with the dissolution of marriage unless the divorce decree specifically provides for continued residence as part of maintenance.
The wife could be joined as a party and allowed to defend the eviction suit and appeal, but her right to continue depends on the terms of the divorce decree, which were not produced.
doctrines: Right to residence as part of maintenance
Gender justice and equitable relief under Article 142
Privity of contract in landlord-tenant law
Succession of tenancy rights by analogy to heirs or sub-tenants

card.dispute: The Bombay Environmental Action Group challenged the development of surplus mill lands in Mumbai under the DCR 1991, arguing environmental and public interest concerns, while mill owners like Bombay Dyeing sought to develop the land under BIFR rehabilitation schemes.
issues_decided: Whether interim relief should be granted to halt development of mill lands pending final disposal of the writ petition.
Whether delay in filing the public interest litigation affects the grant of interim relief.
Whether transactions under BIFR-approved schemes can proceed despite ongoing litigation.
Whether statutory authorities must comply with planning regulations when processing development applications.
holdings: Interim relief halting development would effectively decide the final outcome and cause irreparable harm; thus, it should not be granted absent extreme hardship.
Unexplained delay in filing PIL weakens the claim for interim relief, especially where third-party rights and significant investments are involved.
Transactions under BIFR schemes may proceed subject to conditions, including potential land adjustment if the petition succeeds.

Statutory authorities must process development applications strictly according to law, and any construction or third-party rights created are at the proponents' risk and subject to final court orders.
doctrines: Balance of convenience in granting interim relief
Irreparable injury and conscience of the court doctrine
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) and delay defeating equity
Interim relief amounting to final relief in rare and exceptional cases

card.dispute: The Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) appealed against a High Court direction to re-convey acquired land to R. Hanumaiah and allot alternative plots to others, following alleged government directions.
issues_decided: Whether the BDA was legally bound to re-convey acquired land to the respondent upon directions from the Chief Minister.
Whether the Government had the power under the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 to direct re-conveyance of land already acquired and possessed.
Whether the promise or direction to re-convey land was consistent with the purpose and provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the BDA Act, 1976.
Whether the respondent was entitled to equitable relief in the form of compensation with interest despite withdrawal of reference petitions.
holdings: The BDA is not bound to re-convey land based on executive directions that contradict the statutory purpose of urban development under the BDA Act, 1976.
The Government cannot issue directions under Section 65 of the BDA Act that are contrary to the Act’s objectives or that destroy the legislative purpose of land acquisition.

Once possession is taken under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, neither the State nor the BDA can re-convey the land to the original owner, as Section 48 restricts such power to cases where possession was not taken.
Equity permits payment of enhanced compensation with interest @ 9% (12% for delay) to the landowner who withdrew reference petitions, but re-conveyance is not permissible in law.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on objective language of orders
Principle that statutory authorities must act in furtherance of legislative purpose
Doctrine of equitable compensation when re-conveyance is legally impermissible
Non-justiciability of executive directions contrary to statutory scheme

card.dispute: Brij Pal Sharma challenged the Ghaziabad Development Authority's failure to allot him plots under two housing schemes, seeking either possession or alternative allotment, while the Authority had refunded amounts with interest.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to specific allotment of a plot instead of refund with interest under the Karpoori Puram Scheme
Whether the appellant could claim both specific performance and compensation at 18% interest under the Govindpuram Scheme
holdings: Where a housing scheme is cancelled and monies are refunded, awarding interest at 18% per annum as compensation is just and fair, irrespective of the reason for cancellation.
An allottee cannot claim both specific performance of plot allotment and compensation via interest; the grant of 18% interest constitutes full compensation for non-allotment.
doctrines: Legitimate expectation
Public interest vs private interest
Compensation for breach of statutory duty

card.dispute: The tenant of a petrol bunk site sought to renew his licence under the Petroleum Rules, but the landlord opposed it after the lease expired, leading to a dispute over whether the tenant had a lawful 'right to the site' and whether he became a statutory tenant under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant-tenant became a statutory tenant entitled to protection under the Pondicherry Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1969 after the lease expired
Whether acceptance of increased rent by the landlord after lease expiry created a new tenancy under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the appellant had a 'right to the site' within the meaning of Rule 153(1)(i) of the Petroleum Rules, 1976 to renew his licence
Whether the landlord was estopped from challenging the tenant's right due to prior conduct, including withdrawal of an eviction suit
holdings: The appellant did not become a statutory tenant because the lease was for vacant land not covered by the Pondicherry Rent Control Act, and no statutory tenancy arose upon lease expiry.

Acceptance of rent after lease expiry, even at increased rates, does not create a new tenancy under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act when the tenant holds over without landlord's assent, especially in the absence of rent control protection.
The 'right to the site' under Rule 153(1)(i) of the Petroleum Rules requires a lawful right, not mere possession; continued occupation after lease expiry does not confer such a right.
Withdrawal of an eviction suit with liberty to file again does not amount to landlord's assent to continued tenancy or create a lawful right in the tenant.
provisions: Pondicherry Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1969
doctrines: Statutory tenancy under rent control laws
Holding over without assent does not create tenancy
Lawful right vs. mere possession
Estoppel by conduct in landlord-tenant relationship

card.dispute: The Church of North India challenged the maintainability of a civil suit filed by respondents over trust property, questioning whether civil court jurisdiction was barred under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit given the provisions of Section 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950?
Whether the dispute pertained to matters within the exclusive domain of the Charity Commissioner under the Act?
Whether the nature of the reliefs claimed fell within the administrative or possessory aspects of trust property?
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction when the dispute concerns questions within the exclusive authority of the Charity Commissioner under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
Section 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act bars civil court jurisdiction if the lis involves administration, possession, or title to trust property.
Where statutory remedies under the Act are complete and adequate, civil courts cannot entertain suits on the same subject matter.
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction by statute
Doctrine of plenary statutory remedy
Adjudicatory powers of statutory authorities

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of joint tenants on grounds of tenancy admission and rent exceeding Rs. 3500, while tenants contested the maintainability of the eviction application and claimed individual tenancies to fall under rent control protections.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy was a joint/composite tenancy or individual tenancies.
Whether an application under Order XII Rule 6 of the CPC was maintainable based on admissions in the lease deed.
Whether the unregistered lease deed could be relied upon for eviction when no term was prescribed.
holdings: The lease deed executed in favor of four brothers jointly created a composite and joint tenancy, not individual tenancies, as the rent was stipulated as a single amount for the entire premises.
An application under Order XII Rule 6 CPC is maintainable where there is a clear admission of facts, such as joint tenancy and rent exceeding Rs. 3500, allowing for a decree without full trial.
The non-registration of a lease deed that does not prescribe a term does not invalidate reliance on it for eviction under Order XII Rule 6 CPC, especially when the objection was raised belatedly.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XII Rule 6
Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 6A read with Section 8
doctrines: Admission of facts in pleadings or documents allows for summary disposal under Order XII Rule 6 CPC
Composite tenancy doctrine: joint tenancy cannot be split to bring it within rent control exemptions
Principle of judicial economy: courts may act on clear admissions to expedite justice

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments fought against P. Shanmugama and others over whether certain properties belonged to a religious institution (Mela Madam) or were private ancestral properties subject to partition.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to hear the second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC without framing a substantial question of law
Whether the suit properties were private ancestral properties entitled to partition or properties belonging to the Mela Madam religious institution
Whether the plaintiff was estopped from claiming the properties as private given prior conduct and records
holdings: The High Court lacked jurisdiction because it failed to frame a substantial question of law as required by Section 100(4) and (5) of the CPC before entertaining the second appeal.
The properties in question were rightfully treated as belonging to the Mela Madam based on consistent documentary and oral evidence over more than a century, and no valid oral partition was proved.

The plaintiff and his family were estopped from claiming the properties as private due to their long-standing recognition of the properties as belonging to the religious institution, including statutory record-keeping under the Tamil Nadu Act.
provisions: Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, Section 63(a)
Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 108
doctrines: Substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC
Estoppel by conduct
Appreciation of evidence in second appeals

card.dispute: The appellant's legal heirs sued for specific performance of an alleged oral sale agreement for a property, while the respondents filed a counter-claim for eviction, leading to a dispute over jurisdiction and the validity of the agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the respondents' counter-claim for eviction under the A.P. Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1963?
Whether the appellant was entitled to specific performance of an alleged oral agreement of sale?
Whether the principle of approbate and reprobate applied to bar the respondents from pursuing eviction after the appellant denied tenancy?
holdings: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the eviction counter-claim as the A.P. Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1963, bars civil courts from adjudicating eviction matters except under specific provisos.
The suit for specific performance of the alleged oral sale agreement was rightly dismissed due to lack of enforceability and insufficient evidence to prove the agreement's existence.
The doctrine of approbate and reprobate does not apply here because the appellant did not gain any advantage by denying tenancy, and no final finding on jurisdiction was made by the Rent Controller.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1963, Section 10(1) and proviso to Section 10(2)(vi)
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional bar under special statutes
Doctrine of approbate and reprobate
Nullity of orders passed without jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) fought to execute a decree for eviction against the respondent (tenant) who resisted possession despite multiple judicial affirmations of the eviction order.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a revision petition under Section 115 CPC against an interlocutory order in execution proceedings?
Whether the respondent could raise fresh pleas of fraud and lack of landlord-tenant relationship after they were conclusively decided in the eviction decree?
Whether the execution of the eviction decree should be stayed to preserve the efficacy of a subsequent civil suit alleging fraud?
holdings: An interlocutory order in execution proceedings, which does not finally decide the lis, is not maintainable in revision under Section 115 CPC after its amendment.
Pleas of fraud and denial of landlord-tenant relationship, not raised during trial, cannot be permitted to reopen issues already concluded by a final decree.
The High Court erred in staying execution of the decree on grounds of a pending civil suit, especially when the suit failed to make out a prima facie case of fraud.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXXIX Rule 1 & 2
doctrines: Res judicata
Fraud unravels all (but must be pleaded and proved)
Finality of decree in execution
Prohibition of re-agitation of decided issues in execution

card.dispute: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. contested the validity of a land acquisition process initiated by the state, challenging whether proper application of mind and due procedure were followed in issuing a declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the state government's declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, without recording reasons, is valid when challenged in court.
Whether the state government applied its mind to the objections of the landowner and the collector's report before confirming the acquisition.
Whether a counter-affidavit filed by a Collector or a Special Deputy Collector can suffice to justify the state government's decision in court.
holdings: A declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, need not contain reasons on its face, but the government must produce the record to show the basis of its satisfaction when challenged in court.
The state government must independently apply its mind to the landowner's objections and the Collector’s report; failure to do so renders the acquisition process legally infirm.

A counter-affidavit by a Collector or an unauthorized officer does not satisfy the requirement of justifying the state government’s decision; only a competent state authority can affirm such an affidavit.
doctrines: Principle of objective decision-making in administrative action
Doctrine of reasoned decision in administrative law
Rule of strict construction of expropriatory legislation

card.dispute: Haryana Urban Development Authority challenged the National Commission's order directing it to pay Rs. 2 lakhs compensation to B.K. Sood for alleged service deficiencies in allotting a booth site.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent's complaint before the State Consumer Commission was barred by limitation under Section 24-A of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986?
Whether the National Commission was justified in awarding Rs. 2 lakhs as compensation for deficiency in service, particularly regarding the removal of bhatties?
Whether the National Commission properly evaluated the factual basis for its finding of service deficiency?
holdings: The complaint was barred by limitation as it was filed in 1997, well beyond the two-year period from the cause of action arising in 1987, and no request for condonation of delay was made.

The award of Rs. 2 lakhs compensation was not justified because the alleged deficiency (presence of bhatties) had ceased in 1994, prior to the filing of the complaint, and no fresh cause of action arose during the pendency of the appeal.

The National Commission erred in fact by stating that the bhatties were removed during the appeal, when records showed they were removed in 1994, making the basis for compensation factually incorrect.
doctrines: Limitation bar under consumer law
Requirement of sufficient cause for delay in filing consumer complaints
Factual accuracy in findings supporting compensation awards

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for unauthorized change of user of the premises and for committing acts of waste by making structural alterations and installing electrical connections.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's use of the premises for selling readymade garments, in addition to shoes and leather goods, constituted a change of user under Section 10(2)(ii)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.

Whether the tenant's installation of signboards, racks, and electrical connections amounted to acts of waste likely to materially impair the value or utility of the building under Section 10(2)(iii) of the Act.
holdings: A tenant's expansion of business to include related goods, without altering the fundamental nature of the permitted use, does not constitute a change of user justifying eviction under Section 10(2)(ii)(b).

Mere installation of signboards, racks, or electrical fixtures for trade purposes, without structural damage or material impairment to the building, does not amount to actionable waste under Section 10(2)(iii).
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(ii)(b)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(iii)
doctrines: Beneficial interpretation of rent control legislation in favor of tenants
Material impairment test for acts of waste in tenancy law

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the High Court's reversal of its earlier order granting them 12% interest on compensation for land taken without formal acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could revisit the issue of granting 12% interest after having already decided it in earlier writ proceedings?
Whether the principle of res judicata or issue estoppel applies to writ orders directing payment of interest in land acquisition cases?
Whether the High Court could raise a new ground not pleaded by the parties while reviewing its earlier decision?
holdings: Once a High Court decides a matter in writ proceedings, it cannot later revisit the same issue if it constitutes a final determination between the parties on that point.
The principles of res judicata and issue estoppel apply to writ proceedings, particularly when the same parties and issues are involved, preventing re-litigation of decided questions.
A court cannot base its decision on a ground not pleaded by the parties, as it would amount to deciding a case not framed by the pleadings, violating principles of fair procedure.
doctrines: Res judicata
Issue estoppel
Cause of action estoppel
Principle of finality of judicial orders
Plea of parties must conform to pleadings

card.dispute: Jaipur Municipal Corporation challenged the High Court's dismissal of its review petition seeking to review an interim order in contempt proceedings related to alleged encroachment by a temple on public park land.
issues_decided: Whether the Jaipur Municipal Corporation could maintain a review petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to review an interim order in a contempt proceeding after the contempt petition was withdrawn?
Whether the interim order dated 24.7.2001 in the contempt petition survived the withdrawal and dismissal of the contempt petition itself?
holdings: A review petition cannot be maintained to challenge an interim order in a contempt proceeding when the main contempt petition has been withdrawn and dismissed, as interim orders merge with the final order and cannot survive independently.
Once a contempt petition is withdrawn and dismissed with liberty to file afresh, prior interim orders cease to operate, leaving no effective order in force for review.
doctrines: Merger of interim orders into final judgment
Maintainability of review petitions
Nature of contempt proceedings as proceedings between court and contemnor

card.dispute: The landlords, Kailash Chand and Nokha Ram, fought to evict tenant Dharam Dass from a rented property in Shimla, claiming need for their own occupation, which the High Court blocked, prompting a Supreme Court appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the landlords had a bona fide requirement of the premises for their own occupation under Section 14(3)(a)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987
Whether the second proviso to Section 14(3)(a) barred the eviction because the landlords had vacated another residential building within five years
Whether the requirement for 'his own occupation' includes family members of the landlord
holdings: The landlords established a genuine and bona fide need for the premises for their family's residence, which qualifies as 'own occupation' under the Act.
The second proviso barring eviction does not apply unless the tenant proves the landlord vacated a residential building mala fide; no such proof was adduced here.
The phrase 'his own occupation' includes the residential needs of the landlord's family, interpreted liberally in light of socio-cultural realities.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, Section 14(3)(a)(i)
Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, Second Proviso to Section 14(3)(a)
