Public sports facilities must remain accessible to all and not be restricted exclusively to club members, ensuring primacy of sports over commercial interests.
The matter requires remand to the High Court to decide on cancellation of the lease and to issue directions for preventing misuse of public sports facilities.
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Principle of Accountability in Public Administration
Right to Equality and Non-Discrimination
Sustainable Development of Sports Infrastructure

card.dispute: The appellants, borrowers and guarantors, challenged the State Bank of India's enforcement of security interest and dispossession of their property under the SARFAESI Act, claiming lack of proper notice and illegal action, while the bank asserted its right to recover dues.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution when an alternative remedy under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act was available?
Whether actions taken under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act fall within the scope of appealable measures under Section 17 of the Act?
Whether the Debts Recovery Tribunal has jurisdiction to adjudicate on post-Section 13(4) actions including dispossession and transfer of secured assets?
holdings: The High Court correctly refused to entertain the writ petition as an efficacious alternative remedy was available under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act.
Actions taken under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, being subsequent to Section 13(4), are subject to scrutiny and challenge before the Debts Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
The DRT has jurisdiction to examine the legality of enforcement actions post-Section 13(4), including restoration of possession, if the action is found to be in violation of the Act.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(4)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
doctrines: Efficacious alternative remedy doctrine
Statutory remedy exclusion principle under constitutional jurisdiction
Doctrine of legislative intent in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellants claimed specific performance of a sale deed, but the respondents argued that title did not pass due to non-payment of consideration and subsequent repudiation.
issues_decided: Whether title in immovable property passes on execution and registration of a sale deed or only upon payment of consideration?
Whether the recitals in a sale deed about payment of consideration and delivery of possession are conclusive?
Whether the practice of 'ta khubzul badlain' in Bihar defers transfer of title until exchange of registration receipt and full payment?
Whether the appellants were entitled to specific performance after failing to pay the full sale price before repudiation?
holdings: Title in property does not pass merely upon execution and registration of a sale deed if the parties intended transfer to occur only upon full payment of consideration.
Recitals in a sale deed about payment and possession are not conclusive and can be rebutted by evidence showing otherwise.
In Bihar, the practice of 'ta khubzul badlain' recognizes that a registered sale deed does not transfer title until the exchange of registration receipt for full consideration.
A vendor may lawfully repudiate a sale if the purchaser fails to pay the full price within a reasonable time, and no right to specific performance arises thereafter.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act)
Doctrine of equitable estoppel
Customary practice of 'ta khubzul badlain'
Intention of parties as determinant of title transfer

card.dispute: Justice P.D. Dinakaran challenged the validity of the Judges Inquiry Committee's proceedings, particularly the inclusion of senior advocate P.P. Rao, alleging bias due to prior legal representation.
issues_decided: Whether the inclusion of P.P. Rao in the Judges Inquiry Committee under Section 3(2)(c) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, resulted in bias invalidating the proceedings
Whether the petitioner waived his right to object to Rao's inclusion by not raising the issue earlier
Whether the proceedings before the Committee were null and void due to alleged bias
holdings: The mere prior professional relationship between P.P. Rao and the petitioner did not automatically constitute bias warranting invalidation of the inquiry.
The petitioner, being aware of the facts, delayed raising the objection, which amounted to a calculated attempt to delay the inquiry and indicated waiver by conduct.
While the objection was not upheld, the Court requested the Chairman to replace P.P. Rao to maintain the appearance of impartiality in the ongoing inquiry.
doctrines: Waiver of statutory rights
Apprehension of bias
Public policy in judicial proceedings
Cuilibet licet renuntiare juri pro se introducto

card.dispute: Khatri Hotels and another appellant claimed title and possession over land in village Kishangarh, Delhi, where the Sahara Restaurant was constructed, against the Union of India and DDA, who asserted that the land vested in the government and was transferred to DDA for development as green area and road.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants proved that the land on which the Sahara Restaurant was constructed fell within Khasra Nos. 2728/1674/2 and 2728/1674/3 and that they had lawful possession thereof.
Whether the appellants approached the court with clean hands, given their failure to produce key documents and unauthorized construction despite court orders.
holdings: The appellants failed to prove that the land occupied by the Sahara Restaurant corresponded to the khasra numbers they claimed, as no site plan, aks-shijra, or demarcation report was produced to establish location or boundaries.

The appellants did not approach the court with clean hands due to suppression of documents, unauthorized large-scale construction in violation of status quo orders, and encroachment on public land meant for roads.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Vesting of land under statutory notification
Burden of proof in property disputes

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the acquisition of his land by the State of Karnataka, claiming it was outside the Framework Agreement and that the acquisition lapsed due to non-compliance with time limits for award issuance.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings under the KIAD Act lapsed due to non-compliance with Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for failure to make an award within two years
Whether the land in question vested in the State automatically upon notification under Section 28(4) of the KIAD Act
Whether the present appeal amounted to an abuse of the judicial process by re-litigating already decided issues
holdings: Acquisition under the KIAD Act does not lapse for non-compliance with Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as KIAD Act is a self-contained code with its own vesting mechanism.
Land vests absolutely in the State government upon publication of declaration under Section 28(4) of the KIAD Act, independent of any award or possession under Section 16.
The appeal is an abuse of the judicial process as it re-litigates issues already finally decided, delaying a project meant for larger public purpose.
provisions: Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, Section 28(4)
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, Section 28(5)
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, Section 16
doctrines: Vesting by operation of law
Self-contained statutory code
Abuse of process of court
Finality of litigation

card.dispute: The appellants (Delhi Airtech Services) challenged the Uttar Pradesh government's acquisition of their land without making the payment mandated under Section 17(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, during emergency acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement of payment under Section 17(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is mandatory or directory in cases of emergency land acquisition.
Whether non-compliance with Section 17(3A) renders the acquisition void and violative of Article 300A of the Constitution.
What relief is available when possession is taken without compliance with Section 17(3A), but third-party interests have since arisen.
holdings: Section 17(3A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is mandatory and constitutes a condition precedent to taking possession in emergency acquisitions.
Non-compliance with Section 17(3A) violates Article 300A of the Constitution, which protects property rights by requiring deprivation only by authority of just and fair law.
Though the acquisition is illegal, restitution is not possible due to third-party interests; compensation must be determined as of the date of the writ petition, not the Section 4 notification.
doctrines: Condition precedent
Due process of law
Rule of law
Liberal interpretation of statutes protecting fundamental rights
Protection of property rights under constitutional law

card.dispute: The appellant, a purchaser of mortgaged property, challenged the High Court's decision to remand the suit for fresh evidence after the plaintiff failed to lead evidence despite multiple opportunities.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with a concurrent judgment of lower courts in a second appeal without formulating a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC?
Whether the High Court could remand the suit for fresh evidence when the plaintiff failed to produce evidence despite adequate opportunities?
holdings: The High Court cannot exercise its second appellate jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC without first formulating a substantial question of law; failure to do so renders its judgment patently illegal.
A plaintiff who fails to lead evidence despite multiple opportunities is not entitled to sympathy or remand; courts must ensure effective progress and not allow abuse of procedural adjournments.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XVII Rule 1
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Judicial discipline in granting adjournments
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed in second appeal

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Karnataka High Court's decision to quash the land acquisition and direct restoration of land to respondent No.1, who claimed the state illegally transferred land acquired for a public purpose to private entities.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land for a Golf-cum-Hotel Resort could be legally transferred to private parties by the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation
Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining the writ petition after delay
Whether the High Court was correct in directing restoration of the land to the respondent
holdings: Land acquired for a public purpose cannot be transferred to private individuals or corporations, as such diversion constitutes fraud on the power of eminent domain.
The delay in filing the writ petition was adequately explained, and the High Court was justified in exercising discretion to hear the case on merits.
Restoration of land to the respondent was justified because the acquisition and subsequent transfer were found to be illegal and fraudulent.
doctrines: Fraud on the power of eminent domain
Judicial discipline (binding nature of Division Bench decisions on Single Bench)
Illegality through diversification of public purpose

card.dispute: The appellant sought appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, for disputes arising from an unregistered 30-year lease deed and an alleged agreement to sell two tea estates, which the respondent resisted on grounds of stamp and registration defects.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitration clause in an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document is enforceable.
Whether an arbitration clause in an unregistered lease deed for 30 years is enforceable under the Registration Act, 1908.
Whether the arbitrator can decide disputes relating to enforcement of the lease or recovery of expenses incurred based on the lease or sale agreement.
holdings: An arbitration agreement in a document liable to stamp duty is unenforceable until the stamp duty and penalty (if any) are paid; the court must first determine stamp duty compliance before appointing an arbitrator.

An arbitration clause in an unregistered lease deed for more than one year is severable and enforceable, but the arbitrator cannot rely on the unregistered deed to enforce lease terms or rights over immovable property.

An arbitrator cannot adjudicate claims for specific performance of an unregistered lease or damages tied to it; however, claims independent of the lease deed may be arbitrable if within the scope of the arbitration clause.
doctrines: Separability of arbitration clause
Doctrine of kompetenz-kompetenz
Enforceability of arbitration agreements in unstamped instruments
Effect of non-registration on enforceability of lease deeds and collateral arbitration

card.dispute: The dispute was between a pharmaceutical company (vendor) and a real estate company (purchaser) over the enforcement of an agreement for sale of agricultural land, where the purchaser sought specific performance after failing to complete payment within the stipulated time.
issues_decided: Whether time was of the essence of the contract between the parties?
Whether the defendant-vendor could lawfully terminate the contract for delay in performance?
Whether the plaintiff-purchaser was entitled to the discretionary relief of specific performance despite suppressing material facts?
holdings: Where a contract explicitly states that time is of the essence and contains no provisions for extension or penalty, delay in performance allows the promisee to treat the contract as voidable.
Under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a party may terminate a contract if time is of the essence and the other party fails to perform by the specified time.

A party seeking specific performance must approach the court with clean hands; suppression of a material fact, such as refusal to accept a returned earnest money cheque, disentitles the party to equitable relief.
doctrines: Time being of the essence in a contract
Discretionary nature of specific performance
Clean hands doctrine in equitable remedies

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of incorporating provisions of the Central Land Acquisition Act into the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning (MRTP) Act, alleging repugnancy and legislative incompetence.
issues_decided: Whether there is repugnancy between the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the MRTP Act that invalidates the state law under Article 254 of the Constitution
Whether provisions of the Central Land Acquisition Act, particularly Section 11A, can be incorporated into the MRTP Act through legislation by incorporation
Whether the MRTP Act is a self-contained code that permits selective incorporation of central law provisions
holdings: There is no repugnancy between the Land Acquisition Act and the MRTP Act as they operate in different fields; the doctrine of pith and substance applies, allowing harmonious construction.

Provisions of the Land Acquisition Act relating to land acquisition, compensation, and legal remedies can be incorporated into the MRTP Act, but only to the extent consistent with its object of planned development.

Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, dealing with default and lapsing of proceedings, cannot be read into the MRTP Act as it would frustrate the state law’s purpose and is not part of the incorporated scheme.
provisions: Schedule VII, List I and List II
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Chapter VII
doctrines: Pith and substance
Legislation by incorporation
Incidental encroachment
Harmonious construction
Self-contained code

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the land acquisition proceedings initiated by the State of West Bengal, alleging denial of a mandatory hearing under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was denied a hearing under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, despite being an authorized representative of the owners.
Whether non-compliance with Section 5A vitiated the declaration under Section 6 of the Act.
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the challenge to the acquisition proceedings.
holdings: The right to hearing under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act is a substantive right, akin to a fundamental right under Article 300-A, and must be effectively granted.
Total or substantial non-compliance with Section 5A renders the acquisition proceedings invalid, and the declaration under Section 6 must be set aside.
The Land Acquisition Officer failed to apply his mind to the objections, merely recording the acquiring body's submissions, which amounts to a failure to comply with Section 5A.
doctrines: Effective hearing doctrine
Substantial compliance vs. non-compliance with statutory mandates
Strict construction of expropriatory legislation
Application of mind by quasi-judicial authorities

card.dispute: The appellant, MSK Projects, claimed compensation for delayed issuance of a traffic notification, while the State of Rajasthan challenged the arbitral award on grounds of non-execution of the second phase of the road project.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitral award granting compensation for loss of toll revenue due to delayed notification could stand despite non-execution of the second phase of the project?
Whether the appellant was entitled to compensation for the entire contract value when it had not invested in the second phase of the work?
Whether the tribunal could consider non-execution of contractual obligations arising after the arbitral reference?
holdings: A party failing to perform its contractual obligations, especially non-execution of a project phase, cannot claim full compensation for losses without accounting for its own breach.
Compensation under a contract must be based on actual investment made; a party cannot claim recovery for amounts not spent, as it would result in a windfall profit.
An arbitral tribunal cannot go beyond the terms of reference, but courts may remit issues for reconsideration to ensure justice and protect public funds.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII Rule 5
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Principle of reasonable compensation for breach of contract
Arbitral jurisdiction limited by terms of reference
Prevention of windfall gain due to partial performance

card.dispute: The National Textile Corporation Ltd. (appellant) fought against the owners of the suit premises, Harichand Roopchand Charity Trust (respondents), over whether the appellant was entitled to protection under the Rent Control Act and could continue as a tenant after the lease expired.
issues_decided: Whether the National Textile Corporation Ltd. qualifies for exemption under Section 3(1)(a) or 3(1)(b) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
Whether the vesting of a textile undertaking under the Act 1995 includes tenancy rights in leased premises
Whether the appellant, as a statutory corporation, could claim to be an agent of the Central Government to avoid eviction
holdings: Section 3(1)(b) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 applies to entities capable of paying market rent, including public sector companies like the appellant, and thus the appellant is not entitled to protection under the Act.

The vesting of a textile undertaking under the Textile Undertakings (Acquisition and Transfer of Property) Act, 1995 transfers only the right, title, and interest of the lessee (Poddar Mills), which was limited to tenancy rights, and does not confer ownership or indefinite possession of the leased premises.

The appellant, though a government-owned corporation, is a separate legal entity and cannot claim to be merely an agent of the Central Government to avoid liability; such a claim must be specifically pleaded and proved, which was not done here.
provisions: Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, Section 3(1)(a) and 3(1)(b)
Textile Undertakings (Acquisition and Transfer of Property) Act, 1995, Section 3(1), Section 3(2), Section 2(g), Section 2(m), Section 4(6)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII Rule 2
doctrines: Vesting doctrine: the term 'vesting' is context-dependent and may mean vesting in title, possession, or interest, but not necessarily absolute ownership
Doctrine of pleading: a party must specifically plead factual claims, such as agency, to rely on them in defense
Principle of statutory interpretation: words in statutes are interpreted based on context and legislative intent

card.dispute: The Narmada Bachao Andolan and affected parties fought the State of Madhya Pradesh and the Narmada Hydro-Development Corporation over the rehabilitation and land acquisition issues concerning the Omkareshwar Dam project.
issues_decided: Whether agricultural land between FRL and BWL in five villages should be acquired due to temporary submergence
Whether landless laborers are entitled to land under the R&R Policy
Whether the NWDT Award applies to the Omkareshwar Dam project
Whether major sons are entitled to separate land allotment as independent families
holdings: Agricultural land between FRL and BWL that faces temporary submergence for less than 15 days during floods need not be acquired, as such submergence is short-term and beneficial for agriculture.
Landless laborers are not entitled to land allotment under the R&R Policy for the Omkareshwar project.
The NWDT Award does not apply to the Omkareshwar Dam project, as it is not covered under the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal’s jurisdiction.
A major son does not have an independent right to land allotment as a separate family under the R&R Policy.
doctrines: Principle of temporary submergence not necessitating acquisition
Judicial reliance on expert technical opinion from Central Water Commission
Conditional application of R&R benefits based on nature of submergence and tenure

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including Section 11A, could be read into the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976, for land acquisition under its scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Act 68 of 1984, can be read into the BDA Act for acquisition of land?
Whether Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act applies to acquisitions under the BDA Act?
Whether the BDA Act is a self-contained code on planned development with incidental acquisition?
holdings: The BDA Act is a self-contained code for planned development, and acquisition of land is only incidental to its main purpose.
Provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, can be read into the BDA Act only to the extent of acquisition, compensation, and legal remedies, where not inconsistent.
Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, which provides for lapsing of acquisition proceedings due to delay, cannot be applied to the BDA Act as it would defeat the scheme of planned development.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entries 5 and 18
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 42
doctrines: Pith and substance
Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers
Doctrine of fragmentation
Legislation by reference

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the acquisition of his agricultural land by the State of Haryana, alleging violation of statutory procedures and natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition process complied with the mandatory provisions of Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether non-compliance with the principles of natural justice vitiated the acquisition proceedings?
Whether the invocation of Section 17 of the Act for urgency was justified in the facts of the case?
holdings: Compliance with Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is mandatory, and failure to provide landowners a fair opportunity to object renders the acquisition void.
The principles of natural justice are integral to the land acquisition process, and their violation invalidates the entire proceeding.
Section 17 cannot be invoked to bypass statutory safeguards arbitrarily, especially when the acquisition process remains dormant for years before sudden enforcement.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Mandatory compliance with statutory procedure
Proportionality in exercise of state power
Sustainable development and protection of agricultural land

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the acquisition of their land by the State of U.P. for industrial development under urgency provisions, alleging violation of constitutional rights and absence of genuine urgency.
issues_decided: Whether the invocation of urgency provisions under Section 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was justified in acquiring the appellants' land for industrial development?
Whether the exclusion of Section 5-A proceedings violated principles of natural justice and the rule of audi alteram partem?
Whether the selective acquisition of land, while exempting other similarly situated parcels, violated Article 14 of the Constitution?
holdings: The State failed to demonstrate real and substantial urgency justifying the use of Section 17(1) and 17(4); the acquisition was primarily for private industrial interests, not urgent public purpose.
Exclusion of Section 5-A inquiry violated the rule of audi alteram partem, as the procedural safeguard cannot be bypassed based on speculative delays.
Selective acquisition of land while exempting others with similar characteristics violated Article 14 due to arbitrary 'pick and choose' policy by authorities.
doctrines: Audi alteram partem
Rule of law
Equality before law
Arbitrariness in executive action

card.dispute: The appellants (lessees/occupants) challenged the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority's actions in restricting or permitting non-residential use of land in sectors designated for residential use under the Master Plan.
issues_decided: Whether the Development Authority can permit non-residential use in areas earmarked for residential use in the Master Plan.
Whether commercial activities like banks and nursing homes can operate in residential sectors.
To what extent professionals like doctors, lawyers, and architects can use residential premises for their clinics or offices.
Whether the Development Authority's actions in cancelling leases or issuing public notices were lawful and uniform.
holdings: The Development Authority cannot permit commercial activities such as banks or nursing homes in sectors designated for residential use under the Master Plan.
Existing commercial operations in residential sectors must cease and premises be restored to residential use within two months.
Doctors, lawyers, and architects may use up to 30% of the ground floor area in residential properties for professional offices or clinics, subject to payment of lawful charges.
The Development Authority must act uniformly and in accordance with law, and cannot arbitrarily treat similarly situated parties differently.
provisions: Master Plan of the New Okhla Industrial Development Area
doctrines: Principle of public trust
Doctrine of sustainable development
Principle of equal treatment under law
Fait accompli cannot validate illegal actions

card.dispute: Family members fought over possession and management of property, with one side seeking mandatory interim injunction for immediate possession while the other resisted it during pending litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the Division Bench was justified in granting a mandatory interim injunction directing possession to be handed over to the respondent.
Whether the Single Judge's limited interim order was arbitrary, capricious, or perverse to warrant interference by the appellate court.
Whether granting the interim relief sought would amount to pre-judging the main suit and effectively grant a decree at the interlocutory stage.
holdings: An interim mandatory injunction can only be granted in exceptional cases where the status quo has been altered and justice requires restoration of the prior position.
The Division Bench erred in interfering with the Single Judge's reasoned order, as the discretion was exercised judicially and not arbitrarily, capriciously, or perversely.
Granting the full relief sought at the interim stage would amount to a pre-trial decree, especially when the appellants were in possession and managing development activities.
doctrines: Interim mandatory injunction doctrine
Principle of non-interference with judicial discretion unless arbitrary or perverse
Status quo ante doctrine in interim relief

card.dispute: The dispute was between shopkeepers of Gandhi Market in Gwalior and the State of Madhya Pradesh over the demolition and reconstruction of the market, including the relocation of shopkeepers and the legality of the High Court's directions for constructing a new market complex.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in directing the Municipal Corporation to construct a new market complex and relocate the shopkeepers.
Whether the shopkeepers were entitled to a refund of the amount they deposited and to recall previous court orders.
Whether the permission granted by the Joint Director, Town and Country Planning, was sufficient for reconstruction or required higher approval.
holdings: The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction in issuing directions for the construction of a new market complex, as the move was in public interest and with the consent of the shopkeepers.

The deposit made by shopkeepers was not for construction charges but for future license fees, and there was no merit in seeking a refund or recalling orders, especially since the process had continued with their implied consent.
The permission granted by the competent authority (Joint Director) was valid, but no construction should proceed contrary to statutory provisions or without proper authorization.
provisions: Town and Country Planning Act, Madhya Pradesh, 1973
doctrines: Judicial restraint in administrative action
Public interest litigation and court-supervised execution
Principle of consent and estoppel in writ proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants (co-owners of land) sued to set aside decrees based on arbitration awards that transferred ownership of their land to the respondents, alleging the awards were fraudulent and unregistered despite affecting immovable property worth over Rs.100.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration awards that created rights in immovable property worth over Rs.100 were compulsorily registrable under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether unregistered arbitration awards creating rights in immovable property can be enforced by a court decree
Whether the arbitration proceedings were collusive and constituted fraud on the court
holdings: Arbitration awards that create, declare, or assign rights in immovable property valued over Rs.100 are compulsorily registrable under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.
Unregistered arbitration awards that are compulsorily registrable cannot be acted upon by courts, nor can decrees be passed in their favour under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908.
Where arbitration is collusive, sham, and used to evade stamp duty and registration, and the court is misled, the resulting decree amounts to fraud on the court and is invalid.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings
Doctrine of compulsory registration of instruments affecting immovable property
Principle that courts cannot act on unregistered documents required to be registered

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over a property in Lajpat Nagar, alleging ownership and partition rights, with the core dispute involving decades-long litigation marked by allegations of abuse of process and false claims.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in imposing costs on the appellants for frivolous and dilatory litigation?
What measures can be adopted to curb delays and abuse of civil litigation process?
Whether the trial court should dispose of the pending suit expeditiously without being influenced by observations in this appeal?
holdings: The imposition of costs by the High Court was justified due to the appellants' prolonged and frivolous litigation over four decades, warranting deterrent costs of Rs. 2,00,000 to prevent abuse of judicial process.
Courts must adopt proactive measures like strict scrutiny of pleadings, early discovery, realistic cost imposition, and timely disposal to curb delays and perjury in civil litigation.
The trial court must decide the pending suit on its merits expeditiously, within three months, without being influenced by observations made in this appeal.
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Principle of restitution
Deterrent costs to prevent frivolous litigation
Judicial economy and expeditious disposal

card.dispute: Rangammal, a third-party property owner, contested a partition suit between two brothers who included her property in the suit based on an alleged sale deed executed by her de facto guardian during her minority.
issues_decided: Whether the burden of proving the validity of a sale deed executed by a de facto guardian of a minor should lie on the plaintiff who relies on it in a partition suit.
Whether the appellant could be denied relief on grounds of limitation when she first came to know of the sale deed upon being impleaded in the partition suit.
holdings: In a partition suit, the burden of proving the validity and legal efficacy of a sale deed, on which the inclusion of a third party's property is based, lies on the plaintiff who asserts title under it, not on the third-party defendant.

The appellant cannot be held barred by limitation for challenging the sale deed when she had no prior knowledge of it and only came to know when impleaded in the suit, especially while being in continuous possession of the property.
doctrines: Burden of proof
Constructive knowledge
Perverse findings
Collusive litigation

card.dispute: Samittri Devi claimed ownership of a house property against Sampuran Singh, who purchased it from her son, alleging the sale was benami and that he had notice of her claim.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for recovery of property filed before the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 came into force is barred by Section 4 of the Act
Whether the notice sent by the appellant to the respondent was duly served, affecting the latter's claim as a bona fide purchaser
holdings: Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not bar a suit filed prior to the Act's enforcement for recovery of property.
A notice sent via postal certificate can raise a presumption of service, which may be drawn if supported by evidence and not rebutted, affecting the purchaser's claim of being without notice.
doctrines: Presumption of service of notice
Burden of proof in benami transactions
Rebuttable presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's quashing of a magistrate's order taking cognizance against a person based on a second protest petition, alleging maintainability of successive complaints under Cr.P.C.
issues_decided: Whether a second protest petition is maintainable when a prior protest petition has been filed but not acted upon before the final report?
Whether the magistrate acted legally in taking cognizance under Section 395 IPC based on the second protest petition?
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the magistrate's order on the ground of non-maintainability of the second protest petition?
holdings: A second protest petition is maintainable in exceptional circumstances, especially when the first petition was not competent or lacked full facts.
A protest petition can be treated as a complaint under Chapter XV Cr.P.C., and cognizance can be taken if sufficient material exists, even if based on a second petition.
The High Court erred in quashing the magistrate's order on technical grounds without considering that the first protest petition was filed before the final report and was not properly entertainable.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice in criminal investigation
Maintainability of second complaint on same facts in exceptional circumstances
Judicial review of magistrate's cognizance order
Protest petition as a complaint under Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: The appellant, Shankara Co-op. Housing Society Ltd., challenged the High Court's decision that invalidated the acquisition of disputed lands under the Displaced Persons Act, which were originally declared as evacuee property after Partition.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed lands, once notified under Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, ceased to be evacuee property under the Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Whether the Chief Settlement Commissioner had jurisdiction under Section 24 of the Displaced Persons Act to revise an order passed by the Deputy Custodian under the Evacuee Property Act
Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining a subsequent writ petition challenging a matter already concluded by a final judgment in an earlier writ petition
holdings: Notification under Section 12 of the Displaced Persons Act extinguishes the status of evacuee property, and such property vests absolutely in the Central Government free from encumbrances.

The Chief Settlement Commissioner lacks jurisdiction under Section 24 of the Displaced Persons Act to revise orders passed by authorities under the Evacuee Property Act, as only specified officers under the Act are subject to revision.
A subsequent writ petition is not maintainable when it re-agitates an issue already finally decided by a prior judgment, especially with inordinate and unexplained delay.
provisions: The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
The Evacuee Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) Act, 1951, Section 46
doctrines: Doctrine of res judicata
Doctrine of jurisdictional limits of administrative authorities
Doctrine of extinguishment of rights upon acquisition under statutory notification

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over the enforcement of an agreement for the sale of land and whether subsequent transactions violated a court order against encumbrances.
issues_decided: Whether the execution of Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) and receipt of advances for future sale agreements constituted encumbrance of property in violation of a court order?
Whether the vendors were liable to refund the amounts received under a cancelled sale agreement, despite conditional offers of refund?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to interest on the refund amount and at what rate?
holdings: Mere execution of MOUs to enter into future sale agreements, without transfer of interest, does not create an encumbrance on the property.
Vendors who conditionally offered to refund advance amounts must do so if the conditions for withdrawal of the offer are not met, especially when the purchaser did not file frivolous suits.
The vendee is entitled to refund of amounts paid with interest at 12% per annum from the date of payment where no forfeiture clause exists and title was disputed.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Doctrine of encumbrance
Conditional offer in contractual liability

card.dispute: The Narmada Bachao Andolan sought expunging of adverse remarks made against it in a prior judgment regarding its conduct in land acquisition litigation.
issues_decided: Whether adverse remarks against Narmada Bachao Andolan in the earlier judgment should be expunged.
Whether the remarks were necessary for the decision and based on record evidence.
holdings: Adverse remarks against a party can be expunged only if they are unjustified, without foundation, or unnecessary for the decision.
The remarks against Narmada Bachao Andolan were justified and necessary, as they pertained to its pleadings and conduct in the case.
doctrines: Judicial restraint in making adverse remarks
Necessity and record-based justification for strictures
Inherent power of court to expunge remarks

card.dispute: The State of Haryana claimed ownership of private land through adverse possession, which the respondents resisted.
issues_decided: Whether the State can acquire private land through adverse possession by clandestine possession over 12 years.
Whether government instrumentalities like the police can invoke the doctrine of adverse possession to claim title over private property.
holdings: The State cannot acquire title to private land through adverse possession, especially when it uses its power to clandestinely occupy property.
Government departments, particularly the police, must not be allowed to benefit from adverse possession as it undermines public trust and justice.
doctrines: Doctrine of Adverse Possession
Principle of Inverse Condemnation
Public Trust Doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the legality of General Power of Attorney Sales (GPA Sales) or SA/GPA/WILL transactions as valid modes of transfer of immovable property, seeking clarification on their legal status.
issues_decided: Whether SA/GPA/WILL transactions constitute valid transfer of title in immovable property
Whether such transactions can be recognized as completed conveyances or be used for mutation in revenue or municipal records
Whether the courts can treat GPA sales as valid deeds of title
holdings: SA/GPA/WILL transactions do not convey title or create any interest in immovable property and cannot be treated as valid transfers under law.
Such transactions cannot be recognized as completed conveyances or used as a basis for mutation in municipal or revenue records.
Courts will not treat GPA sales as valid deeds of title, except to the limited extent permitted under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Powers of Attorney Act, 1882, Section 1A and Section 2
Indian Succession Act, 1925, Section 69 and Section 70
doctrines: Doctrine of agency in power of attorney
Doctrine of transfer by registered instrument
Doctrine of part performance under Section 53A of TP Act
Revocability of power of attorney and will

card.dispute: The petitioner sought enforcement of forest and environmental protection laws against mining and industrial projects, including Lafarge's cross-border mining operation in Meghalaya, alleging illegal forest land diversion without proper clearances.
issues_decided: Whether forest clearance must precede environmental clearance for projects involving forest land.
How to prevent ex facto clearance and ensure transparency in environmental and forest clearance processes.
What institutional mechanisms are needed to accurately identify and monitor forest land under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.
Whether public consultation and disclosure of clearance proceedings are mandatory.
holdings: Forest clearance must be obtained before environmental clearance for any project involving forest land, as mandated by the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.
To prevent ex facto clearances, a panel of accredited institutions must conduct EIAs based on MoEF-formulated terms of reference.
A GIS-based decision support system and updated geo-referenced forest maps must be created to accurately identify forest areas, including those not officially notified.
Public consultation is mandatory, and all minutes of Forest Advisory and Expert Appraisal Committees must be uploaded on the MoEF website for transparency.
doctrines: Precautionary Principle
Sustainable Development
Public Trust Doctrine
Principle of Environmental Impact Assessment

card.dispute: The appellant, a watchman employed by the respondent society, claimed rights over a property dedicated for a Dharamshala, while the society sought to reclaim possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, as a watchman, could acquire any interest in the property through long possession or adverse possession
Whether the appellant's pleadings and documents were false and irrelevant, leading to abuse of the legal process
Whether the court should impose costs and restitution due to misuse of judicial proceedings
holdings: A watchman, caretaker, or servant cannot acquire any right or interest in the property they are employed to guard, regardless of the duration of possession.
The court found that the appellant suppressed material facts, filed irrelevant documents, and raised untenable pleas, thereby abusing the legal process.

While heavy costs and restitution were warranted for misuse of the judicial process, nominal costs of Rs. 25,000 were imposed considering the appellant's financial position, and he was directed to vacate the property.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 35A (Costs in civil proceedings)
doctrines: Restitution
Abuse of process
Equity, justice and good conscience
False pleadings and imposition of realistic costs

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) fought with the respondent (tenant) over recovery of rent arrears and eviction from shop premises.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered rent deed can be relied upon for recovery of rent under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the trial court's decree for rent recovery based on inadmissibility of the unregistered rent deed
Whether the tenant could be evicted based on willful default in rent payment after the trial court's decree
holdings: An unregistered rent deed cannot be admitted as evidence to enforce the main claim of rent recovery under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908.
Despite inadmissibility of the unregistered rent deed, the tenant's own admission of rent liability and non-payment sustains the claim for arrears.
The eviction petition became infructuous due to pendency of appeal before the District Judge; the Supreme Court declined to direct eviction directly.
provisions: Hyderabad Houses (Rent, Eviction and Leases) Control Act, 1954, Section 15
doctrines: Admission against interest
Collateral use of unregistered documents
Infructuousness of appeals due to supervening events

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's quashing of criminal charges against the accused for abetment of suicide and criminal trespass, alleging that the High Court wrongly evaluated evidence at the revisional stage.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Sections 397 and 482 of the CrPC by evaluating evidence while quashing criminal charges?
Whether the allegations in the FIR and suicide note were sufficient to sustain charges under Sections 306 and 107 IPC at the stage of quashing?
holdings: The High Court cannot appreciate or evaluate evidence at the revisional or inherent jurisdiction stage; it can only determine if a case falls within permissible categories for quashing.

Allegations that the accused obtained blank documents, misrepresented facts, and illegally occupied property, leading to suicide, are sufficient to prima facie sustain charges under Sections 306 and 107 IPC.
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional and inherent powers of High Court
Prima facie case doctrine in quashing petitions
Abetment by instigation through creation of circumstances

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Badami challenged the validity of a 1973 consent decree and subsequent judgments, claiming they were based on a fraudulent family settlement that transferred Badami's property to Bhali.
issues_decided: Whether the 1973 judgment and decree in Civil Suit No. 1422 of 1973 is vitiated by fraud and thus a nullity
Whether the subsequent decrees based on the 1973 decree can survive if the foundational decree is fraudulent
Whether a consent decree obtained through collusion and without bona fide family arrangement can be enforced
holdings: A judgment or decree obtained by fraud is a legal nullity and can be set aside even in collateral proceedings, as it violates public policy and the principle of clean hands.
A family arrangement that lacks bona fides, where an illiterate woman allegedly transfers all her property for no consideration, is inherently suspect and indicative of fraud.
Courts must look beyond the formality of consent decrees when fraud is apparent, as such decrees cannot validate transactions rooted in deception.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates all judicial acts
Doctrine of clean hands
Nullity of consent decree obtained by fraud
Bona fide family arrangement as a valid transfer

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether service of an arbitral award on a party's advocate constitutes valid service on the party itself under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
issues_decided: Whether service of a signed arbitral award on a party's advocate amounts to service on the party under Section 31(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
Whether the period for filing a Section 34 petition to set aside the award began when the advocate received the award or when the party itself received it.
holdings: Service of a signed arbitral award on a party's advocate does not amount to service on the party itself under Section 31(5) of the 1996 Act, as the term 'party' refers only to the person who is a party to the arbitration agreement, not their agent or advocate.
The three-month period for filing a petition under Section 34(3) begins only when the party itself receives the signed copy of the award, not when the advocate receives it.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 3 Rule 1
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Distinction between party and agent in arbitration proceedings
Commencement of limitation period based on actual receipt by party

card.dispute: The petitioners (trustees and others) challenged the High Court's direction to auction trust land instead of allowing private sale to them, while the respondent (highest bidder) supported the auction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in directing the Charity Commissioner to proceed with an auction of trust land.
Whether the petitioners were entitled to specific performance of private sale agreements with the trust.
Whether the Charity Commissioner should consider fresh bids and public auction to protect the trust's interests.
holdings: The High Court did not err in directing the auction of trust land despite a possible jurisdictional overreach, as it acted in the best interest of the trust under Section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
The petitioners could not claim specific performance of private sale agreements as conditions were unmet and no sanction was obtained from the Charity Commissioner.
Sale of trust property must ensure maximum value; public auction is preferred over private negotiation to safeguard trust interests, especially when market value has increased.
doctrines: Best interest of the trust
Preference for public auction over private sale of trust property
Judicial non-interference in equitable directions for protection of charitable assets

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the government's acquisition of their land without a hearing under urgency provisions, claiming the delay negated any urgency.
issues_decided: Whether the Government of NCT of Delhi could invoke Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to dispense with the hearing under Section 5A for acquiring land for an electric sub-station.
Whether the delay between the proposal and the notification affected the validity of invoking urgency provisions.
holdings: The government cannot invoke urgency provisions under Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 when there is significant pre-notification delay without justifying the urgency.
The omission of the hearing under Section 5A is invalid if the government fails to produce material showing genuine urgency at the time of notification.
doctrines: Presumption of public purpose under Section 6(3)
Judicial review of urgency in land acquisition
Procedural fairness in acquisition under Section 5A

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the unauthorized construction of a five-storey building in Kolkata, which exceeded the two-storey sanctioned plan, seeking its demolition.
issues_decided: Whether the unauthorized construction beyond the sanctioned plan could be regularized under Rule 25 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Building Rules, 1990
Whether the municipal authorities could permit deviations from the sanctioned plan after completion of illegal construction
Whether the illegal construction should be demolished and penalties imposed for violating building regulations
holdings: Rule 25 does not permit regularization of construction that violates the sanctioned plan and is completed without prior approval.
Deviation from a sanctioned plan is only allowable if applied for before or during construction and does not contravene the Act or Rules.
Unauthorized construction must be demolished, and the builder must compensate flat buyers and pay a penalty for flouting regulations.
provisions: Kolkata Municipal Corporation Building Rules, 1990, Rule 25
doctrines: Principle of planned urban development
Doctrine of strict compliance with building regulations
Public interest in preventing unauthorized constructions

card.dispute: The Haryana State Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. challenged the validity of a land sale transaction in a review petition, seeking to overturn a prior judgment on grounds of alleged error apparent on the face of the record.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner made out a case for review under Article 137 of the Constitution read with Order 47 Rule 1 CPC based on an error apparent on the face of the record?
Whether the discovery of new evidence or documents warranted a review of the judgment?
Whether the petitioner exercised due diligence in producing relevant evidence during the original proceedings?
holdings: A review petition cannot be used as an appeal in disguise; it requires a clear, self-evident error apparent on the record, not one needing detailed legal or factual analysis.
The mere discovery of new evidence or documents does not justify review unless it was beyond the petitioner’s knowledge despite due diligence and could have changed the outcome.
The petitioner failed to show due diligence in not presenting available evidence about land prices during earlier proceedings, and thus cannot rely on such matters for review.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Review not an appeal in disguise
Principle of due diligence in review petitions

card.dispute: I.T.C. Ltd and Adarsh Coop. Housing Soc. Ltd fought over possession of a portion of land in Agra, with I.T.C. claiming it was illegally dispossessed by the Society in November 1988.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court had jurisdiction to decide possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 in the absence of a formal partition?
Whether the plaintiff (I.T.C. Ltd) was in possession of the suit property on the date of dispossession claimed?
Whether the findings of fact by the lower courts on possession could be interfered with in appeal?
holdings: A suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is maintainable to recover possession even without formal partition, as long as the plaintiff was in possession for 12 months prior to dispossession.
The plaintiff was in possession of the suit property on the relevant date, as supported by police records, revenue entries, and the defendant’s own prior litigation conduct.
Findings of fact by the trial and appellate courts based on evidence and preponderance of probabilities are not to be disturbed by the Supreme Court unless perverse.
doctrines: Summary remedy for unlawful dispossession
Preponderance of probabilities
Limited scope of appellate review in factual findings

card.dispute: The appellant, Jayrajsinh Rana, challenged the FIR filed against him for allegedly participating in a property fraud, seeking to quash the FIR after settling with the complainant and disclaiming any interest in the disputed property.
issues_decided: Whether non-compoundable offences under Sections 467, 468, 471, 420, and 120-B IPC can be quashed under Section 482 CrPC despite not being compoundable under Section 320 CrPC?
Whether the High Court or Supreme Court can quash an FIR in light of a settlement between the parties, even if the accused is not the main perpetrator?
holdings: The inherent power under Section 482 CrPC can be exercised to quash proceedings for non-compoundable offences if continuation would be an abuse of process and no conviction is likely.
Where a complainant withdraws opposition and the accused disclaims all rights in the disputed property, quashing the FIR secures ends of justice under Article 142, even for non-compoundable offences.
doctrines: Inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC
Abuse of process of law
Ends of justice
Settlement in criminal proceedings involving non-compoundable offences

card.dispute: A real estate firm contested the government's and municipal authorities' actions preventing it from developing part of a residential colony's open land, claiming ownership, while the authorities contested its rights to develop the space.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing the writ petition on the ground of disputed questions of fact.
Whether the petitioner had the right to develop the open space in the residential colony claimed as its property.
What relief, if any, should be granted to the petitioner given the ongoing development and legal position on ownership of open spaces.
holdings: The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition solely because of disputed facts, as it has jurisdiction to decide factual issues under Article 226, especially when public bodies are involved.
The petitioner does not possess full ownership rights over the open land, which is to be held as a trustee for the public, based on precedent and prior judicial affirmations.

The respondents may complete the ongoing development work, and the petitioner may pursue a claim for compensation, if any, in an appropriate forum, without this order affecting the final determination of title.
doctrines: Trustee doctrine for open spaces in residential developments
Judicial discretion in entertaining writ petitions involving disputed facts
Principle against relegate to civil suit when public interest and efficiency are at stake

card.dispute: The appellants, Mangal Amusement Park (P) Ltd. and its Managing Director, challenged the State of Madhya Pradesh's decision to change the land-use of a parcel allotted for a children’s amusement park to a regional park and to invite fresh tenders, arguing violation of legitimate expectations and mala fides.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government's direction to change land-use and invite fresh tenders was mala fide or beyond its powers?
Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel applied to prevent withdrawal of the allotment?
Whether the modification of the development plan under Section 23-A of the M.P. Town and Country Planning Act, 1973 was validly made?
holdings: The State Government's direction to change land-use and invite fresh tenders was within its policy powers and not mala fide, as final decisions rest with competent authorities in public interest.
The doctrine of promissory estoppel does not apply where the license was not renewed due to non-utilization of land and violation of license terms, and no permanent interest was created.
The modification of the development plan was validly carried out under Section 23-A of the M.P. Town and Country Planning Act, 1973, with due procedure and opportunity to object.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act, 1973, Section 23-A
Madhya Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act, 1973, Section 73
Madhya Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act, 1973, Section 39
doctrines: Doctrine of promissory estoppel
Mala fides in law and fact
Principle of legitimate expectation

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Mahesh Kumar fought against Vinod Kumar and others over the validity of a will that left Harishankar's share in joint family property to Mahesh Kumar.
issues_decided: Whether the Will dated 10.2.1992 executed by Shri Harishankar was validly executed and genuine?
Whether the High Court was justified in holding that the execution of the Will was shrouded with suspicion?
Whether the attesting witnesses signed the Will in the presence of the testator as required under law?
holdings: The Will dated 10.2.1992 was validly executed by Shri Harishankar in the presence of attesting witnesses who signed after him, satisfying the requirements of Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
The High Court erred in doubting the Will's validity based on conjectures; mere presence of a beneficiary during execution does not invalidate a will if proper attestation is proved.

It is not necessary for both attesting witnesses to sign simultaneously; the testimony of one attesting witness is sufficient to prove the will if the testator’s act of signing is proved to have occurred in their presence.
doctrines: Testamentary capacity
Attestation of wills
Presumption of validity of wills
Rejection of suspicious circumstances doctrine in absence of evidence

card.dispute: The appellant, a bank manager, challenged his conviction for criminal conspiracy, cheating, and corruption in sanctioning fraudulent loans in collusion with a property dealer.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B IPC beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the appellant abused his official position as a public servant under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988?
Whether conviction can be based on circumstantial evidence and statements under Section 313 of the CrPC?
Whether departmental action bars subsequent criminal prosecution on the same facts?
holdings: Criminal conspiracy can be proved by circumstantial evidence, especially when direct evidence is unavailable due to the secretive nature of the offence.
A public servant commits an offence under Section 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the PC Act if he abuses his position to cause wrongful gain to any person, even without personal gain.
Statements under Section 313 CrPC, when corroborated by oral and documentary evidence, can support conviction.
Departmental proceedings and criminal prosecution are not mutually exclusive; dismissal from service does not bar criminal prosecution for the same conduct.
doctrines: Circumstantial evidence in conspiracy cases
Abuse of official position under PC Act
Corroboration of Section 313 statements
Non-mutual exclusivity of departmental and criminal proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant sister claimed ownership of a property and sought possession from her brother's legal heirs, who had been in possession as caretakers but refused to vacate.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent brother, as a caretaker, could claim possessory rights against the true owner?
Whether long possession by a caretaker creates any legal interest in the property?
Whether the courts below erred in protecting the possession of a person without title or legal right?
What relief, including mesne profits, is available to the true owner when dispossessed by a caretaker?
holdings: A caretaker or servant does not acquire any right or interest in the property, regardless of the duration of possession, and must vacate on demand by the owner.
Mere physical possession by a caretaker does not amount to legal possession; such possession is always deemed that of the principal.
Courts cannot protect the possession of a person who holds property only as a caretaker, friend, or relative without a valid lease, license, or tenancy agreement.
The true owner is entitled to mesne profits or compensation for use and occupation, and courts must balance equities by awarding interim payments during litigation.
doctrines: Legal possession vs. physical custody
Mesne profits and equitable compensation
No title by adverse possession without animus possidendi
Protection of ownership rights against wrongful possession

card.dispute: Monnet Ispat and Energy Ltd. and other private companies fought against the Union of India and the State of Jharkhand over the withdrawal of recommendations for iron ore mining leases in Ghatkuri, seeking enforcement of their claims under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the State of Jharkhand could lawfully withdraw its recommendation for grant of mining leases to private companies in favor of public sector undertakings.
Whether the notifications issued in 1962, 1969, and 2006 reserving mineral areas for public sector exploitation were valid.
Whether the Ministry of Mines was justified in returning the state's recommendation for private mining leases.
Whether private entities have a vested right to the grant of mining leases.
holdings: The State of Jharkhand had the authority to withdraw its recommendation for mining leases to private companies and reserve the area for public sector use in furtherance of mineral conservation policy.
The notifications from 1962, 1969, and 2006 reserving mineral areas for public sector exploitation are valid and consistent with the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.
The Ministry of Mines acted within its powers in returning the state’s recommendation, as no private party has a vested right to a mining lease.
No private entity has a vested right to the grant or renewal of a mining lease, and the state may prioritize public sector exploitation to serve public interest.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 2
doctrines: Public trust doctrine in mineral resources
Doctrine of state as trustee of mineral wealth
Doctrine of no vested right in grant of mining leases
Principle of conservation and prudent exploitation of minerals

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the decree for specific performance of an agreement for sale of land, executed by his father via power of attorney, which the respondent sought to enforce.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was ready and willing to perform its part of the agreement for sale?
Whether the courts below were justified in decreeing specific performance despite alleged lack of specific pleading on continued readiness and willingness?
Whether escalation in land value constitutes a valid ground to deny specific performance?
holdings: A plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform a contract is determined by conduct and surrounding circumstances, not by a rigid formula; demonstration of willingness to pay at the stipulated time suffices if performance is prevented by the defendant.
Concurrent findings of lower courts on readiness and willingness are binding in the absence of perversity, especially when the defendant fails to adduce evidence to rebut the plaintiff's case.
Escalation in land value alone does not constitute unforeseeable hardship to justify denial of specific performance under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Doctrine of comparative hardship
Discretionary nature of specific performance

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell agricultural land, which the trial court granted, but the first appellate court reversed, awarding only refund of earnest money on grounds of hardship, a decision upheld in second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to specific performance of the agreement for sale?
Whether the first appellate court could consider hardship to the defendant under Section 20(2)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, when no such defence was pleaded or issue framed?
Whether the High Court was right in dismissing the second appeal without examining the lack of evidence on hardship?
holdings: A party is entitled to specific performance if they prove a valid agreement, payment of earnest money, and readiness to perform, and the court must not deny relief on grounds of hardship not pleaded or supported by evidence.

Hardship under Section 20(2)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, cannot be a basis to deny specific performance unless it is specifically pleaded by the defendant and supported by evidence on record.
An appellate court cannot reverse a decree for specific performance on unpleaded grounds of hardship without framing an issue or recording evidence on that aspect.
doctrines: Pleadings and issues must frame the scope of defence in specific performance suits
Equitable discretion under Section 20 must be exercised only on pleaded and proven facts
Appellate courts cannot base decisions on grounds not raised in pleadings

card.dispute: The dispute was between a financial corporation, a purchaser from the corporation, and a private buyer over the validity and priority of property sales where the property was mortgaged and later sold by both the mortgagor and the mortgagee.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could adjudicate private title disputes under Article 226 in a writ petition.
Whether the sale of mortgaged property by the State Financial Corporation under Section 29 was valid.
Whether a private purchaser from the original owner could claim superior title over a purchaser from the Corporation after mortgage.
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by adjudicating private title disputes in a public law remedy under Article 226.
The sale by the State Financial Corporation under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 is valid and vests absolute title in the purchaser.
Private disputes over title and ownership must be resolved in civil courts, not through writ petitions.
doctrines: Separation of public and private law remedies
Doctrine of appropriate forum
Vesting of title under statutory sale

card.dispute: Raheja Universal Limited and NRC Limited disputed over whether the BIFR could suspend a property sale agreement involving NRC Limited, a sick industrial company, under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, despite alleged rights under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
issues_decided: Whether Section 22 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 has an overriding effect over Sections 53A and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882?
Whether the BIFR had jurisdiction to suspend a sale agreement involving a sick industrial company under Section 22(3) of the SICA, 1985?
Whether the BIFR's order directing that sale of company assets required its prior approval was valid and within its statutory powers?
Whether a joint petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution is maintainable?
holdings: The provisions of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, particularly Section 22, have an overriding effect on the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, including Sections 53A and 54.
The BIFR has the jurisdiction under Section 22(3) of the SICA, 1985 to suspend a sale agreement involving a sick company to ensure the revival scheme is not prejudiced.
The BIFR can issue binding directions and prohibitory orders regarding asset disposal by a sick company without violating the rights of parties under private agreements.
The maintainability of a joint petition under Articles 226 and 227 need not be decided when the matter is resolved on merits and the issue is not pressed before the Court.
provisions: Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 22
Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 22A
Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 17
Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 18
doctrines: Doctrine of Overriding Statutory Authority
Doctrine of Part Performance (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act)
Principle of Judicial Non-Interference in Revival Schemes of Sick Companies
Doctrine of Proprio Vigore Powers of BIFR

card.dispute: The Ram Dhari Jindal Memorial Trust challenged the government's invocation of urgency powers to acquire land for the Rohini Residential Scheme without conducting a Section 5A enquiry.
issues_decided: Whether the urgency provisions under Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 were validly invoked for a planned residential development.
Whether the government must justify the dispensation of the Section 5A enquiry by showing real urgency.
Whether the absence of material justifying urgency renders the acquisition proceedings invalid.
holdings: The power under Section 17 to dispense with a Section 5A enquiry must be used only in exceptional cases, not routinely for planned urban development.
The government must demonstrate that urgency was so pressing that completing the Section 5A enquiry would have frustrated the public purpose.
Mere invocation of urgency without recorded material justifying immediate possession renders the acquisition order legally unsustainable.
doctrines: Doctrine of exceptional use of urgency powers
Doctrine of reasoned satisfaction in land acquisition
Balancing act between public purpose and private property rights

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Bhikhu Ram Jain fought with the legal heirs of Anis Ahmed Rushdie over the specific performance of a 1970 property sale agreement concerning a bungalow in Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in implying a term requiring further payment by the plaintiff to the defendant under the agreement.
Whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
Whether specific performance should be granted despite a delay of over 40 years and significant rise in property value.
holdings: The High Court erred in implying a term for additional payment to the defendant, as the agreement clearly limited the plaintiff's payment to Rs.50,000 and obligations to the Income Tax authorities; no such term was necessary for business efficacy.
The plaintiff was consistently ready and willing to perform his contractual obligations, while the defendant defaulted by demanding unjustified additional payments directly from the plaintiff.

Despite the long delay and increased property value, specific performance should be granted as the plaintiffs were not at fault; the sale deed must reflect the current market price to ensure fairness.
doctrines: Business efficacy test for implied terms
Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Discretionary grant of specific performance under Section 20
Fairness and reasonableness in equitable relief

card.dispute: The seller refused to return the earnest money after the purchaser failed to complete the property purchase, leading to a legal dispute over whether the seller could forfeit the amount.
issues_decided: Whether the seller is entitled to forfeit the earnest money when the sale fails due to the purchaser's default
Whether the amount paid qualifies as earnest money eligible for forfeiture or merely as part payment of the purchase price
holdings: The seller is entitled to forfeit the earnest money if the purchaser defaults, provided the contract clearly treats the amount as security for performance.
Earnest money serves both as part payment and security; its character depends on the parties' intention and contract terms, not just the label used.
doctrines: Forfeiture of earnest money upon purchaser's default
Intention of parties determines the nature of payment as earnest money or advance
Earnest money as security for contract performance

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, being siblings and legal heirs of their deceased mother, fought over whether the appellant held the tenancy rights and title to the suit property in a fiduciary capacity after it was transferred solely to him, and whether the suit for declaration of co-ownership was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant stood in a fiduciary capacity vis-à-vis the respondents in relation to the suit property.
Whether the suit filed by the respondents was barred by the Limitation Act due to delay.
holdings: The appellant held the tenancy and title in a fiduciary capacity because the transfer was made to him alone for administrative convenience, not due to abandonment of rights by other legal heirs, and all contributed to the purchase.
The suit was not barred by limitation under Section 4 of the Limitation Act as the fiduciary relationship saved it under Section 4(3)(b), and the plea was validly raised in defense.
provisions: The Karnataka Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1973
doctrines: Fiduciary relationship doctrine
Relation back doctrine under limitation law
Constructive trust

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh appealed against the High Court's decision to quash multiple FIRs and charge-sheets against Surendra Kori, a Deputy Registrar, for allegedly abetting the registration of fictitious sale deeds to fraudulently claim benefits under a rehabilitation project.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in quashing the FIRs and charge-sheets under Section 482 CrPC without allowing the prosecution a full opportunity to present evidence?
Whether the respondent, as a public official, could be held liable for abetting criminal conspiracy and fraud in the registration of forged documents?
Whether the principles of inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC were correctly applied in this case?
holdings: The High Court should not have quashed the FIRs and charge-sheets at the threshold, as the allegations disclosed a serious offence involving large-scale fraud and public official complicity, warranting a full trial.

The respondent, as a Deputy Registrar, had a statutory duty under Section 34 of the Registration Act to verify identities and execution of documents, and failure to do so may amount to abetment if done with intent to cause injury.

Inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC must be exercised sparingly and not to usurp the role of the trial court in evaluating evidence; they cannot be used to terminate proceedings where a prima facie case exists.
doctrines: Inherent powers of the High Court
Presumption of regularity in official acts
Principle of 'quando lex aliquid alicui concedit, concedere videtur et id sine quo res ipsa esse non potest'

card.dispute: The petitioner sought directions to conserve endangered species, particularly wild buffalo and red sandalwood, leading to a dispute over state obligations in species protection and regulation of trade.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government should include red sandalwood (Pterocarpus santalinus) in Schedule VI of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972
Whether sandalwood (Santalum album) requires inclusion in Schedule VI or policy-level intervention due to its vulnerable status
Whether a comprehensive conservation policy and regulatory framework for sandalwood is necessary
holdings: The Central Government must include red sandalwood in Schedule VI of the Wildlife Protection Act within six months, as it is an endangered endemic species requiring urgent protection.
